title_vi: Chapter One: Tomorrow Will Be Nothing Like Today
title_en: Chapter One: Tomorrow Will Be Nothing Like Today
text_en:
Nearly six years had passed since the sky began to close. The sun still hung somewhere above the grey clouds, but most days it left only a pallid glow, enough to tell day from night.

Those who once fled south to escape the cold no longer spoke of the desert's scorching heat. Snow blanketed the Atlas Mountains, froze the irrigation canals and turned the fields around Marrakesh hard as stone.

In a stone house on the city's outskirts, Juliet Spencer woke before five. For four years, she had lit the fire as soon as she opened her eyes. She slipped from beneath the animal-hide blanket, drew her collar close and touched Edward's shoulder to be sure her husband still slept.

Edward lay facing Remi, one arm across the edge of the blanket. The boy slept with his cheek against his father's elbow.

Juliet watched them a moment longer, then rose. She stirred the embers beneath the ash, set a kettle over the hearth and narrowed the draught vent. The wood caught, and warmth crept through the room.

Creaking timber made her turn. Edward sat up, his hair tousled from sleep. He glanced through the window, secured the door latch and looked at his wife.

"How long have you been up?"

Juliet set down the kettle and pointed to the cowshed.

"Not long. The fire's going. Clear out the cowshed before Remi wakes, would you?"

Edward looked back at Remi, still curled beneath the blanket.

"All right. I'll take care of the cowshed."

Juliet shook her head.

"I'll check your work afterwards."

He pulled on his goatskin coat and kissed her temple. Juliet was arranging bread and cheese on a plate, but stopped to catch his wrist.

"It's bitter out there. Come straight back when you're done."

"If the cows will let me."

Juliet laughed and pushed him towards the door.

Edward stepped outside, pulling his hood up against the icy wind. The cowshed stood just over twenty paces away, yet overnight snow reached almost to his ankles. He followed yesterday's packed path, cleared snow from the drain and pushed open the shed door.

Forty-three cattle lay in straw-bedded stalls. Edward topped up their fodder, then shovelled the fouled straw into a wooden barrow. He had kept the shed warm through winter after winter, and the water troughs had never frozen.

He pushed the barrow into the central passage and lifted a ceramic cover beside a brick channel under the floor. His fingers reddened in the light of the red lime Vestigium core as hot air hissed through the conduit. He checked the outlet, replaced the cover and pressed it tight.

The lumps of lime had grown paler since last winter. Edward laid his palm on the warm ceramic and looked towards the roof vent. The first winter, a cracked core had cost him a calf; since then, he checked the heating channel every morning.

Footsteps crunched outside. Remi came in with his woollen cap askew, carrying a short broom nearly as tall as himself. Snow clung to his shoulders; the wind had reddened his cheeks.

"Mother told me to bring the broom and help you, Father."

Edward leaned on his shovel.

"Did she give you the job, or did you ask for it?"

Remi tugged his cap lower before confessing.

"Both, Father."

Edward laughed and showed him where to sweep. Remi worked so eagerly that the broom nearly struck the Vestigium chamber cover.

Edward caught its handle and guided it towards the dry straw. The boy looked up at him and nodded.

"Father, were winters in England this cold too?"

Edward's shovel stopped in the straw.

"Cold enough. But the sky was always bright."

Remi leaned on his broom.

"As bright as the Vestigium lamps in the market?"

"No."

Edward looked through the door at the grey sky.

"Far brighter than that."

"Father, I don't remember what the sky in England looked like."

Edward stopped. Remi rested his chin on the broom and watched him.

Remi was born in 1708, barely a year old when London fell. England existed for him in his parents' stories, a few yellowing book pages and a worn leather map.

Marrakesh was beneath his feet: snow-covered Moorish domes, the road to the market, and the smell of roast potatoes old Omar often pressed into his hands on bitter days.

Edward knelt to meet his eyes.

"It doesn't matter. I'll tell you what I remember. When you're grown, you can decide for yourself whether England is your home."

Remi blinked.

"What if I like Marrakesh better?"

"I've lost my homeland already. I won't make you bear that debt."

Edward ruffled his son's hair and rose. Remi asked nothing more. He swept the straw, sneaking the broom handle against his father's boots until Edward pretended to kick back.

When they returned, Juliet had set three bowls of barley porridge on the table.

Steam carried the scent of beef fat and dried onions. Remi rushed to the table, rocking his chair so hard that Juliet caught him by the collar before it toppled.

Juliet fixed him with a stern look.

"Remi, wash your hands before you eat."

The boy tucked his shivering hands under his arms and pouted.

"But my hands are freezing, Mother!"

Juliet kept hold of his collar.

"Dirty hands get washed, however cold they are. Go on."

Remi trudged to the basin like a defendant denied the right to appeal. Edward sat down to find thick slices of salted meat and cheese beside his porridge.

He looked at Juliet, who did not raise her head.

"Don't look at me like that. You worked through supper last night."

Before Edward could protest, Remi returned from the basin and gleefully betrayed him.

"It's true! Father missed supper!"

Edward propped an elbow on the table.

"Seems I haven't an ally left in this house."

Remi pointed towards the cowshed.

"You still have the cows!"

Juliet burst out laughing. Edward gave his son a look of utter betrayal.

Near the end of breakfast, Remi slipped bread into his pocket, no doubt for the cow with the white patch on its forehead. Edward noticed and shook his head. The boy pretended not to see.

After breakfast, Juliet prepared for market. She checked her delivery ledger, wound a scarf over half her face and put a bundle of tanned hides in her basket for a buyer who had arranged to take them. At the door, Edward repaired her cloak clasp.

"Let me come with you."

"And the storehouse roof? You said it needed mending."

"I can do it this afternoon."

Juliet glanced at Remi, busy practising his letters on a page crowded with crooked strokes.

"Stay and help Remi with his lessons. I'll visit the market, call on old Omar and come home."

Before he could answer, Juliet tugged him down by the collar and kissed him.

"I've walked that road for four years."

The door opened, and a cold gust lifted her cloak.

"Besides, I bargain far better than you."

The door shut. Edward turned to his son.

"Hear that, Remi? Your mother says I can't bargain."

Remi kept forming his letters, answering with perfect calm and without looking up.

"But she's right."

"You little..."

Edward sighed.

Near noon, Juliet reached the heart of Marrakesh's market. Snow covered the Moorish domes above the red earthen walls; deep passages had been dug between the stalls, just wide enough for two people to pass.

A gust struck her sideways. She hunched her shoulders, held her basket against her hip and pushed through the shivering crowd.

Under the market roof, Vestigium lamps cast a gentle amber light. Their warmth kept the stalls busy even in heavy snow. People said Marrakesh still had a heartbeat as long as those lamps burned.

Juliet delivered the hides and bought salt, pepper and dates for Remi. As she finished paying, she noticed a crowd at the official noticeboard.

A clerk had posted three new proclamations. People pressed forward to read, then stayed to talk instead of returning to the stalls. Now and then, someone glanced north.

An old sailor stood motionless before the board, crushing his cap brim in his hands. A Castilian family beside him hurried to pack their wares and leave; the father kept looking north.

Someone spoke behind her.

"News from the fronts."

Juliet adjusted her scarf and headed home.

As Juliet crossed the threshold, she found Edward and Remi at the dining table, a faded leather map spread between them. He was teaching the boy the names of the seas.

"This is the Atlantic Ocean."

Edward touched the vast waters to the west.

Remi traced the coast to Morocco.

"Down here, that's where we live, isn't it, Father?"

"That's right. Our home is here."

Edward touched Morocco. When Remi asked about England, his finger lingered on the northern island.

"And England is here."

Juliet's basket touched the table. Edward looked up at once.

Juliet spoke.

"They've posted new notices at the market. Three, all at once."

Edward waited patiently until she had finished.

"Any definite news?"

"I couldn't get close enough to read them. But judging by the crowd, it can't be good."

Edward folded the map, hiding Europe beneath the worn leather.

"Then we won't bring rumours to the table. When we have reliable news, those responsible will deal with it."

Juliet watched him fold the map but said nothing.

Remi pushed over his unfinished page, one finger holding down the last letter, scratched out in a blur of ink.

"Father, how many Ts are in Atlantic?"

Edward bent over the page, examined the two crooked pen strokes and tapped the place where a letter was missing.

"More than you've written."

"I meant to do that."

Remi snatched back the paper and covered his unfinished letters with his arm.

"Then you can mean to write it five more times."

Edward set down the pen and kept his face stern until Remi's fell.

Remi groaned. Juliet laughed, unwound her scarf and went to the kitchen, leaving father and son to quarrel over Atlantic. Soon the scrape of a broom and the tap of a knife against a chopping board filled the house.

That afternoon, Edward mended the storehouse roof while Remi passed up nails. Juliet put away her purchases and prepared supper. By the time they finished, daylight had faded to a pale smear.

That evening, Remi fitted scraps of wood into a three-masted ship on the floor. Edward tried to mend a rein, threaded the needle wrongly for the third time, laughed and started again. Juliet set soup on the table and called them to eat.

Three measured knocks struck the front door. Everyone stopped. Edward laid down the rein and looked at Juliet.

Remi started up, but Juliet held him seated by the shoulder. Edward went to the door and touched the bolt without speaking.

The knocks came again. A deep male voice, forced flat and devoid of feeling, sounded through the wood.

"Edward Spencer, is that you?"

Edward's hand stopped on the bolt.

"That depends who's asking."

Silence followed. Then a second voice spoke, deeper, heavier and even less pleasant.

"Open the door. We have orders to verify your identity."

Juliet set down the ladle, drew the bread knife from its sheath and held it by her hip, hidden beneath the table. Edward noticed; Remi fell silent.

Edward braced a hand against the door before turning the lock.

"Who gave those orders?"

The voice answered.

"You're in no position to ask questions."

The reply came too smoothly. Edward opened the door just wide enough for one man, his rear foot still braced behind it.

Two tall figures entered with a rush of snow. Thick cloaks covered them, dark scarves hid their faces, and low hoods shadowed their eyes. The snow caked on their shoulders concealed every identifying mark.

The first stepped inside but went no farther. His gaze moved from Edward to Juliet, then settled on Remi. Behind the scarf, his voice emerged as a forced, threatening rasp.

"Edward Spencer. Former admiral of the English Navy. Confirm your identity."

Edward shifted between the strangers and the table before answering.

"You've found the right house. Whether I confirm anything depends on what you mean to do next."

"You may be required to come with us."

Juliet took half a step forward.

"My husband isn't going anywhere until you tell us who you are."

Both strangers turned to Juliet. The leader stayed silent long enough for the bubbling soup and crackling fire to fill the room.

Then his shoulders shook. The man behind him laughed first, and soon both were roaring.

"Bloody hell, I told you not to look Juliet in the face!"

The leader tore off his scarf. Damp, platinum-blond hair, matted by moisture, spilled from his hood. A long scar crossed his chin, and his broad grin swept away every trace of menace.

"Good God, Ed! That look on your face was worth the whole journey!"

The second man lowered his scarf. Marco brushed snow from his hair, disappointed as an actor robbed of his finest scene.

"I meant to keep that going another half-minute. Outrageous."

Edward stood by the door. Juliet laid down the knife and leaned against a chair.

"Romeo? Marco?"

Platinum-haired Romeo spread his arms like an actor awaiting applause.

"At last. Someone in this house recognises an old friend."

Edward did not move. Romeo lowered his arms as his smile faded. Perhaps the joke had gone too far.

Romeo ventured a word.

"Ed?"

Edward answered with a punch to Romeo's shoulder.

Romeo staggered, nearly falling.

"That hurt! You merciless brute! I crossed half of Morocco to see you!"

Before Romeo could complain again, Edward hauled him into a fierce embrace, their thick winter coats colliding. Then he pulled Marco in too.

Marco laughed, pounding his back.

"Easy! You'll break my ribs!"

"You bastards."

Edward released them.

"You're really alive."

Romeo planted his hands on his hips and curled his lip.

"We should be asking you that. Everyone said the former Admiral Spencer had vanished south. Nobody said you'd become a cattle farmer."

Marco laughed.

"I told him to knock like a decent man. But you know Romeo."

Juliet gripped the chair back, laughing.

"You made me reach for the bread knife!"

Remi stood timidly beside his mother, searching his memory for stories of these strangers.

"Are you friends of Father's?"

Romeo crouched to the boy's height.

"Of course! I knew him when he thought three hours' sleep a night made him a genius."

As he bent, a pendant slipped from his collar and swung before Remi.

Remi pointed to the lion's head.

"Uncle Romeo, what's that?"

Romeo held it up. The Castilian lion's head had eyes of orange-red Vestigium and a number engraved below.

"The Royal Guard's badge. I serve with them now."

Marco drew out his own pendant, showing Remi two almost identical lions.

"So do I. We're both in the Royal Guard of Castile."

Edward looked between his friends and laughed.

"You two used to curse sentry duty. Now you're Royal Guards?"

"You think I like it?"

Romeo rose and tucked away the pendant.

"Wait until you hear about my last few nights on watch."

Marco smiled.

"Let him eat first. He complained of hunger more than cold on the way here."

Edward pointed to the table.

"There's hot soup. Sit, both of you, and tell me everything."

Romeo sat, eating the bread Juliet handed him.

"The cloaks are finer, I'll grant you. But our superior can have a man beheaded and report it afterwards."

Marco sat beside him.

"Don't say things like that in front of the boy."

Remi dragged his chair closer to Edward.

"Do they really cut people's heads off, Father?"

"Eat your supper, son."

Edward pulled Remi's soup bowl closer.

Romeo laughed so hard he nearly choked on his soup.

Edward waited until his guests had eaten a few mouthfuls.

"So how did you find me?"

Marco wiped his hands.

"At the breeding-stock depot, everyone knows about an English admiral keeping cattle outside Marrakesh. I asked exactly three people and found you. You seem to be doing well."

Romeo cut in.

"Four people, actually. The first was an old red lime seller. He tried to make me buy a whole bucket before he'd talk."

Edward shrugged.

"I have work here, and a wife and son waiting every evening. No one drags me up to take a ship into battle. That's enough."

Marco studied him.

"I never thought you'd bear being ashore this long."

"Get up in the middle of the night for a cow about to calve and you'll find plenty of rough weather on land."

Edward glanced at Juliet.

"Besides, I have a demanding overseer."

Juliet put down her bowl and smiled.

"How fortunate you'll admit it before witnesses."

Their soup cooled as old stories filled the room. Juliet sometimes corrected Edward's recollections, while Remi sat close, eager to hear of voyages before his birth.

As the talk ebbed, Edward noticed Romeo's sword and the fighting gloves Marco kept near his favoured hand.

Edward put down his bowl.

"Right. Enough playacting, eating and grumbling about your superiors. Tell me what you've been avoiding."

Romeo laid down his spoon and looked at Marco. Neither spoke.

Marco straightened in his chair.

"We aren't the only ones who came looking for you."

Edward propped an elbow on the table and nodded.

"I thought as much."

Wheels ground over snow outside. Hooves approached in steady rhythm and stopped at the gate. Edward looked up; Marco had risen.

Juliet looked out to find a black carriage at the gate, four mounted escorts arrayed beside it. They bore no ostentatious banners, but lions worked into their clothing and saddlery matched the pendants Edward had seen.

Edward glanced at Romeo.

"Your superior?"

Romeo bent over his bowl and drank the last broth, avoiding Edward's eyes.

"I haven't said a thing."

Marco went to the door.

"The person we escorted wishes to see you in person."

"Who?"

Marco hid his pendant inside his collar and faced the door.

"Go and see."

Juliet touched Edward's arm as she passed.

"I'll receive our guest. Brush that straw from your coat."

Edward looked down at himself.

"I thought it made me look honest and trustworthy."

"To cattle, perhaps."

A woman stepped from the carriage. Edward glimpsed a deep crimson cloak trimmed in white fox fur before Juliet led the visitor to a chair by the hearth, opposite the table. Romeo and Marco stood rigidly to attention at the door.

Edward slipped behind the kitchen curtain to pluck straw from his coat. He heard Juliet invite the guest to sit, then smoothed his cuffs and hesitated before returning.

He drew the curtain aside and met Marco's eyes. His old friend nodded once.

The woman by the fire did not rise. Her crimson velvet cloak, edged with white fox fur, draped the chair; dark brown hair was pinned at her nape. Her amber eyes betrayed little.

A ceremonial sword bearing the Castilian arms rested beside her chair. Steam curled from the tea Juliet had poured.

Isabella Testarossa sat straight-backed at the Spencers' scarred wooden table. Edward knew that posture before she spoke.

Isabella looked him over.

"Well, look at you. Still alive."

Edward remained beside the curtain.

"Did you cross half of Morocco in winter just to see if I was breathing?"

Juliet glanced towards the small room beyond the curtain, where Remi had been silent since the carriage arrived.

"I'll see to Remi for a moment. You two can talk."

She folded the scarf on the chair and went inside. Isabella gave her a courteous smile.

The smile faded. Isabella's gaze dropped to Edward's snow-stained boots and coarse goatskin coat.

"Are you truly content to bury yourself here with that woman? Her eyes hold only the commonplace devotion of a servant. You should be beside someone who knows your worth."

Edward glanced at the kitchen curtain.

"You'll never understand that, Isabella. In times like these, ordinary warmth is the rarest luxury."

Behind the curtain, Remi asked whether he could take his wooden ship to bed. Juliet lingered to arrange his blankets. When she returned to stand behind Edward, Isabella's courtesy had returned.

"Thank you, Mrs Spencer."

Isabella set her teacup on the tray.

"I've come to tell you this: tomorrow won't be nearly as peaceful for you as today."

title_vi: Chapter Two: Three Roads
title_en: Chapter Two: Three Roads
text_en:
Isabella watched Edward in silence. He stood by the curtain, still without an answer.

Juliet stood beside her husband and looked at Isabella.

"I'll leave you to speak in private."

"Stay," Isabella told her. "Where Edward goes affects you, as does how you and Remi will live. I want you to hear my proposal for yourself."

Edward pulled out a chair for Juliet. She sat, and he stood behind her.

Isabella glanced at the leather tube on Marco's shoulder.

"The map."

Marco unfastened it and spread a map across the table, far larger than the scrap of paper Edward still used for Remi's lessons. Its edge pressed against a wooden plate, nudging Remi's spoon aside. With one movement, their dining table became the kind of place Edward had spent years trying to escape.

Isabella let him study the names before she spoke.

"Word of the war must have reached the markets of Marrakesh. But the official gazettes tell only a fraction of what is happening at the front."

She laid a finger along the Mediterranean coast.

"The Ottomans have lost most of their European lands. The Western Romans are sweeping into North Africa. Snow has trapped their supply wagons, yet their vanguard presses on."

Marco traced Libya and Egypt.

"Castile sent guns and provisions to hold both defensive lines. Both fell."

Isabella's finger stopped at Tunis.

"Now Tunis is next."

Juliet studied the coastal towns. She could not judge how long an army would take to march between them, but suddenly there seemed far too few places between Tunis and Marrakesh.

"Tunis holds the last harbour and supply stores on this line."

Isabella touched the roads marked between Fes and Taza.

"Both cities still stand, but they must divide their troops to protect the roads behind them. If Tunis falls, our supply wagons will have to pass through the fighting."

Edward leaned over the map.

"Can't you send reinforcements from Iberia?"

Isabella moved her hand towards the Pyrenees, where Iberia's northern frontier curved across the parchment.

"If I had troops to spare, I'd have sent them across the sea already. The French Emperor murdered the Pope in Vienna and broke the treaty. Castile's main army is holding the Pyrenees."

"Pull those men away, and the French will march into Iberia before our reinforcement ships can dock."

Marco spoke more quietly than when he had reported on Tunis.

"Fes needs guns and men. But taking even one more battery from the Pyrenees means leaving the soldiers there to pay for it."

Edward studied the sea between Iberia and North Africa.

"What about the navy? If the roads are blocked, you can still carry troops and provisions by ship."

Isabella glanced at Marco, then back at Edward.

"I thought so too, until word came from the New World."

"The Castilian fleet has lost to Portugal there. Their Vestigium was fearsome enough. Worse, their captains knew when to catch the wind, draw my ships out of formation, and destroy them one at a time."

Edward remembered old voyages spent lying awake, trying to anticipate Portuguese captains.

"How many ships have you lost? How many can still fight?"

"We have yet to account for them all. The intercepting squadron is broken, and what remains afloat cannot properly escort our supply convoys."

Isabella smoothed the map's curling edge.

"Across the ocean, one stronghold after another has fallen silent."

She touched the sea route between the Atlantic and Gibraltar.

"Those Portuguese captains are still out there. When they return, I don't know what I'll have left to stop them before they reach our shores."

A log cracked in the hearth. Edward followed the shipping lanes with his eyes. Even the sea, where he had found escape in his most desperate battles, offered no promise now.

Juliet touched his wrist.

"And the roads out of Marrakesh, Your Majesty? Could the people lose their way out?"

"They could," Isabella answered, looking only at Juliet. "For now, the roads remain open. But the fighting changes them by the day. I cannot promise that a road safe today will remain so next week."

Juliet said nothing more. She drew Remi's plate clear of the map, put the spoon inside it, and set both aside.

Edward sat beside her. He studied Marrakesh and the roads leading north without a word.

Remi stirred in the little bedroom beside the kitchen. Isabella left the map untouched and waited.

At last Edward spoke.

"I understand why you can't withdraw those troops. But why come to me in person?"

"Because I have something to ask of you."

Isabella paused.

"I wanted you to hear it from me, then decide for yourself."

Edward nodded.

"Go on."

Isabella opened her leather portfolio and took out three decrees bearing Castile's seal. She laid them out one by one, giving Edward time to examine each before she continued.

"Three roads," she said. "Hear them all before you choose. I don't need your answer tonight."

"The first takes you back to sea."

She pushed the leftmost decree towards him.

"You will command the Castilian ships still fit to fight, defend Gibraltar and Lisbon, and keep the supply routes to North Africa open. When the Portuguese return, you must meet them before they reach our shores."

Edward read as far as Gibraltar, then looked up.

"You're truly giving me what remains of the fleet?"

"I trust you to keep your men alive before you think of victory."

She waited until he finished reading, then offered the second decree.

"The second: Ravenna."

Isabella touched the parchment.

"I have reason to believe the Crown of Ravenna is a Vestigium of Mythic rank. The strange events that accompany each Western Roman advance point towards it, but its true power remains unknown to us."

"Choose Ravenna, and you will lead a party to the place where the crown is kept and bring it out. If that proves impossible, you may order its destruction."

Edward raised his head.

"You're asking a fleet commander to lead an infiltration, Bella."

"Because you know when to abandon a gamble," Isabella replied. "Those who can approach a Vestigium will do their part. You decide whether to advance or withdraw, and you bring them home."

She lifted the final decree. The lion of England stood beneath the Castilian seal in one corner.

"You return to England."

Edward recognised the emblem. He had touched none of the decrees, but his gaze lingered on this one.

"Choose the north, and you'll return to England with a party small enough to cross lands where government and armies have vanished. Find the surviving communities, then try to make contact with the Danes."

"I'll send members of the Royal Guard and the forces under their command with you."

Isabella drew the map closer.

"If the Danes still hold their ground, you may be able to strike from the north and force the French to look over their shoulders. I only need to give the Pyrenees time to breathe."

"As for England..."

She paused.

"I can get you there. Even I don't know what awaits you on that land."

"Three roads, Edward. You choose."

Edward studied the northern decree, then the blank stretches of the map.

"We'll encounter unclaimed Vestigium. Who deals with them? I'm meant to find survivors, not lead everyone to their deaths over something we don't understand."

"The Royal Guard has people trained to recover and contain Vestigium," Isabella replied. "They have forces of their own. I'll send the right people with you."

"They're coming with me?"

"You choose the route. When you encounter a Vestigium, they take charge of that matter," Isabella said. "You won't have to do their work for them."

Marco looked at Edward.

"Those people know what they're facing, Edward. More than we ever did back in England."

Edward turned to Juliet. She sat quietly beside him, listening.

"And if I go, what happens to Juliet and Remi?"

"They will go to Barcelona."

Isabella handed Juliet a writ of protection.

"They'll have a home, food, a physician, and schooling. If the court moves to Madrid, the writ will still stand."

Juliet drew it closer and read each line.

"How long will the protection last?"

"Until Edward returns. Or until you wish to leave, if circumstances allow."

Edward had yet to touch the three decrees. Instead, he placed a finger on the city's name beneath the wax seal.

"Is Barcelona truly the safest place? Or do you want them close enough to make sure I won't betray Castile?"

Isabella sat straighter.

"Both. Barcelona is still safe, and I can protect them there. I also know that protection will make you think carefully before turning against Castile."

Edward touched the writ.

"At least you'll say it plainly."

"You asked. I answered," Isabella said. "I don't need your good opinion."

She turned to Juliet.

"Mrs Spencer, let me be clear."

"You and Remi will not be hostages. If Edward betrays Castile, he'll face military law. If he has to get you both out of a burning city, I'll let him see his family safe before I call him to account."

Isabella looked back at Edward.

"Juliet and Remi will not pay for your actions. I'll say that only once."

At last Edward drew the writ closer and studied the royal seal.

"Does it still stand if I die? And what if you die first?"

"Yes. If you die, they're still protected. If I die, it will still bear the royal seal and the Council's signatures."

He tapped Barcelona's name.

"The city could fall."

"If Barcelona falls, I'll get them out before I touch the treasury."

Juliet spoke.

"And if Remi and I don't want to go where the court sends us?"

"Except in an emergency evacuation, you choose where to live," Isabella said. "My protection is yours and Remi's. Do you understand?"

Juliet traced the escort's intended route.

"If Remi falls ill on the road, will there be a physician?"

"The escort will carry medicines and have someone to tend the sick. If trouble arises, its commander may change the route."

Edward set down the writ.

"One more question."

"What if I say no?"

Isabella met his gaze.

"You mean to refuse all three decrees?"

"I want to know what you'd do if I took Juliet and Remi out of Marrakesh tonight, turned down your protection, and vanished."

Isabella withdrew her hands from the table and straightened.

"I won't send men to drag you back in chains."

"You have the right to refuse. But once you leave my protection, your family's safety is yours to secure. I can't take food from the army or send the Royal Guard after a man who chose to refuse them."

Edward asked:

"And if we die out there?"

"That will be the consequence of your choice."

Isabella looked straight at him.

"Where would you take Remi, Edward? Give me one place."

Edward frowned.

"Lower your voice. Remi's resting in the next room."

Isabella's chair scraped across the stone floor as she sprang up.

"That is precisely why I have to speak. Remi is in the next room."

Edward stood too.

"Bella."

"You fled the war once. Do you think you can keep running forever?"

Her voice faltered. The hand she had braced on the table fell to her side.

"You led thousands out of London while it burned. You taught me that when people are driven to the edge, they can mistake any road for a way out."

Isabella broke off mid-sentence. She turned away, but a tear had already slipped down her cheek.

"And I've always thought of you as my elder brother."

She wiped her cheek with the back of her hand and steadied herself against the table. Marco and Romeo stood motionless.

"I came because of you, Edward. I don't want to hear one day that your whole family froze to death on some nameless road."

Edward took a cloth from the chair and offered it. He waited until she accepted it.

"Bella."

His voice was low.

"I haven't decided to run. But I had to ask, for Juliet and Remi."

Isabella wiped away her remaining tears and folded the cloth in her palm.

"Do you need more time to answer me?" she asked, her voice calmer.

Edward looked at Juliet. She neither nodded nor shook her head, but closed both hands around his.

He studied the decrees.

"Give me two days to speak with Juliet and put our affairs in order. I'll tell you my decision myself."

Isabella sat down again.

"Very well. Two days."

"Marco will come for your answer in forty-eight hours. If it's no, I want you to tell me yourself."

A wooden cup knocked faintly against something behind the curtain. Juliet turned.

Remi peered through, clutching an empty wooden cup and trying to look solemn.

"I only wanted to ask if anyone needed more water."

Edward eyed the cup.

"With an empty cup?"

Remi set it on the table.

"I was going to ask first, then fetch some."

Romeo laughed. Marco joined him, Juliet shook her head, and Isabella beckoned the boy closer with a laugh.

Remi looked to his father for permission and waited for Edward's nod before approaching.

"I heard them call you Remi. Is that your real name or what they call you at home?"

"Everyone calls me Remi, ma'am."

"Reminisce," Edward supplied, his fingers finding his son's shoulder.

"Reminisce?"

"Yes. Remembrance," Edward said. "We wanted to remember what we'd lost, and what was still worth keeping."

Isabella looked at the boy.

"That's a heavy name, Edward."

Edward smoothed Remi's hair.

"When he's grown, he can decide what to make of it."

"Are you really the Queen?"

"I really am."

Remi studied the silver embroidery on her cloak, forgetting his cup.

"Do you own castles?"

"A few," Isabella said. "Most are colder than this house."

The boy considered the cold rooms, then asked something more practical.

"Are there schools in castles?"

"Not inside them. But Barcelona has schools, teachers, and children your age. You could study there."

Remi looked up at once.

"I could go to school too?"

"If your family moves to Iberia, certainly."

Remi turned towards his parents. Juliet gripped a fold of her clothing, and Isabella noticed. She rested a hand on the boy's shoulder.

"But whether you go is for your parents to decide. You mustn't use school to coax your father. Understood?"

Remi counted on his fingers, then looked up again.

"If I only remind Father once a day, that wouldn't be coaxing, would it?"

Isabella laughed.

"Are you bargaining with me?"

Remi gave a sheepish grin, then returned to studying the silver stitching on her crimson cloak. She caught him looking.

"Why do you keep staring at me?"

"Oh, nothing, ma'am."

Isabella smiled.

"I thought you wanted to ask me something."

"I was looking because you're very beautiful."

Juliet laughed. Edward could guess where Isabella was going with this.

"What sort of wife would you like when you grow up?" Isabella asked.

Remi thought for a moment and looked at his mother.

"Someone pretty and clever... and as kind to me as Mother."

Juliet smiled and waited.

"And if she dressed splendidly like Miss Isabella, that would be best of all!"

Isabella laughed first, then Romeo and Marco joined in.

Juliet gathered Remi into her arms and kissed his hair.

Isabella ruffled it once more, then let him return to his father.

Remi was still smiling when he remembered what he had overheard from behind the curtain. He turned to Edward.

"Father."

Edward saw the change in his face and knelt. Remi caught his goatskin sleeve.

"Do you have to go somewhere?"

"Perhaps. Your mother and I still need to talk."

"Far away?"

"Perhaps very far."

Remi examined his father's old goatskin coat, then its collar, as if this were the most urgent question of all.

"Then take your warmest coat."

Edward stroked his hair. A moment passed before he answered.

"I will."

"And the gloves Mother just mended. Don't take the ones with holes."

Remi still looked worried, but Juliet came to rest a hand on his shoulder.

"All right. Now fetch the water you promised. This time, bring some back in the cup."

"Yes, Mother."

Remi picked up the cup and ran into the kitchen.

Isabella rose and adjusted her cloak.

"I'll leave the writ of protection here," she told Juliet. "Read it carefully. If there's anything you object to, write it down and I'll consider it."

"I will," Juliet said.

Isabella turned to Edward.

"Forty-eight hours. That's all I can give you."

"I remember."

Marco opened the door. Snow-laden wind burst inside and bent the hearth flames sideways.

Isabella crossed the threshold, then stopped.

"Edward."

"Don't choose because I cried."

He did not answer at once.

"I know."

She nodded, raised her collar, and stepped into the snow.

The door closed behind her. Marco went with her to the carriage, while Romeo pulled up his hood and headed towards the mounted escort. Neither asked what Edward would choose.

Marco wiped the mist from the carriage window with the back of his hand.

"Edward seldom smiled like that at the Academy, Your Majesty. I never thought I'd see him at peace in a house with a child running about."

Isabella remembered Remi's empty cup.

"Nor did I."

"I thought Your Majesty might compel him to return to service," Marco said.

"After seeing that house?" Isabella asked. "I know what he'd be leaving behind."

Marco watched her.

"Even if he refuses all three decrees, Your Majesty will accept it?"

"I gave him a choice."

Marco considered that.

"I thought the decree for England would persuade him at once."

"I don't know."

The carriage wheels ground over snow-covered streets. Isabella watched the lights of Marrakesh recede behind the glass.

Night had fully fallen.

Remi had long since fallen asleep, curled beneath his warm blanket. He still clutched a wooden model of a three-masted ship as though letting go would mean losing it.

Juliet sat by the fire for a long time without speaking. Edward did not press her. He gathered the three decrees into a corner of the dining table and placed the writ of protection in the centre.

At last she came to him. Ignoring the chair opposite, she knelt beside him and rested her forehead on his knee.

"Edward, I'm afraid."

He placed a hand behind her neck. Juliet tried to speak, swallowed, then tried again.

"I looked at Marco and Romeo, at their armour, at the map on our table... and I saw London."

Edward closed his eyes.

"I know this isn't London."

Juliet gripped his coat.

"But I can still hear the guns at the docks, the people pushing past one another to flee, and Remi crying himself hoarse because you kept turning back to save someone else."

Edward pulled her to her feet and held her close.

"I'm still here."

"I know," Juliet said through her tears. "That's what frightens me."

He held her while snow lashed the windows.

Edward guided her to the chair beside the hearth and sat with her. A long while passed before she lifted her head.

"You're going to leave, aren't you?" she asked.

Edward glanced at the decrees.

"I haven't told Isabella."

"I'm asking my husband," Juliet said. "Don't answer like an admiral."

"If I stay in Marrakesh, all I can do is wait for the war to find us. If I accept a mission, Isabella will protect you and Remi in Iberia. At least you'd both have somewhere safer to live."

Juliet studied the three decrees.

"You keep avoiding the first two. Since Isabella mentioned England, have you thought seriously about anything else?"

Edward touched the first decree.

"I know how to fight at sea. But the Portuguese control the pace of battle, and I won't send another fleet against captains who choose when to open fire."

Juliet looked at the second.

"And Ravenna?"

"A crown whose power nobody understands. I won't gamble other lives on that."

Juliet drew the decree for England closer.

"Then you've chosen."

"I want to go back to England."

Juliet folded a corner of the paper.

"To help Castile? Or because you remember London so well you can't stop thinking about it?"

"Both," Edward said. "If people still live in the north, I could bring them into contact with the Danes and force France to divide its troops. But I want to see my homeland again too."

Juliet looked towards Remi's room.

"And our son? Are you looking for a battlefield, or a homeland for him?"

"I don't know what's left there. But I want to find out whether anyone survives before telling Remi that England exists only in books."

Juliet sat still, her hand in his.

"You could miss his whole childhood."

"And if you never come back?" She met his eyes. "Tell me the truth."

Edward took several seconds to answer.

"I don't know."

She kept looking at him. He drew her closer.

"If there's nothing left but graves, I'll return. But if people are alive, I want to help them find a way through."

Juliet rested her forehead against his chest.

"I hate that answer."

Edward kissed her hair.

"So do I."

She held him a little longer, then spoke against his chest.

"But I understand."

They stayed together until only red embers glowed in the hearth.

Before rising, Juliet looked about the house.

"Where do we start tomorrow? Remi, the cattle, our belongings... then Isabella?"

Edward looked at the room, the wooden chest, and the decree for England in the middle of the table.

"I'll find a way to send Isabella my answer in the morning. Then we'll tell Remi properly and start making arrangements. We'll keep some cattle for a farewell feast, and give the rest to the Governor and families able to tend them."

He pushed the other two decrees aside, leaving only the last at the centre of the table.

England.

For six years, England had lived in the Spencer household only through maps, old books, and the stories Edward told his son. That night its name lay on the table, upon a decree that could take him home.

title_vi: Chapter Three: Old Friends, New Roads
title_en: Chapter Three: Old Friends, New Roads
text_en:
Next morning, Edward opened his door to two familiar faces he had expected in another two days.

Marco leaned against the fence, his Castilian cloak tight at his throat. Romeo sat on an upturned barrel, trying to break a piece of bread so hard that half fell and stuck in the snow. Two horses stood nearby, their breath white in the cold.

"What the devil are you doing outside my house so early? Isabella said no one would be here for another two days."

Romeo eyed the bread buried in the snow.

"I'd like to ask Her Majesty the same thing. Especially being ordered from a carriage in this cold."

Marco brushed snow from his shoulders.

"We'd scarcely left Marrakesh when Her Majesty ordered us back. She wants us helping you for forty-eight hours."

"What for? I could have managed yesterday."

"Carriages, passes, relay stations, papers for the journey. Things you shouldn't spend half a day queuing to get signed," Marco said. "Her Majesty also ordered that no one press you for an answer before the deadline."

Romeo raised what remained of his bread.

"Her Majesty didn't want us standing indoors like two crows waiting for others to tidy up. The crows were my own addition."

Edward laughed.

"You'd barely left before turning back. Why are you still outside?"

"Marco asked if we both had to return," Romeo said, mimicking Isabella's stern gaze. "One look answered him."

The door behind Edward opened. Juliet came down the steps with a large basket, her headscarf tight and a folded paper at her waistband.

"I invited them in to warm themselves," she told Edward. "They said it was easier to breathe outside."

"We didn't want to wake Remi," Marco replied.

Romeo retrieved his salvageable bread and stayed silent.

Juliet glanced at the firewood beneath the porch.

"I must buy flour before the distribution stores get crowded, then ask about the papers for handing over the breeding stock. Stay with Remi, will you? These two can finish your wood chopping."

Edward looked at her.

"You're setting our guests to work already?"

"They said Her Majesty sent them to help. I'm sparing them idleness."

Marco took Edward's axe and checked its haft and blade. Romeo picked up another and regarded his friend.

"I expected grander deeds in the Royal Guard."

"Finish before noon and there's a hot meal," Juliet replied. "I'll inspect it when I return. Edward, don't forget you're seeing Victoria this afternoon."

"I haven't forgotten. Take care on the road."

Juliet left the yard. Edward watched her disappear behind the stone houses, while Romeo turned to him, grinning.

"Juliet's as frightening as ever. I haven't had a drink of water, and she's already found me a job."

"She's run this house for four years," Edward said, shovelling snow from the stable entrance. "Try doing her work for a morning."

Axes rang through the yard. Marco split along the grain so steadily that his logs formed neat rows; Romeo worked faster, but missed the fourth.

"You're holding the haft too high again," Edward said. "You broke one that way in Caen, remember?"

"You still remember that? I told you it was the cold."

Marco planted his axe and roared with laughter.

"I had to write the report. I dared put down only 'cause unknown'. Telling the colonel that an officer who could take a man's head off had been beaten by a log would have been too humiliating, even for you."

Romeo looked between his friends, then shifted his grip lower on the haft.

"You keep a fine record of my disgrace."

They returned to the wood. Between the axe blows and the crack of splitting logs, Edward realised this might be their last morning working together.

He cleared the last snow from the stable. As Marco hauled another log into place, Edward spoke.

"I've accepted Isabella's offer. Juliet and I talked last night. We've decided to leave Marrakesh."

Romeo stopped swinging his axe, and Marco set down the log. Both turned to Edward.

"Back to the navy?" Romeo asked. "I thought Her Majesty would seize the chance to put a whole fleet under your command."

"I've chosen the North. I'm going home to England."

Wind swept the fence, stripping a thin layer of snow from the stable roof. All three were English, though Marco and Romeo now wore Castilian insignia. Their old harbours, barracks and streets were gone; none knew how many survived across the sea.

At last Marco asked:

"Ed, have you thought it through? Going back may be nothing like you hope."

"I know. But I want to see for myself who's left. Right or wrong, I'll know when I arrive."

Romeo rested his axe on the ground.

"I used to think none of us would ever see England again."

"So did I. Then I talked to Juliet last night, and realised I couldn't pass up the chance."

Edward paused.

"The other reason can wait. I wanted you to hear it from me before the official orders."

Marco looked towards the house, as Remi's shadow crossed the clouded window.

"Leaving can't have been easy for Juliet. What have you arranged for her and the boy?"

"She wanted to stay. Four years here aren't easily left behind."

Edward glanced towards the door.

"But we decided together. We'll all go with the convoy to Gibraltar. Juliet and Remi will be escorted on to Barcelona, and I'll leave the convoy when my orders come."

Romeo asked nothing about their night's conversation. He merely hoisted his axe onto his shoulder.

"So what can we do for you?"

"For now, keep England to yourselves. I'll send my acceptance through Marco."

Edward pointed towards the logs still waiting beneath the porch.

"Before reporting to Her Majesty, finish your work here."

Romeo surveyed the woodpile and laughed.

"From the Royal Guard to splitting firewood. What a career I've had."

Remi came onto the porch carrying a full wooden cup in both hands. He picked his way along the cleared path, careful not to spill a drop.

"Father, I've brought water for you and Uncle Marco and Uncle Romeo. It's full to the top, so drink carefully."

Romeo put down his axe and peered into the cup.

"There's really water in it this time? Yesterday you brought us an empty cup and kept everyone waiting."

"There is, Uncle Romeo! I brought it from the kitchen. Go on, have some!"

Remi offered it to him first, smiling only after Romeo took a sip.

Marco drank next and passed the cup to Edward. Remi stood among the three men, gazing at the axes propped against the woodpile, and asked what he'd been wondering all morning.

"Are you going to England with Father? I heard him say he's going back."

"We've still got work in North Africa, Remi," Marco said. "But your father will have company on the journey. I'll help arrange what your family needs before you leave."

Romeo added:

"And I've got wagons of food to look after. If the soldiers go hungry, they'll have nothing to chew but snow, and snow isn't half as good as your mother's cooking."

Remi glanced towards the kitchen.

"Then will you stay and eat with us? Mother says anyone who finishes chopping before noon gets a hot meal."

"We will, if your mother leaves us any," Romeo said promptly. "I mean to finish quickly and get the best portion."

Remi laughed, then turned to his father.

"So you really have decided to go to England? You and Mother will tell me when we're leaving, won't you?"

Edward crouched to his son's height. He and Juliet had decided the night before, without yet telling Remi everything.

"Yes, I've decided. We'll all sit together tonight. You can ask us anything you like."

Remi thought for a moment and tugged at the hem of his father's goatskin coat.

"Then remember the thickest coat in the house. England's terribly cold. You told me yourself."

Romeo laughed, and Marco joined him. Smiling, Edward gave Remi back the cup and straightened his crooked woollen cap.

"I remember. Now go inside and get warm, before your mother has to come looking for you."

Remi ran inside with the cup clasped to his chest. Edward watched until the door shut, then returned to his friends.

Near noon, logs filled one corner beneath the porch. Marco replaced the last rotten plank in the western feeding trough, while Edward leaned on his shovel and surveyed the cleared yard.

Small wheels crunched in the lane: Juliet was back.

She came through the gate with her basket heavier than before, carrying flour, salt, a fresh coil of rope, packets of herbs and two loaves still warm. Remi rushed to meet her, claimed the lightest thing and declared he was helping.

Juliet inspected the woodpile, the cleared path and the repaired trough. She handed Romeo a warm loaf.

"Thank you both. Edward might have worked until evening and still not finished all this."

Romeo took the loaf, surprised, then glanced at the stable.

"If there's more to do, let me eat some of this first."

Edward took the basket from his wife.

"What did they say at the distribution office? Will they let us transfer the cattle to other households?"

"The original stock belongs to the city's reserve, so we need Victoria's signature or her appointed deputy's. I've got the forms, but see her before we divide the herd."

Juliet brushed snow from her sleeves and glanced towards the square.

"The Governor's Palace is quiet today. Go now to avoid the wait."

"I meant to go this afternoon. I'll change and go."

Romeo brushed sawdust from his hands.

"Excellent. We must report there too. We can go with you."

"You two still have work here," Juliet reminded them.

Romeo and Marco both looked towards the stable.

"Marco, replace the rotten plank in the eastern trough, please. Romeo, move those sacks of hay farther under cover. The snow may be heavier tonight."

Marco nodded. Romeo sighed at the hay piled above his shoulders.

"I'm beginning to see why Her Majesty ordered us back."

"Afterwards, go where you please. I've kept hot food for you both."

Juliet turned to Edward, eyeing his muddy boots and sawdust-covered coat.

"And you. Are you really going to meet the Governor dressed as though you've just come out of the cowshed?"

"Victoria's seen me looking much worse," Edward said, looking down at his coat.

"I believe you. The guards at the gate may not have."

Romeo laughed aloud. Edward joined him, then left his friends to the hay and trough while he changed.

Fifteen minutes later, he returned in a clean woollen jumper, his goatskin coat brushed free of sawdust and his hair hastily combed with water. He handed Marco his signed acceptance and asked him to send it through the royal relay station, then let Juliet straighten his collar.

"That's better," she said.

Edward kissed her forehead and promised to be home before dark.

"And if you drink wine with Victoria, at least remember the way home."

Edward hesitated. Romeo gave an appreciative whistle, and Marco kicked him lightly in the shin before Juliet turned. Edward only smiled and left through the gate alone.

At noon Marrakesh looked strange, born under fierce sun yet living beneath grey-white skies. Wheels and boots had ground the snow into dirty strips along the streets, while wooden props braced terracotta roofs against the weight of ice.

Edward passed through the market Juliet had just visited. Sellers covered vegetables with two layers of heavy cloth and hung meat in sheltered alcoves. Merchants who had once fanned themselves against the heat now burned charcoal at their feet.

News of the war had reached Marrakesh long before Isabella. People spoke of Tunis, the eastern road, rising flour prices and military convoys passing through Tangier. None knew the man in the goatskin coat carried a decision that might return him to a country he had sworn, six years before, never to see again.

title_vi: Chapter Four: At the Governor's Palace
title_en: Chapter Four: At the Governor's Palace
text_en:
The Governor's Palace rose above the main square, a great stone residence repeatedly renovated by the Castilians. Two flags strained atop its low tower: the royal banner and that of Marrakesh.

Juliet had been right. The courtyard before the gates was quieter than usual.

A guard recognised Edward before he could introduce himself. He checked the visitors' book, eyed Edward's goatskin coat and opened the gate.

"Governor Valdes is in her study, sir. You may go straight in."

Edward winced at the formality.

"I'm Edward Spencer. Just call me Edward."

The guard fell silent.

Edward crossed the familiar stone passage. Four years in Marrakesh had brought him here often for ration papers, breeding stock, land taxes and matters he'd never imagined as an admiral.

His first visit had involved no livestock ledger.

He had brought an exhausted Juliet, Remi, then about three, and what remained of their old life in two bags soaked with seawater.

Victoria Valdes had stood at the end of this very passage. She had asked neither how many ships and men Edward had lost nor why England had fallen. She had seen the child in Juliet's arms and ordered a room prepared with a fire.

Edward remembered the warmth of that room, and Victoria raising a hand to have the guard let them through, more clearly than any words of comfort.

He knocked.

"Come in."

The Governor's study smelled as it always had of paper, sealing wax and burning wood. A map of Morocco covered one wall beside a provisions board. Outside the window, snow swept across the low tower's roof.

Victoria stood at the window with a report. Her fair hair was tied neatly at her nape, and red ink stained her fingers. She looked Edward up and down, then laughed.

"Edward, you're still as scruffy as you were when you skipped tactics lessons."

Edward shut the door and glanced at his clean woollen jumper.

"I changed before I came. Juliet even checked my collar."

"Then I must thank her. Left to yourself, you'd still have sawdust on your shoulders."

Edward took off his coat and sat. Victoria fetched two glasses and opened a bottle of red wine from the cabinet beside the hearth.

"Wine? At midday?"

"You used to blame the cold for drinking rum before breakfast aboard ship. I thought I'd follow that admiral's example."

She handed him a glass. Edward studied the wine, then the wall map. At the Academy, all four had believed those borders would outlive their makers.

Victoria sat opposite him.

"For four years you've come only about cattle, taxes or residence papers. Today you seem to want another conversation."

"I really am here about the cattle."

"I know. But whenever you want to dodge a difficult question, you start with figures. At the Academy, before admitting you'd lost the map-room key, you spent ten minutes complaining about the lock."

"Romeo took it. I kept it for him and forgot where."

Victoria sipped her wine, amused.

"I remember. I also remember a second-year cadet standing in the rain for nearly two hours, waiting for me to finish training just so he could ask me to supper."

Edward touched his forehead.

"It wasn't raining when I arrived. You tell it as though I went there expressly to get soaked."

"It started half an hour later. You stayed where you were. When I came out, I could hardly tell what colour your hair was."

They both laughed. That rain had washed away most of what Edward meant to say, until Victoria dragged him into the bakery behind the Academy, set a cup of hot water before him and waited until he stopped shivering.

"And the winter festival on that street? Do you remember it?"

Edward remembered the glove Victoria had dropped into a drain and her cold hand slipping into his. They had walked the length of the street, neither eager to let go.

"Sometimes I thought that if you'd been a little less foolish, we might have had a different story."

Edward looked at her. A log settled in the hearth, throwing sparks against the brass guard. Victoria set down her glass, two fingers still around its stem.

"Juliet knows you saved us during our first winter here," he said. "I haven't found the right moment to tell her about the Academy."

"You make it sound as though you've scheduled a disaster."

"You've never seen Juliet discover I've hidden something from her."

Victoria leaned back, laughing.

"Very well. Show me your cattle before we finish this bottle between us."

Edward took out Juliet's form and pushed it across the desk. In four years the city's breeding stock had grown beyond forty head. Some remained the city's; the rest, by agreement, belonged to the Spencers.

"We're leaving, so I want to return the city's share properly. I'll divide ours between Omar, the Thompson family and a few English households who've only just arrived. Selling them now would help no one much."

Victoria read the form.

"I'll send people to your farm tomorrow to count the city's animals, then gradually pass them on to households that need breeding stock. We'll draw up the deeds for yours on the spot. You won't have to drive forty cattle to the palace again."

"That was the tax clerk's idea, not mine."

"I remember. They filled the square while you tried to account for each one by number."

Edward shook his head, smiling despite himself. He remembered dark mornings carrying a dying calf towards the hearth, nights Juliet watched cows struggle to calve, and Remi taking his first steps among the straw. The memories returned as Victoria folded the paper.

"My people will come tomorrow," she said. "Care for the animals as usual until they're handed over."

"Thank you, Vic."

"Four years ago I gave your family shelter, residence papers and a few breeding animals on loan. But you and Juliet built your life here."

She set the form aside.

"Don't turn all of it into a debt to me."

Edward ran a finger round his glass.

"I still owe you for an open gate."

"Then see that you walk out through it properly."

Victoria rested an elbow on the desk.

"Her Majesty came to your house yesterday. The whole city saw the royal banners, so I needn't pretend to be surprised that you're leaving."

"I've accepted. I chose England."

Victoria was silent for a time. Wind struck the glass; an icy branch scraped the stone frame.

"I thought you would," she said.

"Aren't you going to ask why?"

"You'll tell me if you wish. You've studied maps of home longer than any of us since we arrived."

Edward rested his elbows on his knees.

"I need to see who's left. Perhaps I'll find nothing. I won't spend my life knowing I let this chance pass."

Victoria looked at his calloused hands. Four years ago they shook too badly to hold her bowl of soup. Now calluses crossed his palms like wood grain.

"I knew you before anyone called you Admiral," she said. "Before you had anyone to protect except a few troublesome schoolmates."

Edward looked up.

"And what worried you most?"

"You always believed you ought to be the last to leave."

The fire crackled. Edward looked into his cooling wine and found no joke.

"Juliet said much the same last night," he said at length.

"Then perhaps you should listen to her this time."

Edward rose, passed the map of Morocco and stopped before a map of Europe on the opposite wall. Victoria joined him, touching the sea near the British Isles.

"If the Danes still hold ground, if communities remain on the islands that can be brought together, the French will have to divide their forces. Every month counts in the Pyrenees. Her Majesty has reason to seek you out."

"You still don't want me to go."

"I've disliked plenty of your decisions."

Victoria met his gaze.

"Once I stood under the Academy porch, angry with you yet hoping you wouldn't give up waiting in the rain. That stubbornness has stayed with you."

Edward touched the edge of the map.

"I won't leave Juliet and Remi stranded on the road. We all go with the convoy to Gibraltar. They'll travel under protection to Barcelona, and I'll leave when my orders come."

"Make sure they know where they're going and who's to meet them. You're used to stepping ashore in strange ports with a sword in your hand. Remi is seven."

Edward nodded.

Victoria returned to her desk.

"And the English households Juliet looks after? When winter comes, who will divide the food, find medicine and check which homes have run out of firewood?"

"Juliet handles most of it. I help with the livestock, repairs and transport. We'll hand those duties to people who can take them on, so the neighbourhood has help through winter."

"Give me their names. If a house lacks its coal allowance or no one visits a sick neighbour, I want to know whom to ask."

Victoria gathered the cattle form with other papers.

"And speak to Juliet properly. She'll be furious if you start ordering the whole neighbourhood about."

Edward laughed.

"If you and Juliet sat in one room for an hour, I'd have to seek political asylum."

"Perhaps we'd only be discussing how to manage you."

"That's what frightens me."

A knock came; the door opened before Victoria answered. Marco entered with Romeo, snow on both their shoulders.

"I knocked," Marco said under Victoria's gaze. "And I've sent Ed's letter of acceptance to Her Majesty through the royal relay station."

"You knocked while pushing the door open," Victoria said. "Next time, reverse the order."

Romeo went straight to the hearth and stretched his frozen hands towards the flames.

"Juliet had us repairing troughs, moving hay and carrying water. If the Crown has anything easier, I'll volunteer at once."

"She let you go, then?" Edward asked.

"After Remi made me explain everything the Royal Guard does," Marco said, removing his gloves. "Then he asked why we hadn't finished helping his father before we left."

Edward laughed.

"I'll thank him for you."

Victoria fetched two more chairs. Romeo cupped his water between frozen hands; Marco unwound his damp scarf. Edward moved his wineglass aside for Romeo's elbow, as when all four had crowded round Academy tables.

"All four of us together like this," Romeo said, "and I half expect an instructor to come in and order us into the corridor. At least no one can make me stand there as punishment now."

"They usually called your name first," Marco said.

Victoria laughed, and Edward with her. Old stories returned for a few minutes, until Marco noticed the rolled map on the desk.

Marco spread it across the table.

"When Ed's family leaves Marrakesh, I'm going to Fes. Her Majesty wants the Taza road and depots inspected before the Western Roman army advances."

Victoria put a hand on the eastern side of the map.

"If Taza falls, Fes must hold alone. I won't have Marrakesh dragged onto the front while so many refugees remain here."

"I'll visit the outposts myself," Marco said. "I've read enough fine reports. I want to see whether my men still have bread and ammunition."

Edward traced the retreat road west of Fes.

"And roads for the civilians. If you wait for the enemy guns before finding wagons, you've waited too long."

Marco nodded, taking the warning to heart.

Romeo leaned back in his chair.

"I'll be running between Tangier, Ceuta, Casablanca and here. A ship comes a day late and people go hungry. A depot runs short of coal and the medicines spoil. I'd sooner have a ship to command again."

"When you're in Marrakesh, come to my office first," Victoria said. "Don't let your men arrive at the stores only to find nobody's been warned."

"I know, Vic. You must sign for the provisions here. How could I forget?"

Romeo raised his water and grimaced, remembering wagons still awaiting supplies.

Edward regarded his Academy friends, each serving Castile.

"So we've ended up working together after all."

"At least this time someone is looking after all four of us," Romeo said, meaning Isabella.

Victoria laughed and took a small box from a drawer.

Inside lay Isabella's sealed letter. Victoria opened it before them.

"Her Majesty orders that Marrakesh must not fall. A whole corps is coming to reinforce us."

Romeo almost slammed down his cup.

"An entire corps? When the Pyrenees are already stretched so thin?"

"They'll arrive in stages," Victoria said. "Marrakesh will have to feed men who've just escaped the fighting as well as troops coming to defend North Africa. Feeding and housing them will take work."

Edward studied the dot marked Marrakesh. He had arrived with two bags soaked in seawater and asked only for a roof to shelter his family of three through winter. Now tens of thousands depended on it.

"Can you hold it, Vic?"

Victoria folded the letter.

"I've made a promise to the people here. I'll hold it."

She set the letter on the desk and placed a paperweight over it. Wheels ground over packed snow in the square below, audible at the window. They listened until the convoy passed.

Marco faced Edward.

"We're scattering again. Each to a different road."

"At least we have the Castilian post this time," Romeo said. "I don't care to wait another three years before learning where you are, or whether you're alive, Ed."

"Try answering letters yourself first," Marco said. "The one you sent me through three regiments took seven months to arrive."

Romeo spread his hands.

"But it arrived. I still call that an achievement."

Victoria shook her head, smiling. Edward remembered something he had avoided for four years.

"Vic, I left something here. Do you still have it?"

Victoria met his gaze, and her smile softened.

"I've waited a long time for you to ask."

She went into her private rooms behind the study, leaving the three men by the hearth. Marco stood still; Romeo stopped eyeing the wine. Both knew what she had gone to fetch.

Victoria returned with a Sabre in a black leather scabbard. Edward recognised the silver clasp at its mouth before seeing the hilt.

The day he arrived in Marrakesh, he had unbuckled it and laid it before her. His uniform hung loose; Juliet was exhausted, Remi still tiny. Edward had said a cattle farmer needed no sword.

Victoria held it out.

"Do you remember what you said when you gave it to me? That if you ever drew a sword again, you'd have failed to build another life."

"Did I really say something fit for a gravestone?"

"Worse than that. I had to wait until you'd slept before I dared laugh."

Edward studied the scabbard. Victoria brought it closer, slowing her words.

"But you haven't failed, Edward. Those four years happened. Juliet, Remi, the house, the cattle, the neighbours. Taking up a sword again won't erase them."

Edward reached out, then stopped short of the silver clasp. Stable-hardened fingers brushed the leather; Victoria waited for him to take the sword.

He accepted the Sabre.

The leather remained supple and the silver clasp bright. Even the stitching beneath his old grip was unchanged. Edward drew the blade a finger's breadth, and firelight ran along the steel.

"You've cared for it well."

"I couldn't have you return to find a heap of rust."

Marco stepped forward and put a hand on Edward's shoulder.

"Remember our graduation? All four of us?"

Romeo, who would once have answered for Edward, said nothing. He touched the hilt of the Sabre at his own hip, his eyes fixed on the returned sword.

Victoria took her Sabre from the weapon rack. Edward recognised the old scratches and grooves on his friends' blades.

The smell of oil on steel carried him back to their graduation. The year's four highest cadets had received Sabres with Miracle-grade Vestigium cores, forged from steel confirmed as fragments of Excalibur. Edward forgot the speech's length, but remembered the glowing grooves when they stood together, too astonished to lower their swords.

Edward drew his blade. Marco and Romeo drew theirs, while Victoria took her place on the far side of the circle. The whisper of steel leaving leather silenced the room.

The four sword points met. Gold flashed where they touched and ran through the grooves until the hearth fire seemed pale beside it. They recognised that light despite the years apart.

They held the blades together in the golden glow. Four voices recited their old Academy oath.

"May the Queen light our way. Glory to the Empire on Which the Sun Never Sets!"

Romeo laughed; Marco joined him. Victoria looked at Edward and found him laughing too; then she joined them.

The four blades fell. Their laughter faded, leaving only the wind outside.

"That sounded much grander in those days," Marco said, still smiling.

Romeo glanced at the Castilian insignia on his breast.

"I thought I'd be shouting those words until I was old. Now they hardly sound like mine."

He stroked his Sabre's hilt. Marco's smile faded as well, as gold faded along their lowered blades' grooves.

"Leave that oath at the Academy," Victoria said. "I won't carry a lost throne into the promise we're about to make."

Edward looked at them.

"Then what do we swear to now?"

Marco held his blade across his chest.

"To those still living. War has taken enough from us."

Romeo turned his Sabre in his hand.

"I only want my convoys to arrive in time. Too many people have waited for someone who never came."

Edward remembered Victoria opening her door four years ago, and those who hadn't survived their first Marrakesh winter. Beyond the window, snow covered a city that had once lived beneath the sun.

"When the light fails, we forge a path."

Marco lifted his head. Romeo repeated the words more quietly than usual. Victoria watched Edward, gripping her Sabre.

"That sounds like you," she said.

"If we use it, it belongs to all four of us."

Victoria raised her Sabre first. Marco and Romeo followed, pausing before their points touched. Edward looked at his friends and lifted his own blade last.

Their four points met again. Gold lit their older faces, touched the map by the hearth and climbed the stone walls. For a moment nobody spoke.

"When the light fails, we forge a path."

Four voices fell silent. The glow lingered another heartbeat, then retreated into the grooves. Marco lowered his blade, Romeo followed, and Victoria sheathed hers as she waited for Edward.

The silver clasp snapped shut with a dry click. The sword settled at his hip, where it had been absent for four years.

Romeo eyed Edward's sheathed blade and laughed.

"Next time we meet, please don't make us learn another oath. I've only just remembered this one."

"Remembering it tomorrow would be progress," Marco said.

Victoria straightened Edward's Sabre belt as she had during their Academy uniform inspections.

"I can do that myself, Vic."

"I know. But let me today."

She fastened the crooked buckle, let go and spoke under her breath.

"Go home to Juliet. You've a whole house to put in order."

Edward looked from one friend to the next.

"I want to see all three of you before my family leaves. Don't disappear too early."

Victoria nodded.

"I still have to sign your cattle transfer papers."

Marco promised to help carry their things before departure. Romeo laid a hand on Edward's shoulder, gave it one brief squeeze and let go.

Edward smiled and went to the door. At the threshold he looked back at Victoria.

"Vic, thank you for keeping my sword all these years."

"Thank you for finally coming back for it," she replied.

Edward stepped into the passage. Snow covered Marrakesh's square, and wind swept through terracotta streets once hot beneath the sun. The Sabre tugged at his coat with each step; he adjusted its belt before reaching the last stair.

Less than two days remained to settle the house, hand over the cattle, say farewell to those who helped his family survive and tell Remi his father was going far away.

Edward raised his collar and took the road home. Four old friends had stood together again. None knew when they would do so next.

title_vi: Chapter Five: Ambitions
title_en: Chapter Five: Ambitions
text_en:
Forty-eight hours had sounded generous when Isabella said it. By the time Edward returned from the Governor's Palace that afternoon, Sabre at his hip and Victoria having agreed to take charge of the herd, he realised that four years of life could not be packed into a few trunks simply by working faster.

The Spencer house had become a maze of clothes, books, cord and woollen blankets. Copper pot in hand, Edward stood between two piles and decided to ask before making matters worse.

He raised the pot.

"Take this or leave it? I thought I'd ask, since my right to make decisions in this room seems to have been suspended."

Juliet was examining a blanket.

"Leave it for the Thompsons. Theirs cracked last season. And put it on the right, not the left."

Edward looked at both piles, then at the pot.

"The left was for things we're taking a moment ago."

"It was, until you mixed the piles together and insisted you'd moved only one thing."

She pointed to a woollen shirt beside the medicine basket and two of Remi's books stranded in the tool bag.

"You've said that four times since you came home. A fifth won't put the room back in order."

Edward obediently moved the pot to the right.

"At least I remember what I did. I call that progress."

Juliet took a woollen shirt from the trunk, checked its cuff stitching and set it aside to keep.

"If you want to show progress, take this one. The grey shirt goes to the Thompsons. It's still good, which means someone else can use it."

Edward picked up the grey shirt as though he had discovered an unfortunate law of nature.

"I see. The better something is, the more likely we are to give it away."

"You learn faster than I thought."

Juliet brushed dried mud from the hem of his thickest goatskin coat and tested every clasp. Into its two inner pockets went dried garlic cloves, a clean strip of cloth and a sewing kit.

Edward watched the garlic disappear.

"Is garlic compulsory equipment now?"

She kept her eyes on the coat.

"You once spent three days at sea with a loose button and called it no trouble. I'm not staking my husband's life on his ability to look after himself. The garlic, cloth and needles stay."

"I remember the button differently."

"Of course. I sewed it back on when you reached port."

Remi laughed aloud. As Edward turned, the boy bent over his toys with suspicious industry.

Juliet drew her son's bag closer. She rolled his goatskin stockings into pairs, then packed cough medicine, a spare scarf and the woollen cap patched beside its left ear. She checked everything once more before placing it in his little trunk.

When Edward saw the old leather map in her hand, he reached to stop her.

"We're taking that."

"I know."

Juliet wrapped the map in oilcloth alongside Remi's schoolbooks. Six years ago it had lain on an officer's desk; lately Edward had used it to show his son the Atlantic and the shape of England.

Edward put the copper pot on the floor and stood.

"I'll chop some firewood."

"No."

Juliet indicated the book trunk beside the bed.

"Sit down and choose your books. We can't take them all."

Edward lifted a treatise on naval gunnery.

"Could we leave some clothes instead?"

"No. We can buy books in Iberia. You can't wear them when the snow comes."

Remi looked up from his stack.

"Does Queen Isabella have a library, Father? If she's got lots of books already, could we put yours there?"

Edward was still wondering how to explain that the Royal Library was no storehouse when Juliet laughed.

"I know you're trying to help. You've helped so much that my trunk's barely any lighter."

Remi hugged a book to his chest, oblivious to the complaint.

"Then I'll think of something else."

"That's what worries me."

Remi cradled his wooden ship. He had been told to choose three toys, but after half an hour all six still lay around his feet.

Edward rested his elbows on his knees.

"Finished choosing?"

The boy swept all six into his arms.

"Yes, Father."

"Three toys."

"I chose three times two."

Juliet laughed at the arithmetic and left Edward to negotiate alone.

Edward pointed to the ship, the cloth ball and a wooden horse missing one leg.

"These three."

Remi hugged the ship closer.

"What about these two people?"

Two small wooden figures lay by his feet. One wore a sailor's cap; the other had a cloak Edward claimed belonged to an explorer, though Juliet thought it resembled a sack.

"That makes five."

"But they're smaller than normal toys."

Edward glanced at Juliet. She continued folding clothes, plainly unwilling to rescue him.

Remi placed the figures together.

"They have to stay together. They're a crew."

"You're making your own rules."

"You told me to choose. You didn't say every toy had to be the same size."

Edward studied him, then surrendered.

"Very well. Those two count as one. But you tie your own bag."

Remi nodded at once.

Juliet looked at the drum.

"And the drum?"

"Little Hassan can have it. He likes making noise."

"I'll make sure Hassan knows it was entirely your idea."

Remi looked doubtful but put the drum on the pile to leave behind.

The wooden horse troubled him longer. He turned the three-legged creature in his hands.

"Tom Thompson likes this. Can I give it to him myself?"

Edward nodded.

"Of course. Write Tom's name on a tag and give it to him tomorrow. Then he'll know it's your present, not something Mother and I made you abandon."

Remi set the horse aside and clutched the cloth ball.

"I'm keeping this one. No bargaining."

Edward left it on the pile to take, considering the negotiations finished.

Remi sorted the other toys by recipient while Edward returned to the books. He kept the old sea chart, a coverless Shakespeare, the notebook he used to teach Remi and two histories. The rest went to the refugee quarter's little school and families with children who could read.

Juliet spotted the gunnery treatise among the books to be given away.

"I thought you'd insist on taking that."

Edward leafed through it, then closed it.

"I remember most of it. Besides, if I have to consult a book in battle to remember how to fire a cannon, I've got bigger problems than a missing textbook."

Juliet regarded him.

"I can't decide if that reassures me or makes things worse."

"Keep both feelings. Seems fair."

Eventually, two of the three trunks stood closed. Remi was charged with tying a name tag to every bag. He wrote slowly, misspelt Hassan once and corrected it himself; now and then Edward had to untie a tag the boy had knotted too tightly.

Juliet set a medicine pouch before him.
