"This comes with us. Enough for a few days of trouble, and the escort will have army surgeons."

Edward opened it and inspected each packet, frowning.

"I haven't seen their medical stores. Remi will be travelling in midwinter. I'm uneasy about leaving so much."

"I know. But the Thompsons have a child with a fever, and Hassan has two children. We've stored more than most of our neighbours. We keep enough for the journey and leave the rest."

Edward held the pouch a moment longer. He glanced towards the Thompsons' basket, noted the quantities in both portions and tied it shut.

Juliet's voice gentled.

"I know you're worried about Remi."

"And I know the Thompsons need it."

Edward put the medicines in the neighbours' basket and turned to his son.

"Remi, help Father tie this tag, will you?"

By the time the light outside darkened to slate, the room looked bare. Empty shelves and unused coat hooks had altered the house before anyone had left it.

Juliet shut a trunk, her fingers brushing the invitation in her coat pocket. She left it there.

"While you were at the Governor's Palace, Remi and I went round the neighbourhood. Omar, the Thompsons, Hassan and our closest friends all know. I asked others to tell the farther houses. Word should reach almost the whole quarter by tonight."

Edward looked up from his tool chest.

"All those visits in one afternoon? I thought you'd only just returned from the market."

"That was our last stop."

Juliet drew a chair towards the table.

"If we're leaving Marrakesh, I want to tell the people who've lived beside us for four years myself. Whoever can come is welcome. I've counted more than thirty already."

Edward surveyed the little room and the snowy yard.

"Where will we put thirty people?"

"We won't fit them in here. We'll use the yard, put canvas beside the shed and light both outdoor hearths. If the snow grows heavy, children and older folk come inside. I've settled the seating, so please don't invite half of Marrakesh as well."

Edward set down his tools.

"I've yet to invite anyone, and already my diplomatic powers are restricted?"

"Yes. Now we need to discuss the cattle."

At the word cattle, Remi abandoned his tags and crawled towards the table. Edward sat opposite Juliet.

"Victoria's sending someone to inspect the herd tomorrow morning. She'll handle those belonging to the city fund. I want us three to decide about the rest."

Juliet opened the ledger at its last page and turned it towards him.

"Forty-three head. Thirty-one belong to the city's breeding fund, and we've raised twelve of our own. I'd like those twelve settled before Victoria's people arrive."

Her pen stopped at the entry for the feast.

"There's something I haven't told you. I said to the Thompsons we'd slaughter four."

Edward looked up.

"You promised four before we'd discussed it?"

"Yes. They have a sick child, and I thought of the other families too. If we're inviting people, I want them to take something home."

Edward studied the filled pages.

"Some meat for stew, some for roasting, some for families to carry away. Bones for soup, hides for anyone who needs them. I'll find kitchen helpers. Will you do the butchering and tend both hearths?"

Edward nodded.

"I'll see to the cattle, the knives and the fires. You handle the kitchen and helpers. Waste nothing."

Remi followed the arithmetic and pointed at the remainder.

"What about the other eight, Father?"

Edward drew the ledger towards him.

"Four go to Uncle Omar and the Thompsons. We'll make out the transfer papers for the other four to households needing breeding stock, from the Governor's list. None comes with us."

Remi considered this, then asked what Edward had expected.

"What about Number Seventeen?"

Juliet knew he meant the bull with the white patch on its forehead, the one Remi secretly fed turnip peelings.

"He's one of our twelve."

Remi brightened, but Edward went on.

"I mean to give him to Uncle Omar. He needs a sound bull, and Seventeen's used to people. He'll be easier to keep."

The boy's face fell, but he said nothing.

"Can I tell Uncle Omar he likes turnip peelings better than hay?"

"Of course. That's the most important part of the handover. I wouldn't dare take it from you."

Juliet marked the neck tags to be removed before the inspectors came. Edward took the coil of cord from the table's end. Every animal in the ledger now had a destination.

He drew the cord nearer.

"I'll separate the four for the feast tonight, so they won't get mixed up with tomorrow's herd."

Remi watched his parents bind the trunks.

"Father, you promised we'd all talk tonight."

Edward put down the cord. Juliet set the ledger aside and moved her chair closer to their son.

"I remember. What do you want to ask first?"

"How far do we go together? Mother says Iberia, but you said you have to go back to England."

"We all go to Gibraltar first. Then you and Mother will be taken to Barcelona. I'll return to England when Queen Isabella orders me to."

Remi looked down, straightening the cord around his two wooden figures.

"Will you come to Barcelona with us?"

Edward watched him for a moment.

"I'll find a way back to you both. I don't know when, so I can't promise a day."

"Will you write? I can read now."

"If letters can get through, I will. And you must tell me about your new school and everyone you meet. I want to hear it all."

Juliet rested a hand on Remi's shoulder.

"Queen Isabella has arranged your letters of protection and schooling. I'll be with you. Tomorrow we still have neighbours in Marrakesh to say goodbye to."

Remi glanced at a neighbour's name tag, then looked up.

"Will Queen Isabella come to our feast?"

Edward and Juliet exchanged a glance. He shook his head.

"I don't know. She has a whole court to attend to. I expect she's far from Marrakesh already."

"Could I ask Uncle Marco to invite her? He knows Queen Isabella."

Juliet raised an eyebrow.

"One day with someone from the Royal Guard, and you've made him your messenger?"

Edward drew the boy's chair closer.

"Go on, ask. But invite Queen Isabella because you like her, not because she's a queen."

Remi thought hard.

"If she comes, must we give her the best chair?"

Juliet answered before Edward could.

"No. Our best chair is the only one that doesn't wobble, and Uncle Omar is older. He gets it. Queen Isabella will have to follow the Spencer house rules."

Edward laughed. Remi accepted the arrangement, asking only that Isabella have a place near the fire. Juliet agreed and drew back the ledger.

"One more thing. Who's bringing the wine?"

Edward paused over the trunk's cord.

"Romeo said he would."

Juliet checked the ledger and added a stroke.

"Then put out extra bread and water. When Romeo brings wine, someone always forgets to eat."

Edward set another water jug by the hearth and put on his coat. When he returned from the shed, he'd separated the four cattle for the feast and written their numbers on a slip beside the ledger.

Romeo appeared at dusk with two great wine jugs behind his back, as if Juliet might overlook them. Marco followed with a bag of dry bread and spoke before he was through the door.

"Let me be a witness. I told him one jug was enough."

Romeo placed both jugs on the table like a man completing an important mission.

"Tomorrow is the feast. Tonight we're testing the quality. Imagine discovering a fault only after we've served it."

Juliet looked from the jugs to his face.

"You intend to test both down to the bottom?"

"If duty demands it."

"It doesn't."

Romeo sought support from Edward, who was finishing the cord around the book trunk without looking up.

"I've learned today that arguing with my wife about provisions takes longer than obeying her. Fight your own battle."

Marco put the bread beside the wine.

"You've finally grown up. Late, but worth noting."

At Marco's voice, Remi came running from the inner room. He slowed when he reached him, clutching his shirt hem and looking away as if the words he'd rehearsed had suddenly become difficult.

"Uncle Marco..."

He stretched out the name, then looked up.

"Could you take Queen Isabella my invitation, please?"

Marco stopped brushing snow from his shoulder. He crouched beside Remi and pressed his lips together before answering.

"Of course. I'll send someone after Her Majesty's party. I can't promise she'll return in time, but she'll get your invitation."

Remi stood straighter.

"Really? Tell her the place by the fire is still free!"

Marco regarded him and nodded with exaggerated understanding.

"Ah. I see. You've taken a fancy to Queen Isabella, have you?"

"I haven't!"

Remi nearly jumped, crimson to his ears.

"I only want her to come for supper! And she... she's nice to me. That's different!"

"Of course. Entirely different."

Marco nodded solemnly, only flustering him further.

"I didn't say anything. You've explained it all yourself."

Remi opened his mouth to protest but found Marco waiting. He appealed to Edward, who bent over the trunk and pretended the cord required all his attention. Juliet laughed at their son's aggrieved face.

Romeo looked around.

"And me? I bring wine and nobody thanks me?"

Remi eyed the jugs.

"Mother says when you bring wine, people forget to eat."

Marco and Edward laughed together. Juliet moved the jugs away from the table's edge and left Romeo to defend himself.

Supper should have been soup, bread and yesterday's leftover meat. But four old friends were together again after too many years, Remi kept asking about the Academy, and Romeo insisted that the second jug tasted different from the first. By the time Juliet took Remi to bed, talk had passed from their days of slipping out of lessons to the time Marco set his sleeve on fire during Vestigium practice.

Juliet came back once to tell them to lower their voices.

A second time, she took the wine jug from Romeo.

There was no third visit.

Near midnight, their conversation dwindled to scattered words. Soon there was only the crackle of logs and a long snore Juliet knew belonged to Romeo without needing to look.

She slept for a while before the cold woke her. The space beside her was empty.

Juliet pulled on a fur coat, tied it at her throat and opened the bedroom door. The sitting room looked as though it had survived a tiny, pointless battle. Marco lay curled so close to the hearth that one turn would put him against the fireguard; Romeo lay face down on the table, gripping an empty earthenware cup beside a plate of beef bones.

She hauled Marco away from the flames and covered him with a blanket. After clearing the dishes from around Romeo, she covered him too. By day, these Royal Guardsmen could make sentries stand straight; by midnight, one had nearly slept in the hearth while the other guarded an empty cup from imaginary thieves.

Juliet adjusted Marco's blanket and searched for her husband.

Edward lay beneath the table on an old hide rug. She bent to cover him, but the hand beside his chest caught her wrist.

"I thought you'd left the three of us to freeze out here."

His voice was hoarse with wine, but clear. He drew her down beside him, careful that her head missed the table.

"Or did you miss your husband?"

Juliet braced a hand on his chest and frowned at the smell of wine.

"I came to stop those two killing themselves in their sleep. I'm still deciding about you. How much did you drink?"

"Less than Romeo."

"That's no measure."

Edward laughed and put an arm around her back. She let him kiss her temple, but caught his shoulders when he tried to pull her closer.

"Marco's a few paces away, Romeo's right above us, and Remi is asleep next door. Do you want the whole house to know what we did under the table come morning?"

Edward glanced at the tabletop as if remembering where he was, then released her.

"Put like that, my plan's rather hard to defend."

Juliet pressed her lips together to keep from laughing.

"Good. Lie still and let me cover you."

She was about to crawl out when he caught her hand again, just firmly enough to make her turn. Edward waited for Juliet to lean towards him before kissing her. They had barely begun when Romeo shifted above them and the table shook.

They sprang apart. A tremendous snore rolled down, followed by words neither could make out.

Edward covered his mouth to stifle his laughter. Juliet pushed his shoulder.

"Get out before he rolls off."

Edward crawled out first and helped her after him. He stooped to lift her, but she caught his neck to steady herself and whispered in his ear.

"Drop me in front of those two, and I'll tell Remi about it until he's grown."

"I'm perfectly sober."

"That makes me trust you less."

Edward stepped over Marco and Romeo, carried Juliet to their room and shut the door. He set her on the bed and leaned close, but she pressed both hands against his chest.

"Wait. They're still out there, and Remi's just beyond the wall."

Edward stopped at once. Wine lingered on his breath, yet his voice was clear again.

"You're right. I'm sorry. I wasn't thinking."

Juliet watched to make sure he meant to stop, then lowered her hands. He started to withdraw, but she caught his collar.

She drew him closer and glanced at the door, its bolt still open.

"Lock the door."

Edward looked at her.

"Are you sure?"

"Lock the door, Edward. Don't make me ask a third time."

She waited until he met her eyes, then released him.

Edward slid the bolt home. When he turned, Juliet had pulled back the blanket to make room for him.

Much later, when the room had grown quiet, the wind beating against the stone roof became audible once more.

Juliet lay on her side, the blanket drawn to her shoulders. Edward lay close behind her, his arm across her waist. Firelight slipped through the gap at the door in a thin strip that just reached the Sabre propped beside the bed.

Juliet studied it longer than anything else in the room. For four years, that place had held muddy boots, a wood axe or the knife used for butchering. The blade in its black leather scabbard looked as though it had been left in the wrong house.

"Victoria returned it this afternoon?"

Edward was awake.

"Yes. I left it with her when we first arrived in Marrakesh. I thought I'd never have cause to hold it again."

Juliet turned towards him. His hand lay between them, four years of farming calluses over some of the old scars.

"I'm not asking whether you should have taken it back. I want to know how it felt to hold it."

Edward watched the sword, flexing his right hand.

"Too familiar for comfort. The moment Vic handed it over, my hand knew where to rest, where to brace my thumb, how to turn my wrist to draw. My body remembered before I did."

He rested his head on the pillow.

"Then Marco and Romeo stood beside me, and the four of us raised our swords like we did at the Academy. Only a few minutes, yet I remembered walking into a command room, looking down at a map and knowing thousands of men waited on a word from me. Amid cannon fire, my mind could be frighteningly clear."

Juliet let him speak. Edward closed his hand, then opened it.

"The memory itself doesn't frighten me."

He paused.

"What frightens me is that part of me still likes being good at it."

Juliet placed a hand on his chest.

"I'm not asking you to choose again. We talked about England last night, and I know why you're going. It's Remi I'm worried about."

Edward glanced towards their son's room. Juliet lowered her voice.

"Tomorrow he'll be among people who knew you before Marrakesh. Marco and Romeo will tell Academy stories. If Victoria visits, it will only take a few old victories or your former rank for Remi to hear about a father he's never known."

Edward propped himself on an elbow.

"I hadn't thought of that. He knows I was in the Navy, but I've told him little else."

"I know. There was no need to hurry before."

She took his hand.

"I'm not afraid of him learning that his father was a soldier. I'm afraid he'll hear only the part that makes a child want to become one."

She glanced at the Sabre.

"People will tell him about warships, victories, the times they called you a hero. Few will speak of the nights cannon fire woke you, or those who never returned after following your orders."

Edward looked down at his hands.

"At the Academy, we saw only the fine things. Uniforms, medals, victories. By the time we understood the rest, we each had too much to carry."

He looked towards Remi's room.

"He can become a carpenter, grow crops, teach or sell goods at the market. He'll still need to know how to use a gun and a sword in times like these. But I won't have him think a man needs a uniform to be useful."

Juliet drew his hand closer.

"Then tell him both sides. The victories were real, and so was the price. Don't leave the rest for someone else to tell."

Edward pulled the blanket over half his face.

"You make me sound admirable and rather pathetic at once."

"You have a talent for both."

Edward pinched her side. Juliet batted his hand away and stole the blanket in revenge.

Remi stirred in the next room, then settled. Edward waited for the sound to fade, his hand still in Juliet's.

"I'll tell him myself. Even the things I wish I'd done differently."

Juliet squeezed his hand.

"That's enough for tonight."

Edward rose and picked up the Sabre. Even that small movement straightened his back, his hand finding its place on the hilt before he noticed.

He examined his hand, then wrapped old wool around the scabbard. He laid the Sabre across a low chair by the wall, beneath the goatskin coat he wore to the cattle shed.

"I'll take it when we leave."

Edward returned to bed and drew the blanket over Juliet's shoulder.

"Tonight it can stay there. There's no need to turn our bedroom into a guardroom."

Juliet put an arm around his waist. Beyond the door, Romeo snored like a saw through timber, and Marco turned over, muttering something no one could understand.

Edward closed his eyes. The last thing he saw was the edge of the scabbard protruding beneath the old goatskin coat.

title_vi: Chapter Six: A Marrakesh to Call Home
title_en: Chapter Six: A Marrakesh to Call Home
text_en:
That same day, after Edward left for the Governor's Palace, Juliet led Remi outside, with noon already past.

Wind swept down from the Atlas Mountains in short bursts, flinging powdered snow against the faded red earthen walls of the outskirts. The sun hung low behind thin cloud, bright enough to whiten the icy gutters but too weak to offer warmth.

Four years ago, Juliet had hurried through weather like this, breathless and exhausted after a short walk. Now she turned a shoulder into the wind, kept her pace steady, and chose streets with high walls so Remi could walk in their shelter.

The boy was wrapped so thoroughly that only his eyes showed. Every few minutes Juliet squeezed his fingertips through his gloves to check their warmth, then inspected the tops of his boots for snow. Remi endured both; he had known the routine since he was old enough to walk through snow.

Far ahead, the Moorish domes of Marrakesh rose from the mist like stones adrift on a white sea. The wind pressed chimney smoke flat against the roofs. Road crews shovelled fresh snow from the gutters; the central market was filling after the morning lull.

Juliet studied the city longer than usual. Its domes, its hearths, the streets she walked every week: all had become things to remember before she left.

Edward had offered to join them when she announced her visits, but Juliet steered him back towards the papers he had to hand over. He went to the Governor's Palace; she took Remi along her route. The boy walked at her side, his woollen scarf pulled to his nose and a stack of invitations tucked carefully into his coat.

"Do you remember our first stop?" Juliet asked.

Remi nodded and recited the route as if learning it for the first time: Uncle Omar, the Thompsons, Miss Hassan, and finally the Mariabells.

He repeated each name. Juliet realised he knew their Marrakesh neighbours better than any relative in England. They had been there as he grew up.

They followed a channel cleared through the snow by the road crews the day before, heading for Omar's house.

Remi gripped her hand.

"Mother, will we come back here?"

Juliet remembered their promises to return to London when the fighting eased, to England when the seas were safer. None had come true. She would not make another merely to soften today's farewells.

"I don't know. Neither does your father."

She squeezed his hand.

"That's why we're saying goodbye properly today. We shouldn't leave what needs saying to tomorrow."

Remi thought for a moment, then nodded.

Omar answered their second knock. Moisture clung to his thick beard, and the djellaba he had thrown on hung crookedly from one shoulder.

"Juliet? Remi? What are you two doing out in this cold?"

Juliet lowered her scarf.

"We're having a farewell supper tomorrow. We'd like you and your family to come."

Omar stood still. A younger child peered out, then its mother pulled it inside as cold swept through the door.

"Farewell?"

Omar looked at Juliet's invitations, then at Remi.

"Where are you going?"

"Iberia, for now. Edward has accepted a commission from the Queen."

Omar straightened away from the doorframe. These days, a royal summons seldom promised an easier life.

"Is he a soldier again?"

He turned to Juliet.

"And you and the boy are going north with him, in the middle of winter?"

"Edward really had left the service," Juliet replied.

"But the Queen needs what he once knew how to do. This time he's agreed. Remi and I are going with an escort."

She neither dressed up the journey nor asked Omar's permission.

Omar rested a hand against the frame.

"Four years ago you couldn't even tie a scarf across your face properly. One gust from the Sahara and your skin would crack for a week."

"And you sold me a new scarf for twice the market price."

"That was the price of saving your life," Omar protested.

Juliet reminded him he'd called it a friend's price. He laughed, ruffled Remi's hair, then checked their departure date.

"We'll come tomorrow. And if young Edward plans to slaughter a cow, tell him to save me the hide. I won't take it for nothing. I'll trade firewood."

Juliet nodded.

"Just bring your family. We can settle the hide later."

Omar stepped out and embraced her as Moors did their own kin. Juliet staggered half a step before returning the embrace.

"Go in peace, English girl."

The old name made her blink before she answered.

"I'll try."

By the time they left, noon was further behind them. On the way to the English quarter, Remi looked up.

"Mother, Uncle Omar isn't English. How can he be family?"

Juliet asked what family meant. When he said people from the same country, she reminded him that Omar had nursed him through a fever, Hassan had shared half a sack of flour when their food ran out, and the Thompsons had travelled with them from Gibraltar.

"There are people from our own country we've never met. And there are people born a thousand miles away who stand by us when things are at their worst."

Remi watched the footprints in the snow.

"So is home the people, Mother?"

"I don't know yet."

Juliet straightened his crooked scarf and took his hand again.

The English quarter lay in western Marrakesh. Refugees who had arrived later built with whatever the city could spare. Some homes now had brick walls and tiled roofs, but others still consisted of ship timbers, canvas, old sheet metal and doors taken from other buildings.

A Tudor rose was carved into one door. A London street sign carried across the sea hung on the next house. Here, England survived in things small enough to carry.

Juliet stopped at the Thompsons' house.

Martha opened the door, a scarf wound round her prematurely greying hair. She had grown much thinner since autumn, but pulled the door wide as soon as she saw them.

"Come in, quickly. Don't let the wind in."

Inside stood a small hearth. Three children huddled beneath a blanket, the youngest seized by dry coughing fits that curled the small body like a leaf. Juliet held back her invitation, knelt and pressed the back of her hand to the child's forehead.

"Still feverish?" Juliet asked, keeping her hand there.

Martha nodded.

"Better than yesterday. I'm saving the medicine for tonight."

Juliet took a packet of herbs from her bag.

"Simmer these in water. They won't replace the medicine, but they may ease the breathing."

"You've brought me something again."

Martha held the packet, as though weighing what she could offer in return.

"You can repay me by coming tomorrow and eating all the soup I make."

Martha laughed once, then turned to pull the blanket over the youngest child. Juliet sat beside her and came to the point.

"We're leaving Marrakesh the day after tomorrow."

The smile vanished.

"Because of Edward?"

"He's accepted a commission from the Queen."

Martha needed no explanation. Everyone in the English quarter remembered who Edward was, though he never introduced himself by his former rank.

"So they've finally come for him."

Martha clasped her hands.

"Do you want to go?"

"I want Remi to go to school. I want him to have a room where the water doesn't freeze every morning."

"That's what you want for the boy."

Martha refused the easier answer.

"What do you want?"

Juliet looked round the house, where another family was fighting the same winter.

"I don't know yet."

Martha took her hand.

"Then make sure you find out."

Juliet studied their hands, both roughened by winter. She changed her tone to ease the weight in the room.

"Come tomorrow. We're slaughtering four cows."

"Four?"

Martha stared. Juliet admitted that four was only the number she had settled on in her own head, and Edward might have something to say about it.

Martha shook her head.

"Good Lord. You haven't left Marrakesh and you're already deciding the cattle's fate before your husband gets a word in."

"Perhaps. But at least the children will eat something hot tomorrow."

Juliet tucked the blanket around the youngest. Martha laughed and promised to bring barley bread if the children were well enough to come.

Remi had joined the children and was showing them his wooden ship. He described schools in Iberia as if he had visited them, including a map so vast it took two people to hang it. Juliet had no idea where that detail came from, but let it stand.

They left the Thompsons and headed south to find Hassan. Her house stood lower than the Spencers', with oilcloth covering the windows and an old carpet hung across the doorway against the wind.

Hassan opened the door, flour coating her arms to the elbows. She looked from Juliet to Remi and understood.

"Don't tell me you've come to repay the flour. I told you we'd settle it in spring."

"No."

Juliet lowered her scarf.

"We're leaving Marrakesh the day after tomorrow."

Hassan froze, her flour-covered hand falling to her side. In the kitchen her nearly deaf mother went on rolling dough, unaware of the silence that had fallen.

"Where are you going?"

"Iberia first. Edward has accepted a commission."

Hassan asked no more. She wiped her hands on her apron and pulled Juliet into a swift, fierce, awkward embrace.

"Then I'll bring couscous tomorrow."

Juliet held up her invitations.

"I haven't even asked you yet."

"You're going door to door with the boy and a stack of paper in your pocket. The whole quarter heard before you reached me."

Remi looked at his mother, dismayed by how fast news travelled in Marrakesh. Hassan bent to ask whether he really was going to school. When he nodded, the old woman in the kitchen finally caught the word school and beckoned him over.

She put a piece of warm bread in his hand and spoke in Castilian laced with Arabic, only half of which Remi understood. Juliet translated: learn his letters, remember how to light a fire, and thank anyone who gave him warm bread in the cold.

Remi repeated all three lessons to be sure he had them. The old woman smiled and nudged the bread towards him.

Before they left, Hassan drew Juliet close.

"You're still worrying about the families in the southern row, aren't you?"

Juliet glanced at Hassan's mother, still rolling dough.

"I usually check whether they're short of firewood after a storm."

"I'll go instead."

Hassan brushed the flour from her hands.

"I know which houses have old people in them. You go. Don't climb into that carriage and decide the whole quarter will freeze to death without you."

Juliet began to protest, then stopped herself.

"I'll try."

"No. You'll do it."

Juliet laughed aloud. They clasped hands before parting.

The next visits passed faster, though they weighed no less. A Castilian family of tanners gave them two new coils of rope for their luggage. An old man who had helped Edward treat a sick cow forgave the money still owed to him and called it a gift for the road.

An English widow pressed two hard sweets saved from the last festival into Remi's hand. She made him eat one at once to prove they had not turned to stone.

Nobody let the Spencers leave empty-handed once they heard they were going. Juliet began with invitations, but by the sixth house they were useless: word of the departure, Edward taking command again, Remi starting school and tomorrow's feast had outrun them.

Worse, nearly half the quarter had heard about the four cows Juliet had mentioned only once at the Thompsons'.

Juliet knocked again.

"Anne, it's Juliet."

Wind pushed a little powdered snow against the foot of the door. A man came out of the neighbouring house, removing his hat before he spoke.

"Don't knock again, Mrs Spencer."

Juliet turned. The man held his hat against his chest, his gaze lowered to the snow.

"The Mariabells' fire went out the night before last."

He swallowed.

"We broke down the door this morning. All five froze to death."

Remi gripped his mother's hand. Juliet stood before the door a while longer, the last invitation still in her pocket.

She took it out. Unsure what to do with it, she folded it in half and put it back.

"Come along, son."

They walked the length of the alley in silence. Juliet did not turn towards the market as planned. At the crossroads she stopped, took out the small notebook where she recorded flour, firewood and medicine exchanged between households, and thumbed through pages worn by four winters.

"Do you remember how to get back to Martha's house?" she asked.

Remi nodded, and she led him back rather than continuing their visits.

Martha looked surprised to see them. Juliet stayed near the door instead of entering the room where the feverish child lay, and opened the notebook in her palm.

"I need your help before we leave. After this cold spell, don't let any house go more than two days without a knock at the door, especially those with children or elderly people."

Martha read Juliet's face and understood.

"The Mariabells?"

Juliet nodded and pointed to the names already written down: the Thompsons, Hassan, a widow near the tannery, and two new families who did not yet know how to keep a hearth burning overnight.

"I call on these households when I go to market or share out food. When I leave, someone else needs to keep an eye on them."

Martha accepted the notebook and turned its fraying pages. Juliet showed her the marks for homes short of wood and people who were ill. Soon Martha recognised the signs herself.

"You can't visit them all alone," Juliet said.

"Hassan will see to the southern row. Omar has a cart for carrying firewood. As for medicine, ask me before we leave. After that, go to the herbalist near Bab Doukkala Gate. Give him my name; he knows what I usually buy."

Martha closed the notebook.

"How long have you been planning this?"

"I've kept the notebook a long time."

Juliet looked back towards the alley.

"But I only thought of giving it to you today. I don't want another house found when it's too late."

Remi walked beside her, looking back at the Thompson door as it closed behind them.

"You're handing over your work, aren't you, Mother?"

Juliet straightened his scarf. The notebook would help nobody if it travelled to Iberia in her trunk. She nodded.

"Will you do the same thing in our new home?" Remi asked.

Juliet studied the road ahead before replying.

"I don't know what people need there yet. I'll look first, then decide where I can help."

Remi took her hand and asked more questions about the names Martha had agreed to watch over. Juliet answered as they left the English quarter. Its narrow lanes fell quiet behind them; ahead came the cries of merchants and the rumble of wheels.

By early afternoon, every passage through the Marrakesh market stood open. Amber Vestigium lamps hung from the wooden beams, melting roof snow into dripping water. Moors, Castilians and English jostled between stalls selling turnips, salted meat, lamp oil and firewood, buying what they needed for supper.

The lamps gave a steadier heat than coal, though keeping them lit cost the city dearly when food was scarce. Juliet watched water drip onto the beams and stallholders rub their hands. A spice merchant called her by name.

A Moorish woman waved and asked when Remi would come for bread. Castilian soldiers marched past, boots thudding in time on the snow.

Two English refugees followed with a bundle of wood, speaking in Yorkshire accents Juliet had once needed repeated three times. Now she could pick out every word among the cries.

They stopped for pepper and cinnamon for the next day's meal. Juliet inspected each cinnamon stick and haggled as usual, while Remi grew impatient.

"Mother, we're leaving soon. Must we still haggle?"

"Leaving Marrakesh doesn't mean I should throw money away."

Juliet named a lower price. The merchant grumbled, then nodded.

"What we save will buy medicine or firewood. Those are worth more tomorrow."

Remi nodded as if he had learnt a great principle.

Clouds parted, and sunlight fell on the red domes and snow that shone almost silver. Juliet stopped in the market. London had known days like this, before fire and Portuguese cannon fire obscured her memory of the city.

Westminster lay under snow, its windows lit. Flower sellers wrapped in scarves stood on street corners. Carriages crossed the bridge, wheels splashing mud against the hems of pedestrians' coats.

Edward often came home late then, the smell of salt water and gunpowder still in his hair. Yet he would stop to buy her something, although most of his gifts were useless. Once he brought back an outrageously expensive silver comb.

Juliet scolded him for nearly half an hour. She kept it until the day London fell.

When they fled the house, she left the comb on the table. Beside tens of thousands dead, it was a memory too small to matter, yet it brought a sudden sting to her eyes.

A wooden barrel fell from a stall behind her.

Its lid struck the market floor with a sharp crack. It sounded nothing like cannon fire, yet her body reacted before her mind could tell the difference.

For an instant, the Marrakesh market vanished.

The Vestigium lamps became rings of fire above the Thames. The bargaining around her stretched into screams at the docks; a wheel grinding over ice became a ship's hull breaking under bombardment.

Juliet stopped in the moving crowd, her breath caught high in her chest.

She saw London on its last day: snow fouled by mud and blood, crowds packed onto the quays so tightly children were lifted off their feet, sailors shouting how many places remained. Edward ran against the tide of people, disappearing from view and returning with another person or another order. Remi had been so small that she pressed his face against her chest to keep out the smoke.

A small hand tightened around her glove.

"Mother."

Juliet blinked twice. Cinnamon returned first, then the warmth of the lamps, the low wooden roof, and snow melting from shoppers' coats. Each found its proper place again.

Remi stood close, his wooden ship poking from his pocket. He looked at her, bewildered but worried.

Juliet crouched to his height, still gripping her cloth bag.

"London came back to me all at once."

Remi looked round as if London might be waiting at a nearby stall.

"Because the barrel fell?"

"Yes."

Juliet took a slower breath.

"I know this is Marrakesh. But when I heard that noise, I thought I was in London again."

He thought about that, then took one of her hands in both of his.

"Then let's stand here a while."

Juliet almost refused, but stayed. They stood beside a wooden post until her breathing steadied and the noises around her became only market noises.

She watched his hands around hers and squeezed back.

"Thank you."

Remi gave the same shrug Edward used whenever he did not know how to accept thanks.

"Are you going to buy the cinnamon now?"

Juliet released his hand, paid, and accepted the paper-wrapped cinnamon and pepper. She gave them to Remi to carry.

"Yes. And now we've bought it."

A few steps later, Remi spoke again.

"What did you remember about London, Mother?"

"The silver comb your father bought me."

Juliet wiped the last dampness from her cheek.

"Just a comb. Sometimes the smallest things bring a place back to us."

Remi considered that.

"Does Father still buy useless things?"

"He does," Juliet said.

"Some disasters survive the end of the world."

Later, Remi asked if London was prettier than Marrakesh. Juliet looked back at the receding domes.

"London was beautiful in its own way. Marrakesh is beautiful in another. Remember whichever places you wish, when you're older. Remember the place we're going to as well."

By the time they left the market, the grey light over Marrakesh was turning towards evening. Remi held the spices in both hands, still considering his mother's victory over the pepper merchant a considerable feat. Juliet kept the invitation that would never reach the Mariabells in her pocket.

Edward had not returned from the Governor's Palace when they reached home. On the table by the window lay notes he had left unfinished, an open inkwell and a chair pulled askew. Juliet put down the pepper and cinnamon, removed Remi's scarf and stood a moment in the room, which felt emptier than usual.

"Mother, hasn't Father come home yet?"

"Not yet. Victoria has probably kept him longer than he expected."

Juliet took off her gloves and looked towards the road leading into the city centre.

"Let's put these things away. We still have to settle the matter of the cows with your father tonight. And nobody is sleeping late tomorrow."

Remi put the spices on the table and took the wooden ship from his pocket.

"Mother, are we still keeping places for the Mariabells tomorrow?"

Juliet stopped and touched the last invitation inside her coat.

"Yes."

She pulled the chair by the hearth back into place.

"We'll keep places for them."

Remi nodded without asking more. He sat on the floor, loosening a knot in the cord on his ship, while Juliet put away their purchases and sorted the papers she still had to hand over. Beyond the door, Marrakesh lived on in cartwheels, hammer blows and Vestigium lamps growing brighter as evening settled.

Four years ago, the Spencers had come to Marrakesh with almost nothing. In Juliet's pocket, the Mariabells' invitation still bore its fold. The notebook of neighbours' names rested in Martha's hands, remaining with the city.

title_vi: Chapter Seven: A Feast for Those Who Remain
title_en: Chapter Seven: A Feast for Those Who Remain
text_en:
Dawn came slowly to Marrakesh. The low sun turned the courtyard snow from grey to white, but could not soften the ice on the water barrels. Edward woke before anyone else.

He entered the sitting room washed and dressed, though he had drunk with Marco and Romeo until nearly midnight. The smells of wine, hearth ash, and cold meat lingered. Romeo sprawled across the table; Marco slept so close to the fire that Juliet’s blanket had slipped from his shoulders.

Edward rolled up the fallen blanket and nudged Marco’s leg with his boot.

“Up. Today, two men of the Royal Guard have a duty far more important than watching the city walls.”

Marco opened one eye, his voice thick with sleep.

“If this duty begins before I've had a mouthful of water, I shall resign on the spot.”

Edward turned to Romeo and slapped his shoulder twice.

“You too. Get up. Four cows outside are waiting to learn whether your reputation as Royal Guardsmen is anything more than idle gossip.”

Romeo pulled the blanket over his head.

“Ed, I've saved your life more times than I can count. Surely all those years of friendship have earned me another five minutes?”

“Certainly not.”

Edward planted a bucket beside the table.

“Juliet has reckoned this feast at precisely four cows. If she wakes to find you two still lounging about, even I won't be able to save you from her temper.”

Marco needed both hands against the floor to sit upright.

“Water first. Otherwise I'll be the one on the butcher's table.”

The three men went outside while fresh snow still covered the courtyard bricks. A thin crust of ice lay over the water barrel; Romeo broke it with a bucket handle and splashed the freezing water across his face. Marco muttered a curse, and Edward laughed as he opened the cowshed.

The four cows had been separated from the herd the previous evening. Edward ran his fingers over the tags tied about their necks, lingering beside the last animal. For years, those cattle had bought the Spencer household flour, medicine, and enough time to survive one winter after another.

Romeo glanced towards him.

“Want to change your mind? There's still time.”

Edward shook his head.

“No. Carry on.”

Romeo took the hardest work, and handled it so cleanly that Marco reminded him he was in a cowshed rather than on a battlefield. Edward divided the meat into cuts while Marco held the ropes and helped strip the hides. They carried each portion to the preparation table, working almost without a word.

The first cow had scarcely been butchered when Juliet appeared at the door. Her hair was neatly tied back, a large cloth hung over one arm, and a small ledger was tucked beneath the other.

“I need you three to do something for me.”

She opened the ledger at a marked page. Edward looked up at Juliet.

“Go on, love. I'm listening.”

Juliet touched the page with the tip of her pen.

“Save the hides for those who need them, the bones for soup, and share the fat among households short of lamp oil. Wash the path properly, too. There'll be children running through here this afternoon.”

Romeo pressed a greasy hand to his chest.

“Juliet! You insult the three finest cadets the Royal Academy ever produced!”

“Splendid.”

Juliet closed the ledger and surveyed the bloody stones.

“Then three such distinguished graduates can surely clean a courtyard before the guests arrive.”

Edward heard small feet approaching from the storehouse. He stopped working and looked past Juliet's shoulder.

Remi peered out from behind his mother, his scarf covering half his face. He craned his neck to see past the buckets, ropes, and knives scattered across the courtyard. Edward pointed towards the storehouse at once.

“It's dangerous here. Stay back.”

“I'm only watching!”

The boy's face fell.

“Then watch from somewhere else. Fetch that stack of wooden bowls from the storehouse for Father, and ask Mother whether she needs more firewood.”

Remi tugged his scarf down far enough to show a magnificent pout, but hurried away to obey. Before long, he returned with a stack of bowls reaching his chin. No sooner had he finished than Juliet sent him after cloths, twine, and scraps of paper to mark the cuts of meat.

On his fourth journey across the courtyard, Edward caught him by the shoulders and wrapped another turn of scarf about his neck.

“I'm not cold!”

Remi tried to pull the scarf loose.

“Your ears are bright red. That's what comes of running back and forth. Slow down a little.”

“But Father, you were the one who told me to hurry and fetch the bowls!”

Edward turned to Juliet.

“He's learning to turn our own arguments against us.”

Juliet was still adding up the portions in her ledger.

“And who taught him that?”

They were preparing to butcher the third cow when wheels creaked over the snow beyond the gate. Victoria arrived with four Moorish women and a cart heaped with baskets of herbs, onions, turnips, fresh bread, and two enormous copper pots. She stopped in the courtyard at the sight of three men spattered with cattle blood outside the cowshed.

“So this is what became of the four finest graduates of 1700? Only three of you have turned up. The fourth had the sense to stay clear.”

Edward tightened his grip upon the rope.

“Have you come to lend a hand, or merely to see how far we've fallen?”

“I've come to help someone who actually knows how to arrange a day's work.”

Victoria glanced at Juliet, then back at the men.

“You three may carry on with your butchery.”

Juliet set a stone upon her ledger to keep the wind from turning its pages.

“Thank you. These fellows behave as though slaughtering a cow were the hardest labour in the world.”

Victoria took off her gloves and tucked them into her coat pocket.

“Then let them enjoy their delusion.”

Edward leaned towards Marco.

“I seem to be losing what little authority I have in my own home.”

“You never had any.”

Marco wiped his knife on a cloth beside the chopping block.

From then on, the Spencer household scarcely knew a moment's peace. Juliet and Victoria set helpers to building two outdoor hearths, moving tables into the yard, and stretching canvas beside the cowshed. The Moorish women prepared vegetables, herbs, and bread, while Marco and Romeo continued with the meat.

Edward moved between the two groups carrying bones, only to be called away to check a rope, prop up a table, or lift a cooking pot.

While the furniture was being brought outside, an official from the Governor's Palace accompanied Edward to inspect the herd. He compared the marks on the neck tags with the names of the households due to receive each animal, then gave Victoria a written confirmation, which Edward signed beside the cowshed. The remaining cattle would be led away after the feast; by the time the official departed, snow had covered the tracks of his cart.

Towards noon, neighbours arrived to help. Nobody came empty-handed. Omar brought a cart of firewood and three large butcher's knives; the Hassan family arrived with couscous, cumin, and a pot of spices.

A Castilian family from the tannery brought fresh rope, while the Thompsons supplied barley bread and extra chairs.

Word of the feast had travelled far beyond Juliet's list. Invited guests brought relatives, while families who had merely heard that the Spencers were leaving Marrakesh came with whatever they could spare. By early afternoon, three joined canvas awnings sheltered the courtyard, Vestigium lamps hung from ropes, and long tables had been built from storehouse doors, wagon planks, and anything else flat and sturdy.

The smell of stewed meat and herbs rose beneath the canvas. Bones had simmered in soup since morning, and each batch of roasted meat came off the coals before the edges could burn. Bundles of smoked meat hung beside the storehouse, set aside for families to take home.

People brushed shoulders around the cooking fires, making just enough room for one another to set down a pot.

The hides lay neatly rolled by the storehouse. Juliet glanced across, reminded a helper to keep the snow off them, then hurried back to a stewpot boiling over.

Edward turned to Romeo.

“In all my years commanding a fleet, I've never seen the business of feeding people become quite so fearsome.”

Romeo hoisted a barrel of meat onto his shoulder.

“That's because your fleet never had Juliet.”

“True enough.”

By the time the food was ready, the courtyard resembled a small marketplace. English, Castilian, and Arabic voices mingled beneath the awnings. Children darted between the tables until their elders caught them and hauled them back.

Two English veterans argued with a Castilian blacksmith over the proper way to roast meat. Omar stood by the stewpot, insisting everyone had used the wrong amount of cumin, until Juliet pushed him aside and seasoned it herself.

Edward found himself standing in the middle of the yard with a tray of bread, suddenly uncertain where to go. For four years, he had thought of his family as temporary lodgers in a corner of Marrakesh. Yet now, with nearly a hundred and thirty people gathered beneath the awnings, he could see how many bonds had formed around the three Spencers without any of them stopping to count.

Juliet passed and nudged him with her elbow.

“Don't stand there gawping like a guest.”

“I'm keeping an eye on things.”

“Then keep an eye on the soup. It's nearly boiled dry.”

Edward hurried to the pot and stirred with a ladle.

The meal began without waiting for speeches. Juliet refused to let the elderly and the children sit hungry while their food cooled merely because Edward had yet to offer a few fine words. The first bowl of soup went to the Thompson table.

Juliet broke bread for the child who was still coughing, laid a hand against the youngster's forehead, and reminded Martha to save some herbs for the evening.

At the far end of the tables, one chair remained empty. A small card bearing the Mariabell family name lay upon its seat.

Edward had noticed it from across the yard. He did not ask who had placed it there. When the first bowls began to empty, Omar raised his knife handle and tapped it against his glass.

“Young Spencer.”

He waited for Edward to turn.

“Do you mean to feed half the city with your cows and then slip away without saying a word?”

Laughter rippled along the tables. Edward set down his glass and stepped onto the wooden stair before the porch. Juliet paused beside Martha to watch him, while Remi waited eagerly with half a piece of bread still in his hand.

Edward surveyed the assembled guests and began with the simplest truth.

“Four years ago, when my family came to Marrakesh, we had almost nothing. Victoria gave us a roof and a few cows with which to begin again. Omar taught me how to keep cattle alive through winter. The Thompsons shared their powdered medicine when Remi fell ill, and the Hassan family repaired our cowshed roof. So many others offered kindnesses that, were I to name them all, we’d still be here tomorrow evening.”

Laughter rose from several tables. Edward waited for it to fade.

“I once thought Marrakesh was only a resting place on our road home. Yet my son knows every baker here by name, my wife cannot visit the market without half the street calling to her, and I can tell whose cow is about to calve before its owner can...”

He looked across the gathering.

“Such a place is rather more than a passing refuge.”

The courtyard grew quiet.

“Tomorrow morning, my family will leave Marrakesh together. We shall go first to Gibraltar. Juliet and Remi will then travel on to Barcelona, while I undertake another mission entrusted to me by Queen Isabella of Castile. How far that road will take me, I cannot yet say.”

Edward raised his glass.

“These four cows are no grand offering from an admiral or a soldier. They are simply the Spencer family's thanks to those who sheltered us and stood beside us through four bitter winters.”

Omar raised his glass first.

“To those still alive!”

Juliet joined him.

“To those still alive.”

Voices answered throughout the yard. Wooden cups and earthenware mugs clinked beneath the awnings, and the conversations interrupted by Edward's speech resumed from table to table.

Omar waited until Edward had sat down before drawing his chair closer.

“You spoke of a new mission. Where will it take you?”

Edward glanced at Remi before answering.

“England.”

Omar stopped with his glass halfway to his mouth.

“Back there? I thought those northern lands held only ice, French soldiers, and horrors no one wished to recall.”

“There may still be survivors. Units that escaped destruction.”

Edward took a mouthful of wine.

“I must see it myself before I call England a dead land.”

News of Edward's return to England spread faster than he had expected. The merriment had not yet died, but the English refugees around the courtyard began to turn towards him. For four years they had learned to bury their questions about home; tonight, those questions rose again over supper.

An elderly veteran was the first to stand.

“Sir, are you truly Edward Spencer, who once commanded the celebrated flagship *HMS True Hero*?”

Edward set down his cup before answering.

“I have not been an admiral for many years. But yes, the *True Hero* was once my flagship.”

“Once...”

The old soldier pressed a hand to his chest, his voice faltering.

“My son, James Hartwell, served aboard *HMS True Hero* at La Coruña.”

Edward repeated the name to himself. He remembered a gunner from the middle deck, a stubborn young man who had defied the surgeon's orders to return to his gun before the wound in his shoulder had healed.

“James Hartwell. He was wounded in the shoulder on the second day.”

Tears gathered in the old man's eyes.

“You still remember him, sir?”

“He was a stubborn lad.”

The old man laughed through his tears.

“He takes after his mother.”

At the far end, a middle-aged woman rose, gripping a folded paper worn soft at the edges. Her neighbours fell quiet as she waited for Edward.

“And Timothy Beaumont... do you remember him, sir?”

Edward answered at once, as though the name had never left him.

“Timothy Beaumont. A young gunner of English and French parentage. He was scarcely two or three years older than Remi when he enlisted, yet stubborn beyond belief. Even when ordered off the gun deck, he always found a way to sneak back.”

The woman tightened her grip upon the paper.

“We've waited years for news of him. In his last letter, Timothy wrote that his unit had volunteered to remain behind and cover the evacuation. We've heard nothing from him since...”

“Then... do you know whether he's still alive?”

Edward looked at the paper clenched in her hand and recalled the last report concerning Timothy's unit.

“The last trustworthy dispatch said he was alive. But I don't know where Timothy is now. When London fell, the couriers' routes and the muster rolls were already in ruins, even before the people could escape the harbour.”

The woman lowered her head and stared at the worn paper.

“We only want to know... whether there's still any reason to keep waiting.”

Edward watched her hands close around it.

“I still hope he's alive. But I cannot promise what I do not know. If I find ship's rolls or lists of survivors in the north, I'll look for Timothy Beaumont.”

She handed him the paper. Written upon it were Timothy's name, his former unit, and the last place from which his family had received a letter. Edward folded it carefully and slipped it into the inner pocket of his coat.

Others came forward. One asked about a younger brother in Portsmouth; a former marine wanted to know if his unit had escaped Dover. A Moorish woman whose husband had carried cargo for English ships asked whether civilians at the docks had been entered on the evacuation rolls, or had simply vanished with the city.

Again and again, Edward had only one answer.

“I don't know.”

Marco brought over a blank ledger and began recording the names of the missing, along with the places where they had last been seen. Victoria summoned another official from the Governor's Palace to help, but forbade anyone to raise hopes with promises they could never fulfil.

Almost half an hour later, Marco had filled several pages. People slowly returned to their tables; some left their soup untouched and cold. Others lingered beside him to make certain the names of their loved ones had been written correctly.

Remi stood beside his father, studying the ledger before speaking in a low voice.

“Father, you remember Uncle Hartwell and Uncle Beaumont, but you still don't know where they are?”

Edward nodded.

“I remember their faces, their names, and where they stood on deck. But after London fell, there were days when thousands vanished from the rolls before I could learn where they'd gone.”

Remi watched the people returning to their seats.

“Will they be angry with you?”

“Some will. They have every right.”

Edward looked towards the tables that had fallen quiet.

“Every name here belongs to someone's father, someone's son, someone's husband. At the command table, there were times when I saw little more than lines of writing.”

Remi glanced towards Marco holding the ledger and asked nothing more. Cups sat untouched on the English tables, while talk and laughter still drifted from beneath the farther awnings.

Romeo looked round at the faces turned towards Edward and struck his cup against the table.

“Will you stop looking at Ed as though he's just dug his own grave?”

Several people started. Romeo planted his hands on the table and raised his voice above the wind.

“You know him as the fellow who raises cattle in Marrakesh. But has anyone here heard what happened in Flanders twelve years ago?”

A veteran at the far end called out.

“The Second Agincourt?”

“That very madness.”

Romeo pointed straight at Edward.

“Six thousand Englishmen had scarcely stepped off their ships. Ahead of us stood a French army several times our number, guns drawn up across the whole front, and enough cavalry to grind us into the mud. Everyone thought Ed would retreat.”

Romeo grinned.

“He waited for rain.”

Murmurs spread through the gathering. Romeo went on.

“The rain dampened the French powder and turned the ground to mire. Their horses could no longer charge as they would on firm earth. Ed formed the infantry into squares, broke the first cavalry assault, then drove straight at the guns that had fallen silent.”

Victoria tilted her head.

“Like Henry V at Agincourt.”

“Call it what you will.”

Romeo raised his glass towards Edward.

“I remember that by afternoon, the French guns could scarcely fire, their cavalry had been forced to dismount, and six thousand men who thought they'd be buried in Flanders had fought their own way home.”

The nearest veterans turned their chairs towards Romeo. Marco, silent until now, laid down the meat in his hand.

“That was ashore. What about La Coruña?”

Romeo turned to him with a smile.

“Your turn.”

Marco stood. He had none of Romeo’s extravagance, but his voice reached the farther tables.

“Eleven years ago, four French Atlantic fleets bore down upon La Coruña in a storm. The seas ran so high that gunners had to lash themselves to the rails to keep from being thrown overboard.”

He looked at Edward.

“His fleet fought for nearly sixteen hours through the night. At times, gunsmoke and fog grew so thick that opposing ships knew one another only by the flash of their cannon muzzles. By morning, the French line had broken, and those ships still afloat were forced to withdraw.”

Marco lifted his glass.

“After that battle, the sailors began to call him by the name you've just heard.”

An aged voice from the English table spoke first.

“The Pathfinder.”

Another man repeated it, then several more. Soon the name travelled across the yard, from veterans who had known it for years to Moorish neighbours hearing it for the first time that night.

“The Pathfinder!”

Amid the clinking of cups, Edward retrieved his earthenware mug from the table. He had heard that title thousands of times, but not so near in years.

Romeo was still telling some story, while veterans pressed Marco for more about La Coruña. The feast continued around Edward, yet its sounds receded as though a heavy door had shut.

The fire in the middle of the yard flickered in the wind.

A man stood on the far side of the flames.

A dark blue Royal Navy admiral’s full-dress uniform fitted a younger version of Edward. Medals shone upon his chest, and a bicorne rested neatly on hair untouched by grey. His leather boots were so clean they seemed almost absurd amid the snow and mud.

Edward recognised the face before the man raised his head. Its features were younger, but the eyes were the ones he met in the mirror.

The young man looked at Edward's goatskin coat and smiled.

“They tell it well, don’t they?”

Edward said nothing. The immaculate blue uniform seemed an affront amid the feasting crowd.

“Flanders.”

The young man inclined his head towards Romeo.

“The rain came at exactly the right moment. La Coruña. The current turned at midnight, just as the French formation began to stray. You remember?”

Edward's fingers tightened around the mug.

“If the rain had come an hour later, or the offshore current turned a little later, those stories would have ended differently.”

The young man walked along the edge of the fire.

“You know that better than anyone raising a glass out there.”

“I've left those days behind.”

Edward scarcely heard his own voice.

“Have you?”

The figure looked him over from head to foot.

“You traded an admiral's uniform for goatskin, battle charts for a cowshed. Yet when Romeo spoke of Flanders, you knew precisely where the French guns had stood. When Marco mentioned La Coruña, you remembered which ship lost her mast before dawn.”

Edward looked past the man's shoulder. The crowd still laughed, but nobody seemed to notice the figure between him and the fire.

“You hate being called a genius,” the figure said. “You remember every time you stood one decision, one shower of rain, or one change of current away from disaster. Yet you remember how it felt when everything moved at your command.”

Edward could not deny it. Remembering his formations moving at his command rekindled the old heat, though the mug cooled in his hand.

The younger Edward stopped smiling.

“And what of the time nothing moved as you intended?”

Edward's fingers went cold around the mug, though the flames before him still burned fiercely.

The figure stepped closer.

“Inverness.”

Edward squeezed his eyes shut. The mug was still warm in his hand, but the voices calling his name behind him sounded far away, like echoes rising through deep water.

“Or shall I use the name you still avoid?”

Edward opened his eyes. The fire still burned, but the young man's smile had vanished.

“Criston Wallace.”

A faint crack came from Edward's mug.

Flanders and La Coruña vanished. He saw the filthy snow at Inverness, the ranks stretched too thin, an opening he had mistaken for an opportunity. Then came gunfire, broken orders, and the moment he understood too late that Wallace himself had left that road open for him.

Edward's breath caught. He tried to uncurl his fingers, but his hand would not obey.

The young man stood directly before him.

“The Pathfinder.”

He spoke the name without a trace of pride.

“Wallace showed you a road you failed to see, then let you live long enough to remember it.”

A shard of broken pottery pressed into Edward's palm.

“You've spent eleven years fleeing that name.”

The figure stepped backwards towards the fire.

“Now you're walking towards it of your own accord.”

The flames lurched in the wind. The crowd's voices returned at once, so close and loud that Edward flinched.

“THE PATHFINDER! THE PATHFINDER!”

He had not moved. The mug had cracked in his hand, and a thin line of blood was beginning to seep between his fingers, though he had yet to notice. Amid the people raising their cups in his honour, Edward stared only at the empty space beyond the fire, where nobody stood any longer.

title_vi: Chapter Eight: To Win, Part One
title_en: Chapter Eight: To Win, Part One
text_en:
Juliet saw the blood before Edward knew his hand was wounded. She caught her husband by the elbow and steered him away from the crowd still calling for the Pathfinder beneath the awnings. Marco noticed Edward's hand, caught Juliet's meaning, and clapped Romeo on the shoulder.

Together they turned the talk to another victory, keeping the guests occupied in the courtyard.

Edward looked down at the earthenware cup in his grasp. A crack ran from rim to base, and a sharp fragment had pierced his palm. Fresh blood threaded between his clenched fingers.

"I've broken the cup."

He had to swallow before the words would come.

Juliet prised it from his hand. "I'll buy another. Come inside and let me clean that wound."

He began to protest, but she met his eyes.

"And don't tell me you're all right. I know perfectly well what you were going to say."

Edward let her lead him into the kitchen. The thick stone wall behind it muffled the revelry outside. Juliet set the broken cup beside the basin, removed the fragment from his palm, washed the cut with warm water, and bound it in gauze.

He sat on a low stool, still watching the doorway to the courtyard.

"I heard his name," Edward said.

Juliet held the bandage in place. "Criston Wallace?"

Edward turned sharply. "How do you know that name?"

She tied off the gauze and looked up. "You've spoken it in your sleep. Several times when Remi was small, and once more during last winter's cold."

"I've never told you about him."

"No." Juliet drew up a chair. "And if you're not ready, you needn't. I won't force you."

Edward studied his bandaged hand. "I don't want Remi looking at his father the way those people outside were looking at me."

"He saw you standing still while they cheered, and he saw the cup break in your hand. He doesn't know what frightened you."

Edward tugged at the knot with his thumb. "I hate that he saw it."

"I don't." Juliet leaned against the wall. "What harm is there in knowing his father can be afraid and still do what is right? I only hope he doesn't learn to hide his fears until he makes a fool of himself, as you do."

Edward rested his head against the wall. "You do know how to vex me."

"A wife's duty." Juliet put away the spare gauze.

Edward was beginning to laugh when the voices outside fell away. The hush began at the gate and travelled from table to table. Soon the crackle of firewood and the wind snapping at the awnings were the loudest sounds in the courtyard.

Victoria stepped into the passage and bowed toward the open gate. "My Sultan."

Edward rose. Juliet turned toward the door.

A Moorish man entered with just two guards. He was past fifty, his dark hair silvering at the temples, his lean, sun-browned face marked by deep lines about the eyes and mouth. A dark fur cloak covered a charcoal-grey robe embroidered with gold at the hem.

The Sultan's eyes went first to the empty chair at the end of the Thompsons' table. The invitation for the Mariabell family still lay upon its seat. Victoria waited for him to reach the centre of the courtyard before speaking again, this time with ceremony.

"May I have your silence. We welcome Sultan Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad."

The Moors rose together. The Castilians and English followed a moment later. Omar did not bow deeply, yet he placed his aged hand over his heart with a respect Edward had never seen him offer an official.

Abd al-Rahman lifted a hand. "Sit down. I've come to eat, not to inspect your taxes."

A few people laughed, though they remained on their feet.

The Sultan turned to Victoria. "I heard the Spencers were holding a farewell supper and that half of Marrakesh had invited itself. Had I stayed away, by morning the city would be saying its Sultan was too miserly to spare a parting blessing."

"I can have a table prepared for Your Majesty," Victoria said.

"No need." He surveyed the long tables made from cart planks, storeroom doors, and any timber broad enough to lay a plate upon. "If neighbours are feasting, I shall sit with neighbours."

Omar patted the empty chair beside him. "Then take this one, Your Majesty. Mind you, you're late. Young Romeo has laid waste to most of the best meat!"

"I protest!" Romeo called from the next table.

Laughter ran through the gathering. Without another ceremony, Abd al-Rahman pulled out the chair and sat beside Omar.

Edward remained in the kitchen doorway. He had seen the Sultan only a few times, and always from afar. Yet here he sat among the townspeople like an old acquaintance, accepting a clap on the shoulder from Omar while no one nearby seemed afraid to speak.

Juliet saw him watching. "You've lived here four years and never wondered why they honour him so?"

Edward looked toward Omar, who had welcomed a ruler as he might a neighbour. "I thought it was chiefly because he's the Sultan. Perhaps I was wrong."

"In Marrakesh, people remember deeds better than titles." Juliet nodded toward the courtyard. "Look at Uncle Omar."

Victoria was passing the kitchen when she heard the Sultan mentioned and stopped. "During the first winter, three great families tried to send their grain north. He had their granaries sealed before the wagons could leave."

Edward let her finish without interruption.

"He opened the Ziyad stores first. Then he obliged the other families to sell grain at prices the poor could pay. Fires burned all day in two squares, and Moors, Castilians, and English refugees stood in the same line for soup."

Omar's English rang from the courtyard, loud enough for all to hear. "And don't forget the three merchants he hanged for hoarding!"

Abd al-Rahman turned to correct him. "Two."

"Three," Omar insisted.

"Did the third not fall down the stairs?"

"After your soldiers broke into his warehouse!"

"I can hardly answer for another man's staircase."

Laughter swept the tables, and even Edward joined in.

Victoria waited for it to subside. "That winter earned him Marrakesh's trust. What earned him a place in Iberia's memory came earlier."

"When Charles II still lived, the Habsburgs sent ships through Moroccan ports as though the harbours belonged to Madrid. The House of Ziyad had the wealth and the vessels to make those ships wait offshore."

"Then the War of Succession came. Abd al-Rahman opened his ports to the enemies of the Habsburgs, though Morocco paid in ships and men." Victoria glanced at the Sultan eating with Omar. "He gambled upon another Castile so his own country might live. Isabella was too young then to understand the price."

She looked into the courtyard. "Later, he dared contradict Queen Isabella of Castile before her own Council. Once, the rest had to wait in the corridor until the two had finished arguing."

Edward rested a shoulder against the doorframe. "Because Isabella owes him a debt, or because she trusts his judgement?"

"Both. She may be angered by contradiction, but she is angrier still when a sound objection goes unheard."

Outside, Abd al-Rahman asked Martha after a child troubled by a cough, speaking such fluent English that she stared. He drew an almond sweet from his pocket for Remi, but made the boy share it with a child of the Hassan family standing nearby. Edward waited until the Sultan had put the remaining sweet away before stepping out.

Abd al-Rahman noticed him but did not summon him yet. He continued eating with Omar, speaking of snow on the Atlas Mountains, asking a tanner about lamp oil, and hearing an old woman's complaint that the patrolmen near the market had been taking food without paying. Only when several families with small children began to leave did he put down his bowl.

"The renowned Edward Spencer."

Edward approached. "Your Majesty."

Abd al-Rahman gestured toward a chair beside the fire. "Sit. Let us speak awhile."

The neighbouring tables grew quiet. Edward knew that refusing would only draw more notice, so he sat. Juliet passed him a cup of water from the nearest table, while Marco, Romeo, and Victoria remained close enough to hear without intruding.

The Sultan pointed to the white bandage around Edward's hand. "A trophy won from a broken cup?"

Edward bent two fingers beneath the gauze. "It seems so."

"Good. We have proof that a legend may still bleed when cut by a piece of pottery."

Edward settled against the chair back. "Did Your Majesty come here solely to mock me?"

Abd al-Rahman removed his hood and passed it to a guard. He moved nearer the fire, where every surrounding table could see him, and clasped his hands behind his back.

"I remember four names from the class of 1700. The British Empire displayed those officers before Europe as though their presence alone could make defeat impossible."

He paused, then pointed at Edward.

"Edward Spencer. The Pathfinder. Admiral of the Royal Navy of England."

His finger moved to Marco.

"Marco Stones. The Balancer. Colonel of the English Army. Now of the Royal Guard of Castile, and commander of the Tercio de la Balanza, the Second Corps."

Romeo received his share without the Sultan pointing at him.

"Romeo Harkon. The Headsman. Colonel of the English Expeditionary Forces. Now of the Royal Guard of Castile, commanding the notorious Tercio del Filo, the Third Corps."

At last Abd al-Rahman turned to Victoria.

"Victoria Valdes. The Queen's Gambit. Major General of the English Supply Department. Now Governor of Marrakesh."

Victoria said nothing. She merely stood a little straighter.

"Four officers. Four Silver Cross Medals, bestowed before you had even left the Academy. Four talents of a kind Britain once claimed would take decades to produce again."

The Sultan faced Edward.

"Then tell me this. How did a nation blessed with all four of you fall so utterly?"

Romeo's chair shot backward. A short-barrelled flintlock came from its holster before the chair struck the ground. Its muzzle stopped before Abd al-Rahman's brow.

"Mind your tongue."

Wine still roughened Romeo's voice.

"You're at Ed's family feast."

Victoria sprang up. "Romeo, lower the gun!"

Marco stood at once.

Behind the Sultan, one guard drew his sword halfway from its scabbard. The other slipped toward Romeo's flank, his hand already on his dagger.

title_vi: Chapter Nine: To Win, Part Two
title_en: Chapter Nine: To Win, Part Two
text_en:
Abd al-Rahman raised one finger.

Both guards halted, though neither relaxed. The Sultan stood unmoving before the muzzle.

"If you mean to fire, fire."

He spoke to Romeo, but kept his eyes on Edward.

"Otherwise, lower it. I am speaking with Admiral Spencer."

Marco seized Romeo's wrist. He forced the gun toward the stones before the man's finger could tighten on the trigger.

"Enough. Put it away!" Marco snarled.

Romeo ground his teeth, stared at the Sultan a few moments longer, then shoved the weapon back into its holster. One guard sheathed his sword slowly; the other withdrew at a slight inclination of Abd al-Rahman's head. The click of the fastening rang out across the courtyard.

Abd al-Rahman did not turn. He asked Edward again.

"Why did you lose?"

Edward saw the calamities that had driven England toward ruin: failed harvests, riots, France and Portugal, orders arriving too late from a court still praying that the next victory would save them all. He glanced at Marco, Romeo, and Victoria before facing the Sultan.

"Because of me."

Marco looked round sharply. Victoria locked her hands before her, and Romeo stood silent with his gun put away. But Abd al-Rahman would not let Edward stop there.

"That is a judgement against yourself. It is not an answer."

Edward raised his head. The Sultan waited, offering no escape into silence.

He stepped closer. "I am not asking how fiercely you wish to condemn yourself. Tell me what happened. Tell me the truth."

Edward placed both hands on his knees to steady them. "England was in disorder on every side. I was ordered to subdue Scotland, and I believed I could strike quickly, end the campaign, then return south. My error began there."

"And with the name Criston Wallace."

Abd al-Rahman spoke the name Edward had avoided all evening.

Edward did not answer at once. His bandaged hand brushed the chair; Juliet watched him, while Marco, Romeo, and Victoria turned toward the Sultan.

At last Edward found his voice. "You know of him?"

"I know he took you alive at Inverness. I know he himself chose to set you free."

Edward's fingers contracted beneath the gauze. Pain stabbed through the newly bound cut.

"What do you mean?"

"Before the sea froze, Moroccan merchants sailed from Edinburgh to Dublin, London, and Lisbon. I bought tidings from those ships." Abd al-Rahman held Edward's gaze. "An admiral captured and released by his enemy is hard to hide, however many seals a court sets upon its papers."

Edward stared at a wet ring upon the tabletop and kept silent, leaving the Sultan to decide what came next.

Abd al-Rahman put down his cup of tea. "I know you took Edinburgh, and I know you lost it again. What I want from you is the reason you drove your men farther north when the campaign was already beyond your command. Why did you not stop?"

Marco stirred, but Victoria touched his arm and shook her head. Edward saw them and did not turn.

He reached for the water Juliet had given him, turned the cup once in his hands, and spoke.

"I believed another victory would leave Wallace nowhere to retreat. At Inverness, he let me see exactly what I wished: men withdrawing, a command post laid bare, the chance to end the campaign. I knew anger was leading me, and I called it determination."

Edward set down the cup.

"I followed. Straight into his snare."

The nearest tables fell silent. Edward went on before the Sultan could speak.

"I lost nearly all my best troops and was taken alive. Yet Wallace did not kill me."

Edward remembered the words Criston had spoken eleven years before, and the scorn with which he had pronounced his name.

"Why should I take your life, Edward Spencer? To give England another martyr?"

Edward drank before continuing.

"He sent me back. Not from pity. He wanted England to see me return defeated."

Remi stood beside Juliet, hugging his wooden ship to his chest. He knew little of Inverness or where it lay, but understood enough not to question his father.

The Sultan paced slowly about the fire.

"I know Marco was held at Rennes and Caen, Romeo among the Danes, and Victoria in North Africa." He stopped before Edward. "Tell me the rest. Who brought England to its fall?"

Edward watched a log collapse into the embers. "I helped bring her to it."

"Helped?" Romeo muttered, but Marco laid a hand on his shoulder before he could interrupt.

Abd al-Rahman leaned closer. "Answer as a man recounting the past, not as one condemning himself in the night. Could you alone have brought down all England?"

The old answers rose unbidden in Edward's mind.

*It was my fault. If only I had stayed in the south. If only I had not pursued Wallace.*

*If only I had died at Inverness. If only I had stood firm.*

But now each supposition sounded like a sentence spoken too often to resemble the truth of history.

"No."

He spoke more slowly than before.

"I did not bring about her fall alone. But I will not hide behind hunger, riots, or the failures of others to escape my own share."

The Sultan nodded. "Good. At last you can accept your responsibility without sentencing yourself to it."

Edward sat upright. "Will that make my blunders any less grave?"

"I see no cause to lessen them. You chose poorly where to withdraw, let Wallace lead you by the nose, lost your men, bogged down your army, and left a deadly opening in the south. That is evil enough without adding to it."

Abd al-Rahman tapped the table.

"The harvests failed. The people rose. The court was exhausted, and other commanders lost their battles. Do not shoulder their failings merely to make your own sentence heavier."

Edward watched the fire sink low in the hearth. For a long time he found no answer.
