The Sultan glanced at his wounded hand. "An hour ago, the crowd hailed the Pathfinder as a man who had never been defeated. You loathed that tale and fashioned its opposite: that Edward Spencer alone destroyed a kingdom."

He planted a hand upon the table, drawing nearer.

"Either way, you give yourself too much power."

Edward gripped the chair beneath his bandage. Abd al-Rahman waited through the silence before straightening.

"Now, to the promises you have made."

He pointed to the register of missing persons beside Victoria. "You go north at the Queen's command, seeking those who may still live in your homeland. Tonight you have taken the names of sons, husbands, and brothers from the people gathered here."

Edward looked at the register. "I told them I could promise no one's return. If I find a list, a letter, a trace, I shall follow it. That is all."

"At least you know what a promise can bear." The Sultan stepped closer. "But tell me this: do you go for duty, for the living, or to redeem the name Edward Spencer?"

Romeo rose again, this time without touching his gun. "You have said enough."

"Not yet." Abd al-Rahman barely glanced at him.

Victoria spoke. "Your Majesty, you question a man who leaves his home to carry out the Queen's own charge."

"I know. But a royal seal cannot tell us the purpose of the man who bears it."

The Sultan faced Edward. "For Castile, for the survivors, or to prove you did not die at Inverness?"

Edward let the question rest between them. "Perhaps for all three."

Abd al-Rahman did not praise him. "Then at least you speak truthfully."

Edward gestured toward the crowded tables. "If you think I mean to restore the English throne, you are mistaken. If my homeland is now one great graveyard, I will not make those who remain spill more blood for a flag."

"The English throne is of no concern to me."

The Sultan turned, sweeping his hand across the courtyard. He took in the rough wooden tables, the empty stew pots, and the chair still waiting for the Mariabell family.

"Marrakesh is my concern."

Edward said nothing. Looking at the tables and the vacant chair, he could no longer think of the courtyard merely as a place where he had sheltered.

"Four years ago you arrived here with a wife spent beyond endurance and a child near death from cold. The Moors shared their land and food with you. The Castilian authorities granted you lawful papers, while your neighbours gave you cattle, work, and the time to find yourself again."

Abd al-Rahman glanced at the empty chair. "Some lived long enough to sit at this feast. Some did not."

He turned back to Edward. "And now, with war drawing near, you choose to depart. Before we speak of Scotland again, tell me what Marrakesh is in your eyes. A poor resting place to be cast aside when the Pathfinder finds some grander calling?"

Edward parted his lips, but no answer came.

"That's not true, Your Majesty."

Remi's voice was so small that people farther back leaned forward to hear it. Edward turned.

"Remi."

The boy walked slowly to his father, his wooden ship held against his chest. He placed a small hand upon Edward's knee and stood close despite all the watching faces.

Abd al-Rahman lowered his gaze to the child, his voice deeper and gentler. "You say Marrakesh is no temporary home. What makes you so sure?"

Remi swallowed and glanced at Edward. His father let him speak, the bandaged hand still upon his knee.

"Father says Marrakesh is my home too, Your Majesty." Remi hugged his ship tighter. "I've lived here four years. I know the way to the market, and the cowshed door that sticks whenever it's cold."

"Uncle Omar taught Father to keep cattle. The Thompsons gave us flour when I was ill. Mother knows nearly everyone in the market."

He hesitated, then added, "The woman who sells potatoes gives me an extra one. Mother says she needn't, but she always does."

Omar burst into laughter. Juliet turned aside to hide her smile.

Remi tightened his grip upon the little ship. "Father says we nearly died our first winter here. Without everyone helping us, how could we have a house or even a cowshed? I hardly remember England, but I remember Marrakesh."

The Sultan listened without haste.

"Father says England is his homeland," Remi said. "But when we leave tomorrow, I'll miss Marrakesh so much. Can a person have two homelands, Your Majesty?"

Abd al-Rahman watched him for a long moment, then knelt upon the stones so Remi need not look up at him.

"Yes. A person can belong to more than one place. Sometimes it takes most of a lifetime to learn what he owes to each."

Still uncertain, Remi looked at Edward and leaned close to ask, "If Father goes away tomorrow, does that mean he's abandoning Marrakesh?"

The Sultan smiled instead of replying. He gestured for Edward to answer.

Edward rose and knelt to meet his son's eyes. "No. Father has work to do. We shall board a ship tomorrow, but Uncle Omar will still be Uncle Omar, Mother will still know every stall at the market, and that cowshed will still be the place where I've cursed most in four years."

He rested a hand on Remi's shoulder. "We lived here. Leaving cannot change that."

Remi's round eyes searched his face. "Will Father come back to Marrakesh?"

That question was harder than any the Sultan had asked. Edward set his bandaged hand on the boy's shoulder.

"I'll try with all my might to return. But I won't promise what I cannot be sure of keeping."

Remi pouted. "There it is again. 'Try.' Grown-ups always say that when they don't want to promise."

Edward managed a rueful smile, though his heart was heavy. "Then this time Father gives you leave to hate the word."

Remi nodded, still pouting. Juliet came to take his hand, and Edward stood with his wounded hand held against his side.

Abd al-Rahman rose and brushed snow from his robe. "Your son makes a better argument than you."

"I'm beginning to see that," Edward said with a bitter smile.

"Don't rejoice yet. We are not finished."

Edward's smile vanished. The Sultan came within an arm's length of him.

"If you travel far enough north, you may well encounter Criston Wallace again." Abd al-Rahman watched Edward's hand close at his side. "Do not give me an answer from a campaign plan. What will you do when it is Wallace himself across the table?"

Edward kept his voice level. "I shall try to speak with him. If he refuses, there are others with influence in Scotland. He may hold part of that country, but not all of it."

"You speak as an admiral with a road of retreat still open." The Sultan came nearer. "What if Wallace alone controls the passage you need? If you must face him to go on, will you be so calm then?"

Edward was silent. His hand tightened at his side.

Abd al-Rahman advanced another half-step. "When you face Criston Wallace again, will you approach as an admiral seeking terms? Or will you stand as the prisoner of Inverness, waiting for him to spare you once more?"

Edward pressed his tongue against his teeth and said nothing.

"What if he demands that you kneel?"

Romeo thrust himself from his chair. "Your Majesty, enough!"

Edward raised a hand to quiet him, then answered evenly.

"I would kneel."

Marco turned sharply. Victoria gripped the chair arms, while Juliet watched her husband without speaking. Remi looked from face to face, bewildered that his father's words had stilled everyone.

The Sultan did not react at once. Edward went on before he could ask another question.

"If kneeling would open a road for civilians, bring grain where it is needed, or win one day's truce, I would kneel. If Wallace demanded that I stay as his hostage so the others might pass, I would stay. He has defeated me once already, and what little honour remains to me is worth less than their lives."

"Enough," Abd al-Rahman cut in.

Edward stopped.

"Edward Spencer, you disappoint me."

At the nearest tables, people lowered their spoons. Edward felt their gaze and waited for the Sultan to finish.

Abd al-Rahman circled behind him. "I do not scorn a man willing to kneel. Those who rule must sometimes swallow things more bitter than pride. I am disappointed because you have offered yourself to Wallace as though you were the cheapest thing upon the table."

Edward lifted his chin. "You turn a prudent choice into a sermon on virtue."

"I question whether it is prudent."

The Sultan pointed at Edward's chest. "If staying behind would truly save a hundred souls, I should be the first to bid you stay. In war, lives do not always bear the same weight. Yet you have offered yourself as a hostage without considering what becomes of those in your charge."

He nodded toward Marco. "If Wallace holds you, who leads them on? If he breaks his word, who brings them out of Scotland? You have staked all their lives upon the same throw as your own."

Edward fell silent. So did Marco, though his eyes were fixed upon Edward now, rather than the Sultan.

"Years ago I abandoned an eastern fortress to save three cities," Abd al-Rahman said. "For two years men called me a coward who had handed his fathers' land to the enemy."

"Because the three cities mattered more," Edward said.

"Precisely. And I did not order myself burned with that fortress merely to show the world how bitterly I repented."

The Sultan stopped before Edward. "You are putting a chain about your own neck and naming it duty. A commander who holds his life cheap teaches his enemies how cheaply he may be bought."

Edward clenched his jaw. "You were not at Inverness."

"No," Abd al-Rahman answered plainly. "I did not stand upon a ship and watch southern England burn. I have no right to command you to forget, nor must Wallace forgive you. And no dead man can rise to tell you how to make amends."

The Sultan stepped back a little. "But when you meet him again, if you must bow, then kneel. Only be certain it is an admiral bargaining on his people's behalf, not a prisoner who has already passed sentence on himself."

Edward studied his bandaged hand, then met the Sultan's eyes. "I shall remember."

"You need not remember for life. Only long enough not to die in vain before fulfilling the Queen's charge."

Romeo gave a brief laugh, which ceased when the Sultan glanced at him. Abd al-Rahman turned to Remi, who remained beside Juliet, watching him closely.

The Sultan laughed softly. "Very well. There is one more matter to settle before a child judges my morals."

At his signal, a guard brought a cedarwood case, longer than a man's forearm. Its silver bands were tarnished, but the waves and lightning carved upon the lid showed clearly in the firelight. The Sultan had it placed before Edward.

"I meant to send this to your house tomorrow morning. Since I am here, I can spare my men the journey."

Edward opened the lid.

Upon dark cloth lay a flintlock pistol. Black wood formed its stock, and the barrel gleamed with the reddish hue of copper alloy; old engravings ran from breech to muzzle. Deep inside the metal, a red light stirred like an ember caught beneath the surface.

"I doubt you brought this merely to show me how handsome it is."

"A Miracle-class Vestigium." Abd al-Rahman nodded toward the pistol. "It is called *Storm's Roar*, an heirloom of a branch of the Moroccan royal house, from before Castile and our people learned to live beneath one order without cutting one another's throats each season."

Edward looked up. "A royal heirloom of the Miracle class is hardly a trifle to bring to supper. Do you mean to give it to me?"

"No. I am not so generous as that." Abd al-Rahman laid a hand upon the case. "I lend it until you return to Marrakesh. What is lent must be returned."

He glanced at Remi. "I would not have that boy grow up saying the Sultan of Marrakesh sent his father to Scotland with only a sword and a few words of wisdom."

Edward lifted *Storm's Roar* from its case. The pistol weighed more than its size suggested, and warmth from the barrel reached through the bandage upon his palm.

He raised it to eye level without touching the trigger. "If you have brought this, I ought to know what it can do before Remi decides his father has acquired a new toy."

"It takes ordinary lead shot, but the Vestigium in its barrel makes the charge strike with far greater force. At close quarters, the blow may equal a direct hit from a heavy cannon."

Abd al-Rahman saw Edward glance toward the house. "And before some foolish thought takes hold, do not fire it in your courtyard."

Edward lowered the pistol. "My thanks for measuring my curiosity so accurately."

"I measure it by my experience of officers." The Sultan tapped the lid. "*Storm's Roar* takes time to reload, kicks like a beast, and may deafen everyone you mean to save if fired within four walls. Nor does it make the man holding it immortal."

He regarded Edward. "In short, it is dangerous in the way all fine weapons are dangerous."

Edward returned the pistol to the case. Abd al-Rahman shut the lid and kept his hand upon it.

"*Storm's Roar* is borrowed. Do not make a medal of it, or an excuse for a handsome death."

Edward nodded. "I understand."

"Then bring it back whole when you return to Marrakesh." Abd al-Rahman removed his hand. "And if possible, let the man carrying it return whole as well."

The Sultan took up his cloak and strode toward the gate. As he passed Edward, he stopped.

"When you face Wallace, if kneeling will gain something worth the price, kneel."

Edward raised an eyebrow.

Abd al-Rahman smiled. "But if he refuses to listen, *Storm's Roar* may lend your arguments a sharper edge."

For the first time since Criston Wallace's name had been spoken, Edward truly laughed.

The Sultan and his two guards passed through the gate and faded into the snow. Those gathered in the courtyard watched until all three figures had vanished beyond the houses.

title_vi: Chapter Ten: Farewell to Marrakesh
title_en: Chapter Ten: Farewell to Marrakesh
text_en:
After the Sultan departed, no one attempted to revive the celebration. The remaining meat was divided, the food packed away, and the guests took their leave of the Spencer family one by one.

Omar embraced Edward so fiercely that the bandage on Edward's arm pressed against the old man's back. Martha handed Juliet a small bag of pastries for the journey, then burst into tears before she could finish speaking. The other families departed with smoked meat, bones for soup, or a scrap of paper bearing the Spencers' new address, should their letters ever find a way across the sea.

Victoria instructed two secretaries to take the register of missing persons back to the Governor's Palace and make copies before Marco departed with the original. Edward kept the Beaumont family's note in his inner pocket.

It was late. Fresh snow had begun to fill the footprints trampled across the courtyard throughout the day. Beneath the abandoned banquet canopy, only the Spencer family, Victoria, Marco, Romeo, and a few neighbors helping with the clearing remained.

When Juliet saw Victoria putting on her coat, she held the door.

"Are you really going to wake your entire escort and have the horses harnessed in the middle of the night, just to travel a few streets back to the palace?"

Victoria paused with her fingers on the clasp.

"I have a comfortable bed at the palace, and an entire city to govern tomorrow morning. This house is crowded enough without another governor taking up space."

"We've just fed more than a hundred people in our courtyard." Juliet waved toward the adjoining room. "One more guest won't bring the house down. Besides, I wouldn't want anyone saying I'd treated Ed's dearest friend poorly."

Victoria remained beside the door, coat in hand. She glanced toward Edward, who raised both hands like a man awaiting his sentence.

"Don't look at me. I lost all authority over sleeping arrangements in this house a long time ago."

Romeo raised a hand in testimony.

"I can confirm that. He never possessed such authority in the first place."

Ignoring him, Juliet turned to the two Royal Guards.

"You two should stay as well. We have to leave for the station early."

Marco agreed with a nod. Romeo glanced at the table where he had once fallen asleep and grimaced.

"Just don't make me sleep with my face on that table again."

Juliet indicated three mattresses beside the hearth.

"You can sleep on the floor."

Romeo regarded the thin bedding with theatrical misery.

"Such generous hospitality, Juliet."

She pulled a third blanket from the chest.

"If you find it unsatisfactory, there's still room in the cattle shed."

Romeo immediately leaned toward Marco.

"The floor looks wonderful."

By then, Remi was so exhausted he could barely stand, though he still insisted on helping clear the remaining cups. Edward swept him into his arms before he could protest.

Remi rested his head against his father's shoulder but made a feeble attempt to push away.

"I can walk, Father."

"I know." Edward adjusted his hold. "But you'll fall asleep in the courtyard. We have an early train tomorrow. Save your strength for complaining about the cold."

Remi rubbed his eyes.

"Is Uncle Marco really coming with us, Father? What if he changes his mind at the station?"

Marco finished securing the ropes around the canopy and looked over.

"I'm coming as far as Tangier before heading to Fes. You'll have an entire train journey to pester me."

"Then promise you'll tell me stories about Father when he was young before we part!"

Remi managed to stay awake long enough to make his request.

Edward turned toward his old friend and pointed an accusing finger.

"If you tell him any of the stories I'm thinking of, I'll personally throw you off at the first station."

Marco tossed the folded canopy onto the cart.

"Then I'll have to choose the most scandalous one. The boy deserves to know how thoroughly his father disgraced himself in his youth."

Remi's eyes were almost closed, but his arms remained around his father's neck. Edward laid him on the bed, removed his boots, and drew the blanket up to his chin.

As Edward rose, Remi caught his sleeve.

"Don't oversleep, Father."

"I've never missed a train," Edward replied, pulling the nightcap away from his son's forehead.

Remi nestled deeper into the blankets, suddenly wide awake.

"But Uncle Romeo said you once fell asleep in an ammunition magazine."

Edward's hand froze on the blanket.

From the sitting room, Romeo immediately called out.

"I never said when that happened!"

Remi giggled and tucked the blanket beneath his chin.

"Good night, Father."

Edward rested his hand on the boy's hair one last time.

"Good night, Remi. I'll be right next door."

When Edward closed Remi's door, Juliet had already arranged three mattresses beside the hearth. Marco was unfastening his sabre, while Romeo stared between the bedding and the bedroom door, apparently realizing who would be sleeping outside.

"Wait!" Romeo pointed at the mattresses, then at Edward. "This is his house. Why does he have to sleep out here with us?"

Juliet passed them carrying an armful of blankets.

"Because Victoria is sharing my room. She's our honoured guest, and all three of you have slept on open decks through wind and rain. I'm confident one night on the floor won't defeat you."

Edward surveyed the three prepared mattresses and raised an eyebrow.

"I'm impressed that I was informed only after everything had been settled."

"Then you're finally getting used to married life." Juliet set down the blankets and turned toward Victoria. "Does this arrangement suit you?"

Victoria leaned against the doorframe.

"It's the soundest quartering arrangement I've heard proposed all evening."

Edward pulled his blanket from the pile.

"I should have known you'd judge it like a quartermaster."

Marco dragged his mattress closer to the hearth and lay down.

"Stop fighting it."

Romeo collapsed onto the neighbouring mattress.

"I'd rather sleep on deck. At least there aren't two women stealing our beds and expecting us to be grateful."

Juliet threw a blanket straight into his face.

"Go to sleep, platinum head."

When the bedroom door closed, none of the three men fell asleep immediately. The hearth held enough wood to last until morning, but the corners beyond its glow remained cold.

The case containing *Storm's Roar* rested beneath a chair against the wall, while a cloth-wrapped sabre lay beside Edward's luggage.

Romeo lay on his back with his hands behind his head.

"What I hate most about that old man is that after listening to him, I can't find a single argument worth making."

Marco turned toward him.

"Which part troubled you?"

Romeo pulled his blanket higher.

"What he said about lives never being equal in war. I realised I'd spent nearly half my life acting on precisely that principle."

He fell silent, staring at the ceiling.

"Once, on the Danish front, my unit got behind an enemy force pressing our defences. I saw two things at once: some of our men pinned beneath an embankment, and the enemy command carriage withdrawing north. I had enough men to accomplish one task."

Romeo slipped a hand from beneath his blanket. His index finger curled around an imaginary trigger.

"I pursued the carriage. Twelve of our men died beneath that embankment before reinforcements arrived, but I took the enemy commander's head. In less than ten minutes, three battalions ahead of us had lost their orders, their formations collapsed, and our left flank found a way to withdraw."

He turned his head toward Edward.

"I remember all twelve names. But send me back to that day, and I'd make the same choice. That's what bothers me."

Romeo stared at the ceiling again.

"Twelve of ours against one of theirs, yet his head truly outweighed every one of them."

Edward looked at his friend. Romeo had always described hunting enemy officers like recounting a game of cards, but Edward had never heard him speak of the men left behind.

Marco stared at the ceiling, his hands still upon the blanket.

"I heard his words differently."

He drew one arm free and rested it across his stomach.

"At Rennes, the French outnumbered us almost four to one. A battle in open country would have destroyed us before noon. I demolished two roads, blocked the intersections with supply wagons, drew their artillery into streets too narrow to turn their guns, and forced their cavalry to dismount."

Marco paused.

"Then I stationed a company in the western workshops, deliberately leaving them exposed. Seventy-eight men held that position for nearly two hours. More than half never returned, but five French battalions abandoned their main advance to crush them."

He turned his palm upward, studying its calluses.

"By noon, the French still had four times our numbers. But their formations were scattered, and they could no longer concentrate enough force at a single point."

Romeo looked across at him.

"I never believed those seventy-eight men deserved to live any less than the others," Marco continued, his voice as steady as a battlefield report. "But for those two hours, they were the weight that kept five battalions in the wrong place. I know I made the right decision. That's why the Sultan's words trouble me."

A log cracked in the hearth. Silence held for several seconds.

With his head resting on a rolled coat, Edward spoke.

"Then where is the Sultan right? Romeo traded twelve men for a commander. You sacrificed seventy-eight to hold five battalions. We still make those calculations on the battlefield."

Edward turned toward Marco.

"Why should it be different when it comes to me?"

Marco met his gaze.

"Because you don't value your own life the way you value ours."

Edward frowned.

"I'm calculating effectiveness."

"If it were me, you'd find a way to keep me alive because I could command another day. If it were Romeo, you'd consider every alternative before sacrificing him." Marco propped himself on one elbow. "But when it's your own life, all you ask is what your death might purchase."

Edward watched the fire settle between the logs.

"Because I'm in command."

"Precisely because you're in command. Romeo hunts officers because one man's death can leave hundreds without direction. You understand that principle when it concerns the enemy, me, or him. Everyone except yourself."

Romeo tapped a finger against his mattress.

"And if the enemy learns you'll always trade your life for a hostage, they won't need to hunt you anymore. They'll only need to put the right person in the right place."

Edward lay staring at the ceiling.

"Then how do I tell the difference between a necessary sacrifice and throwing my life away?"

Marco rested his weight on one elbow.

"That's difficult to judge alone. Once you're ready to put yourself on the scales, at least let someone else check the calculation."

Romeo pulled his blanket across his chest.

"Three men past thirty, lying in a snowbound Marrakesh debating the worth of human life. If the old Academy crowd could see us, they'd demand our medals back."

Edward looked from Marco to Romeo as the wind whistled beneath the door.

"If someone had told me fifteen years ago that we'd one day be sleeping in a frozen Marrakesh, with England fallen and a Moorish Sultan lecturing me about dying foolishly, I'd have advised him to drink less."

Marco burst out laughing, reaching toward the sabre propped beside his mattress.

"No. You'd have drawn your sword and challenged him to a duel."

"Nonsense," Romeo objected, waving a hand. "Back then, Ed only liked challenging men. Put a woman in front of him, and he became an entirely different creature."

Edward rolled toward his friends, hauling the blanket to his chest.

"Don't you dare start digging up the past."

Romeo propped himself on one elbow, suddenly wide awake.

"Oh? So you know exactly what I'm about to mention?"

Beyond the wall came a rustle of bedding, followed by Juliet's unmistakable voice.

"Ed, darling, what colour was Victoria's corset that day?"

Edward went rigid.

Marco turned toward the wall while Romeo clapped both hands over his mouth. Edward stared at the bedroom door as though an artillery battery had just opened fire.

"Juliet."

"I'm asking seriously," Juliet replied with perfect composure. "Victoria insists it was dark blue, and I told her that if you truly hadn't looked back, you couldn't possibly know. We need a witness."

Edward parted his lips, then glanced toward Marco and Romeo. Both men held their breath, waiting for him to condemn himself.

Romeo lowered his hands and whispered urgently.

"Say nothing. Preserve the last shred of the Royal Navy's dignity. Don't answer!"

Still facing the wall, Marco added, "Too late. Look at his face. He remembers. Every detail."

"Both of you, shut up."

Edward pulled the blanket higher, as though a thin layer of wool might preserve what remained of his future.

Victoria's voice came through the wall.

"I'd like to know as well, Edward. For more than fifteen years, I've wondered whether you passed the changing room by accident, or whether that book you were holding upside down was genuinely fascinating."

Romeo made a strangled noise and buried his face in the pillow.

Edward drew the blanket halfway over his face and surrendered to the four friends awaiting his answer.

"Dark blue. Lavender lace trim."

Marco and Romeo held their silence for precisely one beat before exploding with laughter. Remi stirred in the adjoining room, prompting Marco to smother his amusement in the pillow.

From the bedroom, Juliet giggled for some time before managing to speak.

"Thank you, darling. That means I won the wager."

Edward lowered the blanket and stared at the ceiling.

"I hate every single person in this house."

Victoria answered serenely from beyond the wall.

"Blame your excellent memory first. I was changing behind a screen, and you only caught a glimpse for a few seconds before I threw a towel straight at your face."

Edward gripped the blanket, which he had already pulled above his chin.

"It wasn't deliberate."

"Yet someone stood outside the door looking utterly bewildered for almost a minute, still holding his book upside down."

Marco sat bolt upright.

"Tell us more! Was that the famous incident in the senior girls' quarters?"

Edward whipped around, half rising from his mattress.

"You knew about that?"

"I'm the one who lent you the book!" Marco wiped tears of laughter from his eyes. "You said you needed a respectable excuse to walk down that corridor. I foolishly assumed you were returning it to a professor."

Romeo lifted his head from the pillow.

"The book is news to me. But I distinctly remember him spending forty minutes choosing a coat."

"Only forty minutes!" Edward corrected instinctively.

Romeo pointed triumphantly.

"See? He even remembers the forty minutes!"

Juliet knocked twice against the wall, still laughing.

"Vic, are there any other interesting stories?"

Edward pushed himself halfway upright.

"Absolutely not. That's everything. Everyone go to sleep!"

"What about the time Edward waited for me in the rain?" Victoria called. "I came down almost two hours later, and he still insisted he was merely passing by."

Marco burrowed deeper into his blanket, struggling to contain his laughter.

"He spent the following morning bedridden."

"I didn't have a fever!"

"Of course. Two pots of hot tea and fourteen consecutive hours of sleep meant absolutely nothing."

Romeo leaned on his elbow.

"He also bought every pear tart in the dining hall because he'd heard Vic say she wanted one."

Edward turned to glare at him.

"I bought them for the whole table!"

"Four people eating, twelve tarts purchased," Marco reminded him, holding up three fingers as though presenting the bill.

Juliet's voice drifted from the bedroom.

"Twelve?"

Victoria added, "And I ate exactly one."

Romeo placed a proud hand over his heart.

"Those surplus tarts were when I first learned to appreciate Ed's love. At least his devotion could feed his friends."

Edward sat hunched on his mattress, clutching his head.

"I've commanded men through countless storms, endured Inverness, and even suffered the Sultan of Marrakesh trampling my dignity before a hundred people. Yet none of it compares to tonight."

Victoria was about to mention the winter festival. Hearing her voice beyond the wall, Edward pulled the blanket over his head, knowing the incident with the glove was coming.

He jerked upright.

"Victoria! I'm begging you!"

Juliet immediately asked, "What happened at the winter festival?"

Marco lay back and pulled the blanket across his stomach.

"The glove?"

Romeo gave an appreciative whistle.

"A classic!"

Edward pointed at them both.

"You two are traitors!"

"I lost a glove at the festival," Victoria explained. "Edward immediately gave me his and spent hours walking barehanded through the snow. His hand was swollen the next morning, but he insisted it was from fencing practice."

Juliet pulled the blanket to her shoulders.

"That sounds familiar. My husband still does things like that."

Romeo tapped a finger against his mattress, recalling another detail.

"And for the next three months, whenever Vic appeared in the dining hall, Ed would suddenly discover he was hungry."

Edward collapsed onto his back.

"If only the Sultan were still here. At least he'd give me a more dignified interrogation."

"Don't hide behind the Sultan," Juliet called from the bedroom. "You still have to stay alive and answer to me."

At last, Edward laughed. Romeo buried his face in the pillow to avoid waking Remi, while Marco drew his blanket over his mouth.

Their laughter gradually faded, leaving only the crackle of the fire.

When the room grew quieter, Marco spoke first.

"All things considered, this is rather nice."

Edward turned his head.

"What do you mean?"

"Back then, all we worried about was who fancied whom, who won the fencing matches, and what we'd eat that evening." Marco watched the ceiling. "Sometimes I remember the war so clearly that I forget we ever had days like those."

Romeo pushed the pillow from his face.

"I never forgot them. Most of my memories still smell of alcohol."

Edward adjusted his blanket.

"At dawn, you'll remain in Marrakesh, Marco will head for Fes, and I'll travel to Tangier and beyond. Tonight, let's pretend the most important matter in the world is a dark blue corset."

Juliet's voice immediately carried through the wall.

"I heard every word. Are you still pining for it?"

Edward closed his eyes and sighed.

"I said it deliberately so you'd hear."

Victoria promptly contradicted him.

"Rubbish. You were just as dreadful a liar at the Academy."

Romeo opened his mouth to contribute another story, but Edward and Marco ordered him to sleep in perfect unison. Juliet laughed again behind the wall.

In the bedroom, Juliet placed the last garment into her trunk before lying down. Victoria drew the blanket over her legs, still able to hear the three men arguing outside.

Juliet turned toward the wall.

"Thank you. I've lived with that man for nine years, and apparently there are still plenty of things I don't know."

Victoria rolled onto her side to face her.

"Don't spend them all at once. Edward can withstand artillery fire, but his defences are appalling when it comes to his past."

"I have an entire train journey tomorrow." Juliet pulled her blanket higher. "I'll make the stories last."

From the sitting room, Edward raised his voice.

"You two remember how thin the walls are, don't you?"

"Of course," Juliet answered calmly.

Victoria immediately added, "That's precisely why we aren't bothering to whisper."

Before long, both rooms fell quiet.

Edward lay between Marco and Romeo, watching the firelight darken across the sabre's scabbard and the case of *Storm's Roar* beside the chair. Juliet and Victoria had stopped talking beyond the wall, while outside, fresh snow covered the last footprints of the celebration.

Tomorrow morning, their carriage would follow the same road Edward had taken to the cattle shed every day.

title_vi: Chapter Eleven: Marrakesh Station
title_en: Chapter Eleven: Marrakesh Station
text_en:
The following morning, Marrakesh Station was far busier than Edward had imagined.

Thin bands of snow lay across the glass roof and iron supports, while the great coal braziers lining the platforms filled the air with smoke and the scent of coffee. Freight trains occupied the outer tracks, their wagons marked for provisions or military supplies. On Platform Three, the locomotive bound for Tangier sent white columns of steam billowing toward the vaulted roof.

Edward stood beside a mountain of luggage he had been certain was packed the previous evening.

At the station, it had somehow acquired two additional bags of food from Juliet's neighbours, a crate of Remi's books, the wooden case containing *Storm's Roar*, and the cloth-wrapped sabre Edward refused to let any porter touch.

Seeing him struggle with the heaviest trunk, Marco seized its handle.

"Just wear your sword and pistol and keep that grim expression you always have before battle. I'll carry this."

Edward glanced apologetically at the trunk.

"Half my wardrobe is in there."

"All the more reason to be careful." Marco adjusted his grip and headed for the passenger carriage. "If I damage anything, Juliet may kill me before the war or my wife gets the chance."

A short distance away, Juliet checked the tickets and travel permits.

"He certainly understands the situation better than you do."

Before Edward could answer, Victoria spoke behind him.

"You're only realising that now?"

The governor arrived with two members of her staff. Snow dusted the shoulders of her heavy cloak, and her golden hair was neatly tucked beneath a fur hat.

Romeo pointed toward Marco.

"I raised my objections last night, if anyone cares to remember."

"Your objections carry very little weight anymore," Victoria replied. "You did point a gun at the Sultan, after all."

Romeo placed a hand over his heart and retreated half a step, looking grievously wronged.

"One day, the world will acknowledge that I was once a highly decorated officer!"

"Everyone remembers," Marco replied beside the luggage cart. "That's what makes it so alarming."

Amid the calls of passengers, the bustle around the luggage trunks, and the rattle of handcart wheels, Edward looked at the four friends who had shared his roof the previous night.

Marco had loaded the luggage, and Juliet kept the tickets secure in her coat. Victoria glanced at the station clock before touching Edward's shoulder.

"Edward Spencer."

"Yes?"

"Stand still."

Before Edward could ask why, Victoria turned to Juliet. Her expression was serious now.

"Juliet, there's something I should have done fifteen years ago. Would you mind if I kissed your husband?"

Edward looked between them in bewilderment.

"Just a moment. Are you two negotiating over me as though I'm not standing here?"

Juliet folded the travel permit and slipped it into her pocket before regarding Victoria.

"All right. One kiss."

"Juliet!"

"On the cheek," Juliet added. "And I want to watch."

Marco released the strap he had been fastening around the trunk. Romeo turned to enjoy the spectacle.

Victoria stepped forward.

"Fifteen years is probably long enough to reward a young man who once waited two hours in the rain, bought twelve pear tarts, and wandered through a winter festival with bare hands, yet never managed to take a single step further."

Edward sensed disaster approaching.

"Vic, we excavated those memories thoroughly last night. Please leave them buried."

"Certainly not."

Victoria rested a hand on Edward's shoulder, leaned forward, and kissed his cheek.

Romeo's delighted exclamation was so loud that several nearby passengers turned to look. Even Marco gave a teasing whistle, something Edward had never imagined hearing from the Balancer at such an early hour.

Edward remained motionless, still gripping his bag, unable to think of a reply.

Romeo doubled over laughing.

"Even the Pathfinder has finally run out of ways forward."

Juliet still wore a smile, but her hands had stopped sorting the travel documents. Edward immediately straightened and turned toward his wife.

"I didn't do anything."

"I know."

"She was the one who kissed me."

"I'm standing right here, Edward."

Victoria stepped back, thoroughly satisfied.

"Well, the reward has finally reached its rightful recipient."

Romeo leaned toward Marco and whispered, "I wager he'll be sleeping in the corridor tonight."

Marco shook his head.

"I never wager on a certainty."

Edward pointed at his two friends.

"Don't forget I used to command both of you!"

"But Juliet decides where you sleep," Romeo replied without hesitation. "And I know perfectly well which of you frightens me more."

Juliet approached, brushed the snow from Edward's shoulder, and straightened his collar.

"Very well. You've received your long overdue reward from your youth. From now on, save the other cheek for me."

"I have two cheeks, you know."

"I'm aware."

Edward decided against asking further questions.

Remi had watched everything, clearly unable to understand how grown men and women could turn a kiss on the cheek into a military incident.

As Victoria turned away, he tugged at her sleeve.

"Aunt Vic."

She looked back.

"Yes, dear?"

Remi hesitated.

"Are you sad?"

Victoria knelt before him, allowing the hem of her cloak to touch the cold platform. Her blue eyes were now level with his.

"Of course I am. Your house has been so lively these past few days that I almost forgot we'd soon be going our separate ways. But before I let myself feel sad, there's something I want you to remember."

Remi immediately stood straighter.

Victoria adjusted his crooked woollen hat.

"After this journey, your father may not be home very often. His duties could take him far away, and even I don't know when things will truly become peaceful again."

A few steps away, the smile faded from Edward's face. Juliet also fell silent, holding the travel documents tightly against her chest.

"But you needn't rush to grow up just to take your father's place," Victoria continued. "You're still a child, Remi. Enjoy your childhood. Study diligently, help your mother with whatever chores you can manage, and don't make Juliet call your name three times before you answer."

Remi lowered his head at the mention of being called three times. Juliet folded her arms but allowed Victoria to continue.

Victoria placed both hands on his shoulders.

"When you're grown, I hope you'll become a man others can rely on. You needn't be an admiral, a Royal Guard, or a hero. All that matters is that when someone turns to you for support, you'll be there, standing firm."

She inclined her head toward Edward, Marco, and Romeo.

"Just like the three men standing beside you now."

Romeo was about to make a show of being moved when Marco shot him a warning glance.

"Don't ruin that."

"I haven't said anything." Romeo placed a hand over his heart and, for once, genuinely kept quiet.

Remi looked from one man to another, lingering longest on his father before turning back to Victoria.

"I'll try."

Victoria frowned immediately.

"There you go again with 'try.'"

Remi hastily corrected himself.

"I will."

"Much better."

Remi pulled his hat lower.

"I've been very happy these past few days."

"Aunt Isabella came to our house, and Uncle Marco, Uncle Romeo, and you too. Everyone stayed last night, talking and laughing for ages."

He glanced at his father, as though afraid he had revealed something forbidden.

"Our house hasn't had so many people in it for a long time. Now everyone's leaving, and it makes me sad."

The teasing stopped.

Remi looked down at his shoes, still clutching a corner of Victoria's cloak.

She rested her hands on his shoulders.

"Then remember the happy days first. Let the grown-ups worry about saying goodbye."

Remi nodded.

"I'll write to you. And to Uncle Romeo, Uncle Marco, and Aunt Isabella too."

Victoria smiled.

"I'll have someone deliver a letter to your house as soon as possible. But if your letter to Isabella is longer than the one you send me, I shall consider it an act of treason."

Edward immediately folded his arms.

"Vic."

"Be quiet, Edward."

Remi burst out laughing, giving Romeo another opportunity to tease Victoria.

Still kneeling before the boy, Victoria abruptly changed the subject.

"Speaking of Isabella, there's one extremely important question I must ask before you board that train."

Remi gave her his full attention.

"What is it?"

Victoria straightened his collar.

"Between Aunt Isabella and me, whom do you think is prettier?"

Marco bent over the trunk, pretending to struggle with its lock. Romeo turned away, his shoulders trembling with suppressed laughter.

Juliet stared at Victoria in disbelief. The governor, a woman approaching thirty who had just offered such heartfelt advice, had willingly walked into this trap.

Remi thought about Isabella for a moment before answering with a solemnity that sent Marco's head straight back toward the trunk.

"Aunt Isabella."

Romeo's laughter erupted first. Marco braced both hands against the trunk and bowed his head.

Edward struggled to contain himself and failed, while even Juliet had to turn away despite her efforts to remain polite.

Victoria remained frozen on one knee.

"After everything I've just told you!"

Realising his mistake, Remi scrambled to recover.

"But you're very pretty too!"

"Too late!"

Victoria pulled his woollen hat down over his eyes, cupped his cheeks through the scarf, and shook his head gently from side to side.

"You little traitor!"

"Aunt Vic!" Remi giggled, struggling to push his hat up. "I never said you weren't pretty!"

"But you still chose her."

Once he could see again, Remi tried to explain.

"It's because Aunt Isabella has golden eyes! You have golden hair, but your eyes are blue. You don't look alike!"

Victoria was speechless. She looked up at Edward.

"Have you never taught your son how to tell a polite lie?"

Edward was still laughing.

"I've only taught him to tell the truth."

Juliet folded her arms.

"I tried to teach him manners, but his father ruined everything."

Remi tugged Victoria's cloak.

"Are you angry with me?"

Victoria held her silence for several seconds before surrendering. She straightened his hat, smoothed the hair flattened against his forehead, and rested a hand on his head.

"No. I've merely learned that even a governor has her limits."

Victoria raised a hand to silence the others.

"All right. Everyone, quiet."

A whistle sounded before she could continue.

Railway attendants called for passengers along the platform while porters secured the last luggage compartments. The entire group turned toward the steaming locomotive.

As the departure time arrived, Romeo was the first to turn toward Remi. He knelt on the platform and extended a fist.

"Right, young man. By the next time we meet, you'd better have grown at least another handspan."

Remi tapped his small fist against Romeo's.

"What if I haven't?"

Romeo stroked his chin thoughtfully.

"Then I'll blame your father. I'll work out the precise accusation later."

Without warning, Remi threw his arms around Romeo's neck. Romeo had to brace one hand against the platform to keep from falling.

He muttered a quiet curse before embracing the boy.

"Remember to write to me," Remi whispered into his ear.

Romeo held him a little tighter.

"Of course. I'll write."

"And don't tell lies in your letters."

Romeo patted his back twice.

"That particular promise might be difficult to keep."

As soon as Remi released Romeo, he turned and embraced Victoria.

She drew him into her cloak, resting her chin against his woollen hat.

"Be good to your mother. Try not to drive your father to distraction. And if you ever visit Madrid and meet Aunt Isabella, under no circumstances mention that question again."

Remi stepped back, puzzled.

"Why not?"

Victoria bent to straighten his hat once more.

"Because I'd like to preserve enough dignity to continue governing Marrakesh."

"Yes. I'll try."

Victoria pressed her fingers to her temple.

"There it is again. 'I'll try.'"

His answer sent the adults laughing once more.

Edward stood beside the carriage door, watching his son with the friends who would remain in Marrakesh.

Victoria embraced Juliet next, holding her longer than the others. The two women exchanged a few words beyond Edward's hearing. Juliet nodded, then held Victoria for another moment before letting go.

As they separated, Victoria pressed a fairly thick envelope into Juliet's hand.

"A letter of introduction from me. Use it as you please, or ignore it if you find it unnecessary. Inside are the addresses of two people in Madrid who can help you manage your affairs."

Victoria glanced toward Edward.

"They're capable people, and neither will presume to supervise or watch over you."

Juliet examined the envelope before slipping it carefully into her inner pocket.

"Thank you."

"There's no need." Victoria tilted her chin toward Edward. "Just don't let him turn this move into a military operation where he gives all the orders and you have no say."

"You needn't worry. I have considerable experience with that."

Edward hoisted the strap of his bag onto his shoulder.

"I'm still standing right here."

"Which is why we're speaking loudly enough for you to hear."

At last, Romeo shook Edward's hand, pulled him into a fierce embrace, and struck his shoulder twice.

"Promise me you won't get yourself killed up north."

He kept one hand on Edward's shoulder.

Edward gripped his friend's shoulder in return.

"And you be careful here."

"Nothing to worry about. The people of Marrakesh adore me."

Victoria looked at Romeo over Edward's shoulder.

"The people of Marrakesh are merely enduring you."

"A mere matter of phrasing."

After seeing the last pieces of luggage aboard, Marco returned to the platform.

He shook Victoria's hand, then embraced Romeo tightly. Neither man spoke of when they might meet again.

Marco gave Romeo a light punch against the chest.

"While I'm away, don't be fool enough to aim your pistol at another sovereign."

Romeo placed a hand over his heart.

"I'll do my best to restrain myself until you return."

"That wasn't the answer I wanted," Marco replied.

Romeo patted his shoulder.

"Then you know me far too well."

At that moment, a second whistle sounded, urging the passengers aboard. Attendants began closing the doors of the forward carriages.

Edward helped Juliet onto the steps. Remi followed, climbing aboard by himself and refusing every offer to carry him. Marco handed the final trunk to the porter before boarding behind Edward.

The moment he entered the carriage, Remi leaned toward the window.

Below, Victoria raised a hand in farewell. Romeo cupped his hands around his mouth and shouted at the top of his lungs.

"REMI! DON'T FORGET THAT AUNT ISABELLA IS PRETTIER!"

Victoria smacked his shoulder.

Laughter erupted from the nearby carriages.

Remi blushed and retreated halfway behind Edward, though he still peered around his father to wave. Juliet bit her lower lip so hard it turned white, while Marco turned completely toward the carriage interior.

Edward glared at Romeo through the window.

"I should have let the Sultan shoot you."

Romeo couldn't hear him, but somehow managed to raise his thumb in reply.

The locomotive gave a gentle jolt. Iron wheels began to turn.

Marrakesh Station slowly slipped backward.

Victoria walked alongside the train for several paces before coming to a stop. Romeo continued waving until a steel pillar at the end of the platform concealed him.

Remi knelt on his seat, pressing both hands against the glass. He searched for them through the gaps between the lamp posts, but as the train gathered speed, their familiar faces grew smaller.

By the end of the platform, Victoria was little more than a dark cloak beside Romeo's pale platinum hair.

Then the snow-covered roof of a warehouse swallowed them both.

Remi pressed his face against the window.

Red earthen rooftops, watchtowers, and ribbons of Vestigium light passed behind the drifting snow. Edward searched for the road leading back to the Spencer estate, but the crowded roofs obscured every familiar route.

Juliet watched the city recede, one hand resting against the back of Remi's seat until the last rooftops disappeared.

Across from them, Marco sat with his hands upon his knees beside his neatly folded military cloak. His gaze followed the railway tracks stretching north.

Even after Marrakesh vanished from sight, Remi kept his hand against the glass.

Edward sat down beside his son and rested a hand on his shoulder, keeping it there until the railway curved away toward the north.

title_vi: Chapter Twelve: The Genius of Castile
title_en: Chapter Twelve: The Genius of Castile
text_en:
The journey from Marrakesh to Tangier-Ceuta was quieter than Edward had expected. After the morning at the station, nearly everyone in the carriage was short of sleep. The steady beat of iron wheels soon lulled them into slumber.

Juliet rested her head against the window, one hand holding the blanket over Remi. The boy hugged his cloth satchel to his chest, as though everything from the home they had left might still be inside it.

Across from them, Marco sat with his folded cloak beside him and a report from Fes spread over his knees. Before he reached the third page, his head had fallen forward as the train crossed the snowbound fields of northern Morocco.

Only Edward remained awake.

He watched the signal posts race past the glass and the twin rails vanish into the mist ahead. On every curve, the wheels gave a brief metallic shriek before returning to their measured rhythm. They travelled so swiftly that the long-distance coaches he had once known seemed to belong to another century.

After a while, Marco stirred and opened his eyes.

Edward continued watching the countryside.

"England has never possessed a railway system on this scale."

Marco straightened and rubbed his neck.

"Neither has France."

Edward turned towards him.

"At the Academy, scholars were still arguing whether it was worth laying stone roads for carriages over a few dozen miles. We've scarcely left Marrakesh, yet we've already covered a journey that once took a week."

Marco lowered his report.

"Thank Isabella for that. Her Majesty insisted upon uniform rails, locomotives, and spare parts across every line. Workshops hundreds of miles apart must produce pieces that fit together, or the fastest train in the world will be stranded by a broken valve."

Edward tapped the window frame.

"That sounds like Isabella."

"How long we keep the advantage is another matter." Marco leaned back. "Once something works, someone will want to take it apart."

Edward turned towards the glass to hide his laughter from the sleeping mother and son. Marco folded the dispatch, and for a time they listened to the iron wheels. It was the last stretch of the journey they would share.

Marco glanced again at the news from Fes.

"Get some sleep," Edward said. "Tangier is still a long way off."

"You could use some yourself." Marco kept reading. "Men on the verge of collapse are particularly fond of claiming they aren't tired."

"Have you been taking lessons from Juliet?"

"I hardly need lessons. Twenty-five years of friendship with you have taught me enough."

…

The train ran through thickening mist. By the time the iron vault of Tangier-Ceuta Station emerged beyond the windows, the passengers were gathering their belongings.

Remi woke last, bolting upright with his hair sticking out on one side. He looked about as though he had slept through something momentous.

"Mother, have I been asleep long?"

Juliet folded the blanket.

"Long enough for Mother to enjoy some peace and quiet."

A whistle sounded outside. The locomotive slowed, wheels grinding against the rails as it entered a station vast enough to make Juliet and Remi look up together.

The glass roof was almost lost among the black iron girders overhead. Pipes along the vault released warm vapour across the platforms, melting newly fallen snow into narrow streams on the panes. Below, passengers wore light woollen coats, a luxury to the family newly arrived from Marrakesh.

The carriage door opened, and Marco stepped down first. He took a heavy trunk from the porter, set it squarely on the platform, and helped unload Remi's chest of books. Edward followed, then Juliet with the still-drowsy boy.

Isabella was waiting a short distance ahead.

The Queen sat on a stone bench beside an iron pillar, legs crossed, a porcelain teacup between her hands. In place of her familiar crimson velvet cloak, she wore a tailored grey-and-white uniform with a high collar, her dark brown hair gathered neatly behind her head.

Fredo stood behind her right shoulder, blond hair swept back, hands clasped behind him. At the sight of Marco, Isabella set her cup on its saucer and rose.

Marco approached, stopped at a respectful distance, and bowed.

"Your Majesty."

He turned towards Fredo.

"It has been a long time."

The men exchanged nods. Fredo drew a sealed dispatch from his coat while Isabella watched; her tea remained beside the pillar.

"Fresh intelligence from the east."

Marco broke the seal and scanned the first page, then slowed upon reaching the second. Before Edward was close enough to read it, he saw Marco press his tongue against his cheek.

"When did this happen?"

"The intelligence was confirmed overnight," Fredo replied. "Western Roman forces broke through the Algerian line sooner than anticipated and pushed beyond it. Several of our forward units are withdrawing towards the western assembly points."

Marco folded the dispatch, pressing the edges together.

"Splendid. I haven't even reached Fes, and the enemy has already rewritten my plans."

Isabella took the report, read another line, and lowered it.

"I had hoped you would have a few more days."

Before Marco could answer, she stepped forward and embraced him. The embrace lasted only seconds; when she drew back, her hands remained on his shoulders.

"Do everything you can. Fes will give you few chances to correct a mistake, and I have no one else who can take your place there. Hold the line for me, Marco. Then come home."

"At your command, Your Majesty." Marco blinked. "Though if Millennia hears that Her Majesty embraced me in the middle of a railway station, Fes may not be the most dangerous place awaiting me."

Isabella stepped back.

"I shall issue a declaration confirming that it was the Queen's express wish."

"That declaration is precisely what would get me confined to the house."

Edward reached them as Marco returned to the Spencer family. Marco surveyed the luggage and checked the station clock.

"Well, this is where our journey together ends."

Juliet offered her hand.

"Thank you for accompanying us, Marco."

Marco enclosed her hand between both of his.

"Juliet, if you encounter any difficulties in Madrid, seek out Millennia. She's there with Dante."

"Your son has just turned seven, hasn't he?"

"Indeed. Dante Stones, seven years old." Marco nodded. "A gentler boy than his father, fortunately for him."

Isabella confirmed the arrangements.

"Millennia and Dante were sent to Madrid some time ago. The Spencer family will join them."

Juliet turned in surprise.

"I thought we were bound for Barcelona, Your Majesty?"

"Not any longer. I'll explain the change on our way."

Marco glanced at Edward with a crooked smile.

"There, you see? You close your eyes for one train journey, and someone moves the capital."

Edward turned towards Isabella.

"Now I understand why Marco says even the fastest railway cannot keep pace with you."

"You seem remarkably quick to grasp the situation."

Marco bent to retrieve his travelling bag.

"Well, if I survive this expedition to Fes..."

Edward immediately raised a finger.

"Stop there. Nothing good has ever followed an opening like that."

Marco stared at him.

"I hadn't finished. I meant that if I return before you, I intend to visit your house in Madrid and have a proper meal."

Edward regarded him.

"So you've invited misfortune upon yourself, and mean to put it right with dinner?"

Marco shrugged.

"I expect that should do it."

Edward stepped closer, and they embraced. Marco patted his back twice; Edward kept a hand on his shoulder a few seconds longer before letting go.

Amid the hiss of steam beneath the station roof, Edward raised his fist. Marco brought his own forward, and their knuckles met. Neither withdrew.

Marco tapped twice against Edward's knuckles with his thumb, following an old rhythm from their Academy days. Edward answered with a single tap, his fist still held against Marco's.

To the east, the Second Corps, *Tercio de la Balanza*, had assembled along the military platforms. Carriages loaded with guns and provisions stretched beyond the far end of the station roof.

A whistle echoed through the iron girders. Marco glanced towards his waiting troops, then back at Edward. Their fists were still touching when he spoke the farewell their group had always used before being sent to separate commands.

"I'll see you on the other side of this war."

Edward met his gaze and squeezed Marco's shoulder firmly.

"Yes. We'll meet there."

Marco had barely turned when Remi stepped out from Juliet's side and caught the hem of his cloak.

"Uncle Marco, I'm sorry I slept through nearly the whole journey. You promised to tell me stories about Father when he was young, and I thought I was only closing my eyes for a little while."

Remi spoke in a rush, then lowered his gaze to his shoes.

"Father says Uncle Romeo exaggerates, but you promised to tell the truth. I wanted to know which subjects Father was bad at, whether he was ever punished, and whether he was as strict then as he is now."

Marco knelt until he was level with the boy, hands on his knees, and heard him out.

"Were you planning an entire interrogation?"

Remi looked up, still clutching the cloak.

"I started preparing when you said you were coming with us. I wanted to ask whether Father had ever been frightened of anything, too. But now you're leaving, and I don't know when I'll get to ask."

Marco studied him, then smoothed the hair standing up on one side of his head.

"Then keep that list safe. Don't let your father see it, particularly the last question."

Edward stood behind them with folded arms.

"I heard every word."

Remi turned at once.

"I didn't say anything bad about Father."

"I know. That's what concerns me."

Marco ruffled Remi's hair.

"In Madrid you'll meet Dante, my son. He's seven, like you, though you're rather different. Dante is gentle and quiet, and takes his time with strangers."

Remi listened carefully and nodded with grave conviction.

"Then I'll speak first. I'm very good at talking."

"That I believe." Marco brushed the hair from his forehead. "But don't take his silence as an invitation to drag him into every scheme you devise."

"If he doesn't want to climb onto a roof, don't dare him. If he loses a game, don't laugh at him all afternoon. And never imagine that because he's gentle you may bully him."

Remi frowned, looking thoroughly wronged.

"I don't bully anyone. I just... talk a little too much sometimes. And if Dante doesn't like climbing roofs, I could show him my maps."

"I've got Father's map of England. I'd like to see your map of Fes, too."

At the mention of Fes, Marco stopped smoothing his hair and tapped him lightly on the forehead.

"Maps are perfectly acceptable. I have several more at home, and Millennia knows where they are kept. Just ask before turning my study upside down."

"I will." Remi adjusted his satchel. "And if I meet Dante before you come home, I'll tell him you're well. I'll play with him so he won't feel lonely."

Marco rested a hand against the back of Remi's neck before answering.

"I don't need you to be a grown man on Dante's behalf. You two need only be children. Play together, quarrel a little, and give him time when he grows quiet."

"He's not weak. He's simply gentler than his father."

Remi pressed his lips together to suppress a smile.

"I won't tell him that last part."

"Wise decision."

The boy stood still another moment before throwing his arms around Marco's neck. Marco embraced him at once, one hand cradling his head while the other patted his back.

"Please come home, Uncle Marco," Remi whispered against his shoulder. "I've still got so many questions. And if you don't come back, nobody will tell me how foolish Father was when he was young."

Edward grumbled behind them. Marco kept one hand against Remi's neck.

"I'll do everything I can to come back and discover just how much trouble you and Dante have caused in Madrid."

He drew back enough to look the boy in the face.

"And if you meet Dante first, remember what I told you. Don't torment my son."

Remi nodded vigorously.

"I promise. But you must try to come back so you can look after him yourself."

"A fair bargain."

Marco ruffled his hair once more and stood.

Isabella, who had been watching with folded arms, finally spoke.

"Have you two just divided the responsibilities of raising children in the middle of my railway station?"

Marco straightened his collar.

"Rest assured, Your Majesty. I have entrusted the most dangerous part to Remi."

The boy immediately looked up.

"I can manage it!"

Juliet laughed, while Edward shook his head. Marco looked at each of them once more, accepted his bag from Fredo, and slung it over his shoulder. A short whistle sounded from the eastern military platforms.

This time, he did not linger.

He touched two fingers to his temple in farewell and walked into the crowd of soldiers, porters, and officers. His brown hair vanished behind woollen caps; his dark cloak appeared a few more times between passing figures, then disappeared as well.

Edward remained watching. Remi could not take his eyes from the place where Marco had vanished, one hand clutching Juliet's coat as though to remember the precise spot.

Only when Marco was lost among the people and steam did Isabella finish her cold tea and set the cup on its tray.

"Come along," she told them. "Marco has an entire front to reach, and we have business of our own."

She led them from the military platforms through a broad passage into the civilian concourse. Tangier-Ceuta impressed them less with its vaulted roof or its steam pipes than with the speed at which ordinary life reclaimed the space left by departing troops.

A baker carried a tray of steaming brown loaves from his oven. Two elderly women shared a newspaper beside a heating pillar, while children with writing slates ran past, their woollen scarves loose around their necks.

On a neighbouring track, another military train began to move. Field guns were chained to flatbed carriages, soldiers crowded the windows, and the final two coaches bore the insignia of the Castilian medical corps.

People stepped aside when the warning bell rang. Once the train had passed, tea sellers resumed pouring, children ran on, and a mother bent to straighten her child's cap. An army leaving the city had become another part of the morning.

Remi watched the train disappear behind the iron pillars, then glanced towards the civilian concourse.

"Father, is there really a war going on here? I can see cannons and soldiers, but everyone is still shopping and going to school as though nothing has happened."

Edward laid a hand on his son's shoulder.

"There is. But the people here have learnt not to let war take possession of their entire morning."

Isabella heard him but offered no comment. She led them on through the cries of vendors and the clatter of crockery that had filled the silence after the train's departure.

Fredo took two valises from Edward, who retained only his sabre and the case containing *Storm's Roar*.

Isabella touched the lid.

"The weapon the Sultan lent you?"

Edward held it close.

"On loan. He insisted I return it personally."

"Then you had better not keep him waiting."

She tapped the lid once more and walked on.

As they passed the ticket offices, Isabella slowed beside Juliet. Her gaze settled on the hand gripping Juliet's bag, where calluses and winter cracks remained visible despite the ointment applied the previous evening.

"Is something troubling you, Juliet?" Isabella asked.

Juliet looked up at the familiar address, her hand still on the strap. Isabella extended her own hand and waited until Juliet chose to place hers within it.

"The years in Marrakesh have left their marks on your hands," Isabella said, meeting her eyes. "There are fine ointments and skilled craftsmen in Madrid. I should like you to rest those hands for a while."

She examined the cracks more closely.

"You have endured far too much hard labour. I'll have medicine brought when we arrive. These wounds need cause you no further pain."

Juliet regarded her, then withdrew her hand and pulled her glove over her wrist.

"They have served me well. I'm not ashamed of them."

"I should also like to take you to the dressmakers in Madrid," Isabella continued. "You may choose whatever pleases you. After so many difficult years, you deserve clothes chosen for your own enjoyment."

Juliet kept her head raised and met Isabella's gaze.

"Your kindness is appreciated. But Edward has seen me in torn clothes, covered in mud, blood, and things far worse. He married me all the same. I believe he can endure the sight of my hands."

Isabella fell silent for a moment. Her courteous smile returned so smoothly that Fredo immediately found the valises in his hands worthy of his undivided attention.

"I know," she replied. "Edward has always been remarkably steadfast in certain preferences."

Juliet raised an eyebrow.

"At least we agree on one thing."

"Perhaps we shall find others."

Isabella resumed walking, then added as though remembering a matter of business.

"Nevertheless, I'll send the ointment and soaking preparations. A wound need not remain painful merely to prove you can bear it."

Edward bent to straighten Remi's scarf. Behind them, Fredo continued to pretend the luggage required all his attention.

title_vi: Chapter Thirteen: Ceuta Harbour
title_en: Chapter Thirteen: Ceuta Harbour
text_en:
The Royal carriage waited outside the station.

Warmth spread through its interior from concealed metal vents beneath the seats, without the least smell of coal or sulphur. Instead, a delicate, faintly sweet fragrance lingered in the air, unfamiliar enough that Edward looked up as he sat down.

"I've never encountered that scent."

He pointed towards a silver sphere suspended near the window.

"Don't tell me you've installed another invention in your carriage."

Isabella turned the silver pomander between her fingers.

"Cherry blossoms. The essential oil comes from an island nation in the Far East. When the trees flower, people sit beneath the branches, drink wine, and spend whole afternoons watching the petals fall."

Edward leaned back.

"In times such as these?"

"Especially in times such as these."

She returned the pomander to its hook.

"Six years of winter have yet to persuade them to abandon something as thoroughly unprofitable as admiring flowers. I find that rather admirable."

The carriage rolled away from the station square. Tangier-Ceuta unfolded beyond its windows, bearing little resemblance to a great fortress, though the entire city had been built to become one whenever necessary.

The principal avenues were almost free of ice, kept clear by heating pipes beneath the paving stones. Shops stood beside glass-fronted buildings, bakeries displayed fresh barley loaves, and tea houses set tables along galleries warmed by pipes at the base of the walls.

Labourers leaving their shift crowded around a soup cart, their coats dusted with coal. Farther along, two elderly men played chess while a young woman passed with a child wrapped tightly in wool.

Branch railway lines ran beside warehouses, carrying coal, ammunition, and provisions towards the harbour. Wagons carrying wounded soldiers, escorted by military surgeons, occasionally crossed the avenues between companies of infantry returning to barracks. Citizens made way, then resumed their business without lingering to stare.

Remi pressed his face against the glass. He had barely finished pointing at a cavalry patrol before his attention shifted to children throwing snowballs in a schoolyard. Juliet twice pulled him back by the collar as he leaned forward for a better view.

Juliet watched a fishmonger lift his basket out of the path of a supply convoy. The man calmly set it down and resumed weighing fish.

"In Marrakesh, an artillery column passing through would bring an entire neighbourhood to a standstill. Here, people simply step aside and return to their work."

"That is precisely what makes this difficult to preserve," Isabella replied. "I need this place to withstand war while its people continue living, trading, and sending their children to school."

Edward studied the drains and steam outlets along the streets.

"To accomplish that, you've had to make the entire city function like a machine."

"A road must carry vegetables as readily as military supplies," Isabella said, gesturing outside. "Hospitals must stand well away from ammunition stores, and waste heat from the workshops must reach people's homes. The woman going to market need only find the road free of ice; the calculations are my responsibility."

Edward pointed towards the snow beyond the heated streets.

"You speak as though ordering winter out of the way were a simple matter of administration."

Isabella watched snow sweep across the distant rooftops.

"Winter need not give its consent. Neither does anyone who wishes to kill my people."

The carriage continued towards the harbour. Beyond successive districts, agricultural domes appeared across the lowlands connecting Tangier and Ceuta. Long stretches of green barley grew beneath their coverings, an almost impossible colour amid the surrounding white.

Juliet watched the domes recede and ran her thumb along the seam of her glove.

"How long can the treasury sustain all this?"

Isabella did not evade the question.

"Not very long, if one considers each expense separately. The Council reminds me every morning."

She inclined her head towards the granaries and cranes appearing near the coast.

"But however costly Tangier-Ceuta becomes, it will remain cheaper than losing this strait."

Edward ceased looking at individual buildings. In the map taking shape within his mind, Iberia and North Africa were joined by the narrow corridor through which they travelled.

"Food, coal, steel, wounded soldiers, reinforcements. Everything must pass through here," Isabella said. "If Tangier-Ceuta becomes obstructed, Fes will starve before the Roman armies exhaust their ammunition. Lose Gibraltar, and our rear is exposed."

Edward turned towards her.

"So you're pouring resources into this city because the Pyrenees are already burning."

"Precisely."

Isabella kept her eyes on the city.

"I did not build this place to look impressive on a map. I built it so Castile would still have the means to survive when another front collapses."

Beyond the window, children leaving school passed labourers changing shifts. Across the street, a field gun rolled slowly towards the harbour.

Edward watched them.

"How much sleep have you had this week?"

Isabella narrowed her eyes.

"Less than I permit any general under my command. And before you lecture me about proper rest, remember which of us has just returned from Marrakesh after six years."

Juliet folded her arms.

"On that matter, I can testify against both of you."

Isabella turned towards her. The two women exchanged a look, and Edward could find no safe grounds on which to intervene.

…

A row of Castilian banners passed outside, reminding Remi of a question he had held back since Marco mentioned Madrid. He turned from the window, tugged at Juliet's sleeve, and looked towards Isabella.

"Aunt Isabella, when you were in Marrakesh, you said we were going to Barcelona. But Uncle Marco says Madrid. So where are we actually going to live?"

"Madrid," Isabella answered. "Since leaving Marrakesh, I've received three further reports from the Pyrenees. French pressure is mounting faster than expected, and Barcelona lies closer to the threatened approaches than I'm prepared to accept."

"Last night, I signed the order transferring the essential offices of government to Madrid."

Juliet looked at her.

"Can an entire royal court truly be moved by a single signature?"

"A signature does not pack trunks or take maps down from walls."

Isabella straightened her glove.

"But there comes a moment when deliberation must end. I chose that moment. It will take the others several days to move the government; my duty is to see that they begin before the French force us into a panic."

She explained that Madrid lay farther inland, allowing the Crown to coordinate all three fronts while offering greater safety for Remi. Millennia and Dante had already been sent there, and three houses awaited the Spencer family's consideration: one near a school, another near the medical district, and a third near the palace.

Edward turned fully towards his younger cousin.

"You prepared all three before you even knew whether I would accept the commission?"

"Of course."

Isabella made no attempt to appear innocent.

"Did you imagine I travelled to Marrakesh armed with nothing but hope? I respect your right to choose, Edward. That does not oblige me to wish you would choose differently."

Juliet had another question.

"And if I dislike all three houses?"

"Then tell me what you require, and I'll find a fourth."

Isabella answered without hesitation.

"I want Edward's family in Madrid, Juliet. I have no desire to imprison you in a house you detest."

Juliet considered the answer, then nodded. Remi had only two concerns: whether he could attend school in Madrid, and whether he could meet Dante. Isabella assured him of the first, while the second required Millennia's consent.

For a seven-year-old, that was reason enough to accept a new capital.

Isabella opened a silver-plated box beside her seat and took out a warm butter biscuit. Remi reached for it, but Juliet reminded him that he had eaten on the train, and the Queen's hand stopped at once.

Isabella turned towards Juliet.

"Just one, if you permit it. He is your son, after all."

Juliet looked at the biscuit, then at the hope so poorly concealed on Remi's face.

"One."

"Thank your mother first."

Isabella handed him the biscuit, waited until he obeyed, then stroked his hair.

Juliet studied her.

"So even a Queen knows how to ask another person's permission."

"I have always known how."

Isabella settled back.

"I do not always care for the answer. Remi is another matter."

Juliet leaned against the cushions.

"Good. Then perhaps we shall manage to live together after all."

"That is quite enough for our first day."

Edward closed his eyes for a moment. At the front of the carriage, Fredo remained the only person who appeared entirely innocent of the conversation.

…

The deeper they travelled towards Ceuta, the farther civilian life receded. Bakeries and schools gave way to steel warehouses, engine works, and training grounds. Freight lines multiplied beside ammunition stores and repair yards, while civilian vehicles grew scarce among soldiers, artillery teams, and crates bearing the Royal seal.

Fredo opened the small forward hatch to announce that they would arrive in five minutes. Isabella sat straighter and turned towards Edward.

"The city is what I wanted you to understand," she said. "What comes next is what I've truly been longing to show you."

Edward smiled.

"I'm beginning to pity your treasury."

"Not yet. You haven't seen what made it weep."

The carriage stopped before the military gates of Ceuta Harbour. The moment the door opened, bitter sea wind swept inside, making Remi shrink into his coat. Within a few steps, the city's warmth gave way to salt, engine oil, and cold iron.

Fredo brought four heavy woollen coats from the rear trunk. Isabella settled hers over her shoulders and urged the others to follow suit.

"Within the city, I can still oblige winter to remain outside the door. But down on the quays, the cold has yet to learn any manners."

Edward helped Juliet into her coat before kneeling to straighten Remi's sleeves. Isabella watched without interfering; only when the boy was bundled against the cold did she lead them through the military checkpoint.

Hammers struck steel in ceaseless succession between the docks. White steam rose from great pipes, mingling with coal smoke and sea mist. Traditional sailing warships lay along distant quays, their masts rising like a familiar forest of timber to Edward's eyes.

Then he saw what lay ahead.

An immense black mass pressed against the quay, as though someone had cut a fortress from the land and launched it into the sea.

It sat lower than the three-masted warships Edward had commanded, but its hull was broader and heavier. Armour plates ran from bow to stern, their seams tracing hard dark lines along the steel. A great funnel rose amidships, hemmed in by valves, pipes, air shafts, and fittings that a sailor might mistake for the innards of a floating foundry.

Before Edward could speak, the steam behind the dockyard parted. Beyond it, other black hulls stood under scaffolding, still taking shape.
