One had received armour along only half its side. Another revealed its frames and propeller shafts. A crane lowered a vast steel plate onto the deck of a third, its chains rattling over the thunder of the yard.

Edward stopped. He stripped off a glove and pressed his palm against the cold armour. It did not tremble with the swell as timber would; through it he felt only the steady pulse of engines deep below deck.

"Isabella, what in God's name have you done here?"

The Queen was already partway up the gangway. She turned to face him, standing straighter than she had in the carriage. Sea wind pulled her grey-and-white uniform taut, steam billowed behind her, and the monstrous hull beneath her feet growled like a sleeping beast.

"You told me the Castilian railways were faster than anything England possessed," Isabella called down. "Yet your ships must still beg the wind for passage and turn their broadsides to fire. One burning shot through a wooden hull, and hundreds of sailors die."

"I wanted to build something free of those limitations."

Edward looked up.

"Railway boilers. Pumps from the deep mines. Toledo steel. Machine tools from Valencia."

Isabella gripped the railing.

"Every workshop told me the parts could never be joined. I made them try until this great weight of steel floated."

She pointed towards the unfinished ships.

"One vessel does not make a fleet. It is the yards capable of building the second and third that give me the confidence to stand here."

Isabella climbed higher. Behind her, black hulls rose in succession beneath the cranes; below, Edward kept his palm against the armour.

"Look carefully, Edward Spencer."

She spoke his full name as a summons, not a greeting.

"Lisbon still builds sailing ships. France crowds more guns along its broadsides. Ravenna relies on ramming bows and Greek fire."

Her gaze swept the armoured deck.

"I intend to make our enemies reconsider their battle plans the moment they sight this ship at sea."

A steam hammer fell somewhere behind the slips, its blow passing across the harbour water. Isabella did not raise her voice.

"She sails under her own power. She need not wait for the wind, and enemy shot must pierce steel before it reaches her crew. Even the admiral who commands her will have to learn his trade anew."

Edward looked up at her.

"Then it isn't merely warfare you intend to change."

Isabella turned towards the scaffolding.

"People call Tangier-Ceuta the Beacon of Europe. They see the light. I must see that the furnace never goes out."

Edward's hand remained upon the cold steel.

"And you truly believe these ironclads will change the course of war?"

"I believe they'll compel every fleet to learn how to fight again," Isabella answered, looking down at him.

A valve opened beneath the deck. Its long hiss filled the pause.

"And the yards will build other things besides."

She rested her hand on the railing.

"Tonight they are masses of steel beside the harbour. Tomorrow, men must know how to take them to sea."

Valves opened in succession along the ironclad and through the dockyards beyond. White steam swept over the quay, coiled around the gangway, and shredded in the salt wind. Edward stood beside the armoured hull, his hand still resting on the steel.

To the north, news of the fighting was arriving faster than the shipyard hammers could strike.

title_vi: Chapter Fourteen: A Title Restored
title_en: Chapter Fourteen: A Title Restored
text_en:
Edward still stood beside the ironclad's rail when boots thundered up the gangway. An officer brought Isabella a dispatch, breathless.

"Your Majesty, the French are crossing the Pyrenees. Signals are coming in from the border forts without cease."

Isabella gripped the rail and demanded their positions. The officer bent over his map.

She turned to Fredo.

"Fredo, take Edward and his family to their quarters at once. See that they have everything they need."

Isabella went straight to the command deck.

Fredo collected the Spencers' luggage and escorted them below. Their cabin lay amidships, warm, a heating pipe hidden behind the steel bulkhead. Fredo set down their belongings, bowed, and closed the door.

The engines sent a steady vibration through the floor.

Remi pulled off his boots and crawled into bed. Within minutes, he was asleep.

Once he slept soundly, Juliet sat beside the small table. She clasped her hands before looking up at Edward.

"Isabella doesn't hate me. I know that."

Edward drew a chair closer.

"But?"

Juliet glanced towards Remi and lowered her voice.

"She knows you too well. Things it took me six years to understand, she sees in a glance. I'm not afraid she'll take you from me. I'm afraid you'll become Sir Edward again, and stay that way until the man who comes home is someone I no longer know."

Edward knelt and took her work-worn hands.

"Bella knew me before London. You knew me after London." His fingers tightened around hers. "Both men are me. I won't put on a uniform and pretend the last six years never happened."

"You can't promise you won't change."

"No."

He held her hands tighter.

"But I can promise this. If I ever see nothing but maps, battlefields, and duties waiting to be done, bring me back. Don't stand aside and wait for me to remember on my own."

Juliet studied him, then nodded.

"All right."

Edward kissed her cold-cracked knuckles.

"I need to visit the command deck. I want to know how bad things have become in the north before we reach Gibraltar."

Juliet caught his hand.

"Go, then. But come back before they turn you into an admiral."

Edward kissed her.

"I'll try."

When the door closed behind him, Juliet lay beside Remi. She watched it for some time.

Edward straightened his collar and followed the steel passage to the command deck.

The air inside reeked of hot iron and machine oil. A dozen officers crowded around the charts, while a head-sized Vestigium communications orb glowed blue. Each burst of interference fractured voices from the front, mingling them with artillery fire.

Edward remained outside the council.

Within, Isabella stood over the chart table, steadying the map as reports poured through the orb.

"Your Majesty, the *Tercio del Rayo* cannot hold the western Pyrenean corridor!"

Cannon fire swallowed the words. The speaker shouted over it.

"Our main force is falling back towards San Sebastián. We're joining the garrisons to defend the remaining towns. French artillery is still pursuing us."

Isabella signalled the communications operator.

"Cut that connection. Put me through to Bilbao."

She faced the operator.

"Priority connection to the Northern General Staff. I need to know which positions are still holding."

The operator adjusted the brass joints beneath the sphere. Blue light flared and died.

He tried again, but heard only interference. On the fourth attempt, the orb cracked sharply and trembled. Quarrelling voices from the Knights' Council General Staff Headquarters in Bilbao flooded the command deck.

"Bilbao, give me the whole situation," Isabella demanded. "Begin with the positions we've lost."

The reply faltered beneath artillery fire.

Isabella waited, her hand on the mountain passes.

"Then tell me where we still have artillery and reserves enough to turn this around."

"Your Majesty, the Pyrenean line is breaking at several points. Without reinforcements, we cannot hold the entire front."

A staff general answered amid gunfire and orders.

"The Fourth Corps is encircled at Pamplona. The Fifth and Sixth Corps are scattered across the passes," he reported. "In the east, the Seventh Corps still holds Perpignan, but its ammunition is nearly exhausted. Our supply routes are severed."

Isabella indicated San Sebastián.

"Send reserves from the nearest towns. Secure the road to the harbour first."

Her palm struck the chart table.

"If the Pyrenean line collapses, the defences behind it will follow. I want to know when each formation can reach its destination."

Voices quarrelled; chairs scraped.

An elderly general seized the transmitter.

"Your Majesty, the harbours around San Sebastián are burning. French ships are still bombarding them, and our supply lines have been severed. Where do you expect us to find more troops?"

"So you've exhausted every possibility?" Isabella asked sharply.

Then her restraint broke.

"You have five corps and a chain of fortresses prepared for years. How have you lost so much in three days?" She kept one hand upon the map. "I want figures and explanations, not excuses."

"Do not presume to lay the blame upon us!"

The staff general's voice shrieked through the orb, over blows upon a table.

"The weather has been merciless! Blizzards have crippled our weapons while the French deploy new siege Vestigia! And besides..."

He paused, then pressed on.

"Your Majesty personally tore a hole in our defences when you withdrew ten thousand men from the Eleventh Corps, the *Tercio del Acero*, and sent them to that wretched corner of North Africa! Without ten thousand of our finest soldiers, what do you expect us to fight with?"

Fredo stepped towards the orb, hand on his dagger.

"Those men were redeployed to defend our rear. You still command five corps. State where the enemy broke through before blaming everything upon that order."

"Enough, Fredo!"

Isabella raised a hand.

Three days was too little time for her to accept blizzards and depleted manpower as the entire explanation. Yet Bilbao still commanded essential forces, and she had no evidence with which to accuse anyone while the front collapsed.

Ordering the General Staff arrested now could turn suspicion into mutiny where she most needed men to hold their ground.

She studied the map. San Sebastián still held, but each angry exchange drove the officers in Bilbao into louder arguments.

She followed the eastern railway from Perpignan to Barcelona.

Quarrelling would send no soldiers north. She turned to the communications officer.

"Change channels. Connect me to Barcelona. I want Cassandra."

The officer reached for the brass ring and waited out the interference.

"Put me through to Barcelona Military District Headquarters immediately! I want Colonel Cassandra!"

He turned the pedestal's rings. The orb flickered before its glow steadied.

Cassandra's voice came clearly from Barcelona, amid hurried footsteps.

"Your Majesty, I am listening."

Cassandra bore the designation Diez within the Royal Guard and presently commanded Barcelona's defence.

Isabella knew her old friend could receive orders in the middle of the night without ceremony.

"Cassandra, assemble two hundred Conquistadores immediately. Put them aboard trains for Perpignan."

Cassandra awaited her next instruction. Only boots sounded in the duty room.

"The Seventh Corps is trapped there. Break the siege before the railway is cut."

Isabella marked Perpignan on the chart.

Several officers looked up.

A senior fleet officer blocked Isabella's path.

"Your Majesty, I beg you to reconsider!"

He gestured towards the orb.

"Two hundred Conquistadores are a force we cannot replace in a single winter. If we lose them at Perpignan, we'll have nothing of equal strength to reinforce the next threatened front."

"Return to your post," Isabella told him. "Your objection has been heard."

She indicated his place beside the table.

The officer refused to move. The arguments swelled.

"Send two hundred Conquistadores into Perpignan now, and they'll be trapped inside the encirclement! Withdraw another three thousand garrison troops from Barcelona, and Catalonia will be exposed. Your Majesty, we may lose both!"

Isabella leaned towards the orb again.

"Give the Conquistadores priority over every other movement on the Barcelona railway. I want them in Perpignan before dawn."

Cassandra waited out the uproar.

"And after we've broken the siege?"

"Take what remains of the Seventh Corps westward," Isabella replied. "Strike the French flanks before their advancing columns can join forces."

She marked a route west from Perpignan along the southern foothills of the Pyrenees.

"Cut off the reinforcements following them. Strike quickly, then withdraw beyond French artillery range before they can turn against you."

Cassandra confirmed her orders.

"Understood! I'll have the Conquistadores assembled and the train whistles sounding at once!"

Isabella cut the connection and faced her officers.

"Record those orders. Now, to the fleet."

No one spoke.

"Castile still stands," she said, folding her arms. "I expect you to hold your posts and obey your orders. Spare me any further oaths of courage."

She rested a hand against the chart.

"If San Sebastián falls, we lose our northern approach." Her gaze shifted to the ships marked beyond the strait. "Give me a plan to break the siege from the sea."

She approached the officers.

"The steel-armoured ships at Ceuta are complete. I intend to send them north if there's still time. Any man who objects may show me his reasons on this chart."

"But Your Majesty!"

A naval colonel stepped forward.

"If we withdraw the entire fleet from Gibraltar, we expose our rear. Western Rome is concentrating its forces at Palma, and Portugal could return at any moment. We might save the north only to lose the southern gateway."

Officers nodded towards Gibraltar and Palma.

Isabella offered no rebuke. She measured the route from Ceuta to San Sebastián, then checked the distances to Palma and Lisbon.

She studied the waters north of Gibraltar.

Sending the fleet north would leave the southern approaches undefended. Keeping it here would condemn San Sebastián's defenders to face the French guns alone.

She checked the distances again.

"Yes, our rear will be exposed. But if San Sebastián falls, the northern gate stands wide open. I accept that risk."

She planted her pen upon San Sebastián and ordered the warships prepared.

The officers returned to their stations.

"Gather the ships around Gibraltar tonight. The armoured squadron at Ceuta is to prepare to weigh anchor. Our objective is to break the naval blockade off San Sebastián."

Pens resumed.

Isabella had barely raised her hand to summon the communications officer when Edward spoke from the doorway.

"Forgive me, Your Majesty, but the ironclad fleet cannot be sent to San Sebastián."

Every head turned.

Edward emerged, his woollen coat chilled by the open deck. An officer moved to intercept him, but Fredo raised a hand.

"Stand aside. Let him finish."

Isabella frowned.

"How much did you hear?"

"Enough to know you're about to send your newest ships to perform a task they were never built for."

Edward came forward.

"Give me three minutes."

She folded her arms.

"You have three minutes."

Edward set a finger upon Ceuta and followed the Atlantic coast northward.

"These ironclads have guns and armour that wooden warships cannot withstand in a direct engagement. But they're still first-generation designs. Their weakness isn't their artillery. It's their endurance."

He tapped the Strait of Gibraltar.

"Here, they're close to the Vestigium fuel stores, workshops, and supply depots on both shores. If a boiler fails, they can be repaired. If they burn through their fuel faster than expected, they can replenish their stores."

His hand moved north.

"Send the fleet around the Atlantic coast to San Sebastián, and you're asking boilers that have never endured a long passage to run continuously through winter seas. One storm, one delayed supply vessel, one machinery failure beyond repair at sea, and your strongest warship becomes a mass of steel unable to move under its own power."

The colonel studied the route.

"Then San Sebastián must rely upon sailing ships?"

"It must still be relieved," Edward interrupted. "By vessels with the endurance to reach it."

He turned towards Isabella.

"The sailing fleet may be slower, weaker, and older. But those ships can survive for weeks upon the open ocean. Your ironclads, for the present, are a wall of steel."

Edward touched Gibraltar.

"Keep that wall here, and it guards the southern approaches to Iberia and North Africa. Send it north, and you abandon that protection while staking every new advantage you've built upon a voyage these ships have never attempted."

The naval colonel bent over Edward's proposed route.

Isabella rested a fingertip upon Lisbon.

"Then which fleet would you send north?"

"Keep every ironclad in the strait. Let their presence give Portugal and Western Rome good reason to hesitate."

Edward looked towards Lisbon.

"For San Sebastián, assemble the wooden fleet. Those ships have the range. Replenish their stores at Lisbon, then strike the French navy from the sea."

Isabella examined the route between Ceuta and San Sebastián again.

"You've just saved me from turning everything I spent the afternoon boasting about into a heap of dead iron in the Atlantic."

Edward shrugged.

"I've only seen those ships for a few minutes, and I've already found plenty to dislike."

Several officers lowered their faces towards the charts to conceal their smiles.

Isabella turned to Fredo.

"Lend me your sabre."

Pens ceased scratching. All eyes turned to Fredo.

He drew his sword and offered it with both hands.

Isabella took the sword and stood before Edward.

"Kneel, Edward Spencer."

Edward did not immediately obey.

He looked at the blade, then at Isabella, and understood her intention.

"Isabella..."

"Kneel."

Her voice neither rose nor softened.

The officers fell silent.

Edward lowered himself onto one knee upon the steel floor. Cold pierced the cloth.

Six years had passed since he had last knelt in a military ceremony. Long enough for the old titles to sound as though they belonged to a man who had died somewhere beyond London.

Isabella rested the flat of the blade upon his left shoulder, then his right.

"On behalf of the lost Kingdom of England, and by the authority of the Crown of Castile, I restore the knighthood that war took from you, though it never made you unworthy of bearing it."

The blade lifted from his right shoulder.

"Rise, Sir Edward Spencer."

No one on the command deck repeated the title.

Edward stayed kneeling.

His hand closed against his thigh. The calluses left by reins, shovels, cargo crates, and livestock pens pressed against his palm.

They were still there.

The woollen coat he had worn in Marrakesh had not vanished because a sword had touched his shoulders.

Then Edward rose.

Isabella lowered the sabre.

"This title cannot bring England back."

Edward held her gaze.

"But it still belongs to you."

She returned the sword to Fredo and looked towards the chart.

"Sir Edward Spencer, I place the fleet assembling at Lisbon under your command. The sailing vessels you once commanded are stationed there, along with one hundred Conquistadores who will accompany you north."

Isabella placed the final marker upon the map while Fredo recorded her orders.

Edward examined the route from Lisbon to San Sebastián.

"And the ironclad fleet?"

"Will remain at Gibraltar, precisely as you requested."

Isabella placed a steel marker upon the strait.

"You want a road back to England. I cannot give you England, but I can give you the sea."

Edward studied the northern waters drawn across the chart.

"You may refuse," she continued. "I need an admiral willing to contradict me when I'm about to do something foolish. If all I wanted was a man who knew how to nod, this room has no shortage of them."

Several officers lowered their eyes.

Edward looked at Isabella.

The Vestigium's blue light made the dark circles beneath her eyes more apparent than they had been on the quay.

"What about Juliet and Remi?"

"Madrid," Isabella answered at once. "Barcelona is no longer safe enough after what's happened. Millennia and Dante are already in Madrid, and your family will stay near them. I'll take Juliet and Remi there myself and ensure no one harms them."

Edward rested both hands upon the table.

"If I accept this command, I'll conduct it my way."

Isabella glanced at the calluses upon his hands.

"That's why I put the sword to your shoulders."

Edward took one last look at the northern sea route and nodded.

"Then I accept."

Isabella turned to Fredo.

"Prepare Sir Edward's full dress uniform. Inspect his weapons and arrange the route to Lisbon. He must be ready to depart the moment we reach Gibraltar."

Fredo snapped his heels together.

"At once, Your Majesty."

Edward remained beside the chart table.

For the first time in six years, someone behind him addressed him as Sir Edward, and he felt no need to turn around to discover whom they meant.

A knock woke Juliet from a brief sleep.

She straightened her collar and opened the door.

The steel panel slid aside.

Juliet stood motionless.

Edward waited in the passage with Fredo.

Hours earlier, he'd worn the old woollen coat from Marrakesh. Now his hair was neatly trimmed, his face clean-shaven, and he wore the dark blue full dress uniform of a Castilian naval admiral, its high collar edged with gold embroidery.

It fitted so well that Juliet hated how handsome he looked.

Her eyes rose from the brass buttons to his face.

"I told you to come back before they had time to turn you into an admiral."

Edward glanced down at his uniform.

"I thought I had rather more time myself."

Fredo looked between them, entered the cabin to collect the luggage, and carried it into the passage before closing the door.

Edward had barely turned back when Juliet reached for his collar. She touched the gold embroidery, testing its reality.

"It suits you," she said.

After a moment, she added, "I hate that."

Edward did not jest.

"I know."

"Where must you go?"

"Lisbon first. Then north to relieve San Sebastián."

He took the hand resting against his chest.

"I leave as soon as we dock at Gibraltar."

Juliet kept her hand upon his uniform.

"Could you have refused?"

"Yes."

"And you accepted anyway."

Edward nodded.

Juliet gripped the gold embroidery.

"I don't need you to become a legend again, Edward. I don't need them to give you back every old title, either, if the price is standing on some harbour quay, wondering which of those names will come home to me."

"Neither do I."

Edward lifted her hand to his lips.

"I accepted because I can do the work. And this time, I have a home to return to. I won't throw my life away for something, then call it duty because the sacrifice sounds noble."

He managed a faint smile.

"The Sultan has already scolded me enough for that."

Juliet wiped beneath her eyes with the back of her hand.

"Then remember it. I'm not frightened of this uniform. I'm frightened you'll wear it so long that you'll forget there's a wife and child waiting for you in Madrid."

Edward rested his forehead against hers.

"If I ever forget, just call me Edward."

"I've always called you that."

Behind them came the rustle of bedclothes.

Remi was awake, his hair sticking up on one side. He rubbed his eyes, looked his father up and down, then sat bolt upright.

"Father, you look like someone from a painting!"

Edward turned.

"Is that a polite way of telling me I look ridiculous?"

Remi shook his head fiercely, sprang out of bed, and ran over to touch the brass buttons.

"No! You look splendid, Father! Are you wearing this because you're going to fight?"

"Yes."

Edward knelt until their eyes were level.

"I have something I must do at sea."

Remi fell quiet.

His small hands remained curled around the dark blue coat.

"Will you come back to me and Mother?"

Edward smoothed his son's dishevelled hair.

"I'll do everything I can to come home."

He looked directly into the boy's eyes.

"But while I'm away, you don't have to take my place. No foolish schemes about protecting Mother. Listen to her, attend your lessons, play with Dante if you two get along, and save plenty of stories for when I return."

Remi considered this gravely, then nodded.

"I'll keep a list of questions about when you were young, too."

"Now that does worry me."

"Uncle Marco said I mustn't let you see it."

Juliet laughed through her tears.

Edward gathered his wife and son into his arms. Remi clung to his father's neck, while Juliet buried her face against his shoulder, gripping the stiff cloth of his new uniform.

For a while, none of them spoke.

Beneath the floor, the engines carried their steady rhythm through the three bodies holding one another.

By the time they left the cabin, Gibraltar had emerged through the snowy mist, its lights glowing gold.

Isabella and Fredo waited on deck.

A steam whistle sounded as the warship neared the quay.

Two carriages stood ready on the waterfront. The one bearing the royal crest would carry Isabella, Juliet, and Remi to Madrid. The other, painted military grey, awaited Edward and Fredo for the journey towards Lisbon.

Remi threw his arms around his father's neck once more on the dockside.

Edward let the boy cling to him before setting him down. Juliet stepped forward and straightened his collar twice, though it needed no correction.

"Edward."

"I'm here."

She looked at him.

The tears finally spilled over, but her voice remained steady.

"Come home."

Edward wiped a tear from her cheek with his thumb.

"I will."

Juliet caught his lapel one last time.

"Sir Edward Spencer may go to war. But the man who comes home to me must be Edward."

Edward covered her hand with his.

"I'll remember."

He kissed her without haste, then bent to kiss Remi's forehead.

When he straightened, he kept hold of Juliet's hand until Fredo called from beside the carriage.

Edward approached Isabella.

"I know you'll keep your word. But Bella, don't torment Juliet just because you can't resist."

Isabella glanced towards the woman holding Remi beside the royal carriage.

"Do you truly imagine I have that much leisure?"

She turned back to him.

"There are things I may dislike, but I will not hurt the woman who kept you alive for six years. See to your ships."

Edward nodded.

"Thank you."

Fredo clicked his heels together.

"Your Majesty, with your permission, I shall escort Sir Edward on his journey."

"Go. And see that you both return."

The two carriages departed the harbour in opposite directions.

Remi pressed both palms against the royal carriage window. Juliet sat beside him without moving, watching the grey carriage diminish in the snow.

Inside the westbound carriage, Edward kept looking back.

Fredo sat opposite, until Gibraltar's lights dwindled to a narrow band.

"I once believed Sir Edward Spencer was a man who had lost almost everything."

Edward turned towards him.

"So did I."

Fredo glanced back along the road.

"It seems you miscalculated, Sir Edward."

Edward rested his head against the carriage wall.

"I'm glad I was wrong."

Fredo extended his scarred hand.

"From this day forward, I serve under your command. It is an honour to stand beside you, Sir Edward."

Edward clasped Fredo's hand.

The restored title still sounded strange, but he no longer shrank from it.

"Then we shall look after one another, Fredo."

The carriage wheels struck a steady rhythm against the stone road.

Gibraltar vanished behind them, and the road to Lisbon opened ahead through the blizzard.

title_vi: Chapter Fifteen: Untested in Blood
title_en: Chapter Fifteen: Untested in Blood
text_en:
Events between Ceuta and Gibraltar had come too swiftly for Edward to set them in order. Their carriage had barely stopped at Jerez de la Frontera station when Fredo secured passage on the first train bound for Lisbon. Now Edward sat by the window, reading the orders Fredo had prepared for the journey, trying to make sense of the past two days.

These carriages travelling through the Iberian interior were unlike those Edward had known in North Africa. Steel, steam, and the smell of engine oil remained familiar, but springs and buffers beneath the floor softened the wheels' iron clatter. Warmth spread steadily from the seats and walls.

Edward struggled with a chair fitted with more brass valves than seemed necessary. Fredo set his valise in the corner, watched for a moment, then pointed beneath the armrest.

"Sir Edward, there's a brass valve underneath. Turn it to the right and the seat will grow warm."

Fredo poured a glass of warm water and passed it to him.

"The first trial carriage ran in North Africa. After several years spent putting right one fault after another, the design was brought onto the inland lines. They run a little more smoothly now, and hold their warmth far better. In Castile, those things are worth more than fine upholstery."

Edward drank, watching Fredo straighten his cuffs.

"You seem to know a great deal about what Isabella is doing."

"It's my duty."

Fredo glanced at his notebook.

"If Her Majesty signs an order, I must know which machine, which unit, and which man it will affect. Otherwise, I'm little more than someone carrying papers from one end of the palace to the other."

Edward's attention shifted to the dark grey leather book Fredo always kept close. Its cover had grown rough with handling, its corners worn almost white.

"I took that for a book of secret orders."

Fredo held it by the spine and shook his head.

"The Queen's appointments are kept elsewhere. This is a manuscript I work on during the long watches at night."

Edward looked again.

"A novel? What is it about?"

Fredo turned the book in his hands, his gaze resting on his reflection in the glass.

"A man trying to find his way home through a snowstorm."

He ran a finger over a frayed page.

"A man rather like you."

He glanced at Edward and hastened to add:

"I began it before the Queen sent anyone to Marrakesh to look for you. The likeness is a coincidence."

Edward settled back.

"Ha. An interesting coincidence. Tell me, then, what possessed a man so accustomed to a sword and pistol to write about a lonely exile?"

Fredo rubbed his thumb along the worn paper.

"I don't believe words ought to shout that a man is suffering. On the battlefield, men seldom have time to say they're afraid. A soldier might slip an unsent letter inside his coat before a charge, and the fellow beside him will understand enough."

He turned his pen between his fingers.

"Perhaps that's why I write so slowly. I've killed too many men to believe grief can be dressed in pretty phrases. Sometimes I wonder whether every sentence I put on the page carries the reproach of the dead."

Edward studied the notebook.

"And what answer have you found?"

Fredo rested two fingers against the page.

"Not in the sentences I manage to write, Sir Edward. It lies in the ones I cannot bring myself to finish."

He half closed the notebook but did not put it away.

"Perhaps that's why the story remains unfinished. On watch at the palace, I find myself writing about somewhere a man might return to. The colder the world grows, the more clearly he remembers how warm his home once was."

Fredo smoothed a curling corner of the page.

"That reminds me," Edward said. "Where is your family now, Fredo?"

Fredo closed the book before answering.

"My father is dead. My mother still lives in San Sebastián, in a little house beside the sea."

He gripped the notebook on his knees. At the mention of San Sebastián, he kept one hand on its spine and looked out of the window.

A long blast of the locomotive's whistle broke their conversation. Edward turned just as a train carrying wounded soldiers rushed past in the opposite direction, wrapped in white steam. It passed too quickly for him to distinguish faces at the windows, and the thunder of wheels and escaping air dwindled behind them.

The hospital train vanished. Fredo kept his notebook on his knees as Edward watched the last carriage disappear.

Edward finished his water before Fredo could change the subject.

"I grew up on the outskirts of Nottingham," he said, still looking towards the place where the train had disappeared.

He remembered damp earth at the edge of Sherwood Forest.

"As a boy I ran through Sherwood all day. I'd heard so many tales of Robin Hood that I once thought a bow was all a man needed to become a hero."

Fredo turned to listen.

"My father was a soldier in the castle garrison. My mother had worked in a brothel. When I was born, she left it, learned weaving, and earned her bread with her own hands."

Edward looked at his glass.

"We were poor, but it was a home."

Fredo laid his notebook on the table.

"And your parents, sir? Are they keeping well through this endless winter?"

Edward rubbed the glass's rim.

"They're both gone. They died defending Nottingham against the brutal raids of the Portuguese."

"I'm very sorry, sir."

Fredo lowered his eyes. Edward rose and set a hand on his shoulder.

"Don't apologise. Orders I once gave helped bring England to that day."

He took his hand away.

"For years, I woke each morning and used that knowledge to pass sentence on myself all over again."

Edward held Fredo's gaze.

"Your mother is still alive. Don't bury her in your thoughts before the war has done it for you."

Fredo looked straight back at him.

"Are you asking me to believe everything will turn out well?"

"No. I'm asking you to prepare for the worst without deciding that it must happen."

Edward glanced at a freight train travelling alongside them.

"Before Inverness, I thought an admiral who doubted himself wasn't fit to command. After Inverness, I feared hesitation so much that I hurried to settle every decision. Either way, I misread the battlefield."

"And now, Sir Edward? Do you still doubt yourself?"

Edward touched the cooling glass.

"I do. But now I doubt myself to test a decision, not to ask whether I'm worthy of giving orders."

Fredo laughed and shook his head.

"You're still young, yet you speak as though you've lived three lifetimes. Leave a little youth for the rest of us before we reach Lisbon."

Edward sat down, still smiling.

Fredo closed his book and drew a pendant from beneath his collar.

"I haven't begun writing San Sebastián's funeral sermon. My mother is more formidable than the Queen. She's cautious enough to rob me of sleep on behalf of the entire general staff."

The pendant bore a Castilian lion's head. Two Vestigium crystals glowed reddish orange in its eyes, giving off heat. Beneath its chin, the word Tres was cut deep into the metal.

Fredo tapped the lion.

"To spare us another introduction: Tres. Number Three."

"Marco is Ocho, and Romeo is Doce. If you're wondering whether I'm better than either of them, the answer is still yes."

He settled the pendant against his chest.

"As for San Sebastián, I'd rather get there myself before I declare victory."

Edward looked from the lion to Fredo.

"Ah. Royal Guard Number Three has returned."

"I never went away," Fredo replied, perfectly solemn.

"What a pity."

Both laughed. Fredo leaned back, one hand resting on his stomach.

"Are you hungry yet, Sir Edward? I expect your stomach has begun to make itself heard."

Edward glanced at the empty plate on the side table and nodded. He had eaten no proper meal since Ceuta.

"Splendid."

Fredo pulled the cord of a brass bell near the carriage ceiling.

"I'll have a proper meal brought in. Eat your fill, because the moment we reach Lisbon we'll be off this train and putting to sea."

While they waited, Edward glanced at the place beneath Fredo's collar where the Tres pendant had disappeared. He tapped the table.

"Tres, Ocho, Doce. What do those numbers signify? A ranking of fighting ability?"

"Hardly. Isabella places people according to how much she needs to trust them. The lower numbers tend to carry duties where a mistake costs dearly."

"So Number Three doesn't necessarily mean you could defeat Marco, Number Eight?"

"In a serious fight, I'd still win."

Fredo shrugged, openly smug.

Edward shook his head.

"I'm beginning to see why you're so difficult to like."

Fredo opened his notebook. With a touch of the quill he drew a small circle and wrote Isabella's name within it.

"One hundred members of the Royal Guard answer directly to the Queen," he said, studying the circle. "Some guard the palace, some command troops, and others keep watch over intelligence from the front. When an order must go out at once, she knows exactly whom to summon."

Edward pointed at the name.

"A hundred people to keep the whole army loyal?"

"To learn what's happening before it's too late. Men on the front line cannot wait for an order to pass through every level of headquarters."

Fredo glanced at the carriage door and lowered his voice.

"Though I sometimes think Her Majesty has news from someone even the Royal Guard has never met."

Edward raised an eyebrow.

"A Vestigium?"

"There have been times when the Queen knew something far too early. The report hadn't arrived, no one had dared speak a certain name, yet she already had her reply ready."

Fredo paused.

"I've recognised traces of a Legendary-class Vestigium in such matters. But I don't know what being is behind them, and I've never met it."

Edward remembered Isabella answering before official reports arrived.

"So whenever that girl answers too quickly, I'll have one more thing to be suspicious of."

Edward asked no more. As Fredo prepared to draw further branches from the circle, the door opened.

"Your meal, gentlemen."

A female attendant wheeled a small serving cart into the compartment. Two steaming plates of lamb stewed with vegetables, crisp toasted bread, and potatoes dressed with butter soon covered the table. Fredo rescued his notebook from the gravy.

"Salvation, and just in time," he said, breaking bread into the stew. "At least the railway cooks remember that soldiers must eat."

Edward cut into the tender lamb while watching dark freight wagons on the neighbouring line. Through the misted glass he saw wheat, salted meat, and military stores stamped with the royal seal, bound north.

He pointed at the passing wagons.

"The Royal Guard helps Isabella give orders. But what army can hold the front when those supplies are late?"

Fredo lowered his fork.

"The Tercio are the men who must hold the roads and strongholds. Without those wagons of grain, ammunition, and coal, more soldiers would do us little good."

Fredo pushed his plate aside as the train shuddered.

"The infantry bear the heaviest burden. They hold the line long enough for the others to come up."

He drew a small map closer.

"In the south we have Moorish, Berber, and Algerian troops accustomed to the climate. The Crown is also gathering the displaced English into the English Exile Corps."

Edward stopped with his fork inches from his mouth.

"Exile..."

He watched the freight wagons. Fredo said nothing, lowering his gaze to his food while Edward watched the lit windows slip away behind them.

"One day," Edward said, "that word will no longer have to stand before the name of an Englishman."

He ate another mouthful, then deliberately changed the subject.

"Speaking of army corps, where did you eat the worst field rations of your life?"

Fredo pinned a piece of bread with his fork.

"Perpignan. Our supplies failed during the siege. We found some crescent-shaped pastries in an abandoned bakery, and they tasted better than anything I've had at a royal feast."

Edward burst out laughing.

"In northern France, we had mouldy bread. Half the men were praying they'd find a privy before the day was out."

Fredo joined him, and for a while their talk of rations displaced the arrows on the map.

Their stories passed from army fare to stomach complaints and the tricks practised by field cooks. At last Fredo mopped up the remaining gravy with his final morsel of bread and rested an elbow on the table.

He pointed at the last smear of sauce.

"Conquistador troops break what the Tercio cannot penetrate. The Reliquiario go after things a whole regiment of riflemen wouldn't know how to bring down."

Edward set down his fork.

"With their Vestigium equipment, the Conquistador can break a defended position, even withstand the force of a Miracle for a short while. But they cannot do the work of an entire corps."

Fredo drew a line through the moisture on the table.

"The Reliquiario hunt original Vestigium and malformed beings. In those battles, a rifle is scarcely enough to show a man which way to turn."

Edward nodded.

"One breaks an enemy's line. The other deals with things that have no business appearing on a battlefield."

"Exactly."

The train began to slow. Through the window, the lamps of Sevilla station emerged amid a thin covering of snow.

"And the last branch?" Edward asked, rising to put on his coat before the train stopped.

Fredo shut his book, donned his coat, and followed him onto the platform.

"The garrisons hold the stores, streets, and fortresses until the Tercio arrive," he explained as they stepped down. "Few remember them when the victory is won, but without them there would be no road left for the others to take."

They had some thirty minutes before the train continued to Lisbon. Raised voices near the ticket barrier began to drown out the whistles.

Beneath a brass lamp, a drunken man in a coat bearing yellow stripes on red was snarling at the station staff. He waved an old Don's insignia at the barrier, demanding to pass without showing a ticket. Two employees tried to keep the way clear; when he began shoving passengers, Fredo gave Edward his valise and stepped forward.

"Please stand back, everyone. Leave this to me."

Recognising his Royal Guard insignia, the station workers withdrew to let him speak. Edward stayed close, ready to help anyone pushed from the queue.

"You've had too much to drink, sir," Fredo said, offering his hand rather than advancing on him. "Let me see your ticket. I'll have someone take you somewhere to rest."

The man struck Fredo's hand aside.

"Who the devil are you to lecture me? You snot-nosed brat! These stupid women don't know who I am, and you..."

He thrust a liquor-reeking finger towards Fredo and the female attendants.

"You whores are all in league with that..."

He swung at an attendant approaching him. Fredo stopped him with a short punch.

The drunk struck the stone floor. Fredo checked that he was breathing, then handed him over to the garrison soldiers arriving at a run.

"Take him to the guardhouse and have a physician examine him. Then draw up a report and send the matter to the proper authorities for judgement."

The garrison commander bowed and ordered his men to carry the man clear of the passengers.

"At once, sir!"

The crowd parted for the stretcher. Edward watched it pass and turned to Fredo.

"I see what the garrison does. But what of that Don's insignia?"

Fredo folded his handkerchief.

"I take it you mean the title Don?"

"And the fact that you can knock its bearer senseless and order him arrested before an entire station."

A whistle sounded. They returned to their carriage before the doors shut.

As the train drew out of Sevilla, Edward looked back along the platform.

"A Don can bully railway staff, yet you can detain him without trouble. What power does the Council of Knights truly hold?"

Fredo watched his tea tremble with the wheels.

"The people of Castile, Aragon, Navarre, León, Valencia, Andalusia, and the great houses must all sit at one table. Some have lands and soldiers of their own. Others possess little more than an old title."

"Yet those soldiers took your orders rather than his."

"A Don may have an entire square bow to him and still have no authority over the Royal Guard or the Tercio. Respect and the right to command are two different things."

Fredo tapped his cup.

"Local troops still defend their own lands. But in matters concerning the fleet or the Tercio, a private coat of arms is no substitute for military orders."

He arranged three little groups of sugar crystals on the table.

"The Council has one hundred and twenty seats. Forty belong to the Royal Guard, and twenty-five to nobles sworn to Isabella, Victoria Valdes among them."

Edward nudged two groups together with his spoon.

"So Isabella has a hand upon more than half the chamber before debate even begins."

"Isabella calls it a way of keeping the Council from arguing until the frontier is in flames."

Fredo pushed a grain of sugar towards Edward.

"Able men still receive their duties. I don't care for every nobleman, but at sea you cannot choose your comrades merely because you like them."

Edward leaned back.

"Then Isabella restored my title of Sir to give me a place in that structure? To let me stand before the Council in my own right?"

Fredo considered this, then shook his head.

"Perhaps in part. But I won't invent the Queen's intentions to satisfy your curiosity. There are things I don't know."

Edward let the matter rest. He took a sip of tea, watching the steam quiver above the cup as the wheels turned, until Fredo tapped the window.

"Look outside, sir."

Snow-covered fields reached to the horizon. Farther off, a river lay frozen into a dull white road, with a convoy of wagons making its way across the ice.

"You held command of the Atlantic before this winter," Fredo said, pointing to the wagons. "How greatly has war at sea changed?"

Edward watched for several moments, then took a notebook from his travelling bag.

"From the ground beneath us to the sea beyond it."

He sketched a coastline.

"The North Sea, the Baltic, and the English Channel are so thick with drifting ice that a fleet may lose ships by straying from a safe passage. West of England and France there's still open water, but no captain can sail blindly by his old charts."

"Parts of the Seine, Rhine, and Danube freeze hard enough to carry gun wagons. The sea has fallen, laying bare shoals and reefs," Edward said, marking the coast. "A captain must remember where there used to be water."

He pointed south.

"The Mediterranean still holds some warmth, and storms rise where cold water meets warmer air. We must sound the passages afresh each year."

Fredo studied the crowded page.

"Your body may have left the service years ago, but your mind never left the sea."

Edward drew the notebook closer.

"Running away didn't make the ocean cease to exist. I only prepared for whatever might one day follow me home."

He pushed the book between them.

"And Castile? What doctrine does your general staff trust?"

Fredo took the pen.

"Once, fleets held their line, gained the weather gauge, and fired broadsides. Formation, speed of loading, and the wind decided nearly everything."

He drew two parallel lines of ships and struck them through.

"The line of battle depended on wind and the guns' rate of fire. Now drifting ice turns it into a row of targets. We call the new doctrine 'Open Corridors and Close-Quarters Engagement.'"

Edward gave a small gesture for him to continue.

"First, the light vessels."

Fredo sketched a frigate beside a three-decked ship of the line.

"Frigates, corvettes, and galleys can pass through shallow waters. Their bows are plated with steel reinforced with Vestigium to break thin ice. The great warships strike harder, but turn more slowly."

Edward pointed his pen at the frigate's masts.

"A lighter vessel is less steady when weight gathers aloft. A snowstorm can coat its rigging and sails with inches of ice, adding tons high above the deck. How does a frigate rolling in heavy seas bear such a burden?"

Fredo's pen came to rest.

"The crews are ordered to break ice from the rigging continually and shorten sail when storms approach."

"If they have time. And if the storm breaks during an engagement?"

Fredo examined the drawing.

"The general staff has found no complete answer."

He turned the page.

"Next, closing with the enemy. Long-range gunnery is uncertain in fog and ice, so we wait until we're close enough to sweep their decks with grapeshot."

"If the enemy allows you to close," Edward said, touching the sketch.

Fredo followed his pen.

"What do you mean?"

"Fire rafts. Shipboard mortars. Gunboats bearing Vestigium that can summon fire."

Edward marked the diagram.

"An enemy need only keep beyond your guns and make you give chase. How do you force him within range?"

Fredo bent over the drawing and, rather than arguing, wrote in the margin.

"Force the range. I see."

Edward tapped the three notes.

"And your last pillar?"

"Terrain."

Fredo sketched San Sebastián Bay.

"Draw the enemy into the bay mouth, between shoals and drifting ice. Small ships lure him in, while boats sound bells or send false signals through the fog."

Edward traced a line from the bay towards Biscay.

"Who has the better charts?"

Fredo stopped writing.

"That depends on the waters."

"I mean San Sebastián and the Bay of Biscay."

Fredo could name no one. Edward touched the sketched entrance to the bay.

"A trap works only when the hunter knows the ground better than his prey. If the enemy captain knows the shoals and currents, and sees through your signals, that same narrow passage will cut off your own retreat. Your decoy may become the one trapped."

Fredo set down his pen and reread the three pages, marking each fault Edward had raised. He underlined three lines.

"Light vessels gather ice on their rigging. Close action needs a way to force the range. A coastal trap needs better charts than the enemy's."

He read his notes once more and looked up.

"Anything else, Admiral?"

Edward rested his elbows on the table.

"One question, more important than all the others."

"Ask it, sir."

"Since the Long Frost began, has Castile won a single true naval battle by this doctrine?"

Fredo fell silent. He turned through his notes without finding a victory to offer in reply.

Edward drew the notebook towards him and shut it.

"Theory isn't useless, Fredo. It becomes dangerous when men take something never tested in blood for the truth."

He looked into the darkness beyond the glass.

"It's late. Get some rest. We have a naval base to reach tomorrow."

Fredo nodded, though the notebook remained open on his knees.

"Yes, Admiral."

Edward had barely leaned back before he sat upright again.

"Wait. Before you sleep, establish contact with Lisbon Naval Command."

Fredo straightened at once.

"Do you mean to change the doctrine?"

"Not yet. I mean to deal with something that could kill us before we meet the enemy."

Edward pointed to the frost forming on the carriage window.

"Tell Lisbon to try mixing heat-giving Vestigium powder with whale fat, then paint it onto sails and rigging. The fat should keep the water off, and the Vestigium keep them warm. Have them test it before sending ships to sea."

Fredo snatched the communication sphere from his baggage, but Edward raised a finger before he could activate it.

"And have at least three great ships of the line made ready, each with four gun decks. Check that they're fit to sail. I'll inspect them myself when we arrive."

Fredo blinked.

"You've just told me how unwieldy those great ships are."

"I said casting them aside altogether was a wager, not that they were worthless. Light ships give us freedom to manoeuvre. Heavy ships give us something the frozen sea cannot replace: a gun platform that can stand punishment when the enemy refuses to fight by our rules."

Fredo looked at the two requests he had written down.

"I understand."

The Vestigium sphere flared blue in Fredo's hands, illuminating the fresh notes upon the page. He relayed both orders to Lisbon and waited until each had been acknowledged. With that done, Edward settled into his seat while Fredo continued writing beside the pages once reserved for his novel.

When the sphere's light went out, the first lights of Lisbon had appeared on the far horizon. Fredo still held his pen over the unfinished manuscript, while Edward sat motionless, watching the lights grow larger beyond the cold glass.

title_vi: Chapter Sixteen: A Day in Juliet's Life
title_en: Chapter Sixteen: A Day in Juliet's Life
text_en:
The train from Gibraltar reached Madrid shortly after noon, its whistle echoing between the walls surrounding the capital. By the time the three travellers boarded the royal carriage, lamps were burning beneath the grey skies of the Long Frost.

Juliet sat beside the window, her work-roughened hands resting upon the goatskin skirt she had brought from Marrakesh. Remi had all but pressed his nose to the glass and kept tugging at her sleeve to point out one marvel after another.

"Mother! Mother, look!"

He pulled at her sleeve again.

"I can see, Remi. Don't press your face against the glass. It's cold."

"But look, Mother! All the snow has melted off the rooftops!"

Juliet looked up despite herself. Beyond the carriage window, Madrid extended beneath the sombre winter sky, a world so unlike Marrakesh that the two cities scarcely seemed to belong to the same age.

Grey and red sandstone houses stood in ranks along the streets. Above the central thoroughfares, great panes of glass arched over black iron frames, sheltering the roadway from falling snow. Beneath the paving stones on either side of the avenues ran networks of copper pipes, their vents breathing thin white steam.

Snow that strayed beneath the canopies melted as it touched the warm stone. Water trickled towards the gutters and vanished into the drains.

Here there were no leaning mudbrick houses hoarding what warmth they could from blocks of heated red limestone. No thin oxen dragged carts through drifts so deep that every step seemed an ordeal.

Instead, carriages rolled along clear roads. Soldiers marched in orderly files, well clad against the cold, and shopfronts shone with Vestigium lamps so brilliant that Juliet had to narrow her eyes.

In the middle of a square, a fountain was running.

Juliet watched the water leap and fall into an unfrozen basin. She thought of the bucket at home in Marrakesh, whose ice she had broken every morning with the back of a knife so Edward and Remi might wash their faces.

Here, water rose freely into the freezing air merely to give passersby something pleasant to look at.

She gently drew Remi away from the glass. She could not tell whether the sight made her glad or angry; she only knew that hands accustomed to saving every ladle of water suddenly seemed to have no place here.

"Beautiful, isn't it, Juliet?"

Isabella's voice came from the opposite seat.

The Queen wore her grey and white military uniform, with cream gloves unstained by coal dust. Juliet looked at those immaculate hands, then down at her own worn clothing.

"Your Majesty... it is magnificent."

"Only magnificent?"

Isabella tilted her head, the hint of a smile touching her mouth.

Juliet searched for some fitting reply and found none. Her gaze fell to her faded leather shoes before she ventured an explanation.

"In Marrakesh... if we had a street as fine as this, without a trace of ice, I daresay people would carry their beds outside and sleep there just to keep warm."

Isabella laughed. Even the coachman had to turn away to conceal a smile.

"Perhaps you ought to try it."

The Queen's eyes glinted with mischief.

"If you truly mean to spread a bed across Calle Mayor, I'll order the soldiers to close the whole street for you."

"Oh, no! I never meant anything of the kind!"

Juliet waved her hands in dismay, which only made Isabella laugh harder. Remi joined in, his small shoulders shaking, though he understood little of the joke. Juliet lowered her head, her ears burning.

The feeling had followed her all through the journey. People here seemed to know by instinct how to conduct themselves.

They laughed at the proper moment and sat with the proper bearing. They knew which spoon to take for each course, where to rest their hands, and how far to bow without seeming awkward or uncouth.

And what did Juliet know?

She could tell how many frosts a turnip had endured. She knew how much wood a stew needed to last through the night without scorching, how to read a gathering storm in the clouds, and how to recognise a cow nearing labour from the rhythm of its breathing.

Madrid had not made such knowledge worthless. It was simply the first place in years where her family's survival did not depend on her putting it to use every day.

The carriage stopped before a three-storey villa in a quiet residential quarter. Isabella descended first, helped Remi from the step, then moved aside for Juliet.

Juliet carried her worn leather valise. Remi clutched a cloth bag containing his wooden ship and several pieces of wood he had yet to finish carving. They waited before the great oak door while Isabella fitted a key into the lock.

"This is your home now. The ground floor has a sitting room and a bedroom for you and Edward. On the first floor are Remi's room and the guest room; the second has a study, a sewing room, and a balcony overlooking the canal."

Juliet entered.

Waxed pine boards gleamed beneath her shoes, and dry wood scented the air around the built-in hearth. Without thinking, she searched beside the door for a water bucket, a basket of logs, and somewhere to hang wet clothes.

In Marrakesh, those things had always been close at hand.

"The house has been paid for, and my men are stationed at either end of the street," Isabella continued. "Millennia Stones will come round first thing tomorrow. Afterwards, someone from the Ministry of the Interior will ask what else you need. Tell them plainly, whatever it is."

Juliet set down the valise and gripped her faded ash-grey skirt between her rough fingers. She bowed her head.

"Thank you, Your Majesty. You have done so much for Remi and me already."

Isabella studied the weariness in Juliet's face, and the deep cracks that years of work and cold had left in her hands. Then she looked away, gave a small nod, and drew up the hood of her cloak.

"Rest now, Juliet. Both of you. You've come a long way."

The Queen departed. The sound of carriage wheels dwindled beyond the gate.

Remi dropped his bag and scrambled onto a sheepskin chair, only to jump down again and test the warmth beneath his feet.

"Mother! It's enormous! And the fireplace doesn't sting my eyes with smoke like the old one!"

Juliet shut the oak door and slid its brass bolt home.

Remi kicked off his battered shoes and scampered over the polished pine boards, his bare feet pattering through the rooms. Then he halted in a corner of the sitting room, crouched down, and pressed both palms flat against the floor.

"Mother! There's a fire underneath, isn't there? It's lovely and warm!"

"I don't believe it's fire, darling. There must be hot-water pipes under the boards."

Juliet left her valise at the foot of the stairs and knelt beside him. She rested her hand on the warm wood.

For four winters she had known the sting of walking barefoot over damp, cold floors. Now Remi merely wanted to know where the pipes ran, and she had to blink several times before she answered.

In the kitchen, Remi discovered a curved copper tap above a white stone basin. He rose on tiptoe and turned its valve.

Clear water rushed out, struck the side of the basin, and splashed across his shirt. He stumbled backwards, eyes round with the horror of a boy convinced he had done something dreadful.

"Good heavens!"

Juliet rushed over and wrestled with the unfamiliar brass handle. A little jet struck her nose and sprayed the hair at her temples before she finally managed to shut it off.

Remi took one look at his mother's dripping face. For a moment he stared, then folded over with laughter.

"Mother, you look like a drowned rat!"

"Do I indeed? And since when have you been bold enough to tease your mother?"

Juliet wiped her nose and laughed, then flicked a few drops of water at his forehead. Remi shrieked happily and fled through the kitchen door into the next room.

At the end of the ground floor passage lay the master bedroom. Remi hurled himself onto the enormous bed and sank into its thick, soft mattress. He rolled across the sheets, slapped them with both hands, and looked up at her.

"Mother! Your bed and Father's is twice as big as ours in Marrakesh!"

Juliet followed him inside. Tall glass doors overlooked a little garden and the artificial canal behind the villa. Beside the bedroom was a bathing chamber lined in white marble, with a deep stone tub.

She touched the warm wall, smiling faintly at the comforts Isabella had thought to provide.

"Come along, sailor! Off the bed!"

Juliet clapped her hands.

"Let's see what's waiting in your room upstairs."

Remi bounded from the mattress and dashed up the stairs to the first floor, his skinny bare feet thumping on the boards.

He pushed open the first bedroom door overlooking the street and gave a cry of wonder. Daylight poured through the broad window onto a polished oak writing desk and shelves fitted neatly against the wall.

Holding his cloth bag close, he approached the desk with unusual care. He took out his little wooden ship, set it on the polished surface, and stroked the grain.

"Mother... is this where I'll learn to write Latin, the way Father told me?"

His eyes shone. There was a tremor in his voice that Juliet seldom heard.

"Yes, sweetheart. You'll study here and learn all sorts of wonderful things."

She drew his head against her and smoothed his unruly hair.

They explored the guest chamber and a smaller study at the end of the passage. Remi cared little for either, but was delighted by a wardrobe of fragrant wood, into which he promptly disappeared.

Juliet pretended to look for him, then pulled the laughing boy from his hiding place. Their laughter rang through the floor.

"There is another storey yet. Shall we see what's up there?"

Together they climbed to the second floor, the highest in the house. The air here seemed quieter, almost solemn.

Edward's study lay straight ahead, furnished with a great map table, shelves rising to the ceiling, and a brass telescope beside the window.

Remi stood on tiptoe to peer through the telescope at the red roofs of Madrid beyond.

"Mother! I can even see carriages on the avenue!"

Juliet wandered into the room opposite. It was a workroom prepared for her, with an ebony sewing table and an embroidery frame standing in the light of the window.

Double doors at the far end of the passage opened upon a broad balcony above the warm canal. A winter breeze caught loose strands of Juliet's hair, bringing with it the scent of frost and fragrant garden herbs.

Remi ran out and flung his arms around her waist. Side by side at the sandstone balustrade, they watched brilliant red maples reflected in the slow-moving water below.

Grey afternoon light faded beyond the villa's windows. After Juliet had arranged what little they owned from her worn valise and Remi's cloth bag, the boy's first-floor bedroom had begun to look inhabited.

Remi sat upon the woollen rug at the foot of his bed, both hands pressed to his stomach.

"Mother... my tummy's rumbling. Have we got anything for supper?"

Juliet stopped what she was doing. Throughout the journey from Gibraltar she had thought only of shelter and their safety, scarcely once considering how she would feed them when they arrived.

She stroked his hair.

"Give me a moment, darling. I'll look in the kitchen."

She went downstairs, passed through the dining room, and opened an oak pantry door in the kitchen. The sight within brought her to an astonished halt.

Every shelf was filled. There were bags of fine flour, rolled oats, salted butter in waxed paper, smoked sausages, hard cheeses, fresh eggs, and jars of fruit preserves, all arranged in tidy compartments.

A small parchment had been fixed inside the door. Its writing was fine, neat, and decisive.

*All provisions have been stored according to royal household standards. Should any food approach spoilage, kindly wrap it in waxed paper and place it upon the shelf outside the front gate. The supply staff will take it to the farms for animal feed.*

The note bore the signature Isabella Testarossa.

Juliet read it for a long while, grateful that supper was already provided and almost ashamed to find that someone had even made arrangements for their scraps.

She rolled up her sleeves and set to work with flour, eggs, and a few slices of smoked sausage. Soon the kitchen was filled with the smell of buttery toast and eggs sizzling in the pan.

They ate together at the pine table. Remi cleared his plate in a hurry, praising every mouthful.

After supper, Juliet took him to the bathing chamber on the ground floor. The deep stone tub and its array of turning valves proved nearly as bewildering as the kitchen tap.

She tried each valve with care until hot water filled the tub and clouds of steam misted the mirror.

"Come along, my little sailor."

Juliet washed the dust of the journey from his skin and worked jasmine-scented soap through his tangled hair. As she poured warm water over his shoulders, she gave him a gentle warning.

"Mother is only showing you how to wash properly this once. Tomorrow you'll bathe yourself before bed, because you're a big boy now. Do you understand?"

"Yes, Mother! I understand!"

His eyes were screwed shut against the soap, but he nodded eagerly and smiled. Juliet dried him, dressed him in a soft linen nightshirt, and handed him a lamp.

She watched him trot upstairs towards his bedroom, carrying his light with care.

Only when she was alone in the steam-filled chamber did Juliet remove her old ash-grey travelling dress, still heavy with dust from the road. She lowered herself into the hot water and closed her eyes.

The ache of six years' hard labour seemed to loosen in the warmth. Yet the silence and luxury surrounding her left her uneasy, troubled by thoughts she could not quite name.

She stayed until her pale skin had turned comfortably pink, then rose reluctantly from the tub. Taking a thick cotton towel from its hook, she dried her hair and the droplets lingering upon her shoulders.

Then she reached, from force of habit, towards the other hook where her clean clothes ought to be.

Her hand found nothing.

Juliet stared at the bare wood. Only then did she remember carrying all her spare clothes from Marrakesh up to the sewing room on the second floor earlier that afternoon.

"Oh, heavens above..."

She shut her eyes and pressed a hand to her forehead. After attending to everything else, she had forgotten the simplest thing of all.

To fetch her clothes, she would have to cross the ground floor passage, climb the main staircase, pass along the first-floor landing, and ascend another flight of stairs. Doing so in a bath towel meant staking the dignity of a respectable mother upon the dismal odds of Remi remaining quietly in his room.

Seven years of motherhood had taught Juliet one certainty: her son invariably appeared at the very moment she most needed a little peace.

The slightest sound in the passage might bring that tousled head peering around a corner. And if the towel should happen to slip just then...

Juliet shivered and tightened its fold across her chest.

"No. Absolutely not."

She could, of course, put her travelling dress back on. The old grey wool lay crumpled on a chair, black with coal dust along the hem and still carrying the sharp odour of locomotive smoke from the journey.

Juliet looked at the dress. The dress seemed to look back.

After several miserable moments, she wrinkled her nose and shook her head.

"I'd sooner die than put that on after a bath."

She wrapped the towel as firmly as she could, tucking its edge under one arm, and crept towards the door. Opening it a crack, she peered down the passage like a thief searching for patrolling soldiers.

Only when she was satisfied that Remi was still upstairs did she hurry across to the master bedroom next door.

She closed the door softly and breathed out. Her fingers remained pressed to the towel at her chest, partly from modesty and partly from caution.

In the mellow light of the lamps, a towering walnut wardrobe stood against the wall. Juliet took hold of its brass handles and opened both doors.

The catches clicked. She stood rooted to the spot.

Like the pantry, the wardrobe had been stocked for the two people who were meant to occupy the room. On one side hung immaculate white shirts, a dark blue officer's dress uniform, and stout coats cut to Edward's measurements.

So much careful provision spoke plainly of the regard in which the royal household held her husband.

The other half had been reserved for Juliet. Its contents were rather more difficult to understand.

Glittering evening gowns hung alongside nightdresses made from silk so thin she could nearly see through it. She lifted one, turning it in her hands, unable to imagine what occasion might call for such a garment.

The lowest drawer was stranger still. Inside lay tiny pieces of coloured silk, held together by narrow ribbons and delicate straps.

Juliet picked one up between finger and thumb, wondering if it might be a handkerchief. A second examination persuaded her to put it down.

"Do women in Madrid truly wear these things?"

She glanced at the towel around her body and closed the drawer before imagination could supply an answer.

"Certainly not today."

She wanted only something clean, respectable, and properly sewn, fit for an ordinary woman to wear without embarrassment. Perhaps the smaller wardrobe held better prospects.

Its first gown was crimson silk, so heavily embroidered with gold that Juliet passed over it at once. A second, in pale cream, had a neckline little more reassuring than the nightdresses.

At last she found a dark blue-grey gown, modest across the bodice, with a high enough collar, sleeves reaching below the elbows, and a skirt nearly brushing her ankles.

She held it up and studied it, then cast a wary look at the other wardrobe, half expecting those curious silk triangles to crawl from their drawer unaided.

"Well... at least this looks like clothing."

Whether the gown belonged at a dinner, a ball, or an audience with the Queen no longer mattered. Juliet hugged it to herself with the gratitude of a woman who had just found a lifeline.

A few minutes later she emerged from the bedroom arrayed in altogether more splendour than the occasion warranted. The skirt swept softly across the boards, while her damp hair had been gathered in haste at the nape of her neck.

Anyone seeing her might have thought she was preparing for a royal banquet. Juliet was merely trying to retrieve her nightdress.

Gathering the blue-grey silk in both rough hands, she climbed the stairs. More than once the unfamiliar weight and length threatened to trip her, but she reached the sewing room on the second floor and collected her old clothes.

On the way down she stopped on the first-floor landing and opened the door to Remi's room.

He was already asleep. Curled beneath a spotless white sheepskin blanket, he held his half-finished wooden ship against his chest.

Juliet drew the blanket over his shoulders and kissed his forehead. His hair smelled faintly of jasmine now, rather than the coal smoke and desert dust of Marrakesh.

When she shut the door, leaving his quiet breathing behind, the stillness of the large villa seemed to gather about her.

Back in the ground-floor bedroom, she took off the cumbersome gown and dressed in her familiar nightdress of coarse cotton. She pushed the costly silks into a corner of the wardrobe, then carefully hung her old grey dresses and faded, oft-mended clothes beside Edward's uniforms.

They looked absurd together. Yet when the frayed hem of one dress touched the dark wool of her husband's coat, a small peace settled over her.

Juliet blew out the candle on the ebony table and lay down upon the enormous bed. Its soft mattress gave beneath her tired body, but that very softness kept her awake.

For four winters in Marrakesh she had slept on a narrow, hard bed. She was accustomed to waking when wind found a gap in the door, or when the fire's crackle faded into silence.

Without thinking, her body tensed and she began to sit up.

It was time to check the cloth stuffed about the window frame, lest the wind had loosened it. Then she ought to go downstairs, stir the ashes over the coals to keep the fire alive until morning, and look at the water bucket while she was there.

If a skin of ice had formed, she would move the bucket nearer the hearth. Otherwise they would be breaking it with the back of a knife at dawn.

Half upright, Juliet stopped.

The double-glazed windows were firmly closed. No draught stirred their edges, and hot water ran quietly through pipes beneath the floorboards. The built-in hearth could keep its coals alight until morning without anyone rising to tend it.

She sat motionless for some time.

In Marrakesh, the cold had never allowed her hands to rest. There was always a gap to seal, a fire to guard, a bucket to save from freezing, or a blanket to pull higher over Remi.

Every worry had given her something to do.

Here there was nothing. The house asked nothing of her, needed nothing rescued.

Her calloused hands lay idle upon the soft coverlet, strangely without purpose.

At last she lay back and turned on her side. Through the tall glass doors, the glow of carbide streetlamps drew pale golden bands across the room. Snow gathered on the bare maple branches in the garden, unable to pass through the thick glass.

A narrow band of light fell over the other half of the bed. Juliet looked at it.

This bedroom had been prepared for husband and wife. Behind her, Edward's uniforms hung ready in the wardrobe, and on the highest floor his study awaited him, with its map table, shelves, and telescope by the window.

There was a place for Edward everywhere in the house. Yet Edward had never crossed its threshold.

His half of the bed lay smooth and untouched.

Juliet drew up her knees, suddenly longing for the cramped room they had left behind. In Marrakesh, their bed had been so narrow that an accidental turn in the night could bring her arm against his body.

Here, she had to reach across a great expanse of linen. Her rough fingertips travelled slowly over the sheet, finding only cold cloth where the familiar warmth of his breathing chest ought to have been.

She left her hand where it was, on the part of the bed meant for him. A long time passed before she spoke.

"Is it terribly cold at sea tonight... Edward?"

Her voice was scarcely louder than a breath. Juliet closed her eyes, and the weariness of the journey began at last to draw her into sleep.

Warm water continued flowing beneath the floor, keeping the room comfortable through the winter night. Her hand remained stretched across the empty half of the bed.

title_vi: Chapter Seventeen: Morning in Madrid
title_en: Chapter Seventeen: Morning in Madrid
text_en:
Knock. Knock. Knock.

A measured tapping sounded at the front door while the first mist of morning still clung to the windows.

Juliet woke with a start.

For a few moments she lay still, staring at the unfamiliar ceiling, unable to remember where she was. Her hand was still extended towards the other half of the bed, her fingers cold against the uncreased linen.

Then she remembered Madrid.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

Someone was at the door again.

"Oh, heavens..."

Juliet sat up hurriedly, smoothed her tangled hair, and straightened her nightdress. Still barefoot, she crossed the passage, drew back the brass bolt, and opened the oak door a little.

Cold morning air swept in, bringing with it a voice full of unexpected cheer.

"Good morning!"

Juliet stopped short.

On the doorstep stood a woman of about her own age, wearing a simple cream woollen cloak. Her blonde hair had been cut to her collarbone, and tiny snowflakes clung to the strands stirred by the breeze.

She wore scarcely any powder. The cold had brought a little colour to her cheeks.

But it was her eyes Juliet noticed first. They were bright and gentle, creasing with a smile that asked for neither a bow nor a carefully chosen word of respect.

The woman seemed genuinely pleased to see her.

"You're Juliet Spencer, aren't you?"

Juliet straightened instinctively.

"Y-Yes... yes, I am."

"Oh, wonderful."

The woman gave a relieved sigh, as though she had just concluded an important errand. Then her smile broadened.

"I'm Millennia Stones. Marco Stones is my husband."

Juliet blinked.

"Marco...?"

"Yes. The great big fellow who speaks loudly enough for three men and thinks himself a magnificent singer whenever he's had a drink."

Juliet laughed. For the first time since waking, she was laughing for herself rather than to reassure Remi.

Millennia seemed quite at ease with Juliet's reserve. She brushed snow from her shoulder and lifted the large bag she carried.

"Marco wrote home a few days ago. He told me again and again that you and Remi were coming to Madrid. I thought I'd better come early this morning, or you'd have no notion when the Royal Academy's opening ceremony begins."

Juliet went pale.

"The opening ceremony is today?"

"It is."

"Good heavens..."

Juliet turned towards the house in alarm.

"I haven't a uniform for him, I don't know the way to the Academy, and I haven't even combed his hair..."

"Juliet."

Millennia's gentle voice interrupted her. Still standing on the threshold, she lifted the bag until Juliet could see a corner of navy-blue fabric beneath the wrapping paper.

"I've brought his uniform. I know when the ceremony begins, and a carriage is waiting outside."

Millennia held up three fingers.

"Now all you need do is let me in before the snow freezes in my hair."

A gust of wind made Millennia hunch her shoulders into her scarf. Juliet realised she was still blocking the doorway and stepped hastily aside.

"Oh! Forgive me!"

She opened the door wider.

"Please, do come in. Quickly."

Millennia laughed and crossed the threshold.

"And call me Millennia, please. We're both married to men who make a habit of giving other people cause to worry."

Juliet laughed again, more freely this time.

Millennia removed her woollen gloves and laid them neatly on the shelf beside the door. Rather than looking about like a guest taking stock of an unfamiliar house, she merely bent to brush the snow from her shoes, as though she had visited a hundred times before.

Small footsteps sounded upon the stairs. Remi appeared behind the banister, clutching his wooden ship and peeping out through a tangle of freshly woken hair.

Millennia crouched, pretending to inspect both the ship and the boy's unruly head.

"Let me guess... That hair, that little ship, and the face of a sailor caught napping on deck... You must be Remi!"

The boy hid a little farther behind the banister before he gave a shy laugh.

"How did you know?"

Millennia placed a finger against her lips.

"A grown-up's secret. But I know something else as well."

"What is it?"

"In the carriage outside, someone just your age has already asked me four times when Remi Spencer will come out so you can go to school together."

Remi hurried down two more steps.

"What's their name?"

"You'll have to come outside and ask."

Soon Remi was at the bottom of the stairs, asking question after question about the child waiting in the carriage. Juliet stood by the door and watched him forget all his caution around the stranger.

She still feared saying the wrong thing in Madrid. Yet Millennia had been in the house less than ten minutes, and somehow Juliet had scarcely had time to feel out of place.

"Now then."

Millennia stood and brushed her knees, turning towards Juliet.

"It's your turn."

"My turn?"

"Your clothes."

She gestured towards Juliet's plain nightdress.

"You could go to the Academy in that, of course. But I suspect the other parents would remember you rather better than the ceremony."

Juliet glanced down. Her cheeks coloured.

"Oh, heavens!"
