Millennia laughed, and to Juliet's surprise there was no sting in it. The sound was so open and friendly that she wanted to laugh herself.

"Come along. Let's see what Her Majesty has provided for you."

Juliet hesitated, then led her into the master bedroom. In the wardrobe, new gowns hung beside Juliet's old grey dresses and Edward's uniforms.

She opened the bottom drawer, where Isabella's attendants had placed soft fabrics unlike anything she had seen in Marrakesh.

"I don't know what to do with any of these," Juliet confessed, setting down a piece of silk. "Everything here must be worth more than the whole trunk I brought with me."

Millennia peered into the drawer and covered her mouth with her hand.

Juliet flushed.

"Are you laughing at me?"

"I'm laughing because Her Majesty has bought far too much. Don't be embarrassed. I designed some of these myself, so I know which are useful."

Millennia lifted one piece and inspected its seams.

"I design things to be worn next to the skin, then sell my patterns to the dressmakers in Madrid. I believe the Ministry must have bought the entire shop."

Juliet looked up.

"You design undergarments?"

"Let me find you a few that are warm and easy to wear first. Remi has his first day of school to think of."

Millennia arranged the pieces on a chair. Beneath the unfamiliar silk, Juliet recognised the workmanship of a good seam; she had mended enough clothes for her family to judge a stitch.

"Soft cotton is all you need next to the skin," Millennia said, selecting a plain set. "It's warm and comfortable. The fancy things can wait until you actually wish to attend a ball."

Juliet ran a thumb along the stitching and nodded.

"I could work all day in this."

Millennia returned the silks to their drawer, and the room began to feel less like a store of someone else's possessions. She chose a soft undergarment and a cream-coloured corset, briefly explaining what might be suitable for walking about.

Juliet remembered having her ribs bound so tightly she could scarcely breathe, and shook her head at once.

"Then we shall do without it today," Millennia said, putting the corset away. "You'll be chasing Remi about before long."

Juliet laughed when she noticed Millennia trying to hide a seam that had evidently been unpicked and sewn again more than once. Even the designer, it seemed, had suffered for her inventions.

Millennia kept only a few cotton garments, woollen stockings, and an outer dress.

"Choose what feels easiest. There's nothing more wearying than spending the day pulling at your sleeves and putting your skirt to rights."

She added, with a smile:

"And anything that stops you lifting your son should be left at home."

Juliet nodded.

"That sounds the wisest rule of all."

Millennia turned to the hanging dresses.

"Now, what shall you wear to Remi's school?"

Juliet held up a wine-red gown. Millennia inspected the dense silver embroidery around its collar and shook her head, passing over the other splendid evening dresses as well.

"Arrive at the Academy in that, and everyone will think Edward has conquered another kingdom."

Juliet laughed aloud.

"We'd better leave it here, then."

She settled on a moss-green woollen dress with a modest rounded collar and long sleeves, thick enough for a Madrid morning. Holding it before the mirror, she bent to pick up the little ship Remi had left behind; the skirt fell neatly about her without getting in the way.

Juliet looked towards the half-open drawer.

"I truly don't need a corset?"

"Not today."

Millennia closed the drawer.

"You're going to school with your son, not attending a military parade."

Juliet studied the clothes laid upon the bed. At last she had found garments she could put on without help, wash herself, and mend when necessary.

"Men have spent years making their guns fire faster," Millennia remarked. "Surely women may spend a little time making clothes that let them breathe."

Juliet laughed, loudly enough that Remi called to her from the passage.

Millennia handed her the chosen clothes.

"Get dressed. I'll wait downstairs with Remi."

At the door, she looked back.

"If you need anything, just call."

Juliet looked at the little bundle in her hands.

"Millennia?"

"Yes?"

"That... undergarment."

"Yes?"

Juliet's face grew hot.

"The wider part goes at the back, doesn't it?"

Millennia stood quite still. Then her shoulders began to shake.

"You promised you wouldn't laugh at me!"

"I'm not laughing!"

Juliet eyed her trembling shoulders.

"You most certainly are!"

"Forgive me!"

They both broke into laughter. Beyond the door, Remi had begun demanding to know when they were leaving for school.

Millennia returned to the sitting room and opened the bag she had brought. Inside lay a neatly pressed navy-blue Academy uniform, with thick woollen stockings and a little scarf.

Remi hurried over.

"Oh!"

"Stand still a moment."

Millennia held the uniform against him and narrowed her eyes, judging its fit.

"Hmm... just right."

She glanced towards Juliet, who stood by the bedroom door, and her familiar mischief returned.

"You see?"

She smiled.

"There's nothing to worry about."

Juliet looked from Remi, busy with the blue uniform, to Millennia. Everything remained strange, but at least there was someone she could ask.

Remi chattered excitedly about teachers he had yet to meet. Millennia fastened his buttons, then asked Juliet to help; the two women worked side by side as naturally as though they had known each other in Marrakesh.

Morning sunlight streamed through the glass and cast a golden stripe across the old valise beside the bed. Juliet laid down the moss-green dress and stepped into the passage, where Remi was calling for his mother to come and see his uniform.

title_vi: Chapter Eighteen: The Admirals of Lisbon
title_en: Chapter Eighteen: The Admirals of Lisbon
text_en:
By morning, the lamps of Lisbon station glimmered through fog thick enough to swallow the far end of the platform. Edward studied the two requests sent to the fleet the previous night, knowing that words on paper had saved no one yet. Fredo had scarcely slept; his pen was still moving when the station lights appeared.

"Keep staring and those words still won't turn into warships," Fredo said, putting down his pen as the train slowed.

Edward gathered his coat. "I want to see the ships Lisbon means to give us. Figures aren't enough."

Fredo rose, stiff from hours in his seat. "Find some cold water first. I'd rather not fall asleep before the Council's Navy."

Edward took up his valise, noting the shadows beneath Fredo's eyes. "I thought you had another chapter of naval doctrine prepared."

"Save it for the deck." Fredo closed his notebook. "First, I need to wake up and eat."

Carrying his valise and leather-bound notebook, Fredo followed him onto the platform. Passengers pressed beneath the glass roof, their breath white in the air. Pale light caught the frost on the rails but did little against the cold beyond the doors.

Cold water cleared Edward's head. He returned to the waiting hall and sat on a bench beside the ticket barrier.

A father nearby knelt to readjust his son's scarf while the mother held the boy's other hand. The three hurried towards the exit, debating as they walked whether they could still catch a carriage to the eastern quarter of the city. Edward watched them go, then touched the place where Juliet had straightened his collar before they parted in Gibraltar.

Fredo returned with his hair combed and his collar straight, though the shadows beneath his eyes remained. He sat beside Edward.

"You've been watching them a while," Fredo said. "Missing Juliet and Remi?"

Edward lowered his hand. "I miss Juliet and Remi. That's all."

He glanced towards the gates once more. "Let's settle Lisbon and get home. I don't want Juliet's first news of her husband to be a casualty report."

Fredo fastened his cuff. "Nor do I care to tell her why he never came home, especially before we've even sighted the enemy."

Edward studied Fredo's epaulettes and the Tres pendant resting against his collar. "A few minutes, and you look like a Castilian admiral again. Does the washroom work miracles on collars?"

"Cold water, a comb, and the fear of disgracing Her Majesty." Fredo inspected his cuff. "Quite sufficient."

He headed for the exit before Edward could tease him again.

Edward followed, remembering the stripes on his companion's shoulders. "Wait. Isabella sent two admirals to relieve San Sebastián. Are there others at the harbour?"

"There are." Fredo kept walking. "You'll see them at the naval base."

Edward followed with his valise. Fredo was already through the barrier.

A bitter wind struck them outside. A carriage fitted with a Vestigium heater stood by the road; Fredo opened its door, and warmth rose through the wooden floor. They travelled through snowbound streets towards the Tagus estuary, where masts began to appear through the mist.

Lisbon's naval harbour emerged beneath a veil of fog, whale-oil lamps and suspended Vestigium bars casting amber streaks across the water. Before Edward could make out the warships, he heard hammers striking rivets, pulleys knocking against ropes, winches groaning under heavy loads, and officers calling the change of watch. Tar, gun oil and Atlantic salt filled the carriage as the sea wind swept in through the open door, sharp enough to sting Edward's face.

The moment he stepped onto the quay, Edward checked the angles of the masts, the slack in the rigging, the powder barrels being hoisted aboard, and the gaps between ships at anchor. Amid hundreds of dockside sounds, he could still pick out the hard report of a gun under test. Six years away from a flagship had not erased those habits; Marrakesh had merely given them no occasion to surface.

A party of Castilian sailors hauled an ammunition cart past as a shout in English came from the nearest frigate's lower deck.

"Steady on the port side! Don't let that breeching rope twist!"

The Portsmouth accent made Edward turn. Two more men in grey-and-white uniforms counted the hauling rhythm in English before their voices disappeared amid Castilian orders.

Fredo heard them but said nothing. Edward slowed to observe an old gunner with a faded anchor tattoo on his wrist, then a sailor whose neckcloth bore a knot once common among English squadrons before London's fall. No one approached him or called out the Pathfinder's name, though several watched him a moment longer than courtesy required.

The harbour had grown familiar in a way Edward found difficult to bear. English sailors had not vanished from the seas. They had changed uniforms and flags, taking wages from another crown to continue the work they had once done for their lost homeland.

Two admirals waited near the main quay. The first was a broad, scarred man of middle years, his reddish beard curling down either side of his mouth and a gilded badge of the Castilian Council of Knights shining on his chest. Beside him stood a tall woman, lean and straight as a blade, with black hair pinned high and a lion pendant marked Veinticinco resting against her collar.

Martinez clicked her heels together in salute. "All preparations under the sealed orders are complete."

She handed Fredo a sheaf of papers. "All one hundred Conquistadores have been transferred. Weapons inspected twice. The men are aboard, awaiting final confirmation of the rolls."

Fredo skimmed the pages. Martinez frowned at his weary face.

"You look dreadful, Fredo. Were you two discussing tactics all night? I hadn't thought a council of war in a railway carriage could be so punishing."

Fredo closed the papers and glanced at Edward. "Don't blame Sir Edward for all of it. There was a question I couldn't answer myself."

He tapped his notebook. "I'll check it here. Perhaps the night wasn't wasted."

Martinez nodded, tapped the notebook's edge, then withdrew to her proper place in the Royal Guard.

The red-bearded man turned towards Edward and froze. "Bloody hell!"

Trafalgar pushed past two soldiers carrying a crate and broke into a broad laugh. "Edward Spencer! I thought you'd given up the sea for good!"

Before Edward could do more than smile, Trafalgar seized his arm. "It really is you!"

He pulled Edward into an embrace that sent the valise knocking against their legs. "Six years without a word. I thought you'd found yourself a decent death in the English Channel."

"I considered it."

Edward thumped his old friend twice on the back, then pushed him away far enough to inspect the unruly beard. "But when I heard that ugly face of yours was still alive, I decided I couldn't die yet."

Trafalgar glared.

Edward pointed at his beard. "Someone has to remind you that La Coruña wasn't Don Trafalgar's personal victory."

"You bloody bastard."

Trafalgar doubled over laughing, one hand still gripping Edward's shoulder as though the moment he let go, his old friend might disappear for another six years. He finally let go, clapped Edward on the shoulder, and turned to Fredo and Martinez, eager for an audience.

"Don't listen to him rewriting history. At La Coruña, if my squadron hadn't struck the French flank when it did, his English gunboats would've been fish soup before dawn."

Edward folded his arms, amusement lingering in his voice. "If my gunboats hadn't held the covering line, your glorious squadron would've gone to the bottom before it struck any flank. Keep your beard and your honour, Trafalgar, but leave the rest of us our share of the credit."

Their laughter drew glances from dockworkers, but Edward watched how the sailors responded to each admiral. Older men saluted Trafalgar with the ease of long service; when Martinez turned, two ranks of Conquistadores corrected their spacing without an order.

Fredo had only to open his notebook for a supply clerk to bring the muster rolls. Edward commanded no unit in Lisbon, yet several English gunners on a distant deck paused at the sight of him before returning to work.

Trafalgar followed his gaze across the crowded anchorage and understood what he was seeking. When they began walking towards the quay's edge, his voice softened.

"Looking for the *True Hero*?"

He shook his head. "Don't trouble yourself. Since England fell, she hasn't appeared on a Lisbon register. I've heard no reliable report of her either."

Edward kept his eyes on the dark hulls beyond the quay, where one vessel's mast overlapped the next. "I know. I didn't truly expect to find her here."

His gaze settled between two masts. "But whenever I enter a naval harbour, my eyes still search for that particular bow."

He turned back to the fleet before him.

Trafalgar led them to the edge of the quay, where the thinning mist revealed the ships in ranks across the water. "Old stories can wait. Look at what Lisbon has managed to preserve. If we're going to San Sebastián, these are the ships that must carry us out of the estuary."

Edward counted the bows and clusters of masts from left to right, then counted again. "Fourteen vessels fit to leave harbour."

He pointed towards the outer channel. "But the three furthest out need their rigging checked. That one has just had her mizzenmast replaced, and the next has two gunports boarded over."

He faced Trafalgar. "The figures on paper flatter them."

Trafalgar nodded without offence. "Quite right. Eleven frigates and corvettes, three warships carrying four gun decks."

He indicated the larger vessels. "Their icebreaking bows have been reinforced. The rigging and sails of all three were treated with whale fat and powdered Vestigium last night, as your instructions required. Those two you pointed out have only just returned from escort duty in the south. We're still replacing their timbers."

They walked another stretch along the quay, close enough now to examine the repairs without the shelter of the carriage. A frigate's hull had been patched with pale timber distinct from its old oak, the new fastenings not yet darkened by salt. On the next vessel, the upper aftermast was lighter than the rest, while one stretch of rigging had been spliced from three kinds of rope, as though the stores had yielded every usable coil.

Near a gun deck, Edward saw a watch roster with names struck out and replaced in different ink. An eight-man gun crew had only six men at their stations; during a drill, two young sailors left the sail-handling party and ran below to make up the number.

Trafalgar stopped beside the patched frigate. His earlier swagger had vanished.

"Don't trust the paint."

He struck the new planking with his palm. "Lisbon has repaired these ships time and again. Some look worse than they are, others better. But they float, their guns fire, and their crews still answer the call."

Edward watched the carpenters at work. "Before I board, I need two answers. How many can sail at once, and how many have enough men to fight another battle?"

Trafalgar looked at the depleted gun crews. "Five thousand eight hundred, including the hundred Conquistadores. Enough to work fourteen ships, so long as we lose no more men."

Fredo opened his notebook to the strength authorised by the sealed orders. "Wait. The orders specify six admirals and nearly three thousand more men. I see only four of us and five thousand eight hundred troops."

He looked towards the barracks. "Where are the other two admirals? Where are those men?"

Trafalgar started to speak, but Fredo closed his notebook. "I need an answer before I accept the formation."

A voice reached them through the mist.

"Don't make Trafalgar answer for it alone."

Several officers straightened before the speaker appeared.

"They're still in Lisbon. We kept those three thousand men ashore."

Two figures emerged from the fog. The man leading them had silver-threaded hair, a neatly trimmed grey beard, and deep shadows beneath his eyes that suggested several nights without proper rest. The slender woman beside him wore a black velvet cloak edged in silver and surveyed the decks and crews with the attention others reserved for written reports.

Edward recognised Don José and Dame Elizabeth. A supply officer hurried to José with a muster book without being summoned. Elizabeth glanced at the nearest frigate, and its officer stopped calling orders and came down to await her instructions.

All six admirals now stood on one quay. Fredo and Martinez carried the Queen's orders; Trafalgar had his veteran squadrons; José and Elizabeth held their own contingents. For all their ranks and royal commissions, no one had yet said who would command them all once the ships left harbour.

Edward faced them. "One question before we go further. If the formation breaks after the first enemy shot, who gives orders to all fourteen ships?"

He looked from one to another. "I'm asking about the first ten minutes of battle, when ships cannot wait for someone ashore to stamp a document."

Fredo stopped turning pages. Martinez glanced at Trafalgar; José kept a hand on the muster book. No one hurried to claim command.

José held the open page with his thumb. "On paper? Her Majesty's sealed orders define the campaign's objectives and give the Royal Guard authority to enforce them."

He glanced towards the Council's ships. "But each squadron answers to its admiral. A decision beyond one squadron requires our agreement."

Edward watched a mast sway in the wind. "Then there's a breach already. Storms don't wait for six men to agree. Neither does enemy fire."

José closed the book. "A fair question. But we have a more immediate concern."

He pointed to the barracks beyond the warehouses. "Three thousand men are quartered there. I signed the order keeping them ashore."

He looked at Martinez. "I've read the sealed orders. I know the Royal Guard won't be pleased."

He turned back. "But a royal seal won't make a poor plan sound."

Martinez kept her hand clear of her sword, though her shoulders stiffened. José looked over the patched hulls in the bay.

"Castile has yet to win a victory at sea great enough to make the Portuguese change their methods. They have better charts, know the storms better, and possess seven Legendary-class Vestigium we still cannot counter."

Elizabeth raised her cloak's collar and nodded towards the pale planking on the frigate. "Look at that."

She waited for Edward to follow her gaze. "Our lessons these past years were paid for with ships returning in that condition."

Her eyes remained on the repairs. "Courage won't tell us how to defeat those weapons. Call us overcautious if you wish, but consider who pays the balance."

Fredo folded the sealed orders. "Then you need a sound plan, not another seal authorising departure. You need to know those three thousand men won't repeat our last defeats."

He turned to José. "If someone can prove it, will you open the gates?"

"Yes."

José removed his gloves, gripping them in one hand. "Give me a sound plan, and I'll open the gates myself and go aboard."

He looked towards the barracks. "But I won't send another three thousand men into the sea to make a report to Madrid look better. Families in Lisbon don't bury documents. They bury people."

Trafalgar tightened his glove strap but offered no argument, though moments earlier he had been eager enough to dispute an old battle. Elizabeth watched a gunner aboard the nearest frigate tying the same knot for the third time, while a young sailor at a gunport stared into the water. Behind them, an officer checked the muster at a steady pace, as though the familiar routine might hold everything together.

Another young sailor kept hauling a rope despite fingers reddened by cold. José watched him.

"It's because they still obey that we must take care."

He pulled his gloves back on. "Discipline can put a man aboard even when he expects to die. I don't need more men obedient enough to sink with their ships. I need them to believe they can win."

Elizabeth turned to Edward. "Sir Edward, if you want the remaining troops, tell us precisely how you intend to bring them home."

She glanced at the patched hulls. "Then we can discuss who commands."

Wind drew the flags taut above the Tagus estuary. Edward studied the pale repairs, the English gunners in Castilian uniforms, and the crews still mending rigging in the cold. Beside them, a plan no one had yet agreed upon rested on six pairs of shoulders.

title_vi: Chapter Nineteen: Treason in Lisbon
title_en: Chapter Nineteen: Treason in Lisbon
text_en:
Grey light rose through the mist over Lisbon Bay, glinting on icy railings without easing the cold. Don José adjusted his coat, spoke briefly to Elizabeth, and turned towards the barracks as though the argument were over.

"Wait, Don José."

Edward followed. José stopped and surveyed him.

"So you've decided to speak at last, Sir Edward? Let me guess. You'll remind us of La Coruña and all those battles you never lost, then tell five thousand men that if they trust the Pathfinder, the ocean itself will clear a passage."

Edward had intended precisely that opening. His discomfort lasted long enough for Elizabeth to notice.

"You're half right."

Beyond the masts, fourteen battered warships lay patched but afloat, armed, and manned.

"I've used old victories as proof that new decisions must be right. I've paid dearly enough for that habit."

He turned back to José.

"But San Sebastián is still being strangled. If it falls, the northern sea route lies open. That danger won't vanish because we despise the present plan."

José did not answer at once. He set his muster book on a crate, pinning the page with one finger.

"True. San Sebastián must be relieved."

He tapped the casualty figures at the bottom of the page.

"But a worthy objective doesn't make every means of achieving it worthy. I can love Castile enough to die for it and still have the sense not to throw three thousand men into an unfinished calculation."

Elizabeth returned. Edward had sensed her anger since José mentioned the dead.

"You want to discuss the price of losing San Sebastián? Then let's discuss the price of the way you prefer to win, Edward."

She gestured towards Trafalgar, then the ships.

"La Coruña. You remember? You turned straight into the French guns, dragged your division after you, and won. All England called you invincible."

Elizabeth stopped, her jaw tightening.

"My closest friend never came home from that victory."

Edward held his tongue.

"I don't deny that you saved the day. I deny the notion that a fine result makes every life spent purchasing it a reasonable expense."

She indicated the sailors.

"These men have heard 'just one more battle' more often than you imagine."

She pointed to the nearest frigate, where the undermanned gun crew still checked its breeching ropes.

"That gun should have eight men. Today it has six. Those places aren't empty because two sailors overslept in barracks."

Elizabeth faced him.

"I know the names of those who never returned. José knows which streets their families live on. Trafalgar has written so many letters to bereaved families that he no longer asks his secretary to do it."

Trafalgar said nothing, tightening his gloves as he watched the decks.

"My men need no lessons in how to die for Castile," he said. "What they want to know is whether dying this time will purchase anything beyond a handsome report for Madrid."

Martinez stepped forward, hand resting on her sheathed sword.

"Dame Elizabeth, criticising Sir Edward doesn't alter the fact that the general mobilisation bears Queen Isabella's seal. The Council may object to the plan, but withholding ships and men already called into service exceeds your authority. If every squadron obeyed only the orders it approved of, we would cease to possess a united navy."

José closed his book and faced Martinez.

"Before you lecture me further on authority, answer one question. If Madrid believes San Sebastián is worth sacrificing a fleet, why is the first fleet offered up the Council's fleet here in Lisbon?"

He pointed out towards the fourteen hulls.

"Lisbon keeps these ships afloat. Those sailors are paid and fed from the Council's treasury and stores. These dockyards have patched them together after defeat upon defeat."

He kept his hand raised.

"The Queen's order has arrived. What has yet to arrive is an explanation of why the Crown's own warships weren't counted before ours."

Fredo closed the book in his hands.

"I don't know the full disposition of the Crown's other squadrons. The sealed order assigns the relief of San Sebastián to Lisbon because this force can assemble in time. Had another fleet been close enough to take its place, the order would have named it."

José nodded grimly.

"So you cannot tell me where the Crown's fleet is. You can only tell me mine happens to be nearest. Do you understand why my sailors hear that and conclude they're the cheapest part of the calculation?"

Elizabeth turned towards Martinez.

"Don't call our men cowards because they ask why Madrid won't risk its own ships first. If the Crown lacks vessels, say so. If Lisbon alone can reach San Sebastián in time, prove it. But don't offer discipline in place of an answer."

Martinez released her sword hilt, her voice firm.

"Military duty doesn't oblige the high command to disclose an entire war before every departure. If every unit demanded that Madrid spread its strategic maps across the quay before deciding whether to obey, the Empire would have fallen in the first winter."

"Quite," José replied. "A common sailor needn't see the whole map. An admiral must see enough to know where he's sending his men. I demand no guarantee of victory, only a plan explaining why we won't lose men as we did before."

He pointed towards the mouth of the Tagus.

"If a Portuguese warship appeared out there today, I'd be the first man aboard. Give me a way to answer their Vestigium weapons, and I'll lead this squadron to sea myself. I don't need favourable odds or promises that we'll all return."

José looked directly at Fredo.

"But don't mistake my refusal to slaughter my men for fear of fighting."

Several Council officers tightened their musket grips. Sailors held their posts, a sergeant continued his muster, and frigate gunners replaced breeching ropes despite the guns.

Edward had seen mutinous soldiers and panicked sailors hearing that a ship was sinking. This was neither.

Fredo stepped forward.

"The Queen's order remains in force. I've heard your arguments, but the Council's continued detention of these vessels constitutes disobedience in wartime. The Royal Guard has the authority to strip you of your commands and bring you before a tribunal in Madrid."

Elizabeth laughed shortly and spread her arms.

"Then arrest me. But first, ask yourself why those thousands of men still stand behind us when they know Madrid will call this insubordination."

She looked towards the assembled sailors.

"They stand here because when a ship goes down, the first officers they see in the boats are officers of the Council, not a seal upon a secret order."

Martinez studied the ranks. No cheers, no shouts, no desertions.

José walked to the quay's edge.

"Listen!"

His voice carried across the ships. Gun crews stopped; watch officers turned; men at the ropes stood still without letting go.

"I will order no man to desert or rise against the Queen. But neither will I compel my sailors to enter a campaign whose commanders cannot demonstrate how they intend to bring them home, or at least how their deaths might purchase a genuine military result."

He looked from deck to deck.

"Any man who supports the Council's decision will finish his duty, make his guns safe, seal the powder magazines, and disembark with his unit. There will be no disorder, no damage to our ships. We are refusing an order, not destroying our own navy."

The first to leave was a grey-haired gunner. He checked the securing pin, closed the powder chest, and shouldered his musket.

A six-man gun crew followed in two files to their sergeant's cadence. The last man turned back to chock the wheels of the nearest cannon.

Then another deck fell silent. Across fourteen warships, sailors closed hatches, secured rigging, stowed ammunition chests, and disembarked by unit. Within minutes, thousands stood ranked along the harbour, muskets shouldered, officers before them.

Fredo watched. Anger gave way to a more troublesome realisation.

The men stood at attention, watching Fredo and their officers.

"Do you understand what you're doing?"

José glanced at his formation before answering.

"We understand perfectly. If Madrid wishes to call this wartime insubordination, let it call it by its proper name. If an order comes for my arrest tomorrow, I'll be here to receive it."

He indicated the ranks.

"But do not call these men cowards."

Fredo slipped his book into his coat. His pistol cleared its holster with practised calm.

"Article Fourteen of the Royal Code grants the Royal Guard authority to deal immediately with any nobleman or officer who endangers the Empire's security. Don José, if you continue turning this garrison against the Crown, you'll leave me no other choice."

Two hammers clicked back almost together.

Elizabeth had drawn both pistols. One barrel rested against Fredo's temple, the other pointed towards Martinez, whose sword was beginning to leave its scabbard.

"Then don't make that choice."

Dozens of Council soldiers raised their muskets together; none charged. At their officers' commands, they covered separate firing lanes and held their distance from the Royal Guard with drilled precision.

Fredo kept his pistol trained on José.

"You're pointing weapons at the Royal Guard."

"And you're pointing one at their admiral."

Elizabeth never took her eyes off Fredo.

"Don't force these men to decide which of their oaths deserves to be kept."

José refused to prolong the confrontation. He turned towards Trafalgar.

Fredo followed his gaze.

"Admiral Trafalgar, order your men to lower their weapons."

Trafalgar stood motionless, then drew his pistol away from José.

"I'm sorry, Fredo."

The muzzle settled towards the Royal Guard.

"I will not shoot my own men to prove my loyalty to the very country they're trying to defend."

Edward scanned the officers and the harbour formations. Fredo had the Queen's seal; José and Elizabeth, men who had survived defeat beside them. Edward had an old title and memories of a vanished navy.

A gunshot here would merely leave more dead without resolving a thing.

"Damn it," Edward muttered.

Amid clicking gunlocks and slapping ropes, Edward saw a figure on the nearest frigate's rail. Dark blue uniform, gold epaulettes, white gloves. The face was fifteen years younger, confident as an admiral who had yet to lose his country.

"You're trying to defeat José and Elizabeth," the younger man said. "Meanwhile, their sailors are still waiting."

Edward kept his eyes upon the gun barrels.

"If they won't yield, where am I supposed to find ships to take to sea?"

"You once thought the same of Wallace."

Edward remembered a Scottish camp where rival clans fought over provisions and tent sites, yet held formation when Wallace advanced. He had scarcely believed they could.

The apparition walked between the formations.

"Look how they hold their positions for one another. They've depended on the man beside them to survive."

Edward raised his eyes. A Castilian gunner wore a familiar double knot on his musket sling; farther on, a sergeant shifted position to three commands once used by English crews belowdecks. Old habits survived between opposing muskets.

"They served together," Edward said. "Their officers have divided them, but aboard ship they remember who holds the tackle and who loads the guns."

His younger self looked at him.

"Then call upon the men you actually need."

A hammer cocked behind him, breaking his attention.

"If I call the Englishmen out of their ranks, José will say I'm raising another faction."

"Tell them plainly what you intend, then let them choose."

The apparition glanced towards the quay. The wind stretched Castilian flags taut as his younger self studied the second rank on the left.

"Begin with the man who remembers a sinking ship most clearly. He won't listen to another empty promise of victory."

Edward followed his gaze. The dark uniform vanished among masts and mist. Boots scraped the quay as a familiar face emerged in the ranks.

He searched the men before him. Castilians, Moroccans, a scattering of French exiles. In the second rank on the left he found a gaunt face, a crescent scar beside one eye.

"Timothy Beaumont!"

The young man flinched. His musket still pointed at the Royal Guard, but his finger left the trigger.

"You still remember me, sir?"

Edward stepped forward despite Fredo's attempt to stop him.

"You were the youngest gunner's mate aboard my ship. You nearly set your hair alight at Skagerrak because you ran against the wind carrying a bag of powder."

Timothy laughed hoarsely, bowed his head, and lowered his musket.

"I thought you'd forgotten."

"I haven't."

Edward stopped before him.

"But I'd like to know why a man who once shared a deck with me is now pointing a musket at someone serving beneath the same flag."

Timothy gripped the stock.

"Because I'm tired, sir."

He raised his head, his voice beginning to crack.

"For years, every time we've put to sea, they've told us the next battle would be different. Then another ship sinks, more men disappear, and when we return, there's a new officer waiting to explain why the latest defeat was necessary."

Timothy pointed towards Trafalgar.

"Vila do Porto."

His shoulders contracted as though someone had pulled a cord running down his spine. His eyes slipped past Trafalgar and fixed upon the black water between the quay and the nearest frigate.

"My ship broke in two offshore. More than a hundred men died before morning."

Trafalgar made no attempt to avoid the accusing finger. He lowered his pistol and listened.

"That battle was my responsibility. If you're looking for someone to blame, begin with me."

Timothy laughed without pleasure. His hand travelled from stock to barrel to trigger guard, never touching the lock.

"Do you think I'm only angry because the orders were wrong?"

He turned towards Edward. His breaths shortened; he swallowed between phrases.

"I clung to a plank in the open sea for two days. On the first day, I could still hear men calling to one another. By the second night, the voices had nearly died away."

His eyes remained fixed on the water.

"There was a fellow who'd slept in the hammock above mine for almost a year. That morning his hands were frozen around the edge of our plank. I had to break his fingers one by one to free his body because the plank couldn't bear another man's weight."

The sailors watched in silence. Timothy touched his lips as though tasting seawater again.

"When they hauled me aboard, I vomited until I had nothing left. Three days later, I woke in the infirmary and immediately asked whether Number Six gun was all right. It took me until evening to ask who had survived."

Behind them, an iron hook struck a ship's hull. Timothy flinched towards it before anyone else turned.

Edward noticed.

Timothy realised he had.

"It's been like this for years."

He touched his temple, then lowered his hand.

"Whenever we receive orders to sail, I check the ladder to the gun deck before inspecting my gun. I count the nearest gunports. I sleep in my boots because if the ship lists, I won't waste time finding them."

His voice grew quieter.

"Some nights, a rope creaks louder than usual, and I wake thinking the hull is splitting again."

He looked towards the ships, anger giving way to shame.

"And the worst part is that before I've even seen the enemy, I'm already thinking about sinking."

Council sailors shifted uneasily. A rear-rank sailor, burned to one ear, tightened his grip without lowering his gaze.

Timothy spoke faster.

"I used to step aboard and wonder which enemy ship I'd hit first. Now I wonder which gunport will flood first."

He looked directly at Edward.

"Do you understand, Admiral? It isn't a cannonball killing me that frightens me. It's the feeling that we've already lost before weighing anchor."

Edward remained silent. So did Trafalgar.

Elizabeth lowered one pistol, keeping Fredo covered with the other, and stayed back from Timothy.

"Timothy."

The young man shook his head.

"I'm not finished, Elizabeth."

"I know."

Her voice remained severe.

"But you're about to turn what happened to you into a sentence passed upon an entire navy."

"Because they're Castilian by blood, sir."

Timothy addressed Edward, though his eyes remained fixed on Elizabeth.

"There's a truth everyone knows and nobody wants to say aloud. Without the English Royal Navy, the Castilian Navy has too often been little more than wooden targets waiting for another fleet to tear them apart."

A curse rang out from the sailors. The man with the burn scar stepped half a pace out of formation.

"Say that again."

Several Council muskets shifted. Nearby men turned on Timothy; officers raised their hands to hold the ranks.

Timothy faced the scarred sailor.

"I said you've been losing for too long."

"No. You called us wooden targets."

The sailor bared a pale scar from collarbone to ear.

"I got this jumping into a burning gun deck to pull out two English lads. One survived. The other died in my arms before the boat reached the ship."

Timothy opened his mouth, but no answer came.

Elizabeth approached without embracing him. She jabbed two fingers into his chest.

"I sat outside your infirmary for three nights after Vila do Porto. I know you woke asking about Number Six gun. I also know that on the fourth night, you crawled out of bed because someone called a change of watch in the corridor, and you thought you were aboard ship again."

Timothy clenched his teeth.

"Then you of all people should understand."

"I understand perfectly. That's why I'm telling you to stop talking like a fool."

Elizabeth pointed towards the scarred sailor.

"You want to curse Trafalgar, curse me, curse José? Go ahead. We signed the orders. We wear the epaulettes. We had the authority to make those mistakes, and we'll bear responsibility for them."

Her voice hardened.

"But don't take the night you nearly died and throw it in the faces of men who jumped into the sea to pull you and your mates out."

Timothy drew a ragged breath.

"I never said they were cowards."

"Then say what you mean."

Timothy turned towards the ships. His words were clearer now.

"I mean this navy has been losing for too long. We've lost so often that nobody discusses how to win anymore. They only count how many ships we can afford to lose."

He swallowed.

"The sailing orders arrived, and my first thought was whether I should write to my mother before or after supper. I hadn't even asked whether we had enough powder."

The scarred sailor remained silent.

"I mean the Portuguese and the French have taught us to fear the sea. Perhaps you hate me for saying that. I hate myself every time the signal sounds to prepare for departure, and my knees want to carry me back to barracks."

He gripped his sling until his knuckles whitened.

"But I still go aboard. Every single time."

Trafalgar waited for Timothy to meet his eyes.

"And we keep sending you."

Timothy turned towards him.

"Yes."

Trafalgar nodded, his jaw tightening beneath his beard.

"Then the shame isn't that you're afraid. It's that we've made you carry that fear aboard, voyage after voyage, without ever showing you why the next one should be different."

José said nothing. Neither did Fredo.

Elizabeth folded her arms.

"And your foolishness lies in turning your commanders' failures into proof that every Castilian sailor is incompetent. Do that, and you're no better than those nobles in Madrid who think the men down here are merely numbers."

Timothy's lips twitched in protest.

Elizabeth caught it.

"Go on. Argue. I know you want to."

"I still stand by what I said."

Timothy faced Edward again.

"When the English Royal Navy fought beside us, I never went aboard feeling we'd already lost before seeing the enemy. Perhaps that's arrogant. Perhaps it makes everyone angry. But I won't lie about it."

The scarred sailor studied him before answering from the ranks.

"Then don't lie. Just remember the whole of it. When a ship sinks, English blood and Castilian blood are the same colour upon the water."

Timothy lowered his eyes to his musket. At last his hands grew still.

Trafalgar lowered his pistol fully to his thigh.

"That's enough. Beaumont has the right to remember defeat as he experienced it. The rest of you have the right to despise how he speaks of it."

He looked along the ranks.

"But not one man here has the right to call the man beside him a coward merely to make himself feel better."

Edward let silence settle until chains rattled beneath the quay.

"Are you afraid of dying?"

"No, sir."

Timothy answered immediately.

"I'm afraid of dying without knowing what my life is supposed to purchase. I'm afraid of boarding a ship because someone tells me it's my duty, only to discover, when water pours through the gunports, that nobody ashore ever truly knew what they sent us to accomplish."

The words held Edward silent. In Marrakesh, a Sultan had told him that sacrifice meant something only when a commander understood its price.

"If I showed you a plan clear enough for you to understand what we're doing, would you go aboard?"

Timothy studied him more closely.

"You have a real plan, sir? Not a speech. Not another demand that we trust you because you've won before. An actual plan."

"There's one thing I can promise you."

Edward gestured towards the fleet.

"I won't ask a single man to board a ship merely because I won a battle somewhere ten years ago."

He looked across the harbour.

"Before we weigh anchor, you'll know which ships we intend to use, how we mean to fight, and what this battle is meant to accomplish. If you still believe I'm spending men's lives to purchase my own reputation, you'll have the right to step ashore."

Timothy glanced towards Elizabeth. She offered neither a nod nor a shake of her head.

"If you can prove it, I'll go."

Edward turned towards the ranks filling the waterfront. He raised neither his voice nor the promise of a restored England.

"Those of you who once served beneath the ensign of the English Royal Navy, step forward where I can see you."

Several men glanced at one another, but none moved at once. Edward gave them time.

"I'm not asking you to betray Castile. This country gave many of us shelter, food, and a deck beneath our feet when England had nothing left to offer. Some of the men beside you have fought at your side longer than many of your countrymen who are still alive."

His gaze moved from Fredo to José.

"But if I'm to take a ship out of Lisbon, I must know who still remembers how we fought together. I have no intention of resurrecting a dead empire. I need men who know the same commands, the same gun drills, and the same manner of working a ship that I once used."

An elderly sailor missing two fingers stepped forward. He removed his hat, glanced at his Council officer, then joined Timothy.

"I served eight years beneath the Royal ensign."

Nobody cheered. Another man emerged from the gunners' ranks and gave only the name of his birthplace.

"Portsmouth."

Four more followed.

A gun crew shouldered its muskets and joined Timothy. Their sergeant spoke briefly to his Castilian officer, who nodded.

Gaps began to appear along the waterfront.

Elizabeth looked at Timothy.

"Are you certain?"

He turned towards her. Much of his anger had subsided, but his fear remained.

"No. But I'm going anyway."

Elizabeth muttered a curse, straightened his collar, and shoved him back towards Edward.

"If you're going, don't die like a fool."

"I'll try to die according to plan."

"Get out of here."

Several men laughed, including the Castilian who had cursed Timothy. The laughter lasted seconds, easing the threat of gunfire.

English voices rose from the Council ranks: Portsmouth, Bristol, Kent, Yorkshire. Edward had believed he would hear those accents only in memory.

A scarred former gunner stepped forward.

"Sir Edward. If you're at the helm, and you show us the plan before asking us to die for it, we'll go aboard. Many of us owe Castile a roof over our heads, so don't ask us to pretend we never belonged here."

He straightened his musket sling.

"But we haven't forgotten who we were, either. If the red-cross flag has a chance to fly from a mast once more, I don't think any of us would object."

Agreement spread through the ranks, never becoming one great roar. A sailmaker stepped forward, followed by two gunners, and farther down the waterfront three men in garrison uniforms left their formation.

A Castilian caught his departing friend, spoke in Spanish, and slapped his shoulder.

Edward lost count. More than eight hundred English veterans now stood apart beside him. They had chosen whom to follow to sea, without ships or any promise of restoring their homeland.

Timothy looked at Edward, then at the men who had stepped forward with him.

"We haven't forgotten, Admiral."

Edward offered no speech in reply. He merely looked across those faces, then towards José, Elizabeth, and Trafalgar.

Wind swept from the river mouth through gaps in the Council ranks, pulling Castilian flags taut above the quay. No one lowered a weapon, but from that moment the struggle in Lisbon had ceased to be merely a question of whether a fleet would agree to leave harbour.

title_vi: Chapter Twenty: Bound for Battle
title_en: Chapter Twenty: Bound for Battle
text_en:
Clap. Clap. Clap.

Three sharp claps broke the silence settling over the harbour. Elizabeth stepped out from the Council ranks, her pistol undrawn, and surveyed the eight hundred and three British veterans without treating them as enemies. Her gaze settled first on Edward, then on the gaps those men had left in the Castilian formation.

"Impressive, Sir Edward. You failed to persuade the Council, so you found the men who still remember your orders and assembled a crew in the middle of our harbour."

Timothy stiffened. Several veterans behind him tightened their musket slings, but Elizabeth raised a finger towards them.

"Do not mistake my meaning. I heard why each of you stepped forward, and I will not call it treason merely to make the matter easier to settle."

She turned to Edward.

"But eight hundred soldiers in Castilian service have broken ranks to follow a newly reinstated admiral. If you expect me to smile and wish you a pleasant voyage, six years in Marrakesh have made you altogether too optimistic."

Fredo closed his muster book and slipped it inside his coat. His pistol remained in his hand, though he had lowered its muzzle from José when Timothy began speaking of Vila do Porto.

"No one here is raising a force outside Castilian authority, Dame Elizabeth. Sir Edward has made it clear that these men seek neither to restore their former kingdom nor abandon their duty to the Empire. They have volunteered to serve under a commander they trust to reach San Sebastián."

"And that is precisely my concern."

Elizabeth pointed towards the Castilian flag above the harbour fortress.

"An army cannot endure if every soldier who loses faith in his superiors may choose a commander to his liking and call it a reorganisation."

Martinez stepped beside Fredo, resting a hand upon her sword.

"Nor can it endure when fourteen warships and thousands of sailors refuse a general mobilisation without offering another course. We have heard the Council's objections. San Sebastián remains under blockade."

José raised a hand before Elizabeth could reply. He surveyed the British veterans, then the Council sailors still standing in formation behind him.

"Then we have reached the heart of it. None of us lacks an argument. What we lack is a way to leave this harbour without making Lisbon the first battlefield of a civil war."

A musket lock clicked somewhere behind them.

One sound was enough to make the Conquistadors near Martinez shift their footing.

Fredo turned. A hundred elite Castilian soldiers, previously scattered about the quays, had gathered in two lines, blocking every direct approach to Edward and Martinez without levelling their weapons at the Council sailors. Their officers needed no second order.

The Council answered almost at once. José turned his wrist, and reserve companies emerged from the barracks beyond the warehouses, advancing without running or shouting. More than three thousand men occupied the harbour approaches, bringing field guns and ammunition chests still bearing their lead seals.

Martinez watched the artillery being wheeled into place.

"You had three thousand reserves ready beforehand?"

"Lisbon is the largest naval harbour in the west. Did you imagine we would put every soldier on the quay merely to make this debate look better attended?"

Fredo exhaled through his nose.

"If shooting starts, neither side wins."

"At last," José replied, "something upon which we agree."

Edward surveyed the men around him. The Royal Guard carried the authority of the Crown; the Council commanded eight thousand troops and officers who had fought beside them for years. The British veterans had only his promise of a genuine plan.

He looked out over the anchored warships. For the first time since arriving, he searched for only one.

Edward passed Fredo and approached the edge of the quay, studying fourteen dark hulls riding in the bay.

"José."

The old commander looked up.

"I do not need fourteen ships."

The nearby officers fell silent. Edward pointed towards a four-decked warship anchored apart from the squadron, her dark hull patched with Castilian paint over lines he had recognised the moment he arrived in Lisbon.

"That one."

Trafalgar frowned.

"*Red Baron*?"

"Yes."

Fredo followed his outstretched hand.

"One ship?"

"One."

Edward faced them.

"If the Council believes taking the entire fleet to sea is a wager it cannot justify, I will not force them to stake everything. I need a hull large enough for nine hundred and three men, enough guns to break an enemy formation, and a ship these sailors can handle without learning their trade anew."

José studied *Red Baron* longer than the others.

"She is among the oldest vessels here."

"Precisely why I chose her."

For the first time since the confrontation began, Trafalgar laughed.

"Bloody hell. You recognised her?"

"The stern has been rebuilt, and the uppermost gun deck was never part of the original design. But I knew the plans of that class before some men here were old enough to hold a sword."

Edward looked at him.

"*Red Baron* was transferred from the Royal Navy of England to Castile fifteen years ago."

Trafalgar nodded.

"Three gun decks when she arrived. The Castilians added the fourth."

Edward said nothing more. Whatever he intended for that fourth deck could wait until the vessel was under his command. First, he had to get her out of Lisbon.

Fredo understood. He turned towards José, speaking less like a Royal Guard reciting regulations than an officer trying to remove a live shell from between two armies.

"Don José, the Council retains thirteen warships, every Castilian sailor who declines to accompany Sir Edward, the harbour's ammunition stores and the garrison. We take *Red Baron*, eight hundred and three British veterans and one hundred Conquistadors."

José did not answer.

Fredo continued.

"I shall record this as a dispute over command during a state of emergency, not mass desertion. I cannot absolve the Council of every legal responsibility, but I can keep Lisbon from becoming a battlefield today and withhold any indictment for treason until the San Sebastián campaign ends."

Elizabeth regarded him more closely.

"You propose postponing the confrontation, not granting a pardon."

"Correct. If we survive long enough to quarrel again, Madrid can have its turn later."

Trafalgar shook his head.

"You're beginning to sound like Edward."

Fredo opened his mouth, but José silenced him with a raised hand. The old commander walked to the quay's edge, studied *Red Baron*, then turned to the eight hundred and three British sailors behind Edward.

"You want a ship. I can give you one."

He faced them.

"But if you leave Lisbon aboard *Red Baron*, today's crisis must depart with you. I will not have Fredo summon Royal reinforcements to arrest the Council the moment your sails disappear beyond the horizon, nor will I allow you to visit every Council harbour along the northern coast and draw more sailors away from us."

Martinez narrowed her eyes.

"You have conditions."

"Three."

Fredo rubbed his forehead.

"Naturally."

José raised one finger.

"First, the two Vestigium communication spheres belonging to Royal Guards Tres and Veinticinco shall be sealed here in Lisbon until the San Sebastián campaign has an outcome. Not destroyed. Not permanently confiscated. Sealed."

Martinez objected at once.

"Severing our communications with Madrid while we carry out a secret royal directive is a considerable demand."

"As is allowing two Royal Guards to summon Crown forces into a naval harbour that has just refused their orders."

José met her gaze.

"If you expect me to surrender a ship before eight thousand men who believe the Council has spared them a senseless sortie, you must give them reason to believe Royal troops will not arrive tomorrow morning to close this harbour."

Fredo glanced towards Martinez. She clenched her jaw, but José's reasoning forced them both to consider the demand.

The old commander raised a second finger.

"*Red Baron* carries enough heating crystals for a four-decked warship and a crew larger than usual. You may take only half her present reserve."

Timothy spoke from behind them.

"Half?"

Elizabeth turned towards him.

"Lisbon must endure the winter too."

He was about to protest, then looked towards the barracks, the supply warehouses and the thousands of men behind her. He fell silent.

José continued.

"You shall have the ship, provisions for the voyage, fresh water and enough crystals to keep the watch compartments from freezing. The remainder stays here. I will not strip Lisbon of its warmth to finance an expedition I have already refused to undertake."

Edward calculated quickly. Half would be uncomfortable, but with rotating rest shifts, fewer heated compartments and no attempt to warm all four decks at once, they could survive.

"Acceptable."

Martinez turned sharply.

"Sir Edward."

"We need enough warmth to fight, not enough to turn the Atlantic into a drawing room."

José did not smile. He raised his third finger.

"Finally, from the mouth of the Tagus to Lekeitio or San Sebastián, *Red Baron* may enter no harbour under Council authority. No further recruitment, no additional ships, and no armed landings to compel local garrisons to choose sides."

Fredo regarded him.

"And if the ship is damaged?"

"Anchor offshore and send a civilian distress signal. We shall provide assistance where possible, but no Royal Guard shall march into our harbours with eight hundred British soldiers behind him while this dispute remains unresolved."

This time, Trafalgar spoke.

"That is reasonable enough."

Martinez looked at him.

"You support these conditions too?"

"I support keeping one dispute in Lisbon from becoming three more along the coast."

Trafalgar tightened his gloves.

"I still want San Sebastián rescued. I would also prefer not to wake tomorrow and find myself choosing whether to shoot Frenchmen or soldiers serving my own Queen."

Elizabeth turned towards Edward. Her anger remained, but the cold contempt with which she had approached him was gone.

"You promised Timothy that before setting sail, every man following you would know which ship he was boarding, what his objective was and why he should risk his life."

She inclined her head towards *Red Baron*.

"You have your ship. Do not waste the rest of the morning putting on another performance."

Edward nodded.

"I have no intention of doing so."

Timothy stood several paces behind Elizabeth. She looked towards him, her lips parting as though another sentence might follow, but she said nothing. He made no move to approach.

They had said enough to each other upon this quay.

Fredo removed the Vestigium communication sphere from his belt. Rather than throw it down, he placed it upon a cargo crate and looked at José.

"Seal it in our presence. Record who receives it, the hour of transfer and the conditions for its return."

José summoned a clerk. Martinez surrendered her device after Fredo, looking as though she meant to remember every name involved until the campaign was over.

When the Council's wax seals were pressed onto both containers, weapons around the harbour began to lower. José ordered the reserves to return their field guns to the warehouses, officers dismissed their men by unit, and the Conquistadors brought their muskets back to the shoulder.

Edward allowed no time for hesitation. He faced the eight hundred and three British veterans and pointed towards *Red Baron*.

"You wanted a real plan. First, we must discover what we have."

He called Timothy forward.

"Choose two hundred gunners. Board first and inspect every gun deck, the powder, breeching ropes, flints and ammunition ready for use. I want no polished reports. If a gun is useless, mark it useless; if it needs two hours' repair, tell me two hours."

Timothy snapped his heels together.

"Understood, Admiral."

"Then inspect the hand pumps and gunports nearest the waterline. I have no intention of winning our first battle only to sink because of a rotten seal."

Timothy smiled for the first time since confronting Elizabeth.

"Yes, sir."

Edward turned towards the remaining sailors. One group would inspect the sails, rigging, winches and anchors. Another would descend into the hold to examine the hull, water stores and previous repairs; a final group would count provisions and establish exactly how many heating crystals they were permitted to carry after the Council reclaimed its share.

No one was to undertake major repairs without reporting first. For the moment, they needed only to determine precisely how much life remained in *Red Baron*.

The hundred Conquistadors were summoned next. Edward walked along their formation, examining their heavy fur cloaks, long muskets, rows of pistols and sabres.

"Are you preparing to fight upon a ship's deck, or move house?"

Several soldiers exchanged glances. Edward tapped the commander's musket barrel.

"Keep your leather armour and sabres. One pistol per man. The long muskets and remaining weapons go into storage, under seal. If we have to swing aboard another vessel, I would rather half of you did not fall into the sea carrying an entire armoury."

The Conquistador commander looked towards Martinez. She nodded once.

"Follow Sir Edward's orders."

"Yes, ma'am."

Fredo stood beside a cargo crate, watching the harbour change from an armed standoff into preparations for departure so swiftly that he struggled to keep pace.

"And me?"

Edward turned.

"Can you find tea?"

Fredo stared at him.

"I can locate an artillery battery, find a band of assassins or decipher a secret directive. Tea was never part of my Royal Guard training."

"Then today you broaden your expertise."

Martinez failed to suppress a laugh. Fredo gave her an injured look.

Edward pointed towards the supply warehouses.

"Three crates of black tea. Something decent enough to keep eight hundred and three Englishmen from staging a second mutiny before luncheon."

"Sir Edward, I scarcely consider tea a tactical priority."

"I have just watched eight hundred and three men demonstrate that sailors' morale is a tactical priority."

Fredo found no immediate answer. Martinez patted his shoulder.

"Come along, Tres. At least this assignment is unlikely to get you killed."

"You're coming with me."

"Why?"

"Because if I must explain to a merchant that the fate of San Sebastián depends upon tea, I shall require a witness."

The two Royal Guards departed amid the laughter of nearby veterans. Edward watched them go, then turned his attention back to *Red Baron*.

An hour later, the first inspection report reached him. The vessel was not ready for a major engagement, but she was hardly the floating corpse her appearance suggested.

Most guns on the three lower decks remained serviceable, though several carriages needed new pins. Two hand pumps required repairs, the powder magazines were reasonably dry, and the hull showed no dangerous leaks.

The fourth gun deck made her top-heavy. Meanwhile, the noblemen's cabins astern wasted so much space that the figures alone offended Edward.

He ordered nothing dismantled yet.

Timothy returned to the quarterdeck with soot upon his cheek and a roll of old cloth beneath one arm.

"Admiral. You ought to see this."

He laid the bundle upon a crate and unfolded it. Inside lay a red-cross flag edged in gold from the Royal Navy of England, its colours darkened with age but its embroidery intact.

The British sailors nearby fell silent.

Edward touched the edge of the cloth. He did not need to ask how long it had lain beneath the stores, nor why the Castilians had never thrown it away.

José and Elizabeth were still standing upon the quay. Both looked over when Timothy brought out the flag.

Edward turned towards them before issuing his order.

"The Castilian flag flies highest."

José studied him.

"And this one?"

"Beneath it."

Edward looked towards the old banner.

"*Red Baron* is a Castilian warship. The men serving aboard her today merely wish to remember the flag beneath which they first learned to sail."

José remained silent for several moments. Then he nodded.

"Keep them in that order."

Timothy gathered up the flag and hurried towards the halyards. When the red cross rose beneath Castile's colours, the cheering did not erupt into a frenzy of British restoration.

It began among a handful of men, spread through the gunners, sailmakers and old sailors, then settled into a sound loud enough for the entire harbour to hear.

Elizabeth watched Timothy among them. This time, she offered no rebuke.

Trafalgar approached Edward as the first mooring line was hauled aboard.

"You truly need only one ship?"

Edward watched *Red Baron* begin to spread her canvas in the wind sweeping through the Tagus estuary.

"I need a crew that knows what I mean when I order the helm over. One ship will suffice."

"You still haven't told me what you intend to do when you reach La Concha."

"Because I have yet to discover everything this ship can do."

Trafalgar stared at him, then burst into laughter.

"That's a more respectable answer than your old nonsense about never having lost a battle."

Edward extended his hand.

"I'm getting old."

"No. You're getting less stupid."

They shook hands firmly. Trafalgar did not pull Edward into another embrace, but held his old friend's wrist for an extra moment before releasing it.

"Edward."

Edward stopped. Trafalgar looked towards *Red Baron*.

"Don't make your men write another letter announcing a death merely to preserve the legend of the Pathfinder."

Edward did not smile.

"I know."

It was the only answer Trafalgar needed.

Fredo and Martinez returned with three crates of tea just as the last boat prepared to leave the quay. Fredo tossed one crate towards two waiting sailors and climbed the rope ladder, cursing that no secret directive had ever humiliated a Royal Guard quite so thoroughly as this assignment.

Edward waited aboard *Red Baron* until both had come on deck before ordering the gangway withdrawn.

José remained on the quay. The two communication spheres lay in sealed containers, half the heating crystals had been returned to Lisbon's stores, and the other thirteen warships remained under Council command.

The dispute itself had not been settled. Only the weapons had been lowered. No one wore shackles, and the word cowardice was spoken no more.

*Red Baron* still possessed a crew, guns, provisions, two flags and an open passage to the sea.

Edward placed both hands upon the ship's wheel.

"Weigh anchor."

The order travelled through every deck. Iron chain rattled over the windlass, canvas filled with the gathering wind, and the massive four-decked warship began to leave the sheltered waters of the bay. Her bow turned towards the Atlantic.

Fredo stood beside Edward, the scent of tea still clinging to his gloves.

"Sir Edward."

"Hm?"

"May we finally hear what you intend to do?"

Edward felt the weight of the wheel beneath his hands as the cumbersome hull answered sluggishly. He glanced upwards towards the fourth gun deck towering above him.

"First?"

He patted the wheel.

"Put the kettle on. I need to decide what to do with this floating four-storey cupboard before we catch sight of the French."

*Red Baron* passed beyond the mouth of the Tagus with the wind filling her sails, carrying nine hundred and three souls towards a war that no man aboard still expected to unfold according to plan.

title_vi: Chapter Twenty-One: A Ship Under the Knife
title_en: Chapter Twenty-One: A Ship Under the Knife
text_en:
The Atlantic drove heavy swells against the *Red Baron*. In the captain's cabin, a copper kettle boiled over coals. Edward poured water over black tea, set three cups on the chart table, and sat down.

Fredo accepted the first cup. He glanced at the hourglass beside the charts, then at Edward.

"You've just taken nine hundred and three people out of Lisbon aboard a ship you admit you don't fully understand. If this is how Englishmen recover from a failed mutiny, I begin to see why your empire gives Europe such a headache."

"Tea first. Headaches afterwards."

Edward slid the remaining cup towards Martinez. She tested its heat with a fingertip and set it beside Timothy's inspection report.

"You said we must know what ship we're taking into battle, what our objective is, and why we should risk our lives for it before reaching La Concha. I doubt three chests of tea answer any of those questions."

"No. But they keep the man answering them awake."

Fredo sipped, grimaced at the bitterness, and opened the report.

"Then tell us. I've read this twice. Most guns on the lower three decks remain serviceable, two hand pumps need repairs, the powder magazine is dry, and the hull has no dangerous leaks. Our worst problem is the upper deck and how slowly she answers the helm."

Edward drew the chart of La Concha into the centre of the table. He placed a model of the *Red Baron* north of the bay entrance, then marked Santa Clara Island and the French flagship with two counters.

"That would be our worst problem in a conventional engagement. I have another kind of fight in mind."

Martinez leaned forward, holding down the chart as the ship rolled.

"The western channel is deeper. The eastern passage is narrow and strewn with rocks. The French will put lighter ships outside as pickets, with their heavy warships near the entrance to support their troops ashore. Bring in a four-decked ship and they'll see us before we can bring our guns to bear."

Edward touched the northern edge of the chart.

"Unless they see us too late."

Fredo studied the weather symbols along its margin.

"Fog."

"And wind."

Edward moved a counter southwards in a broad arc. His course avoided the entrance and outer pickets, ending at the flagship's stern.

"We'll use the fog to approach from a quarter they don't expect, then cross the flagship's stern. One close rake should smash her rudder, command positions, and part of her rigging. Martinez, take the Conquistadors aboard immediately afterwards. You're not there to capture her deck by deck. Seize the command section and cut the anchor cables."

Martinez withheld her agreement.

"What if the flagship has Gendarmes aboard?"

"Don't offer them an honourable duel. Hold the passages, draw their men away from the anchors and command posts, and fire into gaps in their armour when you have a shot. If they overwhelm you, abandon the attempt to control the whole ship. We need only leave her unable to steer."

"And how do my people return?"

Edward pushed the *Red Baron* close astern of the French ship, then drew the models slightly apart.

"Grappling lines will hold us together. Fredo guards the lines and hauling parties from our deck. If it goes badly, withdraw in groups. Nobody stays behind for an objective that no longer matters."

Fredo planted his hands on the table.

"I prefer a promise of withdrawal to another speech about honour. But the *Red Baron* as she stands can't make the turn you've drawn."

"Correct."

Edward lifted his cup.

"I wanted to be certain that after Lisbon, two members of the Royal Guard still had the sense to say it aloud."

Martinez tapped the model with a fingernail.

"You want her restored to her original configuration."

Edward paused with his cup halfway to his mouth. Fredo glanced from her to the report.

"Three gun decks."

Martinez pulled the papers towards her.

"The fourth deck makes her top-heavy, gives a crosswind more surface to catch, and forces men, shot, water, and provisions higher up. To turn sharply at the entrance, you don't need more guns. You need a ship that stops fighting her own rudder."

Edward put his cup down.

"That's why I asked you both here."

He offered no schoolmaster's praise. He turned an inventory sheet over and sketched the hull in charcoal: three original gun decks beneath the Castilian addition.

Fredo studied the drawing.

"I've read the refitting plans. The fourth deck came after the fighting with Portugal, when Madrid needed a warship to stand off a harbour and sustain bombardment. Queen Isabella of Castile never asked her to race frigates."

"Exactly."

Edward tapped the uppermost deck.

"Isabella didn't design a bad ship. She designed one for a different duty. As a floating fortress, the present *Red Baron* makes sense. But if we're to slip into La Concha, turn, board, and get clear before the fog lifts, she's a four-storey wardrobe that happens to float."

Martinez leaned back.

"So we're asking a floating fortress to do a raider's work."

"And we have a few days to persuade her."

Fredo turned the drawing towards himself.

"How much do you mean to remove?"

"Fourth-deck guns and reserve shot, the partitions, and the structures raised above the original deck," Edward said. "The shipwrights mark every load-bearing member before anyone touches a saw."

Martinez sat back.

"A relief. I thought you meant to give nine hundred people an axe apiece and tell them to chop anything heavy."

Fredo took the charcoal and drew a line on each side of the hull.

"We strip her in balanced pairs, port and starboard. Lowering guns improves the centre of gravity, but doesn't reduce the ship's weight. The surplus must go."

"Those guns belong to the Council," Martinez reminded them.

Fredo muttered that José would kill them on their return.

"He asked for the *Red Baron* back," Edward said, "not an inventory of every gun she carried."

"You're hiding behind the wording."

Fredo set down the charcoal. Edward smiled.

"I'm English. It's a tradition."

Martinez set down her tea before she could laugh. She pointed to the middle of the hull.

"Don't throw everything away. Keep a few guns below as reserves, where they'll help steady her in rough seas. As for the rest, if they're useless in this battle, their price is no reason to let them kill us."

Edward nodded.

"I thought so too."

Fredo folded his arms.

"I want figures before a gun goes overboard. Weight discarded, weight lowered, and the new positions of water and provisions. And I want stopping limits."

Edward looked at him.

"Limits?"

"You're proposing a refit at sea. If the carpenters report movement in a main beam, we stop. If a mast step takes an abnormal load, we stop. If she heels too far in a turn after any stage, we stop. I won't approve a plan that fails when the deck reaches ninety degrees."

Silence fell across the table. Edward reclaimed the charcoal and wrote three words in large letters along the paper's edge.

STOP FOR STRUCTURAL DAMAGE.

"Agreed."

Martinez tapped the crew list.

"And the nine hundred and three aboard? If we dismantle their upper sleeping quarters, where will they go? We have only half our original heating capacity. A faster ship is worthless if, in three days, our gunners are too cold to light their fuses."

Edward wrote another condition.

STOP FOR CREW EXHAUSTION.

"You take charge of that."

"No. Fredo and I share it."

Fredo turned to her.

"How did I get dragged into this?"

"You demanded load tables, work watches, and stopping limits. Don't pretend you only know how to hold a sword."

Edward braced his hands on the table, watching the two Guards divide the duties between them.

"Now you sound like two admirals."

Fredo raised his cup.

"If you'd said that in Lisbon, I'd have felt less like shooting someone."

"You were busy pointing a pistol at the time."

"A minor detail."

Fredo drank, while Martinez laughed into her cup.

Edward spread out another blank sheet. Nobody waited for a lecture; all three divided the work.

First came the inspection. Two English shipwrights familiar with the original class would examine the fourth deck with three Castilian carpenters.

Red chalk would mark each beam, mast support, joint, and place where cutting was forbidden; white would mark later additions. Both parties had to sign before an axe touched timber.

Second came the removal of high loads in balanced pairs. Guns, shot, tool chests, decoration, partitions, and heavy fittings would be weighed using the hoists.

For every load taken off the port side, an equivalent must come off starboard. Retained guns would be lowered and secured in predetermined positions; surplus pieces discarded.

Third, the *Red Baron* would not be refitted under full sail in heavy seas. They would find steadier water, shorten sail, hold her bow oblique to the swell, and work in stages. After each stage, Edward would order a trial run and turns to port and starboard before authorising more dismantling.

Fredo reviewed the roster.

"Three watches, no more than four hours of heavy labour apiece. Anyone who's been on the hoists or sawing timber goes nowhere near a gun crew straight afterwards. I want at least one watch of rest before they return to fighting duty."

Martinez added:

"The Conquistadors aren't carpenters. Let them work the hoists, hold cables, shift timber, and keep the work safe. Don't put a saw in the hands of someone who can't tell what a beam supports."

"I'll tell them you've saved the honour of their corps."

"Try saying that to their faces."

Edward was already studying the last two lines of the report.

"The fourth deck has our twelve heaviest guns. Six go below; six go overboard."

Fredo whistled.

"José will certainly kill us."

Martinez lifted her cup.

"Then we'd better win before we go home."

When Timothy was summoned, the table held no plan written by Edward alone. Three hands crowded the pages amongst corrections, crossed-out passages, columns of duties, and stopping limits enough to satisfy the sternest carpenter.

Timothy read it, lips tightening at the order to throw away the guns.

"Admiral, may I ask something?"

"Go on."

"Are we truly throwing six guns into the sea?"

Timothy looked from one face to another. Fredo pointed at Edward, while Martinez indicated Fredo's load calculations. Edward folded his arms.

"Both members of the Royal Guard approved it."

Timothy drew the plan towards himself.

"Understood. If José asks, I know nothing."

Laughter burst around the table. It stopped when Timothy touched the target speed.

"Ten knots."

"It's a target, not a prophecy."

Edward rose.

"If trials give us nine and a half knots, but she answers the helm better and stays steady enough for the stern rake, I'll still attack. If she makes ten and begins pulling herself apart, we abandon the plan."

Timothy nodded.

"I like that number much better now."

Work began before noon. The *Red Baron* shortened sail in a relatively calm reach of the Atlantic, her bow oblique to the swell. Red and white chalk soon covered the fourth deck.

Two English carpenters argued with a Castilian for ten minutes over transverse beams. Edward climbed up to them, sounded each length with an axe handle, and ordered the entire assembly left intact.

Nobody mocked their caution. The guns came first.

Hoists groaned across the deck as cast-iron barrels rose from their carriages. Fredo stood to starboard, checking matched loads, assigned men, and timing while sailors handled the rigging. Whenever a team tried to hurry, he stopped them.

"Don't challenge a cable to a contest of strength. If it parts, the cable wins."

A burly Conquistador looked offended. Ten minutes later, an auxiliary hook slipped from its groove and lashed against the railing. The warrior said nothing more.

Martinez took the other side. She divided resting areas by watch and moved men with fevers, old injuries, or a tendency to lose body heat towards the remaining heaters. Cabin canvas became windbreaks below; hammocks hung in two tiers wherever headroom allowed.

An officer proposed more hammocks amidships to conserve heat. Martinez measured the clearance before the escape route and shook her head.

"If water comes in, they must get out in the dark. Keep this passage clear."

"But it'll cost us two more heating lamps."
