"Then extinguish the lamps in the officers' quarters, including mine."

Martinez held the officer's gaze until he nodded. From the head of the companionway, Fredo silently amended the allocation sheet.

By mid-afternoon, six fourth-deck guns lay secured low along the ship's centreline. The other six were unfastened, marked, and brought to the rail. No one cheered as each mass of iron plunged from the deck and vanished beneath the water.

Edward stood by the rail for the last one.

"Expensive."

Fredo handed him the load register.

"You can jump after it if you're sorry to see it go."

"You're learning the insolence of the Royal Navy."

"Three days with you have been enough."

After each gun, the crew checked draught against marks fore and aft. The carpenters revisited the red-chalk points, pressed their palms to the timber, and listened to the hull strain against the swell. Nothing shifted out of place.

Only then did work on the added structures begin.

The crews spared every principal post and load-bearing beam of the original three decks. They dismantled the later Castilian additions in order: cabin partitions, high rails, roof frames, ornamental platforms, auxiliary stores, and light flooring. Each section was lowered whole or cut into reusable lengths.

Some timber became spare braces; sound pieces went to repairing damaged gun carriages. Smaller scraps were bundled for the galley and heating stations. Aboard ship, every length of wood had a use.

Timothy ran between decks with two assistants, marking guns fit to fire, guns needing new retaining pins, and guns unfit for battle. By the end of the first watch, soot streaked his face from brow to collar.

"Admiral!"

Edward held one end of a lever for the carpenters.

"What?"

"The port pump is running again. The starboard pump still leaks at its bottom valve, but the men say another two hours will put it right. And Number Fourteen gun ought to be retired before she kills us."

"Mark her dead."

"You don't want another test?"

"Nobody dies to prove an old cannon still has her pride."

Timothy grinned and ran on.

Fredo relieved Edward at the lever unbidden. He stripped off his outer gloves, wound rope around his palms, and heaved alongside two sailors.

Edward watched him.

"Since when did you know how to use that?"

"I don't. But I know when two men are about to collapse."

One sailor laughed. Edward gave up his place and went to inspect another section.

By evening, the *Red Baron* scarcely resembled the vessel that had left Lisbon.

She remained a heavy three-decker, carrying nearly nine hundred people. One day's labour could scarcely make her a frigate. But her upper profile was lower and cleaner; the worst weight was gone, and what remained lay deeper and nearer her centre.

Edward stopped the celebrations before they began.

"Trials first."

They set more sail by degrees.

Timothy went aft with the log line. A sailor cast the small wooden log overboard; the line ran through the counter's hands as the hourglass was turned.

"Seven point eight!"

Edward gave no reaction.

For the second run, they spread more sail and adjusted the ship's trim.

"Eight point six!"

Fredo stood by the wheel, felt her swing round, then looked at Edward.

"Faster. But the greatest change is how willingly she turns."

"Next."

Martinez watched a rough inclinometer fixed beside the mainmast, its plumb line hanging across a marked board. Edward ordered turns to port and starboard; she read the heel each time.

"Steady. Still clear of the red mark."

The wind became more favourable towards evening.

The *Red Baron* filled her ice-treated sails, and the hull shuddered underfoot. The log went overboard for a third time.

Timothy watched the hourglass, counted the knots running past, and snapped his head up.

"Nine point seven!"

A few men began to cheer. Edward raised a hand.

"Again."

Fredo glanced at him.

"You're the sort of man who accepts a gift, then asks for the receipt."

"Again."

For the fourth trial, the crew trimmed the headsails and let the *Red Baron* run before the wind for a short distance. Timothy finished his count, then held the line for another second to check his eyes.

"Ten point one!"

Cheers erupted along the deck.

Edward watched the mainmast, listened to the rigging, and felt the helm's response. The timber gave no unusual sound. Martinez's plumb line settled within the permitted marks.

Only then did he release the wheel.

"Ten is a handsome figure. But remember, we have that speed only when the wind plays its part. If it turns at La Concha, don't expect a miracle."

Fredo raised his register.

"I'll write that down. Next time you boast of your genius, I'll have something to use against you."

"Please do. You're the novelist."

Passing, Martinez tapped Fredo's shoulder with the back of her hand.

"Write down those stopping limits you demanded, too. You've been more useful today than when you went hunting for tea."

"You drank the tea I brought."

"Beside the point."

That evening, supper was laid out on low wooden chests on the middle deck. There was no victory feast, only pea soup, salt meat, hard ship's biscuit, and tea hot enough to restore feeling to stiff fingers.

Edward raised his mug to the men around him.

"Nobody worked a miracle today. We simply stopped asking the *Red Baron* to do something she wasn't built to do."

Timothy finished chewing his biscuit.

"Does ten point one not count as a miracle, sir?"

"It counts as the ship having failed to kill us," Edward said.

Timothy shook his head at that remarkably low standard, but he was still smiling.

"I've learnt to be practical since Lisbon."

Edward raised his tea. A few men laughed, then went on eating to the sound of waves against the hull.

Late that night, Edward stood at the bow with a mug of cold tea. The wind salted his hair and collar; ahead lay darkness and a black stretch of water leading towards the Bay of Biscay.

Martinez approached with a list, looking rather less like a woman condemned to oversee blankets and canvas.

"The new resting watches are settled. The officers' quarters keep one heating lamp. The others have gone to the gunners and the men sleeping nearest the waterline."

Edward read the list.

"You cut your own heating?"

"I said our gunners mustn't freeze before the battle. It would be hard to keep their respect while sleeping beside three lamps."

Edward handed the paper back.

"Thank you."

Martinez leaned her forearms on the railing and looked across the black sea.

"In Lisbon, I thought you dangerous because you were too sure of yourself. Today you wouldn't let the carpenters cut a single piece of timber before they knew what load it carried."

"Disappointed?" Edward asked.

She shrugged.

"Rather less worried."

Fredo arrived with two fresh mugs of tea.

"He's still dangerous. We just know where to stand now when he picks up an axe."

He passed a mug to Martinez, then complained about the three pages of stopping conditions he had been made to sign.

She raised an eyebrow.

"You wrote them yourself."

"Details."

The three stood together facing Biscay. For a long while, none mentioned Lisbon.

Edward stared at the horizon.

"I miss Juliet and Remi."

Fredo offered no consolation. He sipped his tea and watched the sea beside Edward.

Martinez spoke quietly.

"Do you believe they're safe in Madrid?"

"Yes. I trust Isabella to keep her word."

"Then the rest is homesickness."

Edward laughed, but the sound made the word seem too slight for the ache in his chest. He tried again.

"Yes. Homesickness."

Martinez pulled her collar higher against the wind.

"Then come home alive and open your own front door. Don't leave that task to anyone else."

Edward turned to her.

"You make it sound like an order."

"I'm in the Royal Guard. Force of habit."

Fredo raised his mug.

"I support this order. At least it doesn't send me off looking for tea."

"You've just brought us tea."

Fredo looked at the mug in his hand and swore under his breath.

Below, the resting watches took their turns in the hammocks. After each hour of rough seas, carpenters checked the marked joints; Timothy tested both pumps once more before securing the powder magazine.

Before going below, Edward rested a hand on the rim of the wheel. The *Red Baron* answered more quickly than she had that morning, yet when a swell struck her bow, the full weight of wood and iron still travelled into his wrist. The sailor relieving him stepped alongside; Edward surrendered the wheel and went down the companionway.

title_vi: Chapter Twenty-Two: The Night Before La Concha
title_en: Chapter Twenty-Two: The Night Before La Concha
text_en:
Across the northern Bay of Biscay, *Red Baron* drove south through the darkness at nearly ten knots, the wind astern. Her recent alterations had made her quicker to answer the helm, though the weight of three gun decks still shuddered through the wheel whenever she rolled.

Edward sat against the oak wheel housing on the upper deck, a battered leather notebook open across his knees. In the wan light of a storm lantern swinging beside the rail, charcoal marks stirred old memories. Every hurried symbol and sketched arrow recalled the tactical briefings below.

Timothy had accepted command of the broadside with a firm nod, under orders to hold fire until they came within a few fathoms of the enemy flagship's stern. Martinez had listened gravely to her task of containing the French naval Gendarmes aboard that vessel. Fredo had looked less certain when charged with guarding their flank and stopping the enemy from severing the grappling lines between the ships.

Edward's finger settled on the final diagonal stroke: reinforcements arriving while a hundred Conquistadors remained stranded aboard the French flagship. He had set that possibility before Martinez and Fredo over the chart table.

"If our way back is cut off, don't cross the gap between the two lines of guns."

He pointed to the flagship's position.

"Bring down their officers, cut the anchor cables and use the hull to shield yourselves from their fire. Open a passage for our men to reach *Red Baron*."

Edward looked up, leaving the notebook open upon his knees.

For once, the Long Frost had yielded a clear winter sky. Leaden clouds had parted, exposing a scatter of hard, cold stars. Above the mainmast, the Castilian standard flew beside the red-cross ensign of the Royal Navy, both snapping in the salt wind.

It seemed only yesterday he had stood in a cowshed in Marrakesh, waiting for lime to cool. Now San Sebastián lay ahead, and nine hundred men slept, or struggled to sleep, upon the wooden decks beneath his feet.

His gaze returned to that diagonal stroke. If they failed to seize the flagship quickly, how long would he have to bring them back?

He eased the notebook shut but kept hold of its cover. He saw the door of their house in Madrid and heard Remi calling whenever footsteps sounded in the street.

What frightened him was the thought of that door opening to someone else.

The lantern's flame swam before his eyes. Its wavering light carried him back six years, to a snowbound night in London.

Amid the shouting and killing cold of the evacuation, he had shepherded Juliet and their one-year-old son aboard a ship fleeing across the sea. Remi was scarcely more than a bundle of cloth against his mother's breast, his breaths so weak that Edward feared the frost would steal the next one.

In the refugee vessel's damp, mouldy hold, Juliet had crouched beside a storm lantern, cupping both hands around the child's small feet. Each time his breathing faded, she bent to listen, then drew her coat tighter around him.

Edward stared at the lantern until the deck blurred. In Marrakesh, however late he came home, he could always lie beside Juliet and hear what mischief Remi had managed that day.

"Juliet... I miss you so much."

He covered his face. The next words slipped through his fingers.

"My dear little Remi..."

Wind crept down his collar. He bowed his head, struggling to swallow a sob when footsteps sounded on the stairs.

Martinez stopped beside the helm, placed a hand on his shoulder and waited. A few paces back, Fredo and Timothy turned towards the sea, giving him time to wipe his face.

"The wind is bitter here, Sir Edward."

Martinez dragged a wooden chest into the shelter behind the wheel.

"Come and sit over here."

Edward tried to answer, but his throat failed him. He moved aside to make room for her.

"I've checked the firing cords and the order of discharge again," Timothy said as he joined them. "If we must fire while turning, I'll have each gun follow the target's stern. We needn't wait until the whole broadside bears."

"And you?" Edward asked. "Have you slept at all?"

"A little."

Timothy rubbed his palms together.

"Then I went back to the guns. I know they've been checked, but the moment I lie down I start wondering what I've missed."

Edward pulled another chest towards him. Timothy sat, still rubbing warmth into his hands.

Edward brushed away the last tears with the back of his hand and surveyed the three officers.

"So you've all come up at this hour to freeze with me?"

"I've just handed over my watch," Fredo said, leaning against the wheel housing and leaving the helmsman room to pass. "Saw you here and thought I'd stop."

"Thank you."

Edward set the notebook on his knees. A moment passed before he could let go.

Martinez sat on the neighbouring chest.

"Tomorrow we may have no chance to speak except by shouting. We can talk of something else while we still have the chance."

"But we must sleep sometime," Timothy said. "I'd rather not summon you tomorrow and find all three nodding off."

"A little while longer."

Fredo turned up his collar.

"Keep the time. When it's late, send me below."

They drew their chests nearer the lantern, keeping the way to the wheel clear. Martinez had barely settled before she looked at Fredo.

"Sir Edward, have you ever read anything this gentleman has written? In Madrid he could spend an entire afternoon rewriting one sentence about a noblewoman walking down a corridor."

"Because someone kept reading over my shoulder and finding fault," Fredo said, steadying his chest. "You even corrected how a man held his sword during a dance."

"If he held it wrongly, of course I did."

Martinez glanced at Edward.

"And on patrol he stares at the ladies-in-waiting as though searching for his next heroine. Once I had to remind him the Queen was standing that way."

"I was looking at the person behind Her Majesty."

Fredo caught her smile.

"All right. That sounds worse."

Timothy laughed into his collar. Edward joined him, his voice still rough from the cold.

"Speaking of observation," Fredo said, "how many meetings with prospective husbands has the Queen arranged for you? Ten? I remember one fellow asked what you enjoyed, and you told him every way to break his guard."

"He asked about swords first."

"And you answered until the poor fellow begged to leave."

Martinez nudged Fredo's chest with her boot. He seized its edge to steady himself and raised a hand in surrender; she could not keep from laughing.

Timothy looked at Edward through the lantern light.

"You haven't heard about the Admiral's tea. If he goes without a cup in the morning, we pray the French make trouble early so he'll have someone else to be angry with."

"Timothy."

Edward laid a hand on his notebook.

"Think carefully before you say another word."

"Once, in northern France, you took us to a house on a hillside. The family was so frightened they pressed themselves against the wall."

Timothy paused to contain his laughter.

"I thought you'd order a search. Instead, you asked what tea they were drying behind the house."

Fredo turned towards Edward.

"In the middle of a campaign?"

"I still needed directions."

Edward raised one finger towards Timothy.

"And I paid for the tea."

"You did, sir. Then you made me carry it back and warned me not to get it wet. You were no more particular about the powder bags."

Martinez burst out laughing and leaned away from the lantern. Fredo asked whether the tea had been any good, and Edward could only answer once the others had quietened.

More old stories followed, some abandoned when the teller began laughing. At the change-of-watch bell, Timothy pointed to his timepiece; Fredo kept his word and went below with Martinez to rest before assembly.

At four in the morning, their footsteps returned to the stairs. Edward shut his silver watch as Timothy came up last, straightening his collar.

"Have they lit the galley fires, Timothy? If there's time, ask for four cups of tea. I owe you a tasting at dawn."

"You told me to remind everyone to sleep, and now you're sending me for tea."

Timothy looked at Fredo and shook his head.

"Very well. I'll see what they have."

He returned with four steaming cups on a tin tray. The rich scent cut through the salt and whale oil on deck, stilling the conversation for a moment.

Clouds hid the eastern horizon. By the rail, the four warmed their hands around their cups, shifting their feet whenever seawater washed across the planks.

Edward lifted his cup.

"It's still hot. Drink before we have to run again."

"To victory," Fredo said.

Martinez touched her cup to his. Timothy watched the steam curl upwards before raising his own.

"And to the way home."

***

Half past five in the morning.

Fog closed over the bay, wetting the rails and rigging. Beyond the muted lantern glow, Edward could make out only shadows moving to battle stations.

He straightened his bicorne, pulled his grey-and-white uniform coat close and walked the ranks. Eight hundred British veterans held rifles firing armour-piercing Vestigium rounds; a hundred Castilian Conquistadors stood among them, leather armour fitted and sabres ready.

"Listen."

Edward passed the waiting men, close enough to see their hands reddened by cold.

"The French fleet lies ahead. In Lisbon I promised to tell you why we have come: to relieve San Sebastián and open a road home for those still trapped within its walls."

He halted before a young gunner fighting the numbness in his fingers.

"If an order no longer fits what you see, report it at once. Our honour lies with the men who come home, not the dead we leave upon these decks."

Edward looked from the British veterans to the Castilian Conquistadors.

"You prepared this ship together. Last night you shared hot tea. This morning, remember the man beside you."

For a heartbeat, the ranks were silent. Then came the clatter of weapons being loaded along both sides, and Edward pointed towards the fog ahead.

"We reckon the fog will hold until about eight. If the wind changes, it may clear sooner."

He gestured towards the bow.

"We have two and a half hours. Don't waste them. Seize the flagship, break the blockade and keep a way back for the landing force. Understood?"

"AYE, ADMIRAL!"

The answer rolled along the deck, then fell beneath the click of gun locks, the strain of taut rigging and the footfall of men returning to their stations.

title_vi: Chapter Twenty-Three: The Battle of La Concha, Part One
title_en: Chapter Twenty-Three: The Battle of La Concha, Part One
text_en:
Fog swallowed the sea beyond thirty fathoms. The *Red Baron* slipped into the bay before the wind, her masts lost in the low white murk.

Whale grease mixed with powdered Vestigium kept the rigging supple and the blocks quiet. Sailors held loose lines against the hull. Only water lapping the planking betrayed their passage.

Edward kept both hands on the wheel, feeling each swell through its spokes. Fredo and Martinez watched from the rail as dark shapes surfaced and vanished in the fog.

Fredo lowered his Vestigium glass and pointed over the port bow.

"Two patrol frigates, some three hundred and thirty yards off. Their canvas is slack. They seem to be drifting."

Through his own glass, Edward saw French sentries huddled round a brazier. Ice coated their rigging and gun carriages. An alarm would find them slow to respond.

"Leave them."

Edward eased the helm to starboard.

"Keep silent. We're not giving away our position for two guard ships."

Martinez passed the order below. On the gun decks, the English soldiers drew back from the open ports, weapons ready.

The *Red Baron* slid between the frigates. Her crew held every line fast, listening to water slap against enemy hulls beyond the fog. Neither patrol fired.

Past them, the French flagship emerged by degrees. She carried four gun decks beneath the fleur-de-lis and lay at anchor beside the deep channel into San Sebastián, covering the coastal defences. Most of her broadside guns faced shoreward, leaving her stern exposed to the *Red Baron*.

"There she is."

Edward yielded the wheel to Timothy Beaumont. Once the young helmsman had a firm hold, he drew *Storm's Roar*.

Crimson light flared through its engravings. Snow hissed into steam within the grooves, warming his frozen fingers almost to pain.

Edward moved to the rail and aimed at the rudder stock and steering gear. He waited for the flagship's stern to lift upon a swell, tracking the rising target with his barrel.

His finger closed upon the trigger. He held his aim through one more heartbeat.

BOOM!

*Storm's Roar* kicked in his hands. Fire burst from its bronze muzzle, cutting a crimson path through the fog. The report rolled between the ships across the bay.

The fiery shot struck the rudder assembly. Pins flew loose, connecting rods snapped, and a great section of the stern exploded into timber and steel.

The blast shattered the navigation cabin windows. The chart table overturned and the compass flew from its mounting. The watch officer struck the bulkhead amid shouts from below.

"Hard a-port! Rake her stern!"

Edward lowered the smoking weapon and caught the rail as the *Red Baron* swung round.

Timothy spun the wheel. The *Red Baron* crossed the flagship's stern, bringing her broadside almost square to the enemy's keel. At less than twenty-two yards, the lower gunports faced the shattered command cabin.

"Gun crews! Double shot and chain shot! Fire!"

Timothy dropped his raised hand.

The broadside thundered. The *Red Baron* lurched under the recoil, and powder smoke rolled over the water, swallowing the French stern.

Round shot and chain shot tore along the gun decks. Carriages broke from their securing bolts; shattered beams blocked the companionways; men fell among severed ropes. As the smoke thinned, ruin stretched almost to the mainmast, accompanied by screams for help.

Edward waited until the guns had passed the line of her stern, then signalled.

"Shorten the main and foresails! Let go the starboard anchor to check our way!"

Hands hauled in the canvas. The anchor cable jerked taut, shaking the *Red Baron* as she slowed. Timothy fought the wheel to keep the broadside trained upon the wrecked stern.

English soldiers rose in ranks and levelled their muskets over the rail. Fredo drew his sword, waiting until the foremost rank had found its targets.

"Fire by volleys!"

Armour-piercing balls swept the exits from the lower decks, pinning the French marines behind broken timber.

Martinez pointed her sword towards the flagship.

"Conquistadors! Board her!"

Grappling irons bit into the rail and shattered stern framework. The Conquistadors tested their ropes and swung across, the first men covering those landing behind them on the gun-ravaged deck.

Pistols cracked in succession at close range. Sheltering behind wrecked carriages, the shooters held the defenders down while sabre men pushed across the gaps.

"Forward to the bows!"

Martinez pointed towards the anchor capstan and led the first party over the broken planking.

They had scarcely passed amidships when the lower hatches flew open. Gendarmes poured onto the deck, barring the route towards the bow.

Vestigium plate enclosed them from head to foot. Despite their heavy hammers and maces, they moved swiftly across the slick boards, forcing the boarders into narrow passages by sheer weight of iron.

"Gendarmes!"

Martinez caught a descending mace upon her sword. Her heel slid across the wet boards before she recovered her footing.

"Split into two wings! No single combat! Change your angle and aim behind their knees and beneath their helmets! Anchor party, take their flank. Cut that chain at any cost!"

The Conquistadors shifted their fire towards joints at knee and neck. Most balls glanced from the frontal plates. A few found seams, but the armoured line barely slowed.

Hammers and maces crashed against Castilian Vestigium leather. It turned blades and bullets, but could not spare the bones beneath from the force of each blow.

One soldier doubled over after a strike to the breast. His comrade hauled him clear, only to take the next mace himself. The assault fell back towards amidships, with the anchor party trapped behind the iron line.

Martinez stepped into the breach. She activated her Miracle-grade Vestigium sword, turquoise light running along its edge as the joints unfolded into a claymore more than seven feet long.

"Hold both wings! Leave these three to me!"

She went forward alone to meet three Gendarmes.

The first swung his war hammer straight at her head. Martinez lifted the claymore crosswise and met the blow without flinching.

Metal rang against metal. The great blade absorbed the shock; her arms held steady as the astonished soldier stared at the unmoving steel.

Martinez pivoted, turning her guard into a sweeping cut at his neck. He could not recover his hammer.

Steel pierced the gorget. Blood spilled beneath his helmet as he fell, dropping the weapon.

The other two charged together. The one on her left swung a spiked mace across her waist, while the other brought his down at her shoulder.

Martinez dropped low and knocked the first mace aside, then drove her claymore's point into the gap beneath the second man's helm. He fell at his comrade's feet. The survivor recoiled.

"Hold the wings! Anchor party, forward!"

Her cry cut through the smoke as she held the passage open for the surviving Conquistadors.

They followed the gap she had carved, stepping past wounded men, sabres raised, towards the capstan.

Five more Gendarmes surged up the companionway. The opening closed before the assault party could pass.

Martinez snatched back her blade to avoid a falling Castilian. Her next cut missed a neck joint and lodged in the commander's breastplate. She pulled hard, but the steel would not come free.

A Gendarme struck from the flank. Her leather held, but two ribs broke beneath the mace. Martinez coughed blood and fell, losing her grip on the claymore embedded in the enemy's armour.

She braced her boots and sprang up before the mace returned. Seizing the trapped hilt with both hands, she used it to vault from the deck.

Her legs locked around the mace wielder's helmet. With the buried sword as her pivot, Martinez twisted her body. His neck broke beneath the iron, and he collapsed beside her.

She tore the claymore free, cut down another Gendarme barring her path, and ordered her men to reform. Smoke and blood had roughened her voice to a rasp.

A shot cracked behind her. The ball tore through her shoulder, jerking her sword arm aside. Before she could turn, an iron mace haft struck her between the shoulders.

That blow ended her resistance. Her sight dimmed; the claymore slid from numb fingers, and she fell across planks slick with blood and frost.

A Gendarme stepped forward and raised his spiked mace above the fallen member of the Royal Guard for the killing stroke.

From the *Red Baron*, Edward hurried another round into *Storm's Roar*, closed its breech, and aimed. He fired, hurling the attacker aside in a spray of broken armour. The men around him recoiled.

Edward crossed the gap between the ships, his boots sliding upon the frozen deck as he landed. In his hand shone his own sabre, bearing a fragment of *Excalibur*. Steam curled along its edge and ancient grooves.

He fought towards Martinez, beating aside weapons that barred his path. Whenever his blade met Vestigium plate, light ran through the cracks opening in the steel.

Reaching her, Edward swept the enemy back and hauled her upright by an armour strap. Blood darkened her wounded shoulder. Her claymore lay a pace away.

"Can you still breathe, Lady Martinez?"

Martinez coughed blood onto her hand. Her lip was split, yet her eyes stayed on the soldiers approaching through the smoke.

"Not dead yet... so don't trouble yourself."

Edward glanced at her fallen blade and crouched to let her climb onto his back.

"Hold fast. Can you guard my right?"

Martinez gritted her teeth and hooked her left arm over his shoulder.

"I can. Don't push me against the ship's side."

Edward raised his sabre towards the nearest soldiers.

"Conquistadors, guard our flanks! Get the anchor party forward!"

The survivors formed two wings around them. Pistols fired through the gaps; sabres caught descending maces, buying time for the anchor party to advance.

Edward shielded Martinez from blows on his left, turning each away with his sword. They won the deck a pace at a time, between iron-clad bodies.

At the bows, the anchor party knelt beside the chain. Their comrades held the narrow approach while axes struck the links.

The chain parted and plunged through the hawsehole. With rudder and anchor both lost, the French flagship began turning with the current towards the rocks outside San Sebastián.

"Anchor cut! Everyone back to the *Red Baron*!"

Edward turned, sweeping his sabre behind him to signal the retreat.

They had scarcely faced about when a sudden volley struck the gun carriages behind them. Several men fell before they could find cover.

The remaining Conquistadors closed around Edward and Martinez, firing back while dragging wounded comrades behind wrecked guns. Heavy balls hammered their Vestigium leather, dropping men at the edge of the formation. The armour held, but blood poured from their mouths.

Out of the smoke came fresh Gendarmes, accompanied by musketeers in black wool coats embroidered with the French royal arms: Mousquetaires Noirs.

Their long-barrelled muskets fired reinforced steel-cored balls, made to penetrate the heavy plate worn by soldiers of the Holy Roman Empire.

The Gendarmes shielded the front while the Mousquetaires Noirs kept clear firing lanes behind them. Volley after volley drove Edward's men onto the cramped forecastle, where two swordsmen could scarcely turn.

A young officer emerged behind the French line. His blond hair was tied with a black ribbon, his dark blue naval coat worked in silver thread amid the snow-caked armour. He carried two slender curved sabres and approached as though inspecting men already defeated.

He sprang through a gap between two shields. Both blades flashed into the openings beneath arms and at the throat. Three Conquistadors fell before a fourth could retreat to close ranks.

"The officer with the tied hair! Volley fire!"

From the *Red Baron*, Timothy dropped his hand, signalling the English gun crews.

The Gendarmes closed ranks before their commander. Shots from the *Red Baron* pierced the outer plates, but fresh men filled every breach, keeping Pierrot hidden from the guns.

Without warning, the Gendarmes crouched. Through their ranks, the Mousquetaires Noirs fired together, sending steel-cored balls across to the *Red Baron* before the English could reload.

Oak burst into sharp splinters. Shot tore through sandbags and woollen coats, pitching men backwards beside the ports. Sailors dragged the wounded clear while cannon thundered elsewhere in the bay.

Pierrot flicked blood from his sabres and regarded Edward over the closing ranks.

"Do you see the colour of blood against snow, Admiral?"

His eyes travelled over the ruined deck, then returned to Edward. His voice remained intolerably calm.

"Men say war has its own order and beauty. I wonder if you still believe them."

Pierrot bowed amid the wreckage.

"Pierrot de Kenway, captain of *Le Triomphant*. I've long wished to meet the Pathfinder in person."

Edward settled Martinez against a bulkhead and retrieved an ordinary sabre from a fallen Conquistador. His right hand still held his own blade, the one bearing a fragment of *Excalibur*, its Celtic script casting gold across the filthy snow. He weighed the borrowed steel in his left.

Edward inclined the ordinary sabre towards Pierrot, keeping the fragment-bearing weapon near Martinez.

"Pierrot de Kenway. A fitting name for someone who loves a stage."

He met the young captain's eyes.

"Have you finished?"

Pierrot glanced at the sword in Edward's left hand and smiled. He stayed out of reach.

"I didn't come to quarrel, Edward."

He lowered one blade, keeping the other pointed towards Edward.

"I wanted you to understand your position."

Pierrot looked towards the thinning fog.

"It's time you saw the rest of the battle."

A hard west wind swept the deck, tearing the mist into streamers. Edward glanced at his watch: 6:45 a.m., an hour and fifteen minutes earlier than expected.

French signal lamps appeared across the mouth of the bay. Ships of the line and frigates had closed the circle, their broadsides trained upon the *Red Baron* and *Le Triomphant*.

Beyond the entrance, four great Portuguese warships emerged with the westerly wind. Imperial flags showed at their mastheads as the fog peeled away, revealing heavy Vestigium-equipped hulls advancing astern of the *Red Baron*.

"You see, Edward."

Pierrot withdrew behind the wall of iron.

"Today, the way out to sea is barred."

He retreated behind the Gendarmes, leaving the cramped deck to the advancing soldiers. His eyes remained on Edward until the iron ranks hid them both.

The Gendarmes came on step by step, shielding themselves from fire and driving the Conquistadors against the bulwarks. Mousquetaires Noirs fired through gaps in the line. Men fell, leaving spaces Edward had no reserves to fill.

Edward counted the passages between smashed gun carriages. The black musketeers held the rear, the Gendarmes the front, and the way back to the *Red Baron* narrowed. His sword hand grew numb from parrying one crushing blow after another.

Martinez caught his wrist before he could advance again.

Edward bent towards her. She looked up, breathing hard through the pain in her chest and shoulder.

"Look at me, Sir Edward."

She tightened her grip until his eyes met hers.

"Isabella is waiting for you. We must get out of here."

Fighting down a cough that tore through her broken ribs, the member of the Royal Guard ripped the gold chain bearing Castile's royal emblem from her neck. She pressed its lion pendant against the bleeding bullet wound in her shoulder.

The lion shone in her hand. Turquoise light faded from Martinez's fallen claymore, and the great sword contracted into its original sabre form.

With her last strength, she pressed the warm, bloodstained chain into Edward's palm.

"Put it on. It will take one mortal blow in your stead."

She paused to draw breath, still urging the pendant towards him.

"And the sword... you can release its true form."

Edward glanced at her reverted sabre, then closed his fingers around the lion. Turning to shield Martinez from the French, he slipped the chain over his head.

The pendant touched his breast. The number 25 vanished, and heat ran down his spine. Martinez caught his wrist once more before letting go.

"Close your eyes. Think of the weapon you want."

Her breath came in broken gasps.

"You can choose only once. That shape will remain yours forever."

The borrowed sabre dropped from Edward's left hand. He gripped his own Vestigium sword, still bearing the fragment of *Excalibur*, and shut his eyes as iron-shod boots approached.

Gold flooded the grooves of the blade, forcing the nearest Gendarmes to stagger backwards. The sabre lengthened into a straight, double-edged sword; ancient Celtic runes appeared along its fuller, burning through the drifting smoke.

Edward recognised the name engraved upon the steel.

*Excalibur*.

title_vi: Chapter Twenty-Four: The Battle of La Concha, Part Two
title_en: Chapter Twenty-Four: The Battle of La Concha, Part Two
text_en:
The west wind tore the fog from La Concha Bay. Pale water flashed between the dark hulls as the mist broke apart. From the coastal forts of San Sebastián, sentries glimpsed warships trading fire offshore and hurried to alert the Governor.

"Governor Frenesia! There's fighting in the bay. A warship flying Castilian colours is engaging the French!"

Frenesia set down her pen. The officer stood breathless in the doorway, and she beckoned him to her desk.

"One ship? Have we received her signals?"

"Not yet, madam. She's lost her upper deck, so we couldn't identify her from the tower. But we saw the lion banner, and beneath it... the red cross of England."

Ink fell from her pen onto the corner of a document. Frenesia studied the stain, then looked up.

"Have you checked?"

"Three times, through the North Tower's telescope. Four black-sailed Portuguese warships are closing from the west."

Frenesia rose, fastening her gloves as she crossed to the door. Past sixty, she held herself straight beneath her dark military greatcoat.

"Come with me to Monte Urgull."

The doors opened upon salt air thick with sulphur and cannon smoke. She stepped into the cold and headed for the hill above the harbour.

Ammunition carts choked the road, their iron rims grinding over frozen cobbles. Frenesia walked beside the officer, passing militiamen hauling sandbags beneath an awning. Their leader shoved an empty handcart aside to clear her path.

At a field kitchen she stopped. An elderly woman in a woollen shawl was serving dried turnips with a wooden ladle, her fingers stiff with cold. She made to bow.

"Keep serving." Frenesia looked into the soup cauldron. "How long can you keep it warm?"

"With the red lime, until early afternoon, madam. There are two streets still to feed."

"Reduce the salt in the next batch by one fifth. Send the rest to the stores for preserving meat."

She turned to her officer.

"Tell the well guards to keep children clear of the openings. I will not have another fall in."

She pressed on towards Santa Catalina Bridge, joining the two banks of the city.

The bridge formed the defence that kept the French out of the inner city. Two oak barricades spanned its width, rifled muskets trained through loopholes towards the far bank. Ice gathered around the firing slits, where men waited with fingers curled around their triggers.

A young lieutenant, his face black with soot and ice clinging to his hat, snapped to attention and presented arms.

"Governor! The Third Garrison Battalion holds the bridgehead! The French long guns fired three harassing salvoes, but every shot fell into the river!"

Frenesia examined the piers and asked how close the rounds had struck. She ordered another inspection after the next bombardment and told him to hold his position.

In the lanes of Parte Vieja, she moved the surgical station into a cellar, beyond the reach of flying splinters. Patrols were sent for blankets from the churches, to be carried to the shelters against the cold. Messengers departed with each order while she walked.

Behind her, two orderlies bore a stretcher down the cellar steps. Her liaison officer had to run to catch her as she turned uphill.

The cobbled road steepened beneath her boots. Frenesia passed through the gates of La Mota Fortress and climbed the western rampart, where the cannonade carried clearly on the wind. She did not slow until she reached the parapet.

At the highest step, she took a brass telescope from the engineer commander.

Gun smoke rolled over the water, spreading in torn veils where the wind caught it. Through the glass she saw torn canvas, half-burnt hulls, and a warship stripped of her upper deck lying close astern of *Le Triomphant*. The Castilian lion and England's red cross flew together from her signal lines.

She swept the telescope along the battered ship. Hundreds of men in grey and white fired without pause, but one figure near the rail caught her eye.

A blond man moved between firing positions, shooting French soldiers attempting to swing aboard on ropes. Each muzzle flash lit the lion pendant at his breast, marked Tres.

"Fredo..."

She held the glass on him until he vanished behind a mast.

The artillery commander came to her side.

"Madam, they're caught between the French fleet and four Portuguese warships. Shall the coastal batteries give covering fire?"

Frenesia swung the glass towards *Le Triomphant*'s bow. Golden light flickered among the armoured French, revealing a man with a great double-edged sword. His attackers had just been driven back.

She lowered the telescope.

"Beyond our range. Firing now would only waste powder and shot."

She returned the glass and pointed towards the harbour.

"Ready our warships to weigh anchor. When we draw the enemy into range, the fortress guns will support us. Bring the men on that ship home."

***

Golden light coursed through the ancient Celtic inscriptions on *Excalibur*. The blade warmed the icebound deck, illuminating blood pooled in cracks between the planks.

Martinez leaned against a bulkhead, watching the light move along the steel. She gripped Edward's coat and coughed blood before she could speak.

"This power... it doesn't feel like Miracle rank any more."

She lifted her eyes to his.

"It may have reached Legend rank. Use it to open a path."

Her fingers fell from his coat. Edward watched her chest rise and fall, then faced the approaching maces.

He gripped *Excalibur* in both hands, its point low before the advancing Gendarmes.

The guns still thundered, but the pauses between reports lengthened. Edward felt the vibration in the boards beneath his boots linger unnaturally. He saw a Gendarme's fingers shift upon a mace haft, then watched the edge of his breastplate turn with impossible slowness.

Snow drifted before his eyes. The Gendarmes and Pierrot's sabres moved as though dragged through deep water, exposing openings he had missed a heartbeat earlier.

Individual flakes hung almost motionless, falling slowly enough to count. Every twitch, every tightening muscle beneath the Gendarmes' armour stood out as their spiked maces descended. He could trace Pierrot's crawling blades, every blind angle and gap between plates.

"We meet again."

Edward recognised his younger self, dressed in a British admiral's uniform. The apparition walked between the sluggish soldiers and stopped beside him, studying the sword; its customary mockery had softened.

"Not bad."

A white-gloved hand settled on his shoulder.

"But you've still got someone to bring home."

The sound of timber breaking at Inverness returned, a single sharp crack in the silence. He remembered the weight of what he had left there. Edward kept his gaze on the passage towards the stern.

The man he had once been stood beside him, an old sabre in hand. Steel reflected against *Excalibur*, revealing those familiar white gloves. The apparition looked towards *Red Baron*, where the survivors waited.

"You know what to do," the apparition said.

Cannon fire and wind rushed back together. Edward raised his sword and shifted his weight forwards.

He struck the seam of a Gendarme's breastplate. Steel broke beneath *Excalibur*, and force travelled along the blade, knocking back two men pressing from behind.

The shockwave swept the cramped deck, scattering armour plates and hurling nearby soldiers aside. Splinters rattled across the frozen boards. Edward cut to starboard, forcing the Mousquetaires Noirs back from the rail.

The opening let the surviving Conquistadors drag their wounded onwards. One shouted the advance; the others fired along both flanks to cover Edward.

Blood ran down one musketeer's chin. He steadied his barrel on a comrade's shoulder, firing through the narrow gaps Edward carved in the French line. Each sweep of Edward's sword won them a few more steps towards *Red Baron*.

Then a fresh gun deck emerged beyond the smoke.

A French three-decker had closed to 220 yards off *Le Triomphant*'s bow. Her broadside faced the wrecked ship, gunports open and barrels trained upon the men below.

"EVERYONE, ABANDON SHIP!"

Edward's warning had scarcely left his mouth when the planks convulsed beneath him.

Explosions erupted below *Le Triomphant*'s decks. Her powder stores ignited one after another, tearing through the frames and wrenching planking from its fastenings. Each blast came from farther aft, as though fire were racing beneath the survivors.

Timber and iron burst through black smoke. Men from both armies were hurled overboard as the lower decks collapsed, exposing flooded holds beneath.

Red pillars of flame tore upwards through the wreck, dragging smoke towards the sky. The blast crushed timber underfoot and flung soldiers into the freezing sea.

The hull shuddered beneath further cannon fire at close range. Wounded men lay crowded upon the wet deck while those still standing hauled them from the passage and returned to the fight.

The remaining Gendarmes and Mousquetaires Noirs kept advancing, their armour scorched, their flesh blistered. One could scarcely hold his musket yet clung to the man ahead, stumbling over dead comrades. Edward searched their faces and saw no sign of retreat.

"They prepared to blow the ship apart from within."

Edward glanced towards the smoking waist.

"Pierrot knew."

He shifted *Excalibur* into his right hand and caught the nearly unconscious Martinez with his left. Her arm across his shoulders, he picked his way over the soundest planks towards the stern.

The golden inscriptions dimmed with the one-handed grip. He severed a mace haft, but no shockwave followed, and French soldiers surged into the gap.

"Protect the Admiral!"

A Conquistador called his comrades back, scarcely audible over the blasts below.

They closed ranks around Edward and Martinez. Firing as they withdrew, they used musket stocks to fend off descending maces. Whenever a man fell, another filled the breach.

One soldier dropped after intercepting a mace meant for his comrade. Another stepped into his place before the armoured French could break through. Blood soaked the seams of leather armour; empty pistols gave way to sabres, then broken musket stocks.

"ADMIRAL! FALL BACK!"

A Conquistador with a bayonet through his shoulder seized the enemy musket to hold its owner in place. He turned towards Edward.

"We can hold them a little longer. Get Martinez back to *Red Baron*!"

Edward reached *Le Triomphant*'s stern with Martinez supported against him. Of the hundred Conquistadors who had boarded, only three or four could still keep pace, their leather armour torn and soaked with blood.

Another explosion ripped through the lower hull. Water poured through the breach, dragging the bow down and pitching the stern high. The planking buckled beneath men who had not found a handhold.

The swell struck *Red Baron*, lifting her port side. Guns rolled against their breeching ropes, and the grappling lines joining the ships dragged her towards the sinking French hull. The strain carried through the tackle with a sound like splitting wood.

Edward slid across the steepening quarterdeck. *Red Baron* lay more than 35 yards away; every loose rope and swinging line at *Le Triomphant*'s stern had snapped or burnt through. Across the water, Timothy and his sailors hacked at the last chains to free their ship.

Edward looked from Martinez, limp in his arms, to the grappling tackle dragging at *Red Baron*. The sea churned darkly between them. Leave it fast, and the British vessel would capsize too.

He settled Martinez against the wheel pedestal and drew *Storm's Roar*, aiming at the most heavily strained connection.

*Storm's Roar* thundered.

Its crimson projectile struck where tackle met chain, snapping iron links stretched almost to breaking.

The last lines parted. *Red Baron* lurched clear of the French hull and drifted away from the whirlpool forming beside the wreck.

Edward thrust the empty *Storm's Roar* into his belt and hurried back to Martinez.

He carried her into the corner between the wheel pedestal and the stern cabin, away from the sloping deck. He covered her with his coat and wedged a broken beam against the hem as the planks shook.

Edward rose and took *Excalibur* in both hands. Golden light returned to its inscriptions, flickering through the powder smoke.

Below, Gendarmes and Mousquetaires Noirs clambered up broken timbers towards the rising stern. They still bore maces and firearms, though seawater had flooded the two decks forward. Men slipped, recovered, and climbed again over the shoulders of the fallen.

Edward braced himself and held the blade across their approach. He could defend the narrow space before Martinez, but the deck beneath was shrinking by the moment.

"Edward! Duck!"

Fredo's voice came from above. A figure plunged through the smoke and landed beside him.

Fredo's cloak was torn at one shoulder, and salt water dripped from his sleeves. Segmented steel links were retracting into his sabre's hilt, while the far end of *Vinculum* had just released its hold on *Red Baron*, now more than 130 feet away.

"How did you get here?"

Edward watched the segments coil into the weapon.

"Later."

Fredo planted his feet against the tilting deck.

"Pick up Martinez. Hold on to me."

Edward returned *Excalibur* to its sabre form and sheathed it before lifting Martinez. He wrapped his free arm around Fredo's waist, holding tight as the deck tilted further.

Fredo raised his sabre. Steel joints unfolded again, linked by slender Vestigium cables, and *Vinculum* lengthened into a flexible ribbon of blades that followed his wrist.

French muskets rose below. Fredo lashed the weapon over their heads.

The segmented blade snared the barrels of five Mousquetaires Noirs and the gorgets of two leading Gendarmes. Fredo twisted his wrist and hauled, wrenching muskets from hands and dragging both armoured men down.

He reversed the blade into the knees of soldiers struggling uphill. As the front rank recoiled, he sent *Vinculum* towards *Red Baron*'s main yard.

His gaze followed the spar, measuring the gap against his weapon's reach.

"Maximum reach, 180 feet! Hold tight, Sir Edward!"

Fredo's shout fought the wind.

A tremendous crack sounded beneath them. *Le Triomphant*'s stern burst apart as her hull sank amid shattered timber and filthy foam. The deck gave way.

As all three fell, Fredo snapped his wrist and fired *Vinculum* towards *Red Baron*'s yard.

The hook extended its full 180 feet but passed beneath the timber. A wave carried *Red Baron* farther off, opening the gap to nearly 187 feet. No links remained, and all three were still falling.

Timothy saw the hook fall short, then looked towards the gun carriages whose breeching ropes were not fully secured. He called the nearest sailors to starboard.

Seizing the breeching rope of a thirty-two-pounder, he pointed towards the falling figures.

"Ease the breeching! Hold the check ropes! Run that gun to starboard and bring the yard down to them!"

The crew threw their shoulders against the carriage, using the roll to shift its weight. Men on the restraining ropes checked its run before the wheels travelled too far. Other sailors crowded starboard, heeling *Red Baron* towards Fredo.

The ship listed hard enough to send loose snow sliding across the planks. Her mast inclined with the hull, carrying the yard towards the falling figures while the crew fought to keep the cannon from running loose.

The spar swept down, closing the gap to 177 feet. The hook struck wood and its final links locked around the spar, the Vestigium cable taut within its 180-foot limit.

"HE'S CAUGHT IT!"

Timothy saw the hook bite fast. *Vinculum* snapped taut, and Fredo clutched Edward and Martinez as the sudden pull flung all three towards *Red Baron*.

The Vestigium cables strained beneath their combined weight. Fredo twisted into the swing, hauling Edward and Martinez clear of the churning water. Their momentum carried them over the British deck.

All three struck the planks and slid through broken snow, coming to rest beside the mainmast. Edward turned his shoulder to shield Martinez from the final impact. Fredo fell to one knee as *Vinculum* slowly retracted into its hilt.

"RIGHT THE SHIP! ALL HANDS TO YOUR STATIONS! SECURE THE GUN CARRIAGES!"

The gun crews hauled their cannon back and tightened the breeching ropes while sailors shifted to port. *Red Baron* rolled hard once more, then slowly recovered her balance. Timothy held the rope until the final carriage was chocked.

"WE'VE GOT THEM!"

title_vi: Chapter Twenty-Five: The Battle of La Concha, Part Three
title_en: Chapter Twenty-Five: The Battle of La Concha, Part Three
text_en:
"THE ADMIRAL LIVES!"

The cry had scarcely crossed the decks when black columns of water erupted beside the *Red Baron*. The French fleet had closed its ring, and broadsides struck from three directions.

Round shot and explosive shells hammered her hull. Oak beams shuddered in their fastenings, while the crack of splitting timber raced along the lower gun deck.

The *Red Baron* had been built from Sherwood oak, its ancient grain steeped in the influence of Vestigium. That timber could withstand blows which would splinter ordinary shipbuilding wood, and had kept her afloat through the first volleys.

Now deep fissures ran along the starboard side. Planks tore loose and smoke curled from the impact points. Two more concentrated broadsides there would flood the decks below.

Timothy hauled Edward upright and pointed towards the fractures.

"The side's giving way! Two more volleys like that and the gun deck will flood!"

Edward took the southward bow as his bearing. French guns hemmed them in on three sides, while four Portuguese warships advanced across the mouth of the bay. With each swell, the gap between the formations narrowed.

Farther out, a French ship spread her canvas and withdrew. Edward glimpsed Pierrot de Kenway on her deck, retreating while the wreck of *Le Triomphant* sank astern.

Edward glanced at the signal flag thrashing in the wind.

"Set every headsail and mainsail! Take the westerly and make for the mouth of the bay!"

Timothy studied the four black-sailed vessels.

"They're blocking us. At this speed, we'll never clear the leader's bow."

"I need the wind they're driving towards us."

Edward drew *Storm's Roar* and pressed its grip into Timothy's hand.

"I'll take the helm. Break the French pursuit astern, and don't let them force us to turn too soon."

Timothy checked the empty chamber and took ammunition from Edward's pouch.

"I'll call when the stern is clear. Don't put the helm hard over before then."

Edward returned to the wheel and turned the *Red Baron* into the westerly. Her eased sails filled taut; the heavy hull hesitated, then gathered speed.

Gunports opened along her flanks. The crews fired to keep the French pursuers from forcing an early turn.

Below, Timothy loaded *Storm's Roar* as Edward's command rang down from the helm.

"Port bow! Aim low for that French ship's powder magazine! Fire!"

Timothy pulled the trigger. A blazing red projectile buried itself in the enemy's side and ignited her magazine. The explosion tore the warship in two, opening a gap in the pursuit.

Edward steered between towering shell splashes. The *Red Baron* answered her helm more swiftly since the refit, but the weight of her hull still lagged behind each turn.

The Portuguese guns fired alloy shot strengthened by Vestigium. Purple-black streaks shrieked through the air, converging on the *Red Baron's* weakened planking with greater accuracy than the French volleys.

One shell smashed through the upper deck and gouged a smoking crater in the Sherwood oak. Its angle spared the waterline, but flying splinters struck down nearby sailors.

The black-sailed ships spread more canvas, using Vestigium to stir the westerly into a gale. The same gust struck the *Red Baron*, setting her rigging screaming and straining every reinforcement.

Timothy braced *Storm's Roar* against a gunport and waited for the shout from above.

"Port quarter! Second ship of the line!"

"I see her!"

He waited for the hull to rise on a swell before firing. When Edward called out a frigate off the starboard bow, Timothy moved to another port and rammed a fresh round into the scorching weapon.

The barrel of *Storm's Roar* glowed red with each discharge. Timothy watched four French pursuers catch fire, then a fifth, their magazines exploding one after another. The survivors scattered, trimming sail in haste to keep their distance.

Flames split the French formation. Timothy shouted towards the helm.

"Astern is clear! You can turn!"

"Hard to port! Starboard guns, stand ready!"

Edward wrestled the wheel across, waiting until the *Red Baron* had enough way on to sweep across the leading Portuguese warship's bows.

She crossed the black-sailed vessel's stem. Her starboard broadside erupted at point-blank range, smashing the enemy's forward gun mountings and forecastle railings.

But the Portuguese ship was closing too fast. Three quarters of the *Red Baron* had cleared her bow; the stern remained in the path of the charge.

The enemy's Vestigium-armoured ram struck the *Red Baron's* stern. The helm platform and command station splintered, hurling Edward across the wreckage-strewn deck.

He planted his sabre against the planks and struggled upright. Portuguese soldiers were massing on the enemy's bow beyond the broken wheel.

"Infantry! Form a firing line! Make a wall of muskets! Prepare to repel boarders!"

"Timothy! Keep the gunners below at their posts! Fire every broadside gun and *Storm's Roar* at will. Punch through her lower hull where she's rammed our stern!"

Through the wreck of the quarterdeck, Edward saw the other three Portuguese warships swing round behind their leader. Their gun decks turned towards the helpless *Red Baron*. A single raking volley would leave her nowhere to hide.

"KILL ALL THE CASTILIANS!"

Portuguese Conquistadors poured over the shattered timber joining the ships. They wore full iron armour, grey morion helmets and heavy broadswords of an older pattern, unlike the supple leather of Castile's Conquistadors.

"Fire by volley!"

Edward dropped his hand. Four hundred British veterans fired, their Vestigium rounds punching through old plate and staggering the Portuguese front rank.

Breastplates and belly armour split, yet the enemy kept coming. One soldier took shot after shot at close range and fell only when his legs could no longer bear the weight of his harness. The others stepped over him without a glance.

Bullets alone could not stop them. Edward saw men wounded beyond any ordinary body's endurance still raise their swords and march upon the British line, as though pain had been cut from their flesh.

One took nearly a dozen shots through his organs before he staggered and crashed to the deck.

The Portuguese closed. Broadswords pierced British woollen coats, and the men at the front could not retreat from the broken edge of the deck. Their cries vanished beneath the clash of steel on timber.

Edward raised his sabre and activated the pendant Martinez had given him. The blade lengthened into *Excalibur*. Gripping it with both hands, he stepped between the advancing suits of armour.

*Excalibur* sheared through the gorgets of the first two Conquistadors. Both fell, but others with bullets through their chests pressed on.

"Aim for their necks! Take off their heads!"

Fredo sheltered Martinez from the wind in a recess beneath the mizzenmast, then activated *Vinculum*. Its cable-linked blades slid beneath Portuguese gorgets, wrenching the front rank aside and dragging men out of the narrow passages beside the gun carriages.

Still the Portuguese swarmed over the rail. The surviving British soldiers yielded ground around the masts, hauling the wounded behind gun mountings. Snow beneath their boots became dark sludge under trampling feet and blood.

When the tenth enemy fell, Edward had to lean upon his sword to catch his breath. He looked towards the mouth of the bay and saw the black sails changing course.

The remaining three Portuguese warships had completed their encirclement, their gunports opening towards the *Red Baron*. They lay less than a hundred yards away. With the rudder wrecked and the gun deck depleted, Edward knew they could never evade the next volley unaided.

From the southern mouth of the bay, Frenesia's warships struck the Portuguese flank. Castilian triple-barrelled guns fired in rapid succession, punching through the sides of all three vessels poised to rake the *Red Baron*.

The black-sailed ships turned their guns against both foes. A purple volley snapped one of the *Red Baron's* masts and hurled a gun mounting into the air; other broadsides struck the San Sebastián fleet as it struggled to hold its distance.

An explosion thundered beneath the stern just as the Portuguese broadside began. Edward ducked and gripped a railing. The hull shuddered as if snagged on something beneath the water.

Below, Timothy waited for the Portuguese bow to lift on a swell, exposing the hull beyond the broken planks. He braced *Storm's Roar* against the opening and fired.

The enemy's magazine detonated. The shock wave ripped the ships apart, throwing the *Red Baron* clear of the next broadside's line of fire. Seawater poured through the wound torn in her hull.

Timothy was hurled from the gunport. When he struggled upright, water was sweeping ammunition boxes past his legs, and an order rang down from above.

"Abandon ship! Everyone into the sea!"

Edward held the last Portuguese boarders at the companionway with *Excalibur*, clearing a path for the escaping crew.

Fredo carried Martinez from the deck before the water reached them. Timothy and the gunners opened the gunports and swam through broken timber; survivors from above clung to planks and rigging, scattering from the sinking ship.

Beyond the bay's mouth, Frenesia's fleet fought on for hours. Drawn within range of Monte Urgull, the Portuguese ships fell one by one beneath shore batteries and Castilian triple-barrelled fire. All four Portuguese warships found their graves at La Concha.

Four of the six Castilian ships sent to the rescue also sank. The flagship and her surviving escort turned among the burning wrecks, lowering boats wherever the guns had fallen silent.

In the bitter cold of the Long Frost, rescue became another race against time. Wind and current swept shattered planks and living men farther out to sea. Boats from San Sebastián searched through smoke and wreckage for anyone still afloat.

By the time the rescuers reached the drifting timber, most British veterans no longer answered their calls. Some still clutched the planks, ice thick around their hands and shoulders. The sailors entering the water had to prise each frozen hand from the wood before lifting the men into the boats.

title_vi: Chapter Twenty-Six: The Redemption of a Legend
title_en: Chapter Twenty-Six: The Redemption of a Legend
text_en:
The sea wind still screamed, though life upon the water had all but vanished. Hundreds of French, Portuguese, Castilian and British dead drifted across the bay, rising and falling among the wreckage.

Four survivors clung to the last broken rib of the *Red Baron*. Huddled together against the merciless cold of the Long Frost, they fought to keep the little warmth left in their bodies.

Edward gripped the timber with one hand and held *Excalibur* above the water with the other. Its ancient Celtic runes glimmered faintly, giving off just enough heat to reach them all. The pendants at his and Fredo's throats were fading too.

Each wave stole more of that warmth. Edward drew Timothy against him and shifted the sword's hilt in his palm, afraid his numb fingers might release it.

"Hold on... Timothy, keep your eyes open!"

His voice was raw. His teeth chattered as he hooked an arm around the young gunner's neck and pulled him towards the pendant's failing heat.

Timothy shook uncontrollably, his lips a bruised purple. Cramped fingers clutched Edward's sodden woollen coat. All he could do was breathe thin clouds into the air and bury his face against the admiral's shoulder.

Across the timber, Fredo held Martinez in both arms. He kept his back to the oncoming waves, shielding the wounded woman of the Royal Guard from the freezing spray.

Her face had turned the colour of ash. Blood from the bullet wound through her shoulder and the crushing injury to her ribs had frozen in ragged, dark streaks. Her breathing was so shallow that her chest scarcely moved, and frost had settled along her closed lashes.

"Martinez! Wake up, you little brat!"

Fredo called her name and slapped her cheeks with stiffened fingers. He bent close to find her breath, then shouted to Edward when he saw the faintest rise of her chest.

"Don't close your eyes! We're nearly ashore! Look, my mother's coming for us!"

Martinez sagged against his shoulder. Fredo pressed two fingers to her wrist and counted the slowing beats beneath the thunder of the waves.

Another wave struck. He turned to take its full force, keeping her face above the water. Only after it passed did Edward call Timothy again; the boy answered, but his words were lost in the wind.

The cold worked deeper, stripping sensation from Edward's limbs until his body seemed no longer his own. Fredo's cries receded with the roar of the sea, grew faint, then fell silent. Darkness closed over him, and his eyes fell shut.

***

When Edward opened them again, the bitter cold and salt of La Concha had vanished. A milder wind carried the familiar tang of the sea and the earthy scent of wild grass.

He sat upon a white cliff on England's southern coast. Below, the English Channel lay blue beneath an afternoon sky, and gulls wheeled through warmth he had thought he would never feel again.

Beside him sat his younger self in an admiral's uniform, legs dangling over the edge. A gold-trimmed bicorne rested upon his knees.

Edward turned a palm upwards. The calluses and dried blood remained, but the pain and cold were gone. He looked at the man beside him.

"Well, then... has the battle been decided? Or am I dead?"

His younger self gazed across the Channel, turning the hat upon his knees.

"I don't know. They were still beside you when you closed your eyes."

Edward looked down at his dry hands. He could still feel the sword's hilt slipping in his grasp, although the wind was warm enough to make him want to lie down and sleep.

"Timothy was still answering me," he said.

The younger man nodded.

Edward watched the horizon.

"If you could choose, what sort of man would you want Remi to become?"

His younger self raised an eyebrow. He tossed a pebble over the cliff and waited until its fall was swallowed by the surf before answering.

"Anything he likes. A carpenter, a gardener, a schoolmaster in some little village. Just keep him out of the military academies, and away from thieves and brigands."

Edward glanced at the uniform.

"You, saying that? No one could have kept us away in those days."

The young admiral looked down at the blood on his sleeve.

"Aye. That's why I don't want him following us."

Edward plucked a blade of grass and rolled it between his fingers. After a silence, the younger man spoke again.

"If the boy loves books, let him read. Don't send him to sea merely because his father was an admiral."

Edward looked into the eyes of the man he had been at twenty and nodded. For a while they sat together above the Channel, watching gulls turn in the open sky of their homeland.

At last the younger admiral brushed grass from his coat and rose. Without another glance at the sea, he turned towards the footpaths winding inland.

"Where are you going?" Edward called.

His younger self stopped but did not look back. The brim of his bicorne shifted in the breeze.

"Home."

"Home," Edward repeated.

He pushed himself to his feet and followed, step by step.

They crossed the grassy downs of southern England, passing old fields and roads lined with inns. The roofs of Winchester appeared beside the Itchen; farther on, the smell of fresh bread recalled an inn Edward had visited before the war carried him away. His younger self walked beside him without urging him onwards.

When the Trent and the stone walls of Nottingham came into view, Edward knew what lay ahead. The path led them into Sherwood Forest, where oak branches shut out much of the sky and the rustling leaves sounded as they had in childhood.

The younger admiral halted before a modest timber house at the forest's edge. He turned with a smile so untroubled that Edward scarcely recognised it.

"We're home, Edward."

Edward stopped dead. Every muscle in his face tightened as he stared through the open window.

Sunlight filled the room. A middle-aged man in an old garrison uniform sat at a wooden table sharpening a small knife, while a woman beside him worked a shuttle through coarse linen. His father and mother were there, whole and peaceful, untouched by the cannon fire and slaughter that had taken them years ago.

The younger admiral crossed the threshold. Edward's mother laid down her shuttle and looked up, delight brightening her face at the sight of her son.

"Edward? Is that you, my boy? Why have you been away so long?"

His father set aside the whetstone. Stern eyes softened as they settled on the young officer.

"Come and sit down, son. Supper's nearly ready. Your mother's baked fresh barley bread today."

Edward remained on the porch, listening to his father draw out a chair. He tried to answer his mother, but no words came. Tears dropped onto his coat, still soaked with seawater.

The wooden door creaked wider.

A boy of ten stepped outside in an oversized linen tunic, fair hair falling across his brow. He looked up at Edward's scarred face, took his callused hand and drew him towards the firelight.

"Come inside. Everyone's waiting for us."

Edward followed like a sleepwalker. The child led him to a chair beside the table, where his father pulled up a stool and rested a warm hand upon his shoulder.

"Was it a hard journey, lad? How have you been keeping? Has life at sea treated you badly?"

His mother wiped her hands upon her apron and came to touch the scars across his forehead. Grief trembled in her voice.

"Look how thin you've grown... When did you last sit down to a proper hot meal, my boy?"

Edward sat and stared at her hand on his shoulder. He caught it between both of his, meaning to say what he had carried through all those wandering years, but instead buried his face in her apron.

She ran her fingers through his tangled hair. He clasped her around the waist and wept so hard he could scarcely draw breath enough to speak.

By the window, his younger self wore the admiral's uniform once more. He stood with his bicorne held before him, waiting for Edward to raise his head.

"I'm sorry... Mother, Father, I'm so sorry."

Edward clutched his mother's apron and struggled to look up. His words broke apart between ragged breaths.

"It was my fault. My arrogance, my incompetence. I left the southern coast undefended, and the Portuguese came ashore. I gave them our home to burn, and you both died because of me."

His mother cupped his face in her work-worn hands. Her thumb wiped a tear from his cheek, leaving a trace of warmth. Her own eyes had reddened.

"I've heard you, son."

She dabbed his face with a corner of her apron, then did so again when the tears kept falling.

"Just sit here a while."

His father drew a chair close and laid a hand behind Edward's neck. After a long silence, he pushed a bowl of soup towards him.

"Eat what you can. Your mother's only just made it."

They gathered around the plain wooden table. The scent of fresh barley bread mingled with steam from the turnip stew, and the terrible cold of the bay seemed farther away than ever.

His younger self tore off a piece of bread and chewed slowly. Then he raised his eyes to Edward, who sat in silence.

From beside the window, his younger self broke the quiet.

"I still think they were calling our name that day. When the fire reached the forest."

Edward tightened his grip on the spoon. He had never heard those cries, yet on sleepless nights in Marrakesh they sounded close enough to touch.

His mother nudged the soup nearer.

"Tell me, Edward. How has life been treating you?"

He raised his head and managed a frail smile.

"Well enough, Mother. I've wandered through a few places and met some kind people. It's been difficult at times, but I've managed."

She watched him, broke off another piece of bread and laid it beside his bowl. Edward lowered his eyes and ate. Her hand remained on the table, close to his, and she asked nothing more.

Supper passed in a peace he had almost forgotten. When his father finished the last of his soup, he stood and took down two wooden swords hanging on the oak wall. One came sailing towards Edward.

"Come on, Admiral. You've eaten, so let's put those arms to work. A few passes in the yard will tell me whether all your years at sea have sharpened your swordsmanship or let it rust."

Late sunlight lay across the hard-packed earth outside, scattered with dry oak leaves. The only sound was wind moving through Sherwood's trees.

Edward closed his hand around the wooden hilt. Opposite him, the old garrison soldier bent his knees, settled his weight and lifted the practice sword to eye level.

"Come at me, son!"

His father stamped forward and cut diagonally at Edward's shoulder. The stroke was sound, but Edward had survived too many brutal sea battles and desperate fights at close quarters to mistake its course.

He slipped aside, turned and caught the wooden blade on his own. Following the momentum, he lifted his sword and stopped its point a hair's breadth from his father's throat. The entire exchange had taken fewer than three breaths.

The older man stared at the wooden tip, then burst into delighted laughter.

"Well done! No wonder they speak of your blade across the Atlantic. This old fellow can scarcely keep pace with you now."

He lowered his weapon, brushed dust from his trousers and crossed to a bench made from a fallen oak. Patting the seat beside him, he smiled.

"Come and sit with your father a moment."

Edward collected both practice swords, set them against the tree and joined him.

His father picked a leaf from Edward's sleeve.

"How are Juliet and the boy?"

"Well, Father. They were well when I left."

Edward looked towards the two wooden swords.

"I promised I'd come back."

"Then when you do, spend a day with them. Don't sit down to supper already thinking about when you must leave again."

Edward bowed his head.

"There are duties I cannot lay aside."

"I never asked you to."

His father flicked the leaf from his knee.

"But when you're home, do you listen to your wife? Do you know what the boy's taken an interest in?"

"Remi likes questions. He asks about everything."

Edward smiled, but it soon faded.

"I have to bring my men home as well. Out there on the water... I don't even know how many we've lost."

His father sat beside him in silence. Edward waited for an answer, but the old soldier only put a hand upon his shoulder.

Edward went on.

"I'd planned our retreat. Then the fog cleared. Men died right before my eyes."

"When you return, listen to those who survived. Where you made mistakes, you must learn what they were."

"And if I fail them again?"

The hand on his shoulder tightened.

"That's one thing I cannot promise you won't do."

Edward turned towards the trees. He stayed there until the words he had meant to say settled within him, then covered his father's hand with his own.

Dry oak leaves spun across the yard in the faint breeze. Birds called among the branches while Edward rolled a stem of grass between his fingers. At length he spoke.

"Father... There's something I've wondered about for years. Isabella, the girl we knew as my distant cousin."

He remembered a little girl waiting under the eaves for him to come home from school. In this strange homecoming, the question that had troubled him for years finally found its voice.

"She lived with us for only a few years. Then people came from Aragon and took her back to the Castilian mainland. Now that I have seen her on the throne, I cannot help wondering who she truly is."

His father was silent for some time. He picked up a twig and scratched aimless marks in the earth, searching through memories grown faint with age.

"Edward... Isabella was never your cousin. She has no blood tie to our family at all."

Edward stared at him, stunned.

His father stopped drawing in the dirt. Several moments passed before he continued.

"It must be twenty years now. Your mother and I were travelling near Nottingham when we found her. She had just been put into a filthy brothel on the edge of town, and she couldn't have been more than six or seven. All skin and bone, she was, with a face that scarcely moved."

The old soldier shook his head.

"Your mother understood better than most what such a place could do to someone. We saved every coin we could spare and paid to get that poor child out."

His gaze drifted towards the trees.

"For the first few days in our house, she barely spoke. No tears, no laughter. She kept to the shadows, as though she could hide from whatever had happened to her there. Then she met you."

A faint smile touched his mouth.

"She began to talk when you were near. She followed you through Sherwood, climbed trees after you, played in the woods. Little by little, she learned how to be a child again."

He threw the twig aside.

"Then officials of the English Crown arrived with an urgent order. They took her to a delegation of envoys from the Aragonese dynasty, newly landed from across the Channel. Her own aunt was among them."

His father folded his hands.

"Before they took her away, I asked after her parents. I wanted to know how a child of that family had ended up in such a place."

"What did her aunt say?" Edward asked, the question escaping before he could contain it.

"Only this: 'They died for the unity of the Castilian nobility.'"

The old man watched the forest floor.

"Then they escorted her aboard a ship bound south. We never heard another word of her."

Edward looked at his father, waiting for more. The discarded twig lay motionless beside the bench.

His father spoke again.

"When they came for her, she kept looking towards you. I called her to the carriage, but she wouldn't go."

Edward remembered small fingers hooked around his sleeve. He strained to recall what Isabella had said that day, but heard only oak leaves stirring above him.

"You ought to ask her yourself," his father said.

Edward remained seated a while longer. Then he rose, still holding his father's hand.

He stretched and drew a deep breath of the forest air. His father stood beside him, age written across his face, his expression gentle.

Edward turned and clasped the old soldier's rough hand tightly.

"Thank you, Father. For everything you gave me."

He walked back towards the house.

Sunlight poured through the windows. His mother had cleared the table and was waiting with a tender smile. Beside the window stood the Edward of ten years earlier, resplendent in the full dress uniform of a Royal Navy admiral, his gold-edged bicorne set properly upon his head.

The younger admiral regarded him.
