"Well? Still want to stay?"

Edward looked at the chair his mother had pulled out for him. He longed to sit there once more.

"I do," he said. "But I have to go back."

He went to his mother and held her close, pressing his face against her shoulder.

"I've missed you both so much."

She cupped his cheek. Edward leaned into her hand as he had done when he was small and had to leave home before dawn.

"Keep going, my boy. Your father and I, and this old forest of Sherwood... we belong to the past now."

His father stood beside her and held out the bicorne.

"Juliet and Remi are waiting. Go home to them, son."

His younger self laid a hand upon his shoulder for the last time. When Edward looked back, the young admiral had taken his place beside the table, near the two people waiting there.

Edward bowed his head. He embraced his parents and the man he had once been, held them as tightly as he could, then turned and stepped across the wooden threshold.

He left Sherwood by the roads running south-east. Low fields, waterways and rooftops slid past him, and his footsteps made no sound upon the ground.

London greeted him with bells sounding across the Thames. Near Westminster, a row of stone benches brought back Juliet in her rough woollen scarf, huddled beside him as snow fell. They had shared a piece of warm bread and spoken of the home they would build when the war was over.

Edward rested a hand upon the bench, felt the damp moss beneath his fingers, and walked on.

Beyond Kent the wind grew salty again. The white cliffs of Dover rose ahead, overlooking the English Channel. Edward stopped where the grass ran close to the edge, bowed his head towards the homes and fields of his country, then faced the sea.

He stepped to the brink. Wind pulled his coat taut, and as he looked down at the water the cold returned to his hands.

"My wife, my son... I'm coming home."

He closed his eyes and leapt.

Wind screamed past his ears before the water closed above him. Sunlight dwindled in the dark depths until it was little more than a pale blur. The sound of the sea disappeared, and Edward's consciousness sank with it.

title_vi: Chapter Twenty-Seven: Those Who Survived
title_en: Chapter Twenty-Seven: Those Who Survived
text_en:
A log cracked in the hearth, and Edward woke.

For a while he lay still. Herbs scented the bandages around his arm, and each shallow breath brought a dull ache beneath his ribs.

There was no black water beneath him, no blizzard tearing across La Concha Bay. Above him stretched a sandstone ceiling crossed by dark oak beams. He lay on a soft mattress under heavy fur blankets, with the heat of a stone hearth warming one side of the bed.

He tried to lift his arm, but a slight weight at the edge of the mattress made him stop.

Isabella sat against the bedside, her head resting on the coverlet. She slept fitfully, shoulders drawn inward.

Queen Isabella of Castile wore a simple gown of soft grey linen. Firelight touched her pale cheeks and the faint shadows beneath her eyes. Her fingers clung to a fold of his blanket even in sleep.

The familiar fragrance of cherry blossom rose from her tangled hair, gentler than the scents of salve and salt that lingered in the stone chamber.

Edward remembered a child's hand clutching his coat in a dream. He did not know how to ask her what he had heard.

His expression softened. He drew a rough hand from beneath the furs and stroked her hair, just as he had once comforted his little sister beneath the ancient trees of Sherwood.

Isabella woke at his touch. Her amber eyes opened slowly, then widened as she found him watching her with a tenderness she seldom saw.

"Edward... You're awake!"

She leaned forward and flung her arms around his neck. Her grip tightened with the desperation of someone afraid that he might disappear again.

"Ah... That hurts! Bella, you're hurting me!"

Pain flared through his battered chest and shoulders. Edward winced and caught his breath with a low groan.

Isabella let go at once, looking down at his chest as she pulled the blanket aside.

"I'm sorry. I forgot... Where does it hurt?"

He waited for the worst of the pain to pass before showing her the bruise. She helped him sit higher, placed pillows behind his back and reached for the water.

She lifted a cup of warm water, blew across its surface and held it to his mouth. He took several careful sips before she set it down, took up a pair of silver scissors and began removing the old dressings from his arm and chest.

She spread ointment around a wound, then stopped when he flinched.

"The cuts have been treated. But the physicians are still concerned about the injuries within. The force of the recoil was severe."

"From the necklace?"

Isabella nodded and unrolled a clean bandage.

"It was made for the bloodline of the Royal Guard. You used it to release a legendary Vestigium... Your body could not bear the strain."

Edward glanced at the piece of metal beside his bed. Isabella wrapped the linen around his arm, but the loose end slipped from her fingers, and she had to begin again.

"And then you spent hours beneath the water."

Her hands grew still above the damp bandage.

"When they brought you up, I called your name. You never answered."

"I was so frightened..."

The roll of linen slipped from her hands. Isabella bowed over him and wept, pressing her face to his chest and clutching his shirt between her fingers.

"When I heard the French flagship had exploded, and that the Portuguese fleet had surrounded you... I thought I'd lost you for ever! I thought my own orders had sent you to your death. I was so frightened, Edward..."

Edward rested a hand at the back of her neck, careful not to strain his bruised chest. He waited while she wept, until at last her breath came more evenly.

"Thank you, Bella... Thank you for always caring about me."

Isabella raised her head. Tears glistened in her amber eyes as she waited for him to continue.

His hand remained in her hair.

"I still remember the little girl who followed me everywhere through Sherwood. I haven't forgotten you, Bella."

She stopped wiping her cheeks. After a moment she bent to retrieve the bandage from beside her chair.

"I know."

She gathered the loose linen between her fingers.

"I know what place Juliet holds in your heart."

Edward began to answer, but Isabella shook her head. She bound the last turn of linen around his arm, taking care not to draw it too tight.

"At least you've stopped looking at me as though you must hide every knife whenever I enter a room."

She glanced up, smiling through her tears.

"This is much nicer."

Someone knocked at the door. Timothy Beaumont spoke from the corridor.

"Your Majesty, I've brought more medicine."

"Come in."

Isabella turned as Timothy entered. He caught sight of Edward sitting upright and stopped short.

"Admiral!"

He set the tray down and hurried forward to embrace him. Edward hissed through his teeth and struck the young gunner lightly between the shoulders.

"Let go... Are you trying to finish what the French started?"

Timothy sprang back. Isabella caught Edward by the shoulder before he toppled against the headboard.

"He's only just awakened. Be gentle with him."

"I'm sorry."

Timothy bent to straighten the corner of the blanket he had pulled loose.

"I thought you were still unconscious, sir."

His eyes fell upon the physician's notes beside the medicine.

"You've been unconscious for a full month, Admiral. The doctor says you must rest today as well."

Isabella inspected the new dressing before rising.

"Stay here and help Sir Edward. If his pain worsens, fetch the physician. Don't let him walk by himself."

She turned to Edward, her voice taking on the restraint of royal duty.

"I must attend a council meeting. Reinforcements are still being moved, and the Pyrenees front remains unsettled. Rest a little longer, Sir Edward. We shall speak later."

Edward nodded. Timothy bowed until her footsteps faded beyond the bend of the stone corridor.

The chamber fell quiet again, save for the soft crackling of the hearth. Edward pushed himself a little straighter and regarded the young gunner.

"Well, lad? How have you fared since your long swim in the sea?"

"I'm well enough. My fingers are still a little numb."

Timothy spread his hand for Edward to see, then hesitantly placed *Storm's Roar* upon the blanket.

Edward looked from the weapon to the boy's face.

"What's wrong? Did someone fail to make it?"

"No, sir. It's the gun."

Timothy pushed it towards him.

"Salt water got into the loading mechanism. I've cleaned it, but I still can't make it work. It keeps jamming."

Edward examined the salt-stained weapon and laughed softly at Timothy's worry. He patted the lad's upper arm, avoiding his bandaged fingers.

"Let the craftsmen in Toledo see to it. It's done enough already."

He nudged the weapon towards the medicine tray.

"And so have you. Don't take it apart with those bandaged fingers."

Once Timothy seemed reassured, Edward asked:

"And Fredo and Martinez? How are they?"

"Both alive, sir."

Timothy drew his chair closer.

"Fredo used the last steel links of *Vinculum* to catch the side of Governor Frenesia's rescue ship and haul us aboard. He was nearly spent by the time we reached the deck."

"And once he'd recovered, he joined Tercio I del Rayo and two hundred Conquistadors under Her Majesty's command to drive the French from the eastern bank at San Sebastián. Martinez was back on the training ground this morning, though the surgeon was still keeping watch over her."

"Good... Very good."

Edward breathed out, though one question still troubled him.

"And our British veterans, Timothy? How many of our brothers survived?"

Timothy's smile faltered. His voice dropped.

"A little over three hundred."

He glanced towards the door.

"Those who can stand are waiting in the courtyard. Would you like to see them?"

Edward asked Timothy to fetch his dark blue Castilian admiral's dress uniform, edged in gold, from the wooden stand. His joints ached, and the recoil of the Vestigium still left a deep throb in his chest. Yet he insisted on fastening every polished brass button himself.

He settled the heavy cloak across his shoulders and rose with Timothy's help. Leaning heavily on the young man's shoulder, he took one uncertain step after another towards the stone gate of Monte Urgull fortress.

A cold sea wind lifted the hem of his cloak as they emerged into the broad, hard-packed courtyard of the central barracks.

More than three hundred British veterans waited beneath the grey sky in worn uniforms. Some leaned on crutches; others held bandaged arms against their chests. Their ranks had thinned so much that Edward recognised the gaps at once.

At the sight of their admiral upon the stone steps, hundreds of hands rose to their breasts in the solemn salute of the Royal Navy.

Edward removed his hand from Timothy's shoulder and stood straight to return it. Pain pulled through his bruised chest as he raised his arm, but he held the salute, looking down the diminished ranks before him.

title_vi: Chapter Twenty-Eight: The List With No Column for Homecoming
title_en: Chapter Twenty-Eight: The List With No Column for Homecoming
text_en:
Night settled over Monte Urgull. The voices in the courtyard had long fallen silent, yet Edward heard them whenever he closed his eyes. More than three hundred men had stood in the bitter wind, some lacking enough fingers to press a hand properly against their coats, and held their salute until he lowered his own.

He remembered the gaps in the front rank, wide enough to show the fortress wall between the men. A month earlier, those gaps had scarcely existed. He could still picture faces that should have been there, though he could no longer put names to them all.

Timothy helped him out of his coat and offered to summon the physician to examine his chest. Edward took his medicine and endured a fresh dressing without complaint. Only when the sickroom fell quiet did he ask for the key to the records store.

The young aide glanced at the clock beside the door. His admiral had barely emerged from a month of unconsciousness, yet evidently meant to spend the night on his feet. Timothy recognised the set of his jaw and knew argument would achieve little.

"Which ledger do you need, sir? I'll bring it here."

"The list of those who left Lisbon with us. The first one, before anyone died."

Timothy knew where it lay, beneath relabelled ammunition chests in the stores. The casualty roll remained unfinished while recovery parties searched the compartments of sunken ships. The quartermaster had often suggested separating the registers so that the clerks need not see the names of the living beside those of the dead.

"Could it wait until morning, sir? The physician ordered you to rest."

"I'll see those names tomorrow as well," Edward said. "Tonight I want to know whose faces I saluted."

Timothy laid Edward's old coat beside the bed and summoned a sentry in case he collapsed on the stairs. Edward refused to be supported on both sides, but eventually agreed to lean on Timothy's shoulder, as he had in the courtyard.

A heavy door guarded the records store in the lower fortress. The elderly storekeeper lit two lamps beside a long table once used to count rations, brought weak tea and fetched a muster ledger bound with black cord. White salt still marked its spine from the voyage that had claimed the *Red Baron*.

Edward rested his hand upon the cover. The number 803 had been written in blue ink and underlined twice. Each entry gave a name, age, birthplace, station aboard ship and next of kin to notify upon death; the final column had no heading.

The storekeeper unfolded a second register, a roll of the missing begun during the journey from Marrakesh. It included men who had travelled with Edward before the war changed course, though they had never served aboard the *Red Baron*. They belonged to different units and had fallen in different battles.

With the two books side by side, each loss demanded its own reckoning. Edward had grown accustomed to totals on a commander's desk. Here, every line resisted becoming part of a single number.

"The returns from the bay are still incomplete, Admiral," the storekeeper said. "We recovered another identification disc today, but three earlier cases remain unconfirmed. I can mark them separately."

"Keep them in another column. A missing body is no proof of death."

The old man offered the inkpot. Edward tried writing with his bandaged hand, but the nib struck too hard and tore the margin. He changed hands, waited for the pain in his ribs to ease, and began to read.

The first name belonged to a sailmaker who had mended Timothy's coat with thread from the medical stores. Another man had quarrelled over biscuit rations on their first morning out of Lisbon, then been found beneath a plank near the harbour entrance. The entries followed the recruiting officer's order, indifferent to the order in which those men had died.

Edward marked a confirmed casualty, entered the date and source beside the name, and waited for the ink to dry before turning the page. His hand remained on the paper a moment longer than it needed to.

"You needn't do all this yourself," Timothy said. "Three clerks can reconcile the lists, and two men still have the ship's journals."

"I know. But I stood before them today without knowing who had occupied those empty places."

Timothy watched the ink stain Edward's fingers. He had seen him order wounded men from a burning compartment and heard him recall the gun crews before the ship vanished. He had never seen his commander sit over a single name so long, with no order to give when the silence came.

Three clerks were summoned. Edward divided the pages among them and ordered every discrepancy checked against the journals. No unconfirmed name was to enter the roll of the dead.

Footsteps approached and stopped outside. An elderly sergeant stood in the doorway with two young sailors, his naval coat worn thin and a patch of mismatched cloth sewn into its collar. Behind them was a small wooden chest with a bent iron handle.

The sentry moved to announce them, but the sergeant merely asked whether the admiral could spare a moment. Edward recognised the man who had inspected the lashings on the heavy guns and once shouted at a trembling gunner to ask for help if he could no longer load his piece. He was among the few survivors who still possessed an old naval cap.

"Come in. What have you brought?"

"The belongings of men who cannot carry them any longer, sir."

The sergeant placed the chest on the table, clear of the ledgers. A sailor lifted the lid to reveal a pocket watch with cracked glass, embroidered handkerchiefs, buttons, two unsealed letters and a small knife with a broken blade. Every object had been wrapped separately in dry paper.

"We were told to surrender these to the clothing stores," the sergeant said. "Someone suggested burying the chest in the common grave because we cannot identify several owners. I thought you should know before we decided."

Edward lifted the watch and recognised a triangular scratch upon its case. Its owner had once joked that a slow watch ensured he was never late for duty. The hands had stopped at one o'clock, offering no certain evidence of when he had died.

Edward returned it to its wrapping.

"Bury nothing while someone might recognise it. Record where each item was found, and leave the owner's name blank until we know."

The sergeant drew out a chair but remained standing. He looked from Timothy's pistol by the door to the papers spread across the table. Outside, men were still waiting for word of the missing ships.

"There's another question, Admiral. The men asked me to put it to you."

Edward set down his pen.

"Ask it. I'm listening."

"When can we go home to England?"

Timothy looked at him as though the words had touched a place he had avoided all month. The young sailors kept their hands upon the chest. Edward turned towards a rolled sea chart beside the stove and asked the storekeeper to fetch it.

They spread it across the free half of the table. Red pencil lines crossed the old supply routes from Lisbon to northern English ports, marking the shifting war front, coal depots no longer usable and straits locked in ice. One route ran past La Concha and ended at the mark recording where the *Red Baron* had sunk.

He held the chart flat with the inkpot and broken watch against the draught beneath the door.

"We have no date," Edward said. "The Pyrenean line has collapsed. I have no ship, no passage confirmed safe, and no grounds for promising we'll reach an English port before the Long Frost breaks. Anything else would be a lie told to keep you here."

"Then what did those men die for, sir?"

Edward looked at the casualty ledger. His month in darkness had taken from him the chance to stand beside his comrades' graves. Their survivors waited before him in worn coats, with eyes that had grown accustomed to too little sleep.

"They died because of choices made by us and by the enemy," he said. "Some were mine. The storm was beyond our command, but I must answer for the decisions I made."

"You saved everyone you could."

"I also led them there. Both things are true."

Timothy studied the strait upon the chart. He remembered Edward shouting evacuation orders until his voice failed, and Fredo dragging a chain across fractured ice. Then the ammunition chest had exploded, with men still crowding the deck beyond reach of the boats.

Those memories gave him no answer he could offer the sergeant.

One of the young sailors stepped forward. His left hand was bound in cloth, three joints of his ring finger blackened purple. He asked whether Edward would take them across the sea tomorrow if he had a ship.

"Not if the crossing would kill more of you," Edward said. "I'd ask where you wanted to go and how far the physicians thought you fit to travel. Some have families in Marrakesh. Others have no home left in any port."

The sailor looked down at his damaged fingers.

"Am I still an English soldier, sir? If England is gone and I'm wearing a Castilian coat, what does that make me?"

Edward offered no new regimental name. The council on the remaining English forces had yet to meet, and its proposals rested with commanders he had never spoken to. Naming a regiment tonight would imply these men had already been assigned their places without being asked whether they wished to stay.

"You boarded the *Red Baron* under your own name," he said. "You kept it when you stepped aboard the rescue boat. A coat cannot give your country back, and it cannot erase what you've survived."

"But we must belong somewhere."

"Perhaps. I won't decide that for you tonight."

The sergeant asked whether Marrakesh could be reached by land. The storekeeper explained that the staging posts had reopened for civilian convoys and some lightly wounded men had already gone south. Full allowances were unavailable, but Castile held their unpaid wages, and supply wagons would leave when the wind eased.

Edward drew out a clean sheet and asked Timothy to read the discharge regulations for soldiers recruited at Lisbon. They had to establish what still applied now that the unit had lost its ship and its commander had only just awakened. Timothy hesitated over a clause requiring higher approval.

"I cannot sign this part for you, sir. Full travel expenses from the supply fund also require the Admiralty's approval."

"Request it at once. I can authorise an advance for tomorrow's wagons."

Edward drafted an order allowing men who wished to leave the ranks to receive provisional discharge papers and travel to a safe settlement without being treated as deserters while awaiting a formal decision. Those unfit for labour would need a physician's certificate to retain their allowances. The pain in his hand forced him to pause after every few lines.

The sergeant read the order from beginning to end. He pointed to the uncertain passage to England and requested a sentence making clear that overseas travel could be promised only when a transport route reopened. Edward added it, allowed him to read the passage again, and signed.

"Can we truly collect these papers tomorrow?"

"Yes. And none of you need come to my room to explain why you can no longer hold a musket."

The sergeant stood still. He had assumed that the word England, spoken by this admiral, would bring hundreds of men back beneath their colours. Instead, a discharge order lay before him, its ink still wet, offering a choice the soldiers had imagined through sleepless nights but had never dared request.

"If too many leave, who will defend the fortress?" a sailor asked.

"That is a matter for command and me. You will not be made to stay because I cannot balance the muster roll."

The storekeeper blew gently across the ink. Timothy saw that the order imposed no condition requiring the men to serve until the war ended. He wondered what the dead might say, then remembered the nights he had spent alone on deck with that question.

The dead could make no decision for those still alive.

"I still want to know what you intend next," the sergeant said. "You're awake, Admiral, and some of us can still carry arms. How far must we fight before we get home?"

"There are no new orders. I've attended no council and heard none of the proposals," Edward answered. "If orders come, I'll explain what a battle is meant to defend, whom it requires and what losses we expect. I will not offer the word 'homeland' in place of an explanation."

"Can you really tell us everything?"

"No. I'll tell you what I know, what remains uncertain, and answer when I've been wrong."

The sergeant rubbed the scar on his wrist. He had served long enough to know that orders sometimes revealed their dangers only after they were given, and that young men would die despite every risk marked on a chart. Still, an officer admitting the limits of his knowledge meant more than another promise that everyone would return.

He pushed the chest to the centre of the table.

"Then help us send these things to the right people. Three dead men might have owned that handkerchief. Sending it to the wrong family would be worse than sending nothing."

Edward drew a pad of paper towards him. They began with the watch: an older sailor remembered its owner passing it around the gun deck to time sleeping watches, while another recalled the triangular scratch. Both accounts went into the record, with the owner's name left open pending examination of the personal ledger.

The second handkerchief had an M embroidered in one corner, its stitching slanting like a novice's work. The sergeant remembered a seamstress in Marrakesh sending it with supplies, but not who was meant to receive it. Timothy proposed checking the parcel register rather than guessing from an initial, and Edward recorded that lead.

They worked past midnight and for another hour. Pain tightened Edward's chest whenever he bent too long, so Timothy read the smaller script while the sergeant placed hot tea beside his unbandaged hand. Four men sat among the papers, sometimes disputing dates, patient enough to correct each other.

When a memory failed, they returned to the records. Nothing would be gained by supplying a family with a certainty they did not possess.

Near dawn, the sergeant rose to summon soldiers still awake to identify the remaining possessions. He took the discharge order into the courtyard, and Edward told him to pin it to the noticeboard without an appeal for anyone to remain. Whoever decided after breakfast would have his name entered just the same.

Timothy escorted Edward back before his legs gave way. Beyond the corridor windows, the tower's watchfire had dwindled to red coals, while soldiers sat huddled beside a brazier, unused to sleeping without the prospect of gunfire. The storekeeper had asked a carpenter for another table so unidentified keepsakes need no longer lie beneath the paperwork.

"How do you think they'll choose?" Timothy asked, helping Edward onto the bed.

"I don't know. I won't count those who leave as weak and those who stay as loyal."

"They were all waiting for you when you stood before them."

"That's why they must have another way out."

Edward lay down but could not sleep. He studied the dried ink upon his fingers and remembered his first voyage, when English flags still marked the familiar harbours on his chart and sailors joked about returning victorious. He had measured journeys in days then, rather than by the number of men who might live to see port.

The names from the storehouse followed him into the dark. They would not settle into any comforting conclusion.

***

Morning left a skin of frost across Monte Urgull's courtyard. Edward's sealed discharge order hung outside the stores beside notices for wagons to Marrakesh and treatment for frostbitten limbs. Men gathered in small groups, tracing the lines with their fingers or asking comrades to read for eyes still sore from the storm.

No one raised a cheer. They studied the notice with the care of men who knew how much could depend on a single sentence.

Edward stood beneath the awning, his coat collar open to spare the bandage on his chest. Timothy held the discharge forms beside him. The old sergeant tapped the posted order.

"Anyone claiming an allowance, come before the wagons leave. Your names are recorded here."

A young soldier stepped towards the map of the Marrakesh road.

"If I go there, will they send me back to battle tomorrow?"

The sergeant opened his book.

"This order covers your allowance and transport. Exemption from service belongs to the Crown."

Edward held down the edge of the map.

"Mobilisation orders are Castile's decision. I'll sign only what my authority permits."

He looked at the man's bandaged hand.

"But I can record your injury and the recovery period prescribed by the physician. Standing on your feet is no proof you're fit for battle."

The soldier studied his wrapped fingers, then requested transfer to a treatment centre instead of discharge. Timothy entered his name and sent the certificate to the medical station. The man remained in the garrison but was no longer automatically placed on the fighting roster.

Another elderly sailor asked whether his wife in Marrakesh had received his allowance. The storekeeper checked the remittance ledger, found the payment delayed for want of a signature and led him into the next room. The sailor promised to return when it was settled.

Others began asking about their families, injuries, rest and the graves of missing comrades. Questions once unthinkable at a muster now passed from mouth to mouth. They asked with the caution of men uncertain whether the permission would last beyond the morning.

By noon, no one had taken a discharge paper. Some could scarcely hold a cup; others flinched at the wind beyond the door. They spoke of children, wives and friends whose homes lay in the country threatened by war.

The sergeant returned to the store with the casualty ledger. He set it before Edward without saluting, one hand steadying its spine.

"We haven't taken the papers," he said. "We know staying beside you won't keep us alive. I have a daughter in Marrakesh and a grandson who has only just learnt to walk. If the army abandons every road protecting that city, they'll have no ship to escape on."

Edward looked at the men behind him. Some bowed their heads; others met his eyes. He let each speak for himself.

"You may change your minds," he said. "Tomorrow, next week, or after an order you cannot accept."

"We know. Now keep this."

The sergeant pushed the ledger towards him.

"Don't leave it under ammunition chests. Open it before every order to send men into battle. If another name must be written, you'll know those empty places did not appear by themselves."

Edward took the ledger in both hands. Ink-darkened pages pressed against his thumbs, the names of the dead beneath their marks of confirmation. He set it beside the sea chart and opened the first page.

"I'll keep it here. Before every order to put to sea, I'll read these names again."

At noon, Timothy returned to the sickroom, where Edward handed him a clean sheet bearing the family addresses he had copied. There were still places connected with Étienne, Margaret and Elizabeth that Timothy had been unable to reach, and words he had not managed to say throughout the journey. Even with the addresses before him, he could not see how he would deliver them.

He read the familiar lines and folded the sheet into quarters. Outside, the wind off La Concha swept up the rock face, carrying the hammering of shipwrights working in the bay.

Edward sat beside the window with the casualty ledger open upon his knees. Timothy had no wish to ask another question his commander could not answer. He quietly gathered writing paper and his coat, then walked towards the steps leading out to the headland.

title_vi: Chapter Twenty-Nine: The Departed
title_en: Chapter Twenty-Nine: The Departed
text_en:
The wind from La Concha Bay swept up the slopes of Monte Urgull, threading through rock and carrying salt and the lingering taint of gunpowder. Timothy Beaumont sat alone on an outcrop, his legs dangling over the drop, while the sea below slowly returned to its familiar grey-blue.

San Sebastián lay behind him. Hammers, carts and distant voices reached him as fragments scattered by the wind. Ahead, the mouth of the bay opened towards the Atlantic, where a few shattered masts still rose from the water like charred black ribs.

Timothy raised his hands before his face. Several fingers were bandaged, his knuckles split from salt and cold, and powder stained his nails despite repeated washing.

He turned those aching hands over. His right had loaded *Storm's Roar* and held its barrel steady as an enemy warship rose between the waves. His left had gripped the breeching rope of a thirty-two-pounder, helping his comrades bring the *Red Baron* down just far enough for *Vinculum* to reach a crossbeam.

He studied his hands, then laughed. At first the sound was almost lost to the wind, but his shoulders shook, and the laughter grew louder, awkward and broken.

Tears reached his chin before he noticed them.

"We won."

No one answered. Timothy lifted his face towards the sea, letting the wind sting his wet cheeks, and laughed again without trying to hide the tears.

"We really won."

He wiped his face on his sleeve. When he looked at his hands again, he remembered them black with coal dust at ten years old, clutching a powder bag nearly half his size.

They had borne no calluses then. They knew nothing of stubborn gun oil or breaking frozen fingers from wreckage. Timothy had only wanted to board a ship, stand beside the cannons and join the men he watched so hungrily from the quay.

He could still feel the heat of that gun deck. The vessel pitched, boots thudded overhead, and tackles rattled while he crawled from sailcloth where he had hidden since dawn.

His plan was simple: wait until the ship sailed, then emerge. No one would turn back merely to put a boy ashore.

The ingenious plan of a ten-year-old lasted less than half an hour.

A gloved hand seized Timothy by the collar just as he set his powder bag beside the first cannon. He turned to see black boots, a Royal Navy dress uniform and finally his captor.

Edward Spencer looked at Timothy, then at the gunpowder.

"What's this? How old are you?"

Timothy had prepared his answer.

"Fourteen, Admiral, sir."

Edward examined his spindly arms and shoes so large his heels slid inside them.

"I'll give you one last chance not to insult my intelligence."

Timothy swallowed.

"Ten."

A nearby gunner snorted. Edward glanced over, and the man bent over the breech as if deaf.

Timothy argued on. He knew how to carry powder, light a match and count a gun crew; he had watched hundreds of reloads.

Edward heard him out, then marched him along the gun deck by the collar while Timothy nearly struggled out of a shoe.

"Admiral, I can do it! I'm not afraid!"

"I know."

Edward kept walking.

"I can fight!"

"Perhaps."

Timothy twisted in his grip, furious and humiliated.

"Then why are you putting me ashore?"

This time Edward stopped. He released the collar and knelt to Timothy's height amid the smells of leather, powder and black tea.

"Because a boy who knows no fear is the most dangerous thing I could put beside a magazine full of gunpowder."

Timothy hated those words for years.

Edward took out a pencil stub and scrap of paper, wrote sums and a table of figures, then handed them over.

"If you truly want to return, learn to read powder tables, calculate ranges, understand gunnery orders and tell a good shot from a foolish one. When you're old enough to know what you might die for, come and find me."

"When will I be old enough?"

Edward stood and straightened his cuffs.

"When you no longer need to ask me."

Two sailors took Timothy back to the quay in a small boat before the warship had cleared the harbour. He stood on the pier cursing Edward Spencer until the vessel was no more than a patch of sail upon the horizon.

Years later, Timothy boarded another ship. This time no one caught him by the collar and threw him ashore.

He started at the lowest gun station, passing powder, swabbing barrels and hauling ropes, tasks once beneath his dreams of war. The men around him rarely spoke of heroism as the children at the docks did.

They taught him to keep his thumbs clear when a gun recoiled and never to stand behind a carriage wheel when the breeching rope had frayed. An old gunner struck his head with a broom handle for setting powder too close to a lantern, then slipped him half a piece of bread when he missed supper.

The man in charge of the ropes made him tie the same knot until his fingertips bled, only to make him start again the following morning. He once thought them England's most disagreeable men. Only later did he realise they had raised him.

One taught him to read a gun's elevation; another taught him to listen to the timber and hear where a hull was bearing strain. A good gunner, someone told him, must know where his shot would land if the ship rolled another half a degree before he fired.

Edward sometimes appeared below decks. He might simply pass through, draw one finger across a gun carriage and stare at the man on watch until the fellow understood the dressing-down awaiting him.

One day, he stopped before Timothy longer than usual.

"How old are you now?"

Timothy continued cleaning the breech.

"Old enough not to ask you any more."

Edward studied him, burst out laughing and walked on. It was the first time Timothy felt he had bested the Admiral in an exchange of words.

The years passed faster than he had expected. Watches followed watches, campaigns followed campaigns, and sometimes their ship returned with fewer men than had sailed aboard her.

Some died beneath shot. Others went overboard at night, leaving only a cap in the rigging; another lost a leg and spent his days waving the others to sea.

Timothy went on.

The Royal Navy had seemed eternal to him. Flags might tear, ships might burn and admirals might be replaced, yet the next morning someone would ring the watch bell, and the gunners would still have their barrels to clean.

Then England ceased to exist.

There were memories Timothy had never known where to put: harbours crowded with people fighting to board ships, burning roofs behind them, and soldiers who had quarrelled over half a bottle of spirits the night before standing shoulder to shoulder at dawn to keep the quay clear for civilians boarding boats. Red-cross flags vanished from the horizon with dreadful speed.

He could not recall the last day he had called a vessel an English ship. Only waking one morning to find the others serving under different flags.

He went on, not because he had forgotten England. If he stopped, he could think of nothing left to do but remember.

Castilian service taught him another sort of warfare. He learnt new commands, another language of curses and how to drink spirits that tasted like gun solvent.

But a cannon remained a cannon. Gunpowder burned as it always had, and men struck by shot fell in precisely the same way. Then the defeats began to mount.

Some nights he walked the length of the gun deck and realised he was inspecting the exits for a second time. He returned to his hammock and lay there fully dressed, boots on, until the watch changed.

Before checking the guns, he checked the escape routes. Before sailing, he counted the boats, and whenever a rope screamed under strain or timber cracked beneath him in the night, his body reacted before his mind knew why.

Vila do Porto was merely the place where all of it acquired a name.

Timothy remembered the cold water and a sea so wide he could no longer tell where the shore lay. He remembered two days clinging to a plank beside men who had fought alongside him only hours before. The man to his left died first.

At first Timothy did not realise. The man still embraced the wood, his head resting on his arm as though asleep, until a wave knocked them together and Timothy saw his open, unseeing eyes.

The dead man's fingers had frozen around the plank. Timothy prised them loose one by one, hearing the tiny joints break in the vastness of the sea.

The sound remained with him longer than any cannon fire.

When rescuers found him, Timothy could not remember being hauled aboard. Next came the sickbay ceiling, medicinal spirits and Elizabeth outside the door, arms folded as though he had inconvenienced her by nearly dying.

She was not his sister by blood. She had never needed to be.

He remembered waking in the middle of the night, feverish and confused. The changing watch sent him tearing away blankets and scrambling from bed, convinced of an attack; Elizabeth caught him, they swore at each other, and she shoved him back with one hand.

The days afterwards were much the same. Elizabeth brought food, changed his bandages and sat beside the door when he could not sleep, but never asked whether he was frightened.

Each time Timothy woke imagining the hull splitting open, she was still in her chair. Sometimes she fell asleep with a cold bowl balanced on her knees; Timothy watched for a while, then drew up his blanket.

He had never thanked her.

Timothy raised a hand to wipe his face. San Sebastián returned, with La Concha below and a gull skimming the water before climbing into the wind.

He watched until the bird was a white speck beyond the bay, then looked at his right hand. Lisbon came back to him.

Thousands disembarking; Don José before his soldiers, Fredo and Martinez between lines of muskets, Edward among men disputing who should die, and for what. Timothy had said some bitter things that day.

Part of him still believed them. Another part knew that Elizabeth had been right to rebuke him.

But he remembered Edward's words most clearly. The Admiral would not send men aboard merely because he had won ten years earlier; he would give them a plan worth judging against their lives.

Timothy had gone aboard. Eight hundred British veterans and one hundred Conquistadors had sailed on the *Red Baron*.

The night before La Concha, they drank tea, cursed, laughed at death and spoke of foolish things. By morning, fog shrouded the bay, and Timothy stood beside the helm listening to Edward's orders.

For the first time in years, he did not search for an exit. He looked at the target.

Their first shot tore through the French flagship's stern, and then the plan came apart. Martinez fell, the fog lifted too soon and the Portuguese fleet appeared; *Le Triomphant* exploded with Edward still aboard, and Fredo crossed the gap to bring Edward and Martinez home.

Timothy saw the head of Fredo's chain miss the crossbeam. The distance was growing, and 180 feet was too far; before fear could tell him everything would end as it had before, he looked at the cannons beneath his feet.

He ordered them shifted to one side. Hundreds seized ropes and levers, heaving iron weighing thousands of pounds without question.

The *Red Baron* heeled over. Only ten feet, but ten feet were enough.

He remembered the hook striking the beam, and his own scream as Fredo, Edward and Martinez hurtled across and crashed upon the deck. Then came *Storm's Roar*.

The weapon grew so hot that blisters rose on his fingers. Edward called firing angles down the speaking tube while Timothy loaded, aimed, fired, opened the breech and loaded again.

One French warship exploded, then another. Smoke and fire reared behind the *Red Baron*.

When a Portuguese vessel rammed their stern, Timothy was thrown onto the gun deck. He scrambled up, carried *Storm's Roar* below and found a firing angle against the ship lodged in the *Red Baron*.

He was still afraid. His legs trembled, his throat was so dry that swallowing hurt, and a voice within him insisted Vila do Porto had returned, that he would soon be adrift again, breaking a friend's frozen fingers from the last plank.

But this time Timothy pulled the trigger.

The Portuguese magazine exploded. The shock wave wrenched the two ships apart and drove the *Red Baron* clear of the broadside that would have finished her. Then the *Red Baron* herself sank.

Timothy fell into the sea again. God had a wretched sense of humour, but this time, when Timothy was hauled out, the first two men he saw were breathing.

Edward lived. Fredo lived, Martinez lived and Timothy lived. San Sebastián still stood behind them.

Timothy lowered his head, laughing through fresh tears.

"We won."

He no longer wiped his face. Beneath the waters of La Concha lay men who had not been brought ashore, some found still embracing driftwood, others so badly broken they could not be named.

Some he had known since childhood, others since Lisbon, and some were Castilian sailors he had wanted to curse days before. They now lay together in the same stretch of water.

Timothy reached into his coat for a handkerchief and found a folded scrap of paper instead. He opened it on his knees, holding the corners against the wind.

Among the markings left from the battle, Edward had written an address in Marrakesh. Timothy read it twice, steadying the page with his thumb.

Beneath the address was a final line.

*The Beaumont family*.

Timothy stared. Edward had returned the paper in the sickroom on Monte Urgull, when Timothy had been too shaken to read it properly.

Now he read every word. There was a street in Marrakesh he could find, a door at which he could knock and ask for the Beaumont family.

He pressed the paper into his palm and folded over his knees. His laughter broke into sobs.

"Bloody hell."

He kept laughing through his tears.

"You really are a bastard, Admiral."

The sea wind did not answer. He stayed there, holding the scrap as though it were his most precious possession.

Finally he took another sheet and a short pencil from his inner pocket. Resting the paper on his knees, he wrote his first line.

*Dear Dame Elizabeth,*

His pencil stopped. He studied the words, grimaced and crossed them out.

He began again.

*Dear Elizabeth,*

His handwriting ran crookedly. He adjusted the sheet and continued.

*I'm alive.*

He read the words and almost struck them out for being so foolish. Instead, he wrote beneath them.

*We won.*

*This is the first time in a very long while that I've been able to write those words without feeling as though I'm lying to myself. I don't know whether the news from San Sebastián has reached you yet, but I wanted you to hear it from me before somebody turns the whole affair into a ten-page report and sends it back to Lisbon.*

*I went aboard. I was afraid, and this time I can admit I was terribly afraid.*

Timothy paused, the pencil making a dark mark. He remembered Elizabeth's voice upon the quay and wrote on.

*You once told me not to turn my own fear into a sentence passed upon everybody else. At the time I thought you were half wrong, and I still think so, but you were right about the other half.*

*If you've read this far, I imagine you're already preparing to curse me for managing to argue with you in a letter that is supposed to thank you. You can curse me afterwards.*

*The Castilian navy has lost too many battles. I still believe that. But at La Concha I watched the men I had called little more than wooden targets sail out of San Sebastián harbour under Portuguese fire to drag us from the sea.*

*I saw Englishmen and Castilian sailors haul the same cannon. I saw Conquistadors die holding open the Admiral's route of retreat, and I saw men who had pointed muskets at each other only days before leap into the same waters to save one another.*

*I suspect you will be delighted to know I've had to write these words myself.*

Timothy laughed and continued.

*The Admiral kept his word.*

*The battle did not unfold as he intended. At moments everything became such a dreadful bloody mess that I thought, if I survived, the first thing I would do was make him sit down and write a report explaining himself.*

*But we knew what we were doing, and when the plan fell apart, he still knew what needed doing next. So did I.*

Timothy looked at his right hand before putting the pencil to the page again.

*I sank enemy ships, Elizabeth.*

*Not the usual business of firing a hundred rounds and having somebody afterwards suggest we might have struck something. I pulled the trigger myself, watched the magazine explode and saw the hull break apart.*

*I won a battle.*

The last line slanted down the page. Timothy pressed his wrist against his eyes before writing again, more slowly.

*I wish the old lads had been here to see it.*

*There are a great many men who will not be coming home. I don't yet know how to write about them, so I shall not attempt it today.*

*I only wanted you to know that I'm alive, and that I haven't died like a fool.*

Timothy laughed aloud, almost hearing Elizabeth curse him. He added another line.

*Nor have I died according to plan, so I suppose I've managed to keep half my promise.*

This time he had to stop, laughing and weeping until the writing blurred. He waited for his tears to stop falling on the letter.

*Thank you. For those nights you sat outside the sickbay while I pretended to sleep, for never looking at me as though I were a ruined soldier because I was afraid, and for scolding me whenever I said something stupid.*

*I cannot remember when I first began calling you my sister. I hope you understand what I mean, because I don't know how to put it any better.*

Timothy rested a hand upon the Marrakesh address beside his knee and wrote the last part.

*The Admiral has found my family. They're in Marrakesh, and I have their address in my hand.*

*When the work here is done, provided nobody dreams up another idiotic battle to drag me into, I'll go to them. Perhaps I still have somewhere to come home to.*

Timothy paused. The final words came more easily than all the rest.

*Don't worry about me any longer.*

*I'm coming home.*

*Timothy Beaumont.*

He read the letter through. There were spelling mistakes, a crossed-out line and two tear stains, but he corrected nothing.

He folded it into quarters and slipped it into his inner pocket. The Marrakesh address he folded separately, more carefully, placing it in the small pocket nearest his heart and fastening the button.

Timothy braced his hands upon his knees and stood. His numb legs made him stagger; he stamped his heels, dusted his trousers and straightened his uniform.

The wind had strengthened over the bay. He walked to the edge of the outcrop, overlooking almost the entire bay mouth.

The sea had concealed most traces of the battle, leaving only charred timbers and drifting patches of oil. The *Red Baron* lay beneath it, with her hammocks, tin mugs and the men who had never returned. Timothy remembered laughter in Lisbon, commands shouted across the deck and hands reaching out to pull comrades from the cold water.

He stood straighter before the sea. He brought his boot heels together and raised his chin towards the mouth of the bay. His right hand closed into a fist.

Timothy extended that fist towards La Concha. The wind drew his coat taut behind him, and he held the salute before the vast expanse of water.

His arm still ached. He braced his shoulder to keep the fist raised until the wind shifted and carried the smell of smoke from the city out towards the sea.

At last he drew his fist back and pressed it against the centre of his chest. Then he bowed deeply towards the water.

"Thank you."

title_vi: Chapter Thirty: The Woman in the Mirror
title_en: Chapter Thirty: The Woman in the Mirror
text_en:
Oak logs crackled in the hearth of the study at Monte Urgull. Across Isabella's desk, casualty rolls, pension warrants, military maps and letters from the provinces lay in separate stacks, each awaiting her royal seal.

Queen Isabella of Castile sat alone, dipping her quill into the ink for what seemed the hundredth time. A month had passed since the Battle of La Concha. In the streets of northern Castile, people still sang of victory; here, that victory had become hundreds of pages of cold accounting.

Losses to the fleet, ships requiring repair, wounded soldiers, pensions for the families of the dead. Beside them lay requests for heating coal from the Pyrenees, appeals for aid from North Africa, and tax petitions sent without end by the noble houses.

Among the documents rested a particularly thin ledger bearing the red cross of the English exiles. Its list of names was shorter than a corps' muster roll, yet Isabella found her quill growing heavier as she read.

These veterans had followed Edward into La Concha Bay, many after years of quiet existence in refugee settlements. Now each was reduced to a name, a former home and the sum due to surviving kin. More than half had not returned.

Isabella signed the last page, pressed the royal seal beneath the pension authorisation and closed the ledger. For several seconds she regarded the red cross before placing the book among the completed papers.

"It must nearly be time for the meeting."

She checked the lock on the door, exchanged her linen blouse for a silk shirt and lifted her uniform from its stand. As she fastened the buttons, her eyes strayed back to the English ledger.

"Edward... How did you persuade hundreds of men to follow you so willingly?"

One by one, silver buttons engraved with lions and castles slipped into place. The high, rigid collar rose about her throat, hiding the softness of the woman beneath. She tightened her belt, smoothed the folds and settled the uniform around her with almost faultless care.

Isabella had never allowed a maid or servant to touch her during such private moments.

Mud from an inspection of the barracks still clung to the boots beside the stand. She wiped their leather clean and arranged them neatly before taking her seat at the mirror. Soon the generals would expect her answers to the petitions upon her desk.

She drew an ivory comb through her hair and dusted her face with powder to conceal the traces of sleepless nights. A stick of dark crimson wax coloured her lips, completing the appearance the world knew. The Queen had taken her place in the glass, but the memory of a report from Lisbon's naval port stilled her hands.

She remained angry with the men who had allowed Edward to sail with a single ship. Yet their objections were recorded plainly: insufficient troops, disputed authority over deployments, and the danger of leaving a defensive line exposed. Each bore the signature of an officer who would answer if his position fell.

Isabella turned the report face down. La Concha had been won; she still had to explain why those men had been required to fight such a battle.

Her grip tightened around the handle of her cosmetic brush. The jewelled silver snapped against her palm, and a sharp edge sliced her skin. Blood spotted the wood; she watched the cut for a moment, then lifted her gaze to the mirror.

Her left eye had darkened to crimson, while her right remained amber. In the glass, the reflection smiled before Isabella's own lips stirred. A gentle voice spoke within her mind.

"Isabella, how careless you are..."

The shadow whispered with tender regret, its red gaze resting upon the Queen's bleeding hand.

"Those people are not worth an injury to you."

The reflection watched the blood gather in Isabella's palm.

"Please, leave the rest to me."

Isabella held the broken half of the handle without blinking. A crimson mist, fine as silk, slipped from the polished bronze into the room and wound itself about her wrist.

Coolness spread beneath her skin. The ragged cut drew together, flesh knitting perfectly until her palm was whole, as though no drop of blood had fallen.

"I am the shadow born solely to serve you."

The reflection laid a hand against the glass.

"I exist to protect you. If I cannot prevent even a wound to Your Majesty's hand, how can I claim to serve you at all?"

Isabella examined her healed palm. Then her eyes moved to the ledger marked with the red cross.

"Testarossa. If you can mend flesh so easily, why can you not heal those who died in the bay?"

The reflection's smile did not falter.

"Because they are not you. And I am not all-powerful."

Isabella glanced again at the pension ledger. Testarossa waited in the mirror, her hand resting precisely where Isabella's had been.

"The lives of subjects, soldiers, anyone in this world, may be weighed by what they contribute. But Your Majesty is different. There is nothing in existence that could be placed upon the scales against you."

Isabella withdrew her hand, her voice lower now.

"And if an entire city had to be sacrificed to preserve my life?"

"I would burn it."

"An entire corps?"

"I would bury it."

"Even all of Castile?"

Testarossa stopped smiling. She considered Isabella for a moment before replying with the same gentle voice.

"If Castile can endure only through your death, what purpose does such a Castile serve?"

Her crimson eyes curved once more.

"The kingdom exists to serve you, Your Majesty."

Isabella held her gaze. No anger showed upon her face, but the polite smile she so often wore was gone.

"You are wrong."

Testarossa inclined her head.

"Then I beg you to explain."

"I sit upon the throne because Castile needs someone to sit there. If my life must one day be exchanged for this country's survival, I shall be the first to give that order."

A rare displeasure crossed Testarossa's red eyes. The mist around the mirror trembled as if caught in a draught.

"I will not permit it."

"You have no right to permit it."

Isabella spoke quietly, yet her voice seemed to chill the room. Two women with the same face regarded each other across the polished bronze.

Testarossa lowered her head. When she raised it, her smile had returned.

"Then I shall devote all my strength to ensuring that day never comes."

Isabella touched the mirror with one fingertip.

"Do you know why I have kept you with me?"

"Because I understand you."

Testarossa touched the same spot from the other side.

"Or because you still fear my power?"

"Because you speak aloud things I have thought myself."

Isabella drew her finger away.

"Things I must never allow myself to do."

Testarossa's smile widened.

"Then do I not understand you better than anyone alive?"

Isabella did not answer. She looked at the broken brush and covered the blood upon the table with a cloth.

"Very well. Tell me."

She leaned against the dressing table.

"Lisbon. The Council. Where would you begin?"

Testarossa glanced over Isabella's shoulder at the English ledger.

"The north has given you a power the throne would scarcely have dared hope for only a few years ago. Why hurry to punish every man in Lisbon?"

"Are you speaking of Edward?"

Isabella frowned. Testarossa shook her head and gave a clear, delighted little laugh.

"My most exalted Queen, he is hardly the only one."

She leaned towards the glass, raising a spectral hand as though to stroke Isabella's cheek.

"At this moment, the north lays a magnificent chessboard before you. The Pathfinder has returned from death, veterans hunger to restore a symbol of their homeland, and loyal warriors need a victory in which to believe. Others bow before the throne while waiting for its first sign of weakness."

Testarossa paced the length of the mirror and stopped near its edge.

"Do not arrest them yet. Let them believe they are free to choose. As Edward's reputation grows, each will reveal what he means to do."

Isabella set the cloth aside and faced her fully.

"You would use Edward as bait?"

"I would have you see the pieces already in your possession," Testarossa replied.

"Edward, the English exiles, the great houses, even the hatred of those who oppose your throne. Loyalty and fear alike will move men. What matters is knowing whose hand guides them."

Isabella's expression cooled.

"Edward receives his orders as an admiral."

She placed her hand upon the desk.

"Juliet and Remi are not soldiers in my army."

Testarossa's smile faltered.

"You draw a distinction between two things that are equally a man's weaknesses?"

"I do."

Isabella did not let her continue.

"I may order Edward into battle and use his victories to rally the army. But never again suggest that I use his wife and child to compel him."

Testarossa studied her for a long moment.

"Because you love him?"

Isabella met her gaze.

"Because military authority has limits. Cross them, and I shall no longer have an admiral who stands beside me of his own free will. I shall have a prisoner."

The shadow bowed slowly, although her face still betrayed disagreement.

"I shall remember."

Isabella picked up the broken half of the brush and laid it on a silver tray.

"Continue."

Testarossa smiled again.

"Whether their loyalty is blind or their obedience false, all may serve as instruments if placed correctly. Let war force each man to choose his allegiance. Do not offer them a purge through which they may call themselves victims. Grant them enough freedom to cross the very boundaries they pretend to honour."

Testarossa set a fingertip against the glass.

"When they reveal their intentions, Your Majesty will have no need to search for names."

Isabella drew the Lisbon report towards her.

"I shall watch what they do. An objection to an order is not grounds for condemnation. Whoever crosses the line must leave evidence."

She looked into the mirror.

"Thank you, Testarossa."

At the sound of her name, the shadow bowed deeply. Joy kindled the red in her eyes.

"To bear your name is my greatest honour, Your Majesty."

Slowly, Testarossa raised her head and pressed her hand against the bronze. Her crimson eye burned with fierce longing.

"If Your Majesty finds the missing eye, I shall break the limits of a Legendary Vestigium. When the two eyes become one, I shall ascend to the rank of a Mythical Vestigium."

Isabella showed none of the delight Testarossa had expected. She studied the reflection before asking plainly.

"If those eyes are joined, what becomes of you?"

"I shall be complete."

"I asked what becomes of you."

For once, Testarossa did not answer at once. She raised her hand and studied her fingers, her smile settling into a strange tranquillity.

"If I can become a perfect part of you, does my separate existence matter?"

Isabella frowned.

"I did not ask whether you were willing to disappear."

"But that is my answer."

Testarossa spoke with the softness of a prayer.

"I was born to protect you. If my existence can purchase Your Majesty's continued journey, I shall accept it."

Isabella said nothing. The hearthlight shifted across the bronze, superimposing their identical faces until woman and shadow could scarcely be told apart. At last, Testarossa broke the silence.

"When I am complete, even the vast power of the *Crown of Ravenna* will cease to be a considerable threat. I shall break every danger, master every backlash and offer you eternal peace."

Isabella narrowed her eyes.

"You have never seen the *Crown of Ravenna* yourself. Why are you so certain?"

Testarossa laughed, and the red mist trembled against the glass.

"I am not certain."

Seeing Isabella's surprise, she continued.

"But if the *Crown of Ravenna* seeks to seize your will, I shall find a way to stop it. If I fail once, I shall seek another way. So long as I exist, Your Majesty's will shall remain your own."

Her crimson pupil brightened with a devotion both fervent and serene.

"My one and only Queen."

Beyond the locked door, footsteps sounded along the stone corridor. A knock followed, and Martinez's familiar voice announced that the generals had all assembled in the great hall.

Testarossa's smile faded. The mist withdrew into the mirror, and the red light went out in Isabella's left eye, leaving only its familiar amber.

Isabella wiped away the last drop of blood on the dressing table, placed the broken brush in its case and straightened the stiff collar of her uniform. She looked at herself once more in the mirror.

Then she unlocked the door and went out to meet Martinez. Behind her, the hearth continued to cast a red glow upon one eye of the reflection that had just turned away.

title_vi: Chapter Thirty-One: Decisions
title_en: Chapter Thirty-One: Decisions
text_en:
Martinez waited outside the council chamber with a folio beneath her arm. Her Royal Guard uniform was immaculate, though the place reserved for her numbered pendant remained empty. When Isabella emerged, Martinez stepped aside and bowed, holding the papers close with her formerly wounded arm.

"Are you quite well, Your Majesty?"

"I am." Isabella glanced at Martinez's shoulder. "And your wound? Can you sit through a long council?"

"It has healed, Your Majesty." Martinez turned her shoulder to demonstrate, though her uninjured hand still supported the folio. "If I need to rest, I shall say so."

Isabella nodded, and they climbed towards the great hall. Boot heels rang on the steps of Monte Urgull as sentries moved aside.

The doors opened upon a low murmur of conversation. Officers had gathered around Edward to question him about the battle in the bay. He sat beside Fredo, tea in hand, until Martinez announced the Queen.

Everyone stood. Isabella gestured for Edward to remain seated, noticing the hand with which he braced himself against his chair.

"Sir Edward, has your physician given you leave to be out of bed?"

"I went into the courtyard with Timothy, then met Fredo. I wanted to hear the council." Edward put down his cup. "If I cannot endure it, I shall ask to withdraw."

Isabella looked towards Fredo. He drew his chair close enough to assist Edward if necessary.

"Then stay seated. Do not strain yourself for the sake of ceremony."

She took the presiding chair at the head of the table, beside Fredo, Martinez, Governor Frenesia and the garrison commanders. Edward sat opposite her across the campaign map, his tea within reach.

Martinez broke the red wax seal of a leather folio and stood at attention beside the Queen.

"In the name of Queen Isabella Testarossa, I hereby declare this extraordinary military council at the fortress of Monte Urgull convened."

She did not rush through the roll. As each delegation was named, a staff officer set its wooden token upon the map.

"The representatives of Navarre and the Pyrenees Defence Staff; Lord Franco Valdes, representing the House of Castile; Lady Frenesia, Governor of San Sebastián; and Admiral Sir Edward Spencer of the Royal Castilian Navy."

Those four political appointments were marked first. Martinez turned towards the officers seated down either side of the table.

"The commanding officers of Tercio I del Rayo, IV del León, V de la Sombra, VI del Trueno, VIII de la Roca, IX del Escudo and X del Bastión."

Seven grey counters formed a line against the Pyrenees. Edward followed their positions as they settled upon the map rather than memorising the numerals.

Martinez turned the page.

"Colonel Cassandra, Number Ten of the Royal Guard, is attending from the Perpignan front through a Vestigium communication link."

The crystal sphere at the centre of the table flashed blue. Wind whistled through it, mingled with distant explosions, before Cassandra spoke.

"Cassandra present! My respects to Your Majesty and the assembled commanders!"

Isabella acknowledged the greeting and turned to Fredo.

"One front at a time. I would rather everyone not suffocate under the figures before the French have a chance to kill them."

Brief laughter loosened the chamber. Fredo rose and swept the French counters away from San Sebastián.

"We begin in the north. After the French and Portuguese fleets were defeated at La Concha, the royal relief forces counterattacked from both the eastern and western approaches to the Pyrenees. French formations that had penetrated our territory were driven across the frontier. The western flank has been relieved for the present."

Before he could turn the page, the sphere trembled.

"For the present," Cassandra cut in. "French artillery still pounds our outer positions at Perpignan every day. Aragon holds my flank, but if the French send reinforcements, we shall bear the first weight of them."

Fredo inclined his head towards the crystal.

"As her report makes clear, Perpignan remains our most vulnerable point in the east. Cassandra and the Aragonese are holding their positions, but we must strengthen that line before considering an offensive."

Edward studied the seven Tercio counters at the edge of the map. Now he understood why their commanders had been summoned to Monte Urgull together.

Fredo removed the marker for Taza from North Africa. Nearby officers stared at the gap it left.

"Taza has fallen after several days of Western Roman bombardment. Their main army is closing upon Fes. Intelligence estimates more than five hundred thousand soldiers, sustained by forward depots and convoys arriving from the Mediterranean ports."

"Five hundred thousand?"

The chamber erupted in murmurs. Martinez struck the table once with her palm, and silence followed.

"Hear the rest."

Fredo arranged a chain of small counters for the supply convoys running towards Fes from Iberia and North Africa. He took up five legion markers and read their names in order.

"Tercio XVI de la Hazaña, XVII del Pozo, XVIII de las Cadenas, XIX del Silencio and XX del Trono."

The officers placed the five counters around Fes, covering the roads along which grain, ammunition, medicines and fuel had to travel. Opposite stood a red mass representing more than half a million Roman soldiers. The disparity silenced the room.

Fredo did not allow the council to dwell upon Africa. He returned to the peninsula and set three counters sideways upon León, Galicia and Valencia.

"In the rear, León and Galicia still refuse to release grain from their stores or obey the mobilisation orders issued from Madrid. Valencia stood with them until recently, but has reversed its decision. I shall explain its deployment shortly."

A member of the Council frowned.

"Then why have they not been charged with treason?"

Fredo tapped the sideways counters with his pen.

"Because they have not declared themselves enemies of the Queen. Every refusal is dressed up as the 'result of a local vote' or 'the expressed wishes of the provincial garrison'. If the Crown proclaims rebellion without an armed act or proof of collusion, we shall hand them the pretext they need to turn disobedience into war."

Edward gripped the handle of his cup. Three fronts, a lost city, a frontier only just saved, and a rear beginning to turn upon itself. He watched Fredo open the last page.

"How long has all this taken?"

Fredo faced him.

"One month, Admiral."

Edward stopped with his cup halfway to his mouth.

"A month?"

He knew he had lain unconscious for a month. Only the shifting counters revealed what that absence had cost. He said nothing as Franco Valdes rose and brought four pieces bearing red crosses into the centre of the table.

"We have not spent that month merely losing ground," the old lord said. "We have raised a new force as well."

He lined up the four pieces.

"The decree for the general mobilisation of the English exiles has been fulfilled. Four Exiled English Legions have been formed: the White Lion, the Black Rose, the Fallen Oak and the Mist. Their supreme commands have been entrusted to four distinguished former officers of the old Royal English Academy."

Franco picked up the first counter and set it upon Madrid.

"Sir Edward Spencer. You are not to be sent straight to the French frontier. One legion will accompany you to the capital. You will serve as Guardian of the Throne, protecting Her Majesty and your family while ensuring that unrest in the rear cannot become a knife driven into Madrid."

Edward studied the red cross in silence.

Franco carried the second counter across Gibraltar and placed it at Fes.

"Marco Stones will command an English legion fighting directly alongside the Tercios defending Fes."

The third counter went to Tangier and Ceuta.

"Romeo Harkon commands the next legion in cooperation with Tercio III del Filo and Sultan Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad. That position must serve both as a reserve capable of relieving Fes and as the vital gateway should the forward front break."

The fourth piece came to rest upon Marrakesh.

"Victoria Valdes takes charge of the remaining legion alongside Tercio XI del Acero. They will guard our rearward centre and the roads carrying food and weapons to the whole North African theatre."

Franco stepped back to let the arrangement speak. Three English flags anchored the southern positions beside the Tercios and Moors.

"Across North Africa, our Castilian and English formations number one hundred and seventy-five thousand men: eight regular Tercio legions and three Exiled English Legions under Marco, Romeo and Victoria. Add the sixty thousand elite Moorish troops under Sultan Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad, and our combined strength reaches two hundred and thirty-five thousand."

He traced a circle with his silver-tipped cane around Fes, Tangier, Ceuta and Marrakesh.

"That is the price of restraining more than five hundred thousand Western Romans while keeping North Africa linked to Iberia."

No one cheered the figure of two hundred and thirty-five thousand. On the map, their combined forces were still dwarfed by the enemy.

Franco returned his cane to the Pyrenees.

"Now we come to what the men in this chamber must do."

He indicated Martinez's seven grey markers.

"The seven Tercios just called by name will march east from Monte Urgull and assemble under Cassandra's direct command."

Her voice came immediately from the sphere.

"I shall establish a mustering ground behind Perpignan. Send me men, ammunition and food before sending another speech."

A few officers laughed without much mirth. Franco smiled faintly and set Tercio VII del Sol at Perpignan.

"Tercio VII del Sol will continue to hold the stronghold. The Navarrese Knight Legion will reinforce it, while Aragon commits its local troops and treasury to defending the line down to the Mediterranean. Once the seven legions have assembled and Perpignan is secure, Cassandra will have authority to launch a general counteroffensive across the Pyrenees into southern France."

This time the murmurs came from the Navarrese nobles rather than the Tercio officers.

Before objections gathered force, Governor Frenesia rose. Past sixty, the formidable woman planted both hands upon the table and looked directly at Isabella.

"The eastern flank belongs to Cassandra. Leave the western flank to San Sebastián. The former Pyrenees Defence Staff appointed by the Council was dismissed after the recent defeats. I pledge my personal honour that, so long as our flag flies above La Mota, the fortresses of the Bay of Biscay will not let a French army through the western approaches."

Franco nodded and closed the plan. Every piece but Navarre's had been assigned a front.

Its representative drew the mountain-pass map closer.

"Your Majesty, we have defended these passes throughout the campaign. If we send our knights across the frontier, who will protect the roads the French have only just used to invade us?"

He planted a finger on the border.

"An order to defend our territory is not an order to invade France. I must bring the Council a duty with limits, not a promise of a war no one can say when it will end."

Fredo joined him at the map.

"Your first assignment is to reinforce Perpignan. The counteroffensive will not begin until the men are assembled, the defensive line is secure and Cassandra can sustain the flow of supplies."

"Then put those conditions in writing."

Fredo indicated the positions still held by the French.

"I shall. But if we stop at the passes, they will retain their assembly grounds for another assault. We need Navarre to help us advance beyond that line, not stand waiting on this side of it."

The representative glanced at his accompanying officers, then at Isabella. She allowed him to continue.

"The authority to send troops beyond our borders remains with the Council of Navarre. I cannot return with my signature alone and tell every family to surrender its sons to a new campaign."

The officers behind him nodded. Fredo opened the deployment papers and laid another order beside the map.

"Valencia accepted the task of holding Palma a fortnight ago." He touched the seal upon the page. "They objected too, until their assignment and supply routes were made clear."

"Palma is not southern France."

"Indeed. That is why I am not giving you Valencia's orders." Fredo pushed the Navarrese document across. "Show me what is missing from this one."

The representative remained standing, looking from the seven Tercios to Fredo.

Fredo laid the order before him.

"Seven royal legions are gathered in this fortress. If your Council is concerned that Navarre will have too few men to defend its own territory, Her Majesty could leave several of those legions behind to assist you."

The proposal rested among the grey counters. Their authority needed no explanation.

The representative withdrew his hand from the map, glanced at the Tercio commanders and finally drew the paper towards him.

"I understand the proposal. Include the conditions for defending the frontier, and I shall deliver the order to the Council."

No one laughed. Fredo signalled the secretary to add the conditions, while the Navarrese officers sat and conferred quietly over the document.

When the clerk had finished, Fredo looked around the table.

"Are your assignments and the deadlines for mustering understood?"

"UNDERSTOOD, YOUR MAJESTY!"

The officers rose and pressed their hands against their coats in salute. Fredo closed the order book.

"The council is concluded. All units are to return and make ready their provisions according to the deployment schedule."

The delegations filed out. Only Isabella, Fredo, Martinez, Franco and Edward remained.

Franco pulled his chair nearer the map. Once the Navarrese had gone, he swept aside the ceremonial counters with his cane, revealing the western peninsula concealed during the public session.

"That was what we could say before the full Council, Your Majesty. What follows cannot be spoken there."

He set two black pieces upon León and Galicia.

"If those houses openly rebel, their two principal knightly legions, together with the mercenaries they are quietly recruiting, could give the rebels more than fifty thousand armed men. We have indications that they are seeking ties with foreign powers, but no proof sound enough to present before the Council."

Martinez braced one hand upon the table, watching the black counters.

"And Andalusia?"

Franco took out another piece but kept it suspended above the south, as though the house had yet to choose a side.

"Outwardly, they continue to obey. Grain leaves their stores, taxes are paid, and the garrison has made no suspicious movement. But intelligence gathered by the House of Castile confirms that Andalusian representatives travelled secretly to the naval port of Lisbon no fewer than three times this month to contact Don José's faction."

"Three meetings do not tell us what they promised," Fredo said. "I want the names of the couriers and the route of the money before drawing conclusions."

Martinez moved a Conquistador counter towards Santiago.

"If they begin combining their forces, striking their headquarters would cost fewer lives than waiting until they have sixty thousand men. But we must know precisely whom to strike. How many Conquistadors can we withdraw from the Pyrenees?"

Franco did not answer at once. He opened a wooden box and arranged fifteen metal Conquistador company markers in three rows before her.

"This was our strength when the war in the Pyrenees began. More than fifteen hundred men."

He picked up six markers and dropped them into the box one by one. Each struck the wood dryly.

"And this is what remains. Nine hundred."

Martinez stared at the nine pieces. Franco showed her the discarded pieces.

"For the past month they have taken turns holding the mountain flanks against the Gendarmes. Six hundred Conquistadors have been killed, reported missing or rendered unfit for further combat. Every replacement suit of Vestigium armour and every transmission mechanism draws funds away from food, fuel and the foundries already labouring without rest.
