We cannot afford to spend these men on every political dispute."

Martinez looked at the six empty spaces. Her fingers gradually loosened upon her sword hilt.

"If we lose another half of those who remain..."

"Castile will have broken its last shield with its own hands," Franco replied, closing the box upon the six discarded pieces.

A heavy silence settled. At length Martinez looked towards Isabella.

"Then what of the Reliquiario? They are fewer, but if we mean to sever the head of a rebellion instead of fighting an entire legion, would they not be better suited to the task?"

"The Reliquiario are suited to hunting a particular target," Isabella answered. She turned a small marker bearing their insignia between two fingers. "They are trained to hunt original Vestigium, deal with mutated creatures and confront anomalies requiring infiltration or sealing. If we use them to fill every gap in the army's ranks, a handful of battles will destroy the force altogether."

She returned the marker to its box rather than placing it on the map.

"I need them intact for duties no one else can perform. One day Edward must return to England, or our armies may advance deep into southern France, among ruins still touched by magic. When that day comes, a thousand fine soldiers will not replace a Reliquiario team that understands what it is hunting."

Isabella looked towards the far end of the table.

"Sir Edward, you will command the defence of Madrid. Knowing what you know now, what should we do first?"

Edward studied the pieces until he realised all four were watching.

"To tell you the truth... my thoughts are caught on something else."

He set down his teacup.

"I have only just woken to find I have lost an entire month. Before we discuss whom to arrest or whom to lure into treason, tell me how my wife and son are faring in Madrid."

Franco smiled at his impatience. He put away the piece for Andalusia.

"Lady Juliet and young Remi are both safe, Sir Edward. Your family's apartment lies within a closely guarded district in the heart of the capital, and they have no shortage of heat or provisions. According to news received by my household, Lady Juliet has grown accustomed to Madrid and become especially close to Lady Millennia, Colonel Marco Stones's wife. The two visit each other almost daily and are of great comfort to one another."

Fredo added his own reassurance.

"Remi has entered the Royal Academy, in the same class as Marco's son. They have become such friends that their tutors know both names. You may put your mind at ease."

Edward's shoulders eased. He exhaled and drew his chair closer.

"Good. Now tell me precisely what is at my disposal. Spare me another catalogue of figures. Let us build Madrid on this map."

Franco pushed the box of counters towards him.

Edward selected a red-cross marker and placed it upon Madrid.

"My English legion. How many men?"

"Eleven thousand armed men," Franco answered. "They have assembled and received their equipment at barracks on the outskirts of Madrid."

Edward kept one finger upon the piece and looked towards Isabella.

"Eleven thousand people scattered across the peninsula until now. How did Your Majesty bring them together?"

Isabella rose from the presiding chair and joined him at the map.

"News of La Concha reached the towns, mines and refugee settlements before our recruiting officers. I granted them permission to muster beneath the emblem of their homeland. They came."

She touched the red cross beneath his finger.

"They defend Castile, which has given them shelter through this winter of the Long Frost. All four Exiled English Legions may carry their red-cross banners into battle."

Edward regarded the marker for a long moment.

"Their equipment?"

"Equal to the regular Tercios," Isabella said. "Armour made from mutated oxhide and the finest rifles our arsenals can provide. Only their uniforms differ: the English wear deep red wool, while the Crown's regiments wear grey and white."

A slight smile touched her mouth.

"The same colour as the Frostblood Redcoats Legion that Marco raised at Fes. When the North African fighting is over, the Redcoats will be incorporated into the Exiled English Legion under his command."

Edward slowly lowered the piece onto Madrid. Its red cross stood out among the grey blocks.

He picked up a second counter and placed it alongside, leaving room for local troops.

"What of Madrid's own troops? Lord Franco, how many men does the House of Castile retain in the capital?"

Franco laughed proudly, leaning upon his cane.

"The Castilian Knight Legion remains in Madrid. Two thousand knights and heavily armoured men."

Edward looked up.

"Only two thousand? For a house of Castile's standing?"

"Precisely because of its standing," Franco replied, placing the piece beside the English legion. "For centuries, sons of Castile old enough to bear arms have joined the Crown's Tercios. The two thousand knights and heavy troops in Madrid preserve our house's traditions and defend the capital; the greater part of Castile's strength serves in the national army."

Edward nodded and turned towards Fredo and Martinez.

"And Fredo and Martinez? What authority shall I have to deploy them?"

"They will take orders directly from you in Madrid," Isabella replied. "They will also be responsible for coordination with the Royal Guard."

Fredo bowed with one hand on his breast. Martinez gave a short nod.

Edward placed two markers beside the red legion and frowned.

"Something is still missing."

Fredo followed his gaze.

"What are you looking for?"

Edward ran a fingertip along the Tercio symbols at the map's edge.

"At the council we heard I, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX and X. Others are in North Africa. But where are XII, XIII, XIV and XV?"

Fredo took out four pieces and placed them at the approaches to Castile's heartland: Tercio XII de la Cima, XIII del Muro, XIV de la Venganza and XV del Colmillo. Two blocked the mountain roads and main routes of advance, while the other two formed a line behind them.

"All four stand along the borders adjoining territories suspected of sedition. Their orders are to stop any unauthorised movement of troops from León, Galicia or Andalusia before it reaches our heartland."

Edward nudged León's counter towards Madrid. It immediately struck the line of Tercios.

He surveyed the defence: eleven thousand English soldiers in the capital, two thousand Castilian knights, Fredo and Martinez at its centre, and four regular legions guarding the approaches. The Conquistadors and Reliquiario would be spared a ruinous war of attrition.

Edward pulled the map closer, then stopped as pain stabbed through his chest. He shifted in his chair while Fredo cleared away the tea tray to make room for the next pieces.

"We return to Madrid as soon as our men and provisions are ready. Before then, I want to know which approaches will allow us to conceal our reserves."

He pointed out the roads leading into the city.

"Keep enough men openly posted here, at the granaries and along the routes used to bring troops into the capital. But the enemy need not know the full strength of our reserve, nor everyone we have watching them."

"You want them to underestimate us?" Isabella asked. "And if they set their sights on me, or at Juliet and Remi?"

"Then we protect you before they act." Edward kept his hand upon the Madrid marker. "I am not proposing to withdraw guards and create a weakness, nor to place my family in danger and wait for a man with a knife."

Martinez moved a smaller counter beside the palace.

"The Royal Guard will cover the positions closest to Her Majesty. Your troops will hold the roads and their assigned posts. The Reliquiario will receive specific targets, not be scattered throughout the city."

Franco turned to Edward.

"And if the plotters continue to meet but never raise their weapons?"

Edward released the counter.

"Then we continue to observe them. Record the people involved, where the money goes, and where their weapons are carried."

"When they take action sufficient to warrant intervention, we must already have men in position. If they merely oppose the Crown, we have no grounds to arrest them."

Isabella studied the final arrangement.

"Visible defences, concealed reserves and evidence gathered. No civilians used as bait. That is the plan I approve."

Franco rose and pressed his hand to his breast.

"With Your Majesty's permission, I shall withdraw to prepare the troop movements."

The silver-mounted cane tapped steadily across the stone floor and faded down the passage. Only four people remained in the great hall.

Fredo sank into the nearest chair, loosened his collar and sorted the amended orders. Martinez eased her sword belt, while Isabella leant back and rubbed the place on her forehead where the rim of her hat had pressed.

She looked towards Edward.

"Once we are in Madrid, I shall need you healthy enough to carry out everything you have just proposed."

"I should like to make it home in time for dinner myself." Edward put down his cup and braced himself to stand, but needed Fredo's support. "For now, let me get back to my room."

title_vi: Chapter Thirty-Two: Red Ascendant
title_en: Chapter Thirty-Two: Red Ascendant
text_en:
A blizzard had swallowed western León and Galicia. After two great houses refused to aid the war, Queen Isabella of Castile ordered the railway services through their lands suspended. The last train departed, abandoning cities whose only remaining roads to the world were old stone routes buried beneath snow.

In Santiago de Compostela, the steam whistles had fallen silent. Snow choked the drains and rose knee-deep in the streets. Between shuttered shops and narrow lanes, the wind had the city to itself.

Don José climbed the slope of Rúa do Vilar, pulling his collar higher. He passed dark granite houses where Vestigium light had once spilled from merchants' windows onto the cobbles. Now every oak door was barred to preserve a little warmth within.

For weeks, famine and killing cold had gnawed at the ancient city. Beneath low roofs, gaunt figures huddled about dead hearths, winding torn sacks around their limbs. Hungry children cried behind closed windows, their voices mingling with the ragged breathing of those who could scarcely survive another night.

The severed railway had struck at Galicia's very artery of supply. Horse-drawn wagons laden with barley and dried turnips from the southern plains had scarcely cleared their depots before foundering in snowbound mountain passes. There, the storm and marauding thieves took what the drivers could not save.

Occasionally, convoys from Madrid still reached the town gates with flour and salted meat. The escorts called out households by name as they distributed rations. Some of those waiting cursed the great houses for withholding their stores; others cursed the Queen for stopping the trains.

José paused beside a child licking flour from his mother's fingers. He drew his collar close and continued towards the cathedral, thinking of his requests to Madrid for troops and provisions, still unanswered.

Crossing the snow-covered Praza do Obradoiro, Don José passed the main entrance to Santiago de Compostela Cathedral and found the side door leading to the Berenguela bell tower.

He climbed the rough spiral staircase of grey stone, step by deliberate step, while the wind battered the openings in the wall. The higher he rose, the more bitterly the cold entered his bones. The damp odour of ancient moss mingled with a faint, acrid trace of sulphur drifting from the chamber above.

He pressed against a heavy wooden door, found it unbolted, and entered an octagonal room open to the wind.

By a stone arch overlooking the snowbound city, a tall, slender man leaned against an iron railing. A copper brazier burned in the room's centre, its uncertain light striking fire from his shoulder-length red hair.

He gazed down upon the darkened Praza do Obradoiro without turning. A lock of hair stirred aside, revealing one angular cheek and black leather covering an empty eye socket.

"Your footsteps weigh more heavily than a hundred corpses out there, Admiral José."

The man did not turn. José removed his frost-stiffened gloves and bowed beside the brazier.

"Lord Rouge von Habsburg... Your Majesty."

He waited for the other man's coughing to subside.

"I have walked through streets without food or fuel. If my report speaks only of our defeats, it leaves far too much unsaid."

Rouge smiled faintly. The jutting lower jaw of the Habsburg line prevented his lips from closing properly, exposing pointed teeth to the firelight. Beneath the red hair and eyepatch, the deformity seemed more pronounced.

When he turned, the ruin beneath his dark cloak became plain. His left shoulder hung askew above a withered arm, wrapped in heavy cloth and held fast by an iron brace. The curse of the Mutant Two-Headed Eagle upon the dispossessed Habsburg bloodline had ravaged his body until every breath rattled and caught in his throat.

Yet his single grey eye, set in an ashen face, possessed a dreadful, unreadable intensity. He passed the long fingers of his sound right hand through the scarlet hair lying across his chest and spoke with unsettling ease.

"Defeats? Do you mean Edward Spencer's warship crushing the French fleet at San Sebastián, or the Portuguese fleet sinking to the bottom of La Concha Bay?"

José looked up.

"You have heard already?"

"The courier arrived before you."

Rouge tapped the railing.

"And he brought other news. I know Isabella has forced the great houses of Navarre and Valencia to submit. She has also placed the banner of the red cross in the hands of forty thousand English troops, forming four great armies of exiles."

A savage cough convulsed Rouge's narrow chest. He bent double, gripped his misshapen jaw, and spat phlegm laced with dark blood onto the freezing stone. When his broken breathing steadied, he forced the words out through clenched teeth.

"That Aragon girl has learnt the cruelties of power quickly enough. She strangles the railway arteries of León and Galicia, starves our subjects, then doles out flour by the ounce until the people's anger becomes a spear pointed at your heart."

The leather over his hollow eye socket twitched as he raised his face.

"So you are wavering."

Rouge studied José across the brazier.

"You fear the court will brand the Council of Knights traitors, do you not?"

José went down on one knee, his gloves held in both hands.

"I fear marching sixty thousand men into a war for which the people of these cities will pay first. Madrid has troops in position, while we have no grounds to mobilise."

He glanced at the scroll beside the fire.

"Our objections in Lisbon concerned troop strength and the right of command. Victory at La Concha does not turn those objections into an order to begin a civil war."

Rouge laughed hoarsely and limped towards the brazier. His crooked shadow climbed the tower wall, its withered arm almost lost beneath the folds of his cloak.

"More than twenty years ago... in that accursed year of 1690..."

His voice dwindled to a whisper, his remaining eye bright with grief and hatred in the glow of the embers.

"When Bourbon guns and Aragon treachery shattered the Habsburg throne, my father hesitated just as you do. He feared that his own hand might kindle the fire that would bring an empire down."

Rouge touched the edge of his patch with rough, bony fingertips. It was a keepsake of the blaze that had taken his eye when Madrid fell in 1701.

"That hesitation cost us the throne. It passed to an Aragon girl scarcely twelve or thirteen, raised up by the nobility as the emblem of a new order. The proud Habsburgs were driven into this barren country to scurry like filthy rats beneath a bell tower."

His lips curled, revealing the sharp teeth beneath his distorted chin. Twice he rapped the iron brace securing his left arm, then looked at José.

"I have still been fortunate, José..."

The words grated from his throat. Each contraction of his chest released breath thick with sulphur.

"The backlash of the Mutant Two-Headed Eagle should have claimed my last breath long ago. Yet while loyal servants such as you remember that I alone am Spain's lawful sovereign, the curse of Habsburg blood has not managed to bury me."

He fixed the admiral with his single eye.

"I am the lawful monarch, not that wretched Isabella, who stole the throne by deceit and then had the insolence to strip my ancestors' kingdom of its name. She replaced it with that foreign Castilian rubbish!"

José gave no answer to the insult. He took up a poker and pushed a fallen coal back into the brazier; Rouge waited until he stood before speaking again.

"But I am not mad enough to roast sixty thousand men in the trap she has laid at Madrid. Swords and slaughter are the crude devices of men driven into a corner, the last move left to men with no other choice."

From his black wool coat, Rouge drew a parchment scroll sealed with dark red wax and the ancient arms of the double-headed eagle. He threw it at Don José's feet.

"She wants a trap? Then I shall carry the battle into her streets. Use the gold and networks of the West Coast houses to scatter pamphlets across Madrid, dredging up Isabella's origins and the house in Nottingham where she was found. Leave the rest to the tongues of the people."

His solitary eye narrowed in calculation.

"The Church is where we must set our fire. France has just killed the Pope in Vienna. Carry word of the red-cross banners and exiled English armies to every parish, and ask the bishops whether the court still defends the faith or merely wears it as a standard. Once they contend for their pulpits, Madrid must answer its people before it dares answer us."

Beyond the arches of Berenguela, the blizzard rose in another furious gust.

José's weathered hand stopped halfway towards the parchment. The old admiral stared at the crooked back of the red-haired claimant.

"Nottingham?"

He kept the scroll unopened in his hand.

"What proof have you? Such a rumour will not stop at the palace gates."

Rouge did not turn.

"In this world, José..."

He rubbed the hollow beneath the leather patch.

"Not a breath, a trace of blood or a mortal sin escapes the sight of the Two-Headed Eagle. This eye I lost now sees into the darkest corners that Aragon girl has laboured to conceal."

Rouge turned halfway and limped forward. His twisted shadow spread over the old commander, who had lowered himself again to one knee upon the stone.

"When you have sown that filthy truth in the capital, tell every subject of this kingdom that their true sovereign has returned."

Rouge straightened his narrow chest, revealing the double-headed eagle upon the clothing beneath his cloak. His voice rang through the chamber with an authority his ruined body could scarcely contain.

"Remind them of that bitter year, 1690, when my father, King Charles II, closed his eyes for the last time. The world blindly believed he had died without a single child to inherit his throne, leaving it for the Bourbon and Aragon vultures to tear apart. Yet I, Rouge de Habsburgo, am his only blood, the last rightful heir of his sacred line!"

He thrust his sound arm towards the south-east, where Madrid endured the same pitiless storm.

"Let the fire of legitimacy consume that counterfeit throne. Take back everything that belongs to me, José. This very winter!"

José bowed, concealed the unopened scroll beneath his coat, and left the octagonal chamber. The tower bells reverberated down the spiral stair. Feeling his way along the stone wall, he reached the side door, where wind drove the snow of Praza do Obradoiro straight into his face.

A harsh, broken cry pierced the storm, high enough to make him search the grey clouds.

He stopped in the square and turned towards the sound. One hand gripped his collar as an enormous shadow crossed the cloudbank.

Above him, a great eagle circled through the blizzard. Its black feathers clung together in sodden patches, and two necks rose from a single body. Each head bore a pair of fiery red eyes fixed upon the square.

The monstrous bird made one wide circuit of Berenguela's summit, then folded its wings and plunged through the octagonal stone arch. It vanished into Rouge's chamber, bright with the brazier's red glow.

José remained beneath the tower for a while, pressing one hand against the scroll hidden in his coat. From the far end of the street came shouts for men to carry a wooden stretcher. He turned towards the voices and descended the snow-covered steps.

title_vi: Chapter Thirty-Three: Homecoming
title_en: Chapter Thirty-Three: Homecoming
text_en:
The northern train braked into Atocha Station, its iron wheels shrieking before the sound vanished beneath a cloud of white steam. Beyond the great arches of glass, Madrid still shone with lamplight, its daily life far removed from the western provinces besieged by snow and shortages of food.

Four passengers stepped onto the platform. Edward wore a woollen coat reaching past his knees, his hair stirred by the warm air rising from the train's heating pipes. Queen Isabella of Castile walked beside him in a grey-and-white military uniform, while Fredo and Martinez kept a respectful distance behind.

Beneath a brass lamp, Isabella turned to the two members of the Royal Guard.

"The Madrid watch takes charge from here. Once you've handed everything over, return to your quarters and rest. Both of you."

Fredo surveyed the people gathering beyond the station gates.

"I'll notify the guards along the entire route. If Your Majesty changes her destination, please see that the escort is informed."

Martinez waited for the station commander to approach before nodding. Isabella glanced towards Edward, who had changed hands with his bag to relieve his aching shoulder.

Before Martinez could turn away, Edward stepped towards her. He removed the gold chain bearing a lion's head from his chest and carefully returned it to the guard's open palm.

"Thank you, Martinez. Without this, I could never have brought you back. I doubt the four of us would have survived those hours beneath the water."

The chain still held the warmth of his skin. Martinez smiled as she fastened it about her neck, and the moment the metal lion touched her uniform, a pale golden light flared beneath its chin. The word Veinticinco emerged in clear strokes, glowed, then slowly sank back into the metal.

"You did not leave me behind. Until the troop assembly, Sir Edward."

She checked the clasp and saluted him. Fredo offered a salute of his own, and they departed after handing their duties to the Madrid soldiers.

Edward watched them pass through the gates, then turned to Isabella and lowered his voice.

"You planned to give them their leave at the same time, didn't you?"

"They even managed to inspect my entire route before agreeing to go, as you saw. Let them have an evening without anyone giving them orders."

Isabella took his bag, then gently tugged at his coat.

"You've been missing at sea for more than a month. Juliet and Remi must be furious with waiting by now. Could we stop somewhere on the way and buy them a few presents?"

"I'd rather go straight home. They've waited long enough."

"It's on our way, I promise. Ten minutes. There's something Remi will love, and after more than a month away, I doubt Juliet will let you forget it if you come back empty-handed."

When Edward held out his hand, Isabella returned the bag. He hesitated, asked how far the shop was, and followed when she pointed beyond the station's vaulted roof.

She led him out towards Calle Mayor. Beneath the heated glass canopies, melting snow trickled into copper gutters; shop bells sounded above the scent of cinnamon butter drifting from a bakery. Steam from the train still clung to Edward's coat.

Isabella stopped outside a shop selling books and mechanical toys. Beyond its window stood a model warship with three gun decks, its small rudder connected to a set of exposed gears.

"First, something for Remi. He's become quite besotted with those books about ships at school. Look, the gears inside can even turn the rudder."

Edward studied the vessel and smiled.

"He'll have every screw out of it within two days. Still, it's a handsome ship."

Before Isabella could reach for her purse, he placed his money on the counter.

"That ship, please, and a set of quills with a bottle of black ink. Wrap them securely, if you would."

Isabella tilted her head in amusement.

"How generous you've become, Sir Edward. You were rather more careful with your money in Marrakesh."

Edward accepted the parcel from the shopkeeper.

"My admiral's wages come from a certain someone. What use are they if I can't buy my son a present?"

Leaving the bright market behind, Isabella took Edward by the hand and led him towards a quiet row of fashionable tailors. A brass bell rang when she pushed open a pinewood door, and the scents of new linen and beeswax met them inside.

She ran her fingers across the glossy silks, then stopped before a thick, handwoven woollen shawl. Its muted blue-grey was the colour of morning mist spread across an English meadow.

Isabella lifted it to her cheek to feel its softness. A gentle, wistful smile touched her face.

"Juliet has never cared for elaborate things. This colour would suit her, and the wool is thick with a close weave. She could wear it while mending clothes or going into town."

Edward rubbed the edge between thumb and forefinger, testing its weight. He remembered Juliet in Marrakesh, tucking her hands beneath her arms whenever she sat sewing in the cold.

He took the shawl from Isabella and draped it over her shoulders to judge its length. His rough fingers carefully straightened each fold.

"You've always had a better eye for such things than I have, Bella."

At the light touch of his fingers, a blush rose in her pale cheeks. Isabella caught her lower lip between her teeth and gave him a smile of mock hauteur.

"Naturally. If Juliet dislikes it, you may take it to the stables and wrap it round the horses."

"Juliet will like it."

Edward laughed and asked the tailor to wrap the shawl. While the man worked, Edward noticed a velvet tray beside the glass counter, displaying little silver hairpins shaped like oak leaves and set with red agate that glimmered like embers. Without further explanation, he pointed to one and offered the shopkeeper a few more silver coins.

"And wrap this one as well, please."

Outside, they joined the people leaving the market, carrying bags of chestnut cakes still warm from the oven. Edward looked from the shops ahead to the road leading towards the houses.

Beneath a stone archway, he suddenly stopped.

"Bella, stand still a moment."

She turned to him in surprise.

"What is it?"

Edward brought out the small velvet box, opened it and lifted out the silver oak-leaf pin. Bending to meet Isabella's eyes, he lightly patted aside a stray lock at her temple and fastened the ornament into her thick hair. The street lamps had just come alight, and the red stone caught their glow like a tiny flame.

Isabella started, then touched the new ornament with uncertain fingers. Her eyes widened.

"This present... is it really for me?"

"The leaf reminded me of Sherwood. Surely the person who chose everyone else's gifts deserves one too?"

He stepped back to check that the pin was secure. Isabella touched the silver leaf and studied its reflection in a shop window; only when Edward lifted the cakes from her hands did she look round.

"Very well, Sir Edward... I'll forgive you for the moment. Now come along, before the cakes grow cold!"

Her clear laughter accompanied his unhurried footsteps through old streets, past windows filled with porcelain and polished jewellery beneath golden lamps.

As they passed a broad window reflecting the busy road, Isabella faltered for half a step.

Her reflection moved without her. It tilted its head, revealing a left iris burning deep crimson, and an unseen resonance turned Isabella's own left eye red. She blinked sharply, forcing it back to its familiar clear amber.

Testarossa's voice sounded directly in her mind, sweet and bright with mischief.

"Your Majesty, that oak leaf suits your hair exceedingly well... And do the two of you not look ten thousand times more natural together than you ever could beside those false noblemen at court? Say only that you wish to keep Sir Edward for yourself, and I would gladly overturn every earthly law to make it so..."

*Be silent, Testarossa!*

Isabella's brows drew together at her own angry thought. Testarossa only laughed, and in the reflection she raised a hand. A valve on a branch of heating pipe near the eaves sprang open, sending water from a cooling section of pipe down upon the place where Isabella stood.

"Look out!"

Edward pulled Isabella close against the wall and swept his cloak over both their heads. Water struck his back, streamed along his arm and splashed onto the stone pavement.

He lifted the edge of the cloak to examine her face.

"Did any get into your eyes?"

Isabella shook her head, still gripping his sleeve. Edward brushed a drop from her forehead before looking up at the valve, which had stopped spraying.

"Your coat is soaked," she said.

"Only the outside."

He let the cloak fall, rolled his shoulders experimentally and picked up the cakes. Isabella took the bag back, held it before her stomach and turned away before he could see her face.

In the neighbouring shop window, Testarossa was gone. Only the two of them remained in the reflection, sheltering beneath the eaves amid the warm streets of Madrid.

The road towards the villas grew quieter. Edward carried the presents and talked freely of Remi's childhood in Marrakesh, while Isabella listened a pace behind him.

"You know, Bella, when we first came to Marrakesh, Remi had never held a toy as finely made as this. I'd collect scraps of wood from beside the cowshed and carve him little boats with the knife we used for peeling vegetables. The first was so crooked you could scarcely tell what it was, but he treasured it all winter and even hid it in his straw sack when he went to sleep..."

Edward laughed heartily and turned towards his younger sister, his face bright with the memory.

"Just think how he'll jump when he sees a warship with three gun decks and a working rudder! And that woollen shawl for Juliet... She'll scold me for wasting money, then spend an hour before the mirror trying it on tonight."

Isabella said nothing. Her silence seemed stranger beside his cheer.

She slowed, smoothing a crease in the bag of cakes with her thumb. Edward asked whether Remi would dismantle the new ship that very evening, but she had to ask him to repeat the question.

"What's troubling you? Did that water hurt you after all?"

He stopped to look at her.

"No. I'm quite well."

Isabella moved the cakes to her other hand.

"Go on with your story. Did Remi's first boat actually float?"

"It leaned so far to one side that he made me spend the whole evening fixing it," Edward said.

Isabella laughed and followed him into the residential quarter. This time she watched him as he spoke, rather than lowering her eyes to the parcel.

They passed through ornate iron gates into a district much quieter than the streets outside. Sandstone villas stood behind their own gardens, where grass remained green above the buried heating pipes.

Edward had once lived in a great English manor, yet he stopped in disbelief before the three-storey sandstone villa. He looked up at its oak windows with metal frames, then turned to Isabella.

"Are you certain you haven't taken a wrong turn, Bella? This house... it's far too extravagant for a family of refugees like ours."

Isabella surveyed the house and adjusted the pin in her hair. When she faced him again, her teasing smile was gone.

"I promised to find the best home I could for your family. There is no mistake, Sir Edward."

Edward shifted the parcels to his left hand. Isabella waited beside him while he reached for the brass knocker.

Footsteps sounded almost as soon as he knocked.

"Who is it? Just a moment, please..."

The heavy oak door opened slowly. Juliet Spencer appeared in a plain linen dress, her hair gathered neatly at the nape of her neck, her hands hastily wiping themselves on her apron. Then she looked up, and her hands went still.

She stared at Edward, one hand still resting against the apron. He had scarcely said her name before she crossed the threshold and embraced him.

"You're home."

Her words were muffled against his shoulder, and she pulled back just enough to search his face.

"They told me the ship had sunk... Then there was no word for days."

Edward dropped the presents and wrapped his arms around his wife.

"I'm here. I'm home."

Juliet pressed her face into his shoulder once more. He stood quietly and let her hold him, one hand resting against her back, saying nothing about the parcels at their feet.

At last Juliet wiped her tears with the back of her hand. Looking up, she found Isabella on the doorstep with the still-warm cakes in her arms, silently leaving husband and wife their moment of reunion.

Flustered, Juliet stepped back and began to lower herself into a royal curtsy.

"Your... Your Majesty..."

"Please don't, Juliet."

Isabella smiled warmly and came forward to take her elbow before she could kneel. The queen's eyes held none of the pride or chill Juliet remembered from Marrakesh, only unguarded kindness.

"Here, I'm not the queen. I've only brought Edward home."

Juliet stared at this unexpected warmth, then smiled in return. She turned towards the house and called out loudly.

"Remi! Come quickly, darling! Father's home!"

title_vi: Chapter Thirty-Four: A Place at the Table
title_en: Chapter Thirty-Four: A Place at the Table
text_en:
Remi raced down the stairs, checked himself on the final step, then flung both arms around his father's waist. Edward bent to hold him close, while Juliet picked up the bag of presents at his feet and stepped aside to give them room.

"Father, you're really home."

Remi looked up without releasing his coat. Edward stroked his son's hair and answered softly.

"Yes."

Then he led them into the sitting room.

The sandstone kitchen of the villa glowed with lamplight and the warmth of the hearth. Herbs scented the air, mingling with beef broth that simmered gently over the fire.

Isabella paused in the doorway, watching Juliet turn the meat and draw the chopping board closer. She rolled up her sleeves and went to the unpeeled turnips.

"Let me help, Juliet. I can slice the cured meat and peel the turnips for you!"

Juliet glanced up, uncertain.

"Your... Your Majesty, these messy kitchen chores are best left to me."

"From now on, call me Isabella. There's no need for 'Your Majesty' here. I'm perfectly capable of helping!"

Before Juliet could object, Isabella took a round turnip and a small paring knife from her hands.

She pressed the blade too deeply and tried to turn the vegetable against it. The knife slipped, shearing off a great chunk that splashed into the water bucket, and she snatched her thumb back.

"Oh!"

Colour flooded Isabella's cheeks. Testarossa's reflection appeared upon the blade, and a bright voice, barely suppressing its laughter, sounded inside her head.

"How pitiful, my Queen. Do you mean to serve him a plate of mangled turnips, like ships shattered by cannon fire?"

*Be silent and help me at once!*

Isabella's furious command remained inside her thoughts.

"As Your Majesty commands."

Isabella closed her left eye as red began to bloom within it. Under Testarossa's control, her wrist changed angle, and the blade returned to work with a steadier, cleaner stroke.

One eye squeezed shut and the other wide with concentration, she chopped in a swift, even rhythm. Slices of turnip and cured meat fell into immaculate rows, each as thin as a printed page.

Juliet studied the turnips, then Isabella's closed eye.

"You can open both eyes, you know. They're only going into the stew. It doesn't matter if they're a little thicker."

Isabella stopped and waited for Testarossa to withdraw before opening her eye.

"I thought you wanted them thin."

"That's enough of those."

Juliet set the prepared meat aside.

"Would you carry the plates out for me?"

Before long, the long oak table in the sitting room was laden with hot dishes. Beef and turnip soup sent up fragrant steam beside crisp toasted bread spread generously with butter, and the chestnut cakes the two siblings had bought that afternoon filled the room with their sweet scent.

The four gathered in the glow of the stone fireplace. Edward sat opposite Juliet, with Remi beside him eagerly chewing buttered bread, while Isabella occupied the head of the table, looking more content than she ever did at court.

Edward placed a wooden box on the table and turned its ribbon towards Remi.

"I've brought you something. Wipe your hands first, or you'll get butter all over the sails."

Remi's eyes widened. He put his bread on his plate and hurried to his father's side, watching as Edward loosened the ribbon and lifted the lid.

Inside lay a model oak warship with three full gun decks.

"Oh! Father's warship!"

Remi lifted the little vessel with both hands and carefully turned the tiny wheel at its stern. His delight only grew as he discovered its other details.

"It's beautiful, Father! Look, the cannon barrels even slide in and out!"

"Aunt Isabella chose it for you."

Edward ruffled his son's hair and glanced towards his younger sister. Remi turned at once and gave her a very proper bow.

"Thank you, Aunt Isabella! I'll take good care of it!"

"What a good boy."

Isabella smiled and gently smoothed his tousled hair.

Edward placed the second box before Juliet. She opened it, touched the wool within, then looked at her husband.

"How much did this cost?"

"I could afford it."

Edward draped the shawl over her shoulders, then tugged one end down when he saw it hung unevenly.

"Try moving your arms. See whether it gets in the way."

Juliet moved her hands to and fro, then smoothed the weave beneath her fingers.

"It really is warm. But don't spend so much next time."

"I chose it," Isabella said. "If you don't like it, you may blame me."

Juliet looked at her and laughed. She kept the shawl around her shoulders and cleared away the empty box to make room for the cakes.

Supper went on amid easy conversation and laughter. Remi eagerly recounted his lessons in history and mathematics at his new school, while Edward entertained them with tales of Fredo and Martinez quarrelling so absurdly on campaign that no one had known whether to laugh or despair.

Juliet listened as she refilled their cups with hot tea. Isabella lingered over a chestnut cake, quietly watching the happiness on her older brother's face.

Remi tried the ship's wheel again and accidentally knocked its bow against a plate. Juliet moved the plate aside, and Edward steadied the stern while their son showed Isabella how the little gears worked.

At nine o'clock, the cathedral's bronze bells tolled through the night, their sombre notes mingling with the wind whistling through the gaps in the stonework.

Isabella rose and settled her pale grey and white cloak about her shoulders. Fastening the silver castle clasp at her throat, she turned towards the family still gathered at the table.

"It's late. I must return to the palace. Sleep well, all of you."

Edward sprang up and reached for the woollen coat hanging on its wooden stand.

"I'll walk you as far as the palace gates. The streets aren't safe at this hour."

Juliet came beside him and gently nudged his shoulder.

"Please let Edward escort you, Your Majesty. It's terribly cold and dark outside. I'll feel much easier knowing he's with you."

Isabella smiled and shook her head. For a moment she regarded her brother, seeing the weariness in his face and the happiness beneath it, before answering softly.

"There's no need, Juliet. He's only just come home, and I won't steal another half-hour from you. The Royal Guard patrols this road. I can make my own way back."

She bent to stroke Remi's hair, though he barely loosened his embrace of the wooden ship. With a final nod to Edward and Juliet, she crossed the threshold, and the heavy oak door closed behind her, leaving the family's laughter and warmth on one side and the bitter night on the other.

Isabella walked slowly along the smooth paving stones. Beyond a bend in the row of villas, where the streetlamps could no longer reach her, the Queen stopped.

She looked down at a little puddle of thawed water beneath a heating pipe. Its surface lay still as a mirror, reflecting a pale crescent moon.

"Come out, Testarossa."

The puddle rippled. From the deepest shadow beside the stone wall came the measured sound of heels upon the pavement, drawing closer until a woman stepped into the faint light.

She might have been Isabella's twin, so closely did their faces resemble one another. Yet Testarossa's long hair blazed red against the winter darkness, her right eye burned a deep crimson, and her left remained clear amber.

Isabella's own left eye had turned red, as though the colours had exchanged places between them. Around Testarossa's neck swung the golden lion-headed pendant of the Royal Guard, bearing a single unmistakable mark: Uno.

Testarossa tilted her head, a strange, beguiling smile upon her face.

"Did that lovely family supper satisfy my Queen?"

Isabella sat upon a stone step, removed her gloves, and examined the dried trace of turnip on one fingertip.

"I told Juliet I was good at it."

Testarossa stood before her, looking down at that hand, but Isabella raised her head before she could reply.

"Don't laugh. And I know you were behind that business with the heating pipe."

"He caught you very quickly."

"And he'd only just got out of his sickbed."

Isabella pulled her glove back on.

"You mustn't do that again."

Testarossa's smile softened. She came to sit beside Isabella and ran slender fingers through the Queen's disordered hair, soothing her with a voice as gentle as the night breeze.

"I saw that too. But a little embarrassment suits you a thousand times better than that icy expression you wear when giving orders at court, my Queen."

Isabella rose, brushed down her skirts, and straightened the silver oak-leaf hairpin Edward had given her. Testarossa accompanied her towards the palace, close enough that their shoulders occasionally touched on the narrow path.

In the royal apartments, steam rose from a vast marble bath and softened the warm candlelight. They bathed together in water scented with herbal oils, Testarossa seated behind Isabella and passing a soft sponge gently over her bare back, with the tenderness of an elder sister caring for a younger one.

Once they had dried themselves and changed into soft silk nightclothes, Testarossa led Isabella to the ebony dressing table. She took up an ivory comb and patiently freed the damp strands around the Queen's temples, drawing it through her hair until it fell smooth across her shoulders.

Isabella closed her eyes and leaned her head lightly against Testarossa's chest, content to be cared for.

At last Isabella climbed into the great feather bed and curled beneath the thick, warm covers. Testarossa lay beside her and pulled the quilt over her slender shoulders.

By the last flicker of the candle, Testarossa rested her head upon one arm and regarded Isabella with her red eye.

"And what of your plans, Your Majesty? The West Bank is stirring towards rebellion, the Church waits for an opening to tear at us, and you must decide how to play the board."

Isabella drew her pillow beneath her cheek.

"Bring me the reports in the morning. Tonight I don't want to hear another noble family's name."

She closed her eyes. After a little while, she spoke once more.

"I want another supper like that. Just to come, eat with them, and go home."

Testarossa looked towards the silver oak-leaf hairpin, its red agate glinting faintly on the bedside table.

"I shall remember, Isabella."

Isabella made no answer. Her hand relaxed upon the edge of the quilt, and Testarossa reached out to lower the candle flame until the room darkened.

title_vi: Chapter Thirty-Five: The Reward for Surviving
title_en: Chapter Thirty-Five: The Reward for Surviving
text_en:
On the first morning after Edward's return to Madrid, he sat waiting for Remi to finish breakfast. Streetlamps still shone through the curtains. The boy had set the satchel Isabella had given him beside his chair, and his model ship rested beside his bowl.

Juliet straightened the collar of her son's white linen shirt. She wore a simple ash-grey dress and the mist-blue sheep's-wool scarf Edward had given her, its soft folds resting upon her slender shoulders.

"Pay attention to your lessons today, won't you?" she reminded him, her voice gentle but firm.

"Yes, Mother! I'll only keep it in my desk to look at!"

Remi beamed, hurried towards the door and caught his father's hand. Edward smiled and bent to smooth his hair. In his well-cut dark woollen cloak, he looked nothing like the stern commander his soldiers knew on the battlefield.

The three stepped into the clear, dry morning air of central Madrid. Holding Remi between them, Edward and Juliet followed the broad avenue towards the Royal Academy, its imposing stone buildings rising beyond a row of nearly bare maples.

Children of noble families and officers were playing near the gates. When Marco Stones's son waved from the steps, Remi turned and threw his arms around his parents' waists.

"Mother, Father, I'm going to class now!"

"Study hard, my little sailor."

Edward winked and patted his back. Juliet watched Remi disappear through the heavy wooden doors, then released a peaceful sigh and adjusted her scarf.

Edward slipped an arm around her waist and drew her close enough to make her blush. They wandered beneath the shaded glass arcades of the old quarter, with neither carriage nor guards to accompany them. For once, the busy capital offered a moment that belonged to them alone.

"Here we needn't worry about the stove going out in the night," Juliet said as they passed a steam vent. "I still woke up to check during those first few days."

Edward squeezed her hand.

"Are you sleeping better now?"

"Better than before. Except when I was waiting for news of you."

She looked at him and drew him onwards.

"There are so many things I want to do here. First I need to learn my way about."

They turned onto a quiet path beside an artificial canal. Its warm water never froze, and yellowing trees trembled in the reflection.

Juliet pressed close to his side, her fingers entwined with his. Their footsteps sounded upon the granite paving, while the faint scent of herbs and flowers drifted from upper windows. She looked towards the villas with their red sandstone roofs and smiled.

"I still feel as though I'm dreaming, Edward. In Marrakesh, whenever it turned cold, I only wished the fire would last through the night. Now I can step into the street and feel warm steam rising around my feet."

Edward slowed to match her pace and watched the water passing beneath the trees.

"While I was away, how did Isabella treat you and Remi? She didn't make things difficult for you, did she?"

Juliet adjusted the edge of her scarf.

"Isabella was very thoughtful about the house and Remi's schooling. But when we first arrived, I often had to guess whether she wanted me to stay and talk."

"And last night?"

"Last night she ruined half my turnip."

Juliet laughed, then glanced at their joined hands.

"But she stood there and let me show her how to do it. Talking to her felt easier after that."

Edward remembered Isabella at the chopping board, trying to look confident even after Juliet had seen the turnip fly into the bucket. He laughed and asked what other difficulties Juliet had faced during their first days in the new house.

Still holding her hand, he looked down the street.

"Tomorrow I'll have someone bring a few pots of yellow chrysanthemums for the porch. Remi wants a bed of mint behind the house, too. He says he'll make tea for you himself."

"All Remi talks about lately is the sea," Juliet said with a relieved little sigh.

"Yesterday, while he was studying with Marco's son, he boasted that he'd become a captain and sail a ship far bigger than his father's."

Edward laughed, though his fingers tightened at the thought of the model in Remi's satchel.

"Let him study first. There's plenty to learn before going to sea. And being aboard a ship doesn't mean he must fire a cannon like his father."

Juliet laughed at his confident paternal pride.

The thought of North Africa reminded Edward of the comrade who had survived its battles alongside him.

"Speaking of friends, how are you getting on with Lady Millennia? Have you become close?"

Juliet's face lit up, her eyes narrowing into delighted crescents.

"Millennia has been wonderful. At first I didn't know where to buy anything, so she walked me through the streets and showed me the bakeries and the shops selling embroidery thread. She even brought me books on dressmaking."

Juliet studied the dresses in a shop window.

"She's taught me to choose fabrics as well. Sometimes I feel so clumsy beside her that I don't know what to do with my hands."

"Would you like to make yourself a new dress?"

"Yes. One I've chosen myself."

She glanced at him.

"And I mean to walk more instead of sitting with my needlework all day. Now you're home, you can come with me."

Edward nodded. Juliet led him to the window and pointed out a style of sleeve she had admired since the previous week.

A thin autumn breeze lifted a few strands of hair at her temples. Juliet smoothed the scarf at her throat and gazed past the rooftops, her expression turning thoughtful.

"Edward... I don't need a mansion or costly silks. I only want our days to be as ordinary as this. You come home to a hot supper when work is done, and Remi comes back from school with his father here to help him study."

She looked up at him.

"Would a life like that be possible?"

Edward stopped beneath a stone arch thick with green ivy. Turning towards her, he held her thin cheeks between his rough hands. When the breeze lifted the edge of her scarf, he tucked it back into place.

"I'll be home for supper tonight. I won't promise what I can't know about the days after that. But if I have to leave, I'll tell you."

Juliet held his wrists.

"And when you are home, be here with me. Don't make me call twice before you listen."

"I won't."

He kissed her forehead and looked into her face.

"You're beautiful, Juliet."

She laughed, pushing gently against his chest.

"We're having a serious conversation."

"So am I."

He could not promise her every day to come, but for now he could take her home. Hand in hand, they crossed the cobbled streets, leaving the carriage bells and shopkeepers' calls behind.

The oak door closed. Juliet had barely reached for her scarf when Edward drew her into his arms, and they kissed in the entrance hall. Their shopping bag slipped to the floor, unnoticed by either of them.

"It's still daylight, Edward."

Juliet rested her forehead against his shoulder, though her hands kept hold of his coat.

"I know. I kept watching the clock all the way back."

He loosened his embrace enough to see her face.

"I missed you more than I expected."

Juliet stepped away, then led him upstairs by the hand. At the bedroom door she paused to fold the blue-grey scarf he had chosen for her and set it over a chair.

"Wait a moment, my dear Admiral."

She took a ribbon from her dressing table and motioned for him to sit.

"And this time, you must do as I say."

Edward let her blindfold him. He heard the wardrobe open, hangers clattering, and Juliet muttering when a fastening caught around her finger.

When she removed the ribbon, she was standing beside the bed in a cream satin nightdress. She adjusted the lace at her waist, then laughed when Edward remained silent too long.

"Millennia helped me choose it. I meant to keep it hidden until you came home. If you don't like it, my old woollen nightdress is still in the wardrobe."

"I like it."

Edward held out his hand for hers.

"But what I like most is seeing you stand there smiling at me."

Juliet sat beside him, her smile softening when she touched the calluses on the hands that had held a ship's wheel at La Concha.

"Some nights I thought a messenger would reach our door before you," she said. "And the next morning I still had to take Remi to school, buy groceries and answer when he asked where his father was."

Edward held her hand. He remembered the sound of splintering wood and cold water, and knew that nothing he said could make those nights easier. Instead he drew her close.

"I'm sorry I left you waiting in fear."

He rested his forehead against hers.

"Next time, if I can send even one line, I'll send it before you're left to guess."

Juliet answered with a kiss. The words they had carried through their month apart were finally given somewhere to rest. Outside, a delivery cart rattled over the stones, then the sounds of the street faded behind the curtains.

After a while, Juliet took his face between her hands, mischief returning to her eyes.

"One more question, and you must answer at once. No thinking too long."

Edward tilted his head, recognising the playfulness he had missed since Nottingham.

"I've commanded an entire fleet, Juliet. Surely one question from you can't sink me."

"Then which of us is prettier, Isabella or me?"

He went still. Juliet tried to look stern, but her mouth was already curving into a smile.

"You've chosen quite a moment to ask."

Edward regarded her as though plotting a course through hidden reefs.

"You are. I intend to live long enough to take Remi to school tomorrow."

Juliet burst out laughing and tapped his shoulder with a pillow.

"I'll remember that, Admiral Spencer."

He caught the pillow and let her lean against him. They lay together until the last light of noon slipped beneath the curtains. The blue-grey scarf remained undisturbed upon its chair.

When the clock downstairs struck the afternoon hour, Juliet sat up first. Edward hunted for his shirt among the clothes at the foot of the bed, studied the first button, then looked at his still-laughing wife.

"I once thought I'd never come home," he said, fumbling with the second button. "And now all I want to know is what you're cooking this afternoon."

"Beef and mushroom stew, if you'll come downstairs and help."

Juliet corrected his crooked button.

"And come now, before Remi reaches the door."

Knock! Knock! Knock!

Urgent knocks sounded from the entrance hall, interrupting their lazy afternoon. Remi's clear voice rang through the oak door.

"Mother! Father! I'm home from school! Please let me in!"

Juliet pushed herself upright and looked from Edward to the bedroom door. He reached among the clothes on the floor and pulled up her dress by mistake, forcing her to snatch it back.

"Your shirt's over there. Hurry and open the door for him."

"Coming, Remi!"

Edward fastened another button into the wrong hole. Juliet put it right, hiding her laughter as she gathered the bedsheet for washing.

He hurried downstairs, smoothing his rumpled shirt and running a hand through his wild hair, then pulled back the bolt.

Click!

Remi came trotting through the half-open door, hugging his leather satchel and wooden ship. He stopped just inside and gazed around with wide eyes.

The sitting room was dark, for no one had lit the lamps. He set down his satchel, glanced towards the unlit kitchen stove and searched for his mother.

Then he looked up at Edward, who stood against the door with sweat running from his forehead into his partly buttoned collar. His chest still rose and fell as though he had run ten miles.

"Father... why is the house so dark?"

Remi tilted his head and let fly a volley of questions.

"The stove isn't lit either... Where's Mother? Why are you all sweaty? Were you fighting someone in the house?"

Edward followed his gaze towards the kitchen.

"We haven't managed to cook yet. Are you hungry?"

"Yes, Father."

Just then Remi saw Juliet carrying out the washing basin.

"Mother, are you changing the bedsheet again?"

"Yes, I'm taking it to be washed."

Juliet put down the basin and dried her hands on a towel.

"How was school?"

Remi began describing his ship's steering mechanism, but soon asked how long supper would take. Edward interrupted with a suggestion.

"Shall we go out for beef and mushroom stew and cakes tonight?"

"Really? We can eat at a restaurant?!"

Remi turned towards Juliet to make sure. She nodded, and he immediately lifted his satchel and asked whether he could bring his ship.

Edward let out a long breath, as relieved as if he had survived a desperate battle, and exchanged a discreet glance with Juliet. Standing in the corner, she looked equally relieved and gave him an embarrassed smile.

"Go upstairs and change into clean clothes, son. Put your wooden ship in the display cabinet, and we'll leave shortly."

Edward lifted Remi briefly, then set him down and patted his shoulder.

"Yes, Father!"

Remi nodded eagerly, clutched his satchel and ran up the wooden staircase.

Once he had gone to put away his things, Juliet took the basin to the washing corner and returned to the bathroom. Edward followed and knocked twice.

"May I come in?"

Juliet glanced at his disordered shirt and moved aside.

"Yes, but be quick. Remi is waiting for supper."

Edward closed and bolted the door.

"I remember."

He sat beside her and used a sponge to wash her back. Juliet tilted her head to keep her hair clear, occasionally warning him away from a scratch on her skin.

"What are you still laughing at?" she asked, turning.

"Nothing."

Juliet scooped water onto his shoulder. Edward failed to dodge and laughed, then offered her a towel before she could splash him again.

A few minutes later she finished bathing and dressed in an elegant dark-blue velvet gown, pinning her wet hair into a neat bun. She opened the wooden door and stepped into the corridor, only to stop in surprise.

Remi stood directly outside with his woollen beret in his hands. His round eyes moved from his mother to the mist of steam behind her.

"Mother? Why were you and Father bathing in the same room?"

Juliet kept the bathroom door shut behind her.

"Father helped wash my back. Have you got your coat?"

"Yes, Mother. But Father's taking ages."

A water ladle clattered to the floor inside, and Edward called out.

"I'll be ready in a moment!"

Juliet bent to straighten Remi's crooked beret.

"Come and wait by the door with me. This time Father can hurry after us."

By the time Edward had dressed, night had fallen over Madrid. The bustle of the working day gave way to lively evening streets. Glass-enclosed acetylene lamps cast a warm golden glow along the old thoroughfares.

The three walked along the cobbles towards the central square. Edward held Remi's hand as the boy skipped beside him, and clasped Juliet's with his other hand. He looked like any contented father out with his family.

They stopped at a small restaurant beneath a Gothic stone arch. A wooden sign bore the carving of a roasted turnip, and the savoury scent of herb-stewed meat drifted into the street.

Inside, Edward spotted Fredo and Martinez at a corner table. Martinez's black hair was still pinned high, and she put down her spoon when she saw them.

"Having supper alone together, are you?" Edward asked.

Fredo looked at the empty chair beside him, then at Martinez.

"It took me some time to persuade her to come. Please don't turn this into an interrogation."

"Because you took so long choosing the restaurant," Martinez said.

She rose and greeted Juliet.

"Please sit down. The next table is free."

Edward smiled and introduced his family.

"This is my wife, Juliet, and our son, Remi. These are Fredo and Martinez. Without them, I doubt I'd be sitting down to supper with you tonight."

Fredo drew out a chair for Juliet, while Martinez asked the proprietor to join their tables. When Remi asked whether her sword was as long as the table, Fredo lowered his cup and waited for her answer.

"It doesn't need to be that long in here."

Martinez pointed to the model ship Remi had brought out.

"Show me its steering wheel first."

Juliet sat beside Edward, listening to Remi explain the gears. Beneath the table, she sought her husband's hand, and he intertwined his fingers with hers. Then he leaned closer to hear the rest of their son's story.

title_vi: Chapter Thirty-Six: The Exceptional
title_en: Chapter Thirty-Six: The Exceptional
text_en:
Marco Stones had spent weeks on the Fes front since leaving Tangier-Ceuta with the Second Corps. The military train flying red-cross banners had left Tangier-Ceuta before dawn, but this was no first journey to Fes. He was returning from the northern junction, where he had taken command of a newly assigned British corps under an emergency royal decree issued after La Concha.

Four British corps, each roughly eleven thousand strong, had been assigned to Edward, Marco, Romeo and Victoria. Marco's men now filled the carriages winding through North Africa's snow-covered hills, while Edward Spencer still lay unconscious in San Sebastián.

Marco sat beside the command carriage window, elbow resting on its wooden frame, watching the soldiers through the opening between the two carriages. Their laughter sometimes drowned out the iron wheels on the rails.

A fair-haired lad scarcely twenty showed his comrades the small portrait of his fiancée he kept hidden inside his coat. Two others fought over a piece of salted meat, swearing in thick Midlands accents until a nearby sergeant threw a glove at both their heads.

None looked like men travelling to face a Western Roman army many times their size.

Marco watched them, then lowered his eyes to his cold tea. His reflection trembled on the dark surface, older than the man he remembered from his years in northern France.

Ten years earlier, troopships bound for Rennes and Caen had been just as noisy. The young men around him had argued over drink, football, women and the cold meat served in barracks, as though the French army were an inconvenient rainstorm rather than a force capable of tearing a platoon apart in minutes.

Many had never returned.

Marco cupped the tea between his hands. Too many names remained with him. That was what frightened him.

The compartment door opened. The major in charge of supplies looked in, melting snow darkening his shoulders.

"Colonel, we're about two hours from Fes. The train behind reports a coal wagon with a seized axle at Sidi Kacem, but the ammunition and provisions have passed through."

"Leave the wagon for repairs. Don't hold the whole train over one axle." Marco glanced at his papers. "Move half the reserve coal to the other two locomotives. Restore their allocations at Fes."

The major glanced into the adjoining carriage.

"They don't seem afraid."

"They are. They just don't want the next man to see it."

Marco asked how old the men were and how many veterans served in the new companies. He ordered the recruits distributed among platoons with combat experience.

"Don't make a whole company learn to endure shellfire in a single afternoon."

The major left. Marco faced the window again, but the young faces next door had lost their easy charm.

He had once known the French army's rhythm well enough to recognise its artillery habits and predict how a general would respond to a severed supply line. The Western Romans were different: vast numbers, heavy armour, siege engines and engineers using incendiary weapons. He had read every report from Algiers but had never fired upon a Roman formation himself.

He would not hide the truth from himself, nor parade his fears before his soldiers.

He reopened his map. The Taza-Fes road was inked red; the northern Melilla-Nador route was ringed three times in blue pencil.

If the Romans forced the Taza corridor, Fes would take the main blow. If they swept north and descended on Nador, they might cut the Mediterranean supply ports off entirely. If Castilian commanders panicked and massed their troops at Fes, one Roman force could pin them there while the rest broke through weaker positions.

Marco tapped the three axes of advance. He remembered Edward's warning to consider the roads beyond the walls.

The train carried eleven thousand British soldiers towards the fortifications awaiting them at Fes.

Two hours later, the city emerged in its valley, a mass of reddish-brown stone being swallowed by snow from every side.

The train slowed at the military station west of Fes el-Jdid. Hundreds of local soldiers, labourers and men of the Second Corps, stationed here since the front first formed, lined the platforms. The man heading the reception party wore a heavy woollen cloak over his breastplate, not court finery.

Hassan al-Qadiri, Governor of Fes, was in his fifties, with a close-trimmed grey beard and sleepless eyes. He approached as Marco stepped off the last iron stair.

"Colonel Stones."

"Governor."

They shook hands without further ceremony. Hassan looked along the red-cross banners hanging from the troop carriages and breathed out, as if a weight had lifted.

"Your men have come just in time. Taza reports two more Roman columns assembling to the east. We don't know whether they're feinting or preparing to strike."

"We'll find out." Marco passed his gloves to an officer. "First unload the men, feed them something hot, inspect their feet and weapons. I want them to have at least six hours' sleep before anyone drags them off to dig trenches."

Hassan nodded.

"I've prepared barracks to the south."

He hesitated.

"Two others are waiting at the Governor's residence."

Marco stared.

"Who?"

Hassan smiled.

"Better see for yourself."

A closed carriage took Marco through Fes el-Jdid. The city still went about its business, but war had entered every street: sandbags at the gates, provision wagons moving without pause, carpenters making stretchers beneath awnings, children pulled aside whenever the artillery passed.

He watched until the carriage stopped at the residence. He had barely entered the operations room when a familiar voice called from within.

"Finally decided to arrive? I wagered Victoria you'd stop halfway to inspect every bolt on the train."

Marco froze.

Romeo Harkon perched on the map table, one leg swinging, holding a half-eaten red apple. He wore the crimson uniform of the British Legion in Exile as casually as a hunting coat, two collar buttons undone, his gloves tucked through his belt.

By the window, Victoria Valdes turned from a wall map. Her blonde hair was pinned at the nape, her officer's coat buttoned to the throat. She held three folders crowded with tiny notes in blue ink.

Marco looked between them.

"What the hell is this?"

Romeo finished his bite.

"A touching reunion."

Victoria ignored him.

"Supplementary orders from the General Staff. Before I return to Marrakesh and Romeo to Tangier-Ceuta, the three of us must agree on North Africa's defences. Fes, Taza and Melilla-Nador cannot be fought as three separate wars."

Marco put his hat on the table.

"Who thought of that?"

"Franco Valdes."

"I should have known."

Romeo laughed and jumped down.

"I like it. All those years at the same academy, fighting for the same country, and this is the first time we've sat as equals without a professor behind us shouting about a laboratory fire."

Victoria finally glanced at him.

"You started the fire."

"But Marco opened the gas valve."

Marco sat.

"I thought that business died in London."

"Nothing dies while three people remember it." Romeo set down his apple and pulled the map towards him, turning serious. "Not even bad ideas."

Those last words silenced them for several seconds. Nobody mentioned England.

Victoria broke the silence, placing wooden counters on Fes, Tangier-Ceuta and Marrakesh.

"Our assignments remain unchanged. Marco holds Fes with the Second Corps, Tercio de la Balanza, here since the beginning. The remaining five reinforcing Tercios are gathering along the Fes-Taza corridor, while his new British corps serves as the mobile force and reserve."

She touched the other two markers.

"Romeo holds Tangier-Ceuta with Tercio III del Filo and the Sultan's forces. I return to Marrakesh with Tercio XI del Acero, responsible for the reserves, railway, supply workshops and my British corps."

She added a smaller marker at Taza.

"If Taza falls, the consequences won't end there. Nor will a siege of Fes affect Fes alone. And if Melilla-Nador is cut, you'll both learn to eat your reports instead of bread."

Romeo pulled up his chair.

"If the Nador route is lost, how long can Fes feed itself?"

"Four months at peacetime consumption, two and a half while fighting and taking in refugees from Taza." Victoria laid a tally on the map. "Give me six weeks and railway priority, and I'll raise that to nine months. Divert some stone wagons to grain, and it could reach eleven."

Marco considered the unfinished defences. Fes's walls had to close before deeper snow arrived, but starving men could not defend a city. Victoria held her pen above the railway from Marrakesh, awaiting his choice.

"Taza must withstand two weeks of heavy bombardment. Steel takes priority for the guns; use local materials for the remaining walls," Marco said. "Take the other wagons, but leave enough stone for the principal fortifications."

Victoria revised the wagon figures. Romeo muttered that he'd never seen bread bargained over so fiercely.

Marco asked whether he planned anything besides raids on enemy camps. Romeo placed three black markers on roads east of Taza.

"I mean to make them arrive late and hungry. Burn a kitchen at the right moment and you may do more good than by killing a general."

"We talk of fortresses, artillery and food, but Romans don't grow out of the sand. Half a million men need bread, water, powder, horses, wagons and couriers. I don't have to kill half a million; only make enough arrive at Taza late, hungry and uncertain where their neighbouring units are."

Marco leaned over the map. Romeo spread the black markers with his fingertips.

"Independent mobile detachments, thirty to fifty men each. No guns or heavy wagons. Light horses, rifled carbines, short knives, climbing ropes, charges to destroy bridges and five days' dry rations."

"Guerrilla warfare?" Hassan asked from the far end.

"No. Guerrillas fight on their own land and prolong the war. I want to hunt the enemy's nervous system: signal posts, staff officers, couriers, powder stores, field kitchens, little bridges and wheelwrights. Cut one thing every night, vanish before the pursuit arrives each morning."

Marco studied the counters.

"What if they strengthen the escorts?"

"All the better. Every hundred soldiers guarding a flour wagon is a hundred not standing before Taza."

Victoria pointed to a detachment beyond Taza.

"And if they chase glory until light cavalry closes around them?"

"They withdraw before the ring closes. I'll replace any commander who values an exploit above his route home."

Marco held Romeo's gaze until he nodded his assurance, then noted the operational limit beside the map. Romeo's approach was hazardous, but it answered Marco's deepest fear: Rome might crush Taza through numbers, yet every extra soldier lengthened the army's supply line.

Marco marked the limits more firmly.

"No team goes beyond three days' march. No glory hunting, and everyone has a second way out."

Romeo nodded at the ink. Victoria unfolded three inventories, interrupting his next joke.

"My turn. Three sets of figures, each for a different audience."

Marco read them and understood before the others. Victoria indicated each sheet.

"The first gives true strength and supplies to those running the system. The second goes to administrators, with only what they need to know. The third is permitted to fall into enemy hands."

She arranged depot tokens beneath workshops, monasteries, merchants' warehouses and stone cellars.

"Fes won't have a single storehouse the enemy can destroy. Each cluster knows only the station above it and the two beside it."

Marco braced his hands on the table.

"Dispersal slows distribution."

"So I've standardised the rations." Victoria produced a wooden token cut with four grooves. "One package feeds a platoon for a day. No weighing at the front, no handwritten issue record each time. The depot takes a token, issues a package and sends the wagon on its way."

Hassan examined it.

"If it's stolen?"

"The branded mark on the back changes daily."

Romeo whistled.

"You've made bread into ammunition."

"In war, bread is ammunition."

Victoria pointed to the northern road towards Nador.

"Psychological warfare begins here too. If Rome believes Fes has only three months of food, it'll choose a siege over an assault. If Nador looks weak, it may send troops north. Wagons running by day, complaints from merchants, sacks deliberately exposed at stations: such trifles can direct the enemy's gaze."

Marco regarded her.

"You want to feed them false intelligence."

"I want to feed them what they're willing to swallow."

Romeo reclined in his chair.

"I'm starting to find you more frightening than Marco."

Victoria did not react.

"Two false depots along the Taza route, a sham artillery repair station near Guercif, and empty wagon trains under heavy escort. Enemy scouts will report precisely what we want them to see."

Marco considered this, then circled an area west of Taza.

"Put the false depots here. Near enough to seem valuable, far enough from homes that their destruction won't kill anyone."

Victoria nodded.

"Exactly."

Romeo pointed north.

"And Melilla-Nador?"

At that question, the mood in the room changed.

Hassan brought another map. The narrow northern coast was broken by mountains, passes and small ports. Nador was the junction for moving cargo inland; Melilla guarded a vital sea entrance where any landing could open a dangerous breach.

Marco studied it.

"We can't wall off the whole coast."

"Or defend every landing beach," Romeo said.

Victoria placed three coins at the road junctions.

"Then don't hold the coast. Hold the roads."

Marco looked up.

"They can land in many places, but large forces still need a few corridors to bring their guns and supplies inland. Hold the bridges, passes, coal depots and stations. If necessary, let them occupy a few coastal villages and starve there."

Romeo put his finger on Nador.

"I'll station a rapid-response force here. When coastal scouts report a landing, we won't rush the beach. We'll wait until the enemy unloads, then strike its transport columns."

Marco turned to Hassan.

"Have the coastal villages prepared evacuation plans?"

"On paper."

"So they haven't."

Hassan sighed.

"No drills yet."

Marco drew a line south from Melilla to Nador.

"Hold the drills within the next two weeks. Victoria, calculate temporary shelters and rations. Romeo, you need coastal scouts, not just raiders."

Romeo nodded.

"I'll use local fishermen. They recognise ships at a distance better than my men."

"Pay them," Victoria said. "Don't seize their services for nothing, then wonder why no one spots a ship on the third day."

Romeo grinned.

"Yes, madam, housekeeper of the war."

Victoria looked up.

"I'll remember that when I set your rations."

Marco burst out laughing. Hassan finally smiled, the first time since the train arrived.

The meeting continued through lunch.

Servants brought lunch, but none of the officers left the maps. They broke bread one-handed while soup cooled beside the markers, dismantling and rebuilding entire stretches of the defence like a machine.

Marco wanted Taza defended in three successive lines, each lost position forcing the Romans to redeploy their guns. Victoria opposed storing too much food in an outpost that might become enemy spoils. Romeo disputed both, arguing that a fortress too strong would make the enemy cautious, whereas one that seemed just tempting enough might lure them down the chosen corridor.

"You want Taza weakened?" Marco asked.

"I want it to look weaker than it is." Romeo tapped a marker with his spoon. "Quite different."

Victoria set down her bowl.

"If Taza is bait, set the limits first. How many men, for how many days, and when do they withdraw?"

Marco did not answer at once. It was the hardest question on the table.

A fortress could be a wooden counter. Ten thousand people inside it could not.

"No holding to the last man just to make a report look good," he said. "Taza must delay the enemy, force them to expose their artillery, spend ammunition and enter the corridor. Once those three aims are met, the garrison falls back towards Fes in stages."

Romeo nodded.

"I'll harass their pursuit to cover the withdrawal."

Victoria pressed on.

"Who can order Taza abandoned if communications with Fes fail?"

Marco looked at her.

"The commander on the spot."

"Put that in writing."

"Naturally."

"Not naturally." Victoria's voice remained even. "Some men will die for fear of being called cowards before the enemy ever reaches them. If you mean to allow them to retreat, make it explicit. Don't leave them guessing what their superiors call honour."

Marco took his pen, wrote the instruction in the margin of the operational map, and signed it.

Romeo studied the signature without smiling.

"Good. Taza will be a trap, not our men's grave."

Marco leaned back, suddenly tired.

"Yes."

The bell in the courtyard sounded in mid-afternoon. Victoria gathered her inventories, but Marco stopped her.

"What about the system that keeps working when we're no longer in one room?"

Victoria unrolled white cloth and laid out thin metal tokens engraved with wheat, ammunition, medicine, coal, horses, wagons and casualties.

"Lifeblood. Every convoy, intermediate depot and receiving unit uses the same symbols, packing standards and reporting schedule."

Marco took the casualty token. In Fes, a wagon might pass through the hands of Castilian, Arabic, Berber and English speakers in a single morning; the token required none of its handlers to speak all four languages.

Victoria turned the token over, showing a groove for a coloured insert.

"The code changes daily. If a wagon is captured, we cancel its code. If it arrives late, I know where contact was lost."

"You'll find people selling information as well," Romeo said.

He reached for a set of tokens to help him hunt Roman supply trains. Victoria immediately drew the cloth out of reach.

Marco laughed, then fell silent before the symbols linking Marrakesh through Tangier, Nador and Taza to Fes. The branches looked tiny on the map, but one misdirected medicine chest or lost coal convoy could cost lives at the front.

"Run Lifeblood across the whole line," he said. "Hassan appoints the storekeepers. Romeo sees only the codes needed for his missions, never the master register."

Marco rose and drew a broad wooden board away from the wall. Faded English annotations surrounded a long-barrelled gun and a sectional drawing of its breech.

Romeo recognised it first.

"Armstrong."
