"The version we used at Caen." Marco touched the barrel. "I had the Fes workshops build jigs and begin trial barrel conversions weeks ago. We have enough Castilian guns, but most are smoothbores. If Rome brings heavy siege guns, we can't wait for them to close before we can hit them."

Victoria studied the drawings.

"How many will you cast?"

"No time to replace them all. The first conversion prototype is nearly finished, so we'll pursue both approaches. Sound barrels will be rifled and their breech mechanisms improved wherever their construction allows. New steel goes first to complete Armstrong guns."

Marco opened a wooden case and set a hollow steel projectile beside a phial of red crystalline powder.

"Bala de Fuego. Ordinary-grade heat-generating Vestigium powder activates an incendiary compound that clings to timber, cloth, shields and siege engines."

Victoria lifted the projectile.

"How many?"

"Enough to fire throughout a battle. If every shell needs a rare Vestigium stone, I scrap the plan."

Romeo rolled the round between his fingers.

"Hit their powder magazine and you won't need a better name."

Victoria returned it to the case, understanding at last why Marco cared more about workshops than any one weapon.

Romeo produced a short carbine and two smoke canisters from a canvas bag. With its rifled barrel, detachable stock and rope hook beneath, the carbine was compact enough for climbing a fence and making a swift escape.

"My men will work close to the supply roads, fire twice and change position. The canisters make thick smoke, sting the eyes and frighten horses. The men must know which way the wind blows."

Marco handled the carbine and asked its range. Romeo shrugged.

"Shorter than a line infantry musket. I trade range for a way out."

Victoria told him to test the canisters outdoors before issuing them. This time Romeo did not joke.

Through the window, wagons still rolled in the evening shadows. Three former academy students once punished for wrecking a laboratory had now signed plans to be tested in a real war.

By nightfall, scarcely any blank space remained on the map. Marco's red lines closed the Taza corridor and layered Fes's defences. Victoria's Lifeblood network ran from Marrakesh to the junctions, branching into concealed stores, while Romeo's black marks scattered like saw teeth beyond the main front, around Rome's likely routes.

Marco stood before the crowded map.

"Suppose they bypass Taza, swing north towards Nador or cut Fes off from the sea altogether?"

Victoria moved the Tangier counter towards the road junctions.

"Romeo's men hold the supply corridors, not each beach. Our scattered stores will let Fes outlast the siege estimates the enemy can discover."

"And to bypass Taza, they must haul both men and artillery several extra days farther," Romeo said, pointing to his marks outside the front. "I know how to make each day cost them."

Marco regarded both their positions. He still feared the Western Roman army, but now the map had withdrawal routes, limits on how long each position would hold and named officers responsible for each decision.

Romeo noticed his silence.

"Afraid?"

"Yes. I've never fought the Western Romans. Eight calculations can be right, and the ninth can ruin them all."

Romeo pulled out a chair.

"I'm afraid too. I just look more handsome when I am."

Victoria folded her papers.

"I'm afraid the rear will break before the front. Soldiers can endure a few hungry days under orders. A city cannot bear rising food prices, coal shortages and news of dead relatives for ever."

She touched the settlements beyond Fes.

"Our enemy has time on its side, too."

Marco studied the new supply lines.

"Then we must make every day of waiting more costly for them."

Romeo turned a Roman marker between his fingers, accepting the task. All three laughed wearily.

The meeting ended near midnight.

Victoria rose first. Next morning she would inspect the southern depots before returning to Marrakesh. Romeo would stay three days to choose his mobile detachments, then return to Tangier-Ceuta.

Marco would stay in Fes. Before leaving, Victoria gave him a thin sheaf of papers.

"List of things to inspect."

Marco opened it.

"That thin?"

"That's the contents page."

Romeo laughed from the doorway and dodged the rolled map Marco threw after him.

Victoria lingered until his footsteps had faded, then looked at Marco more gravely.

"Millennia asked me to remind you to sleep."

Marco sighed.

"You saw her?"

"Before leaving Madrid."

"And agreed to spy for my wife?"

"I agreed to keep you from dying of stupidity before the Romans get their chance."

Marco leaned against the table.

"What's the difference?"

Victoria gave a slight smile.

"There is one. If the Romans kill you, at least someone might erect a statue."

She left before he could think of a reply.

Alone in the operations room, Marco sat looking at the overlapping ink. The Second Corps, Hassan and the workers of Fes had built the fortifications over the preceding weeks; today Victoria's convoys and Romeo's detachments had joined those separate efforts into a system.

He still did not know if they could defeat the Western Romans. At least someone was now responsible for every position on the map.

title_vi: Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Balancer
title_en: Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Balancer
text_en:
Victoria left Fes before dawn. Marco knew because her carriage was already passing through the gates when he came down the stairs of the Governor's residence. It was still dark, Romeo slept in the eastern guest room, and a small note in familiar, precise handwriting lay on the operations table.

*Get a full six hours' sleep.* Victoria had signed it.

Marco read the note, folded it in half and slipped it into his coat pocket. He had slept three hours and seventeen minutes.

Hassan al-Qadiri waited in the hall with two cups of mint tea. The Governor studied the shadows beneath Marco's eyes, then glanced at the wall clock as though weighing whether to mention Victoria's instruction.

"Don't." Marco took a cup before Hassan could speak. "If you're about to speak for Victoria, I'll put you both on the same train out of here."

Hassan sipped his tea, the corner of his mouth lifting. "I was only going to ask where you'd like to begin."

Marco drank half his cup. "Wherever they say they're best prepared."

"Why?"

"Because that's usually what worries me most."

An hour later, they stood on the eastern wall of Fes el-Jdid, where a bitter wind drove fine snow sideways like sand. The section had been marked complete since summer, its chief engineer having stamped the record three times in green and declared, in elegant handwriting, that it met wartime defensive standards. Marco had walked fewer than fifty paces along the base before stopping.

He crouched, brushed snow from a mortar joint and found a hairline crack running down from the edge of a stone. Drawing his short knife, he slipped the point into the gap and levered gently.

A palm-sized chunk of mortar dropped into the snow.

The chief engineer paled. "Colonel, we've reinforced this section twice. We used the finest lime from the southern kilns."

Marco handed him the fragment. "Good lime won't stop water entering a joint and freezing. You've been repairing the surface while the frost expands inside."

He borrowed a small hammer from a workman and struck the neighbouring stone in three places. The first rang solid, the second sounded dull, and the third answered hollow.

"Cut away the dead material. Pack small stones deep into the wall, then fill the joints in layers. Open every cavity instead of covering it." Marco returned the hammer. "A visible crack is a job. A painted-over crack is a disaster."

The engineer hurried to take notes, but Marco was already approaching the first gun platform, where he stopped to look over the valley.

A smoothbore cannon stood squarely on the parapet, clean beneath its canvas, with shot and powder stacked beside it. On paper, it was perfect. Marco took the gunner's position and sighted along the barrel.

An outcrop to the east obscured almost a third of its low field of fire. Roman infantry advancing beneath the slope would show little more than the tops of their helmets.

"Move it."

The artillery captain blinked. "Sir?"

"Twelve yards higher, about thirty yards to the left. Cut a new platform into the rock."

"But hauling a twelve-pounder up there will take at least two days."

Marco turned. "Then start today and we'll have a gun the day after tomorrow. Wait until the Romans arrive to discover that blind spot, and we'll have a beautiful hole for burying its crew."

He never raised his voice. The captain immediately turned to call for the engineers.

All morning Marco worked along the eastern face, then moved south, demanding proof wherever a section looked sound. Were the powder magazines dry? Could two gun carts pass on the hauling road, would storehouse doors open under another handbreadth of snow, and had the new barracks blocked access to the reserve well?

By noon, muddy snow reached his ankles. Hassan stopped reciting which works had passed inspection and simply summoned the officers responsible. On the southern face, they found something worse.

Nearly two hundred yards of wall rested on ground that had subsided before. New buttresses made it look secure, but frozen water marks at the foundations told Marco it would shift again with each cycle of frost. He stood in the wind, studied the wall and asked how much Lapis Caen remained.

"Thirty-two crates, sir," the engineer officer reported, consulting his ledger. "Twenty are assigned to the eastern gate under the old orders. The rest are for the artillery towers."

"Change that."

"Sir?"

"The eastern gate has sound bedrock. Bring fourteen crates here." Marco lifted a grey sample stone, pale blue veins crossing its surface; its cold seeped through his leather glove. "Grind it fine and mix it into the bonding mortar deep inside, not over the face for show. We need to stop ice tearing the structure apart, not give it grey armour."

The engineer hesitated. "If we use that much here, there won't be enough for the towers."

"Which towers matter most?"

"Two and Four."

"Keep their allocation. Use stone, timber and rammed earth for the others. Lapis Caen is finite." Marco replaced the sample. "Don't spend rare materials making everywhere a little stronger. Spend them where failure is unacceptable."

Hassan had listened closely. "Is that why they call you the Balancer?"

Marco watched labourers carrying stones beneath the wall. "No. Some idiot classmates coined that name when I miscalculated an explosive charge and blew the laboratory door off."

Hassan stared.

Marco kept a straight face for two seconds before laughing. "Romeo has another version. Don't believe him."

***

By afternoon, the inspection turned from stone to men. The Second Corps remained in the southern barracks of Fes el-Jdid, where it had been stationed since Marco first took the front. Felt tents stood in straight, snow-covered rows; Castilian, Moorish and Berber soldiers served in mixed companies, their breastplates marked with the silver scales of the *Tercio de la Balanza*.

Marco refused a parade. He went straight to the kitchens.

The quartermaster major nearly dropped his ladle when his commander appeared amid salted meat, onions and coal smoke. Marco served himself an ordinary soldier's stew, sat by the door and finished it before speaking.

"A little salty."

The cook swallowed. "Sir, the preserved meat in this batch..."

"I'm not complaining. I want to know how much more water the men need after eating it." Marco put down the bowl. "If the ration's salty, the water allowance must reflect that. Don't let the ledger and the stomach tell different stories."

He inspected the sock store, footwear depot, infirmary, latrines and stables before reaching the training ground. At the infirmary he lingered over thirty-seven soldiers suffering cracked feet, fever from cold and infected scratches.

"How many men became unfit for combat this week without an enemy weapon touching them?"

The surgeon checked his register. "One hundred and eighty-two. Most return within two to four days."

Marco addressed his staff officer. "List that number separately in the strength report. I won't accept 'full strength' while some of those men are bedridden by wet boots."

"Understood."

"Issue two more pairs of dry socks per man."

The supply major frowned. "We can't maintain that allowance all winter with our present stocks."

"Commission the civilian weaving workshops."

"The expense..."

Marco looked at him. "Socks cost less than four days of a soldier lying feverish. Cut the decorative cloth from officers' uniforms first, if you must."

Nearby soldiers hid smiles. Marco noticed and said nothing.

On the common training ground, Second Corps units drilled alongside the newly arrived British corps. There Marco found the young company reinforced at Salamanca, the one he had asked about on the train. Nineteen and twenty-year-olds stood among older veterans as ordered, and a brown-haired recruit struggled with his musket sling, his hands shaking mostly from cold.

Marco stopped before him.

"Twenty, Colonel," the young man answered when asked his age. He had heard no real artillery fire beyond training, yet tried to stand straight as Marco questioned him about his first battle.

Marco called over a sergeant with an old burn on his wrist. The man had fought at Oran and Algiers, survived the retreat from Blida, and lost part of his left ear.

"From today you eat, sleep and stand in line together," Marco told them. "When the first shells land, if this lad forgets his lessons, show him what to do first."

The recruit flushed. "I'll try not to panic, Colonel."

"Everyone panics." Marco tapped the stock of the boy's musket. "What matters is whether you can still hear the man beside you afterwards. Don't be reckless just to prove you aren't frightened."

The sergeant nodded and accepted his charge. Marco crossed the rest of the ground, but his own words stayed with him as he approached the steps where a staff officer waited with the artillery-range schedule.

He remembered what he had told Edward after the banquet in Marrakesh, then counted the previous three nights. Together they had given him fewer than ten hours' sleep.

"Colonel, the firing range: now or after dinner?" the officer called.

Marco glanced at his schedule.

"After dinner."

The officer tried to hide his smile. Marco lifted his chin.

"Go on, laugh. Then bring me the reports."

That night he slept five hours. Next morning the guns began to roar.

***

The proving ground lay beyond the western walls, with an old cliff as its backstop. The first gun modified to the *Armstrong* drawings stood on a new wooden carriage, the result of nearly three weeks' quiet work in the Fes workshops. Its steel barrel exceeded ordinary Castilian models in length, and rough tool marks still showed on the breech.

Marco circled it three times.

"Which trial?"

"The eleventh, sir," the foreman replied. "All ten earlier shots went well."

"Pressure?"

The foreman checked the gauge. "Within limits."

"Cracks?"

"None visible."

Marco examined the strengthening bands and wiped a thin film of oil around the breech himself. "Strip it down after the twelfth shot. I want to know how the metal fatigues, not just that it hasn't exploded."

The crew loaded solid shot for an accuracy trial. Everyone withdrew behind the earthen barrier.

"Fire!"

The blast rolled across the valley. The barrel recoiled, its carriage wheels biting into frozen earth, while hundreds of yards away rock burst near the centre of a white-painted ring.

The workmen cheered. Marco did not.

He approached before the smoke cleared and checked the carriage and breech. A mounting bolt had shifted almost half a finger's width.

"Hitting the target doesn't prove it can fire thirty rounds without stopping. Strip the carriage, measure the deformation, then resume." Marco pointed to the loosened bolt, and the foreman summoned the mechanics. Cheers gave way to the clink of tools on steel.

On the third day Marco tested the first complete batch of *Bala de Fuego*, after weeks of separate trials of the casing and incendiary compound.

None of the shells entered the main magazine. An earthen bunker outside the workshops held each in a sand-filled box, with heat-producing Vestigium powder measured to the minimum needed for ignition. Marco rejected a proposal to double the charge for a more spectacular demonstration.

"The enemy won't fear us because the fire looks beautiful," he told the foreman. "They'll fear us when we can fire the hundredth round."

The first shell struck a mock siege wagon. Steel split and the compound clung to the timber, spreading in red-orange ribbons despite the snow beneath its wheels. Burning resin and acrid smoke drifted back on the wind, silencing the observers.

Marco watched the blaze, then turned to the safety team.

"How long to put it out?"

"Sir?"

"If a magazine catches fire, we need to know how to save our own men. Bring sand, thick blankets and water vessels. Test them."

The officer stared. "But it's our weapon."

"Which makes it all the more important to learn how it kills us."

By week's end every new *Armstrong* gun had its own firing log, every batch of *Bala de Fuego* a workshop stamp and production date. Any model whose premature-ignition rate exceeded the limit was dismantled, however badly that reduced the official reserve. Marco preferred ugly, truthful numbers to pretty figures written in dead men's blood.

Romeo left Fes on the third morning. Before mounting, he drew Marco beyond the officers' hearing and pressed a folded sheet into his hand.

"My selected teams. Three at Taza, two slipping east, one watching the Nador route. Every team has the two retreat routes you demanded."

Marco unfolded it. "Only six?"

"For now." Romeo adjusted his gloves. "I'd rather have six teams that know their business than twenty who think they're competing for Roman generals' heads."

Marco eyed him. "At last, something that sounds as though an adult said it."

"Don't tell Victoria. I've a reputation to maintain."

Romeo swung into the saddle, then leaned down. "And Marco."

"What?"

"Don't die inspecting the sock stores."

Marco reached to strike his leg, but Romeo was already riding through the gate, laughing. Fes was left to Marco and the tasks that could not laugh back.

***

He devoted the next week to Taza without going there. Each morning, reports arrived by train or horse: completed defences, artillery rounds, preserved food, wells, the state of retreat routes and Western Roman gun positions found by scouts. Young officers urged him to make Taza a fortress that could never fall; Marco refused to reinforce it without limit.

Taza did not need to last forever. It needed to last long enough.

In the operations room he placed three hourglasses beside the outpost's marker. He labelled them Artillery, Ammunition and Formation, then began drafting orders as Hassan watched.

"Once the enemy has deployed sufficient heavy guns, its ammunition expenditure reaches the threshold confirmed by our scouts, and its main body enters the western corridor, the Taza commander may withdraw on his own judgement if contact with Fes is lost." Marco paused. "He must not wait for orders until the last man."

Hassan reread it. "Are you certain?"

"Yes."

"If they pull out early, the court may call it abandoning the town."

Marco laid down his pen. "Then my name is on the order."

"I didn't ask who would take the blame." Hassan leant over the table. "Can you bear it if they withdraw before the trap works as intended?"

Marco looked at the hourglasses.

"No."

Hassan raised an eyebrow.

"I'll be furious. I might curse them for a week, or decide their commander made the wrong judgement. But if I order ten thousand men to die because I dread hearing the word 'retreat' afterwards, then the first man to have judged wrongly is me."

Hassan fell silent. Marco signed.

Three copies went out: one by train, one by mounted courier, one kept in Fes. Before they were sealed, Marco had the secretary read the withdrawal clause aloud to ensure no one could construe it as permission to retreat only if Marco approved.

That evening he examined three work boards already assigned to engineering, supply and artillery officers. The next morning he summoned eleven departmental heads and placed the assignments before them. He would no longer sign their work for them.

"From today, I won't sign a second approval for work that already has an officer professionally responsible," he said. "Make the reports clear enough for surprise inspections, but the work belongs to whoever takes it."

The engineering major looked surprised. Marco pushed the Number Four wall checklist towards him.

"The name on that report carries responsibility for the work. I'll inspect without doing every job again."

A captain asked whether something had happened.

"Yes," Marco said. "I pay eleven officers and keep trying to do all their jobs."

The captain who laughed was promptly assigned the cross-inspection schedule. Hassan turned to the window to conceal his smile.

Delegation did not immediately lighten Marco's days. It changed his work from counting ammunition crates to settling questions no subordinate had the authority to decide. One surfaced late in the second week.

***

In the eastern refugee quarter of Fes el-Jdid, English drill commands rang from behind stone houses. Marco reined in, gave his horse to a guard and followed the sound into a courtyard. Nearly three hundred men drilled there.

They wore goatskin, brown wool and old Castilian coats, but their musket loading, rank changes and turns into square formation made Marco stop. A middle-aged man with a long scar across his forehead called the cadence.

"Change ranks! Rear rank, advance..."

He turned, his command dying in his mouth.

"Colonel Stones?"

Marco recognised him a heartbeat later.

"Thomas Hale."

The man threw his baton into the snow and approached. They stared at each other until Hale punched Marco hard in the shoulder.

"You bastard. I thought you'd died at Caen."

Marco staggered half a step, then embraced him. "And I thought you'd died in London."

Recognition spread in whispers through the ranks, drawing dozens of ageing, weathered, scarred men towards him. Some had been at Rennes, others had defended Caen. Marco forgot some names but remembered precisely how their owners cursed when a musket jammed.

After Britain's collapse they had drifted to North Africa, becoming blacksmiths, carpenters, railway labourers, coachmen and stallholders. With war approaching Fes, they had taken out their old firearms to practise before anyone asked.

"We could muster nearly two thousand if we call everyone who served," Hale said. "Many still have uniforms."

Marco surveyed the ranks. "How many have children?"

Hale hesitated. "Nearly all."

Marco lowered his voice. "And how many are their families' main breadwinners?"

"Nearly all of us, too." Hale frowned. "Why ask? We know what we're volunteering for."

Marco picked up the baton and handed it back. "I know. I just don't want to see red coats and forget that the men inside them have lived another ten years."

Hale said nothing.

Marco faced the crowd.

"Anyone who wants to return will enlist formally, with pay, rations for your families, disability benefits and a death allowance. Those who don't want a musket can serve in transport, medical care, workshops or training. No one will be called a coward for living long enough to have someone waiting at home."

A voice from the rear shouted, "What about you, Colonel? Is someone waiting for you?"

Laughter rose.

Marco smiled. "Yes. And my wife is more frightening than the Roman army, so I'm trying very hard to get home."

The laughter grew. Three days later, the registration lists were ready.

One thousand eight hundred and seventy-three battle-fit veterans asked to return to the front. More than four hundred others took training, transport, stores and medical duties. Rather than make them an independent corps, Marco formed them into a reserve attached to Fes, under the name they chose from their past.

Redcoats.

When the old red wool coats came out of trunks, many were faded, patched at the elbows or too tight across stomachs that had grown in ten years. Marco refused to replace them all.

"Issue new armour and muskets," he said. "But if a man wants his old coat, let him wear it. We needn't pretend the last ten years didn't happen."

There was no grand speech at the first Redcoats' parade.

Marco walked from platoon to platoon, asking what the men had done before returning. One had baked bread, another repaired locomotives, two brothers had run a shoemaker's shop, and one had just welcomed his third child.

At the end of the line Hale asked softly, "Disappointed? We don't look much like the men at Caen any more."

Marco studied the grey hair among the red coats.

"Thank goodness."

Hale raised an eyebrow.

"Too many of the men at Caen died." Marco straightened a nearby veteran's musket sling. "I need men who know how to survive a battle."

***

Over the next weeks, Fes changed daily. Gun platforms rose on higher slopes, and the southern wall was opened and reinforced with Lapis Caen mortar only where needed. Lifeblood markers appeared on supply wagons, coal stores, infirmaries and powder magazines.

Trains from Marrakesh no longer unloaded into one vast warehouse but dispersed goods among several depots. Even Marco needed the new cipher to locate all the reserves. He was pleased: a defence that one captive could reveal in full was no defence at all.

At the end of the second week a letter came from Madrid. Marco received it near midnight but, instead of opening it at his operations table, took it to his room, removed his armour, washed his hands and sat beside the stove.

The address was in Millennia's handwriting. There were no reproaches inside.

*Our son was made to stand at the back of his classroom because he and Remi took a mechanical clock apart to see how it worked, then couldn't put it together again.*

*Juliet has visited for tea twice this week. She's beginning to find her way around Madrid and absolutely refuses to let me pay for her at the market any more.*

Towards the end, Millennia described meeting Victoria before her departure for Fes. Then came lines meant for Marco alone.

*Victoria told me you're preparing a city for war. I only hope you remember that city needs a commander who can think clearly more than it needs a hero who stays awake all night.*

Marco read the passage twice. Another slip lay in the envelope, covered in a child's uneven script, the ink heavy here and faint there.

*Please remember to come home, Father. Remi and I have bet on whether you or Uncle Edward will come home later. I've put two coins on you.*

Marco laughed aloud, then fell quiet. Holding the paper in both hands, he stared into the flames until his eyes stung and he had to wipe them with the back of his hand.

No one saw. He felt childishly relieved and took out paper for his reply.

He made no promise that the war would end soon. He described the preparations in Fes, how Romeo still talked too much and how Victoria remained right at the most irritating moments. At the end he wrote to his son.

*Keep those two coins. I don't want you to win because something happens to Uncle Edward, and I don't want to lose because I do something foolish. I'll try to get home early enough to take your money myself.*

Marco reread *try* before closing the letter. He knew the boy would keep the coins until his return.

He sealed the envelope and left it by the door. Tomorrow's schedule held six items; he crossed out three already delegated, looked at his desk once more and blew out the candle before midnight.

Next morning he woke after six hours and eleven minutes. Hassan met him in the corridor, glanced at the clock and smiled.

"Shall I send word to Victoria?"

Marco fastened his cloak. "Do you want to survive until the Romans arrive?"

"I understand."

They descended the stairs. Marco had inspected walls, guns, soldiers, stores, infirmaries, retreat routes and the people who would hold them. On the map, Fes was beginning to resemble a fortress that might withstand war.

But outside, civilian wagons were passing the Governor's gates. Two families from Taza sat among blankets, cooking pots and hastily tied bundles, their children crowded between them.

A little girl held a wooden cage with a chicken inside. Her mother clutched a ring of keys, though the house they opened lay hundreds of miles to the east.

Marco watched the wagons pass. Hassan watched too.

"More refugees are arriving," the Governor said. "About three hundred yesterday. It may be twice that next week."

Marco looked towards the crowded roofs of distant Fes el-Bali. Thousands of alleys wound together so tightly that the map showed only a single patch of brown.

For almost two months since leaving Tangier-Ceuta with the Second Corps, he had calculated how many rounds each gun needed, how much bread a platoon ate, how much water a horse drank, and how many blows a wall could take before its gun crew must withdraw.

Yet he did not know how long a mother clutching two children would need to reach shelter from the old quarter when the alarm bells sounded. He turned to Hassan.

"Tomorrow I want to go into Fes el-Bali."

"Which district?"

"Every district the evacuation plan expects civilians to pass through."

Hassan glanced at Marco's freshly cleaned boots. "You'll hate those alleys."

Marco pulled on his gloves. "If the ambulances hate them too, I need to see them all the more."

He stepped into the courtyard, passing the refugee families who had stopped to ask directions. Fes had its walls. Now Marco must learn whether there were still paths within those walls by which its people might survive.

title_vi: Chapter Thirty-Eight: Fes and the War
title_en: Chapter Thirty-Eight: Fes and the War
text_en:
Before Taza fell, Marco entered Fes el-Bali through its western gate shortly after the markets opened. Hassan offered a platoon as escort, but Marco took only four soldiers and threaded between the stalls, studying doorways and tight bends where stretchers would have to pass once the guns opened fire.

The municipal map, only four years old, was wrong from the first alley. On paper, Evacuation Route Three allowed two lines of people abreast; in the street, low awnings, donkey carts and merchandise almost blocked it.

"Was this road drawn at a desk, or did anyone come here to measure it?" Marco asked the clerk. He folded the map. "Send someone with a walking stick and a stretcher along the entire route before you enter it in the evacuation register."

He ordered the clerk to measure the alley. Before the wooden rule touched the opposite wall, a vegetable seller asked them to move for his donkey cart; then came a coal merchant, followed by pupils carrying writing boards from their master's house. Each time the rule had to be withdrawn until the passage cleared.

The clerk grew impatient, but Marco told him to record every delay. The map had forgotten the ordinary business of a morning.

They descended into lanes smelling of leather, lamp oil and fresh bread, with washing swaying overhead. Marco had defended cities whose broad avenues allowed artillery to turn; every bend in Fes led past someone's home. Its markets were still open, and that made it harder to defend than an empty fortress.

In the coppersmiths' square, a watch officer had assembled twelve able-bodied families to test the route. Marco asked for elderly people with walking sticks, mothers carrying infants, handcarts and a stretcher as well, then blocked the main alley with two carts.

"But that's the shortest way," the officer protested.

"Enemy artillery won't ask for directions before firing." Marco withheld the route from the participants and told them to bring what they would truly wish to save. Half an hour later, the bronze bell rang three times.

The trouble began at the doors. A woman returned for blankets, papers and the family's most valuable copper pot; an old man took four minutes to descend his stairs, while a child refused to part with his wooden horse.

At the third alley, the stretcher jammed against a stone doorway. People converging from a side route frightened a boy into tears, and Marco stopped the exercise. Hassan checked his watch: thirty-two minutes instead of the planned eleven.

The officer protested that people had not obeyed instructions.

"Will you argue with every mother on her doorstep while shells fall?" Marco asked. He knelt to ask if the boy was hurt; the child shook his head and pointed to his mother, trapped with her pot. Marco handed the officer the map. "Draw a route for these people. We'll try again."

When the mother finally passed the obstruction, her pot struck the wall with a clang that turned every head. She blushed and hid it behind her, her fingers red from gripping the handle. Marco did not order her to drop it, but asked what she would save if she had to escape alone with two children.

She looked at her crying boy and passed the pot to an acquaintance. The officer began to speak, then stopped when Marco pointed to the chalk marking where the stretcher had jammed.

On the second attempt, children and the stretcher went first, the able-bodied took two other alleys, and handcarts were sent to a collection point near the gate. A man refused to leave his cupboard until Marco pointed to his two children.

"I can't promise your belongings will survive if the city burns. But those two must get out first."

The time fell to nineteen minutes. Marco removed one leaf of an abandoned warehouse door, opened a bypass and changed where the routes met. The third attempt took thirteen minutes, but nobody cheered.

An elderly woman with a stick said thirteen minutes was still too long if the guns fired quickly.

"You're right," Marco said. "I can't make you walk faster. So the bells must ring sooner."

Hassan had the clerks record the elderly group's time separately instead of averaging it with the quickest. The volunteers stayed to identify slippery steps, water points and awnings needing repair, while Marco listened despite the watch ticking in his pocket.

Laughter returned when a craftsman asked whether he must bring a real pot next time. Marco allowed an empty one, provided the man brought his youngest child too. The craftsman glanced at the child's wet shoes and nodded.

Before noon, they found escape routes blocked by doors opening the wrong way, wells hemmed in by neighbouring buildings and poorly lit staircases. In the dyers' quarter, Zahra took Marco into a three-storey house holding thirty-one people, including eleven young children and four elderly residents. Mahmud, upstairs, needed two helpers to descend.

"Who brings him out when the alarm sounds?" Marco asked.

Zahra indicated two young men below. "They usually help Mahmud, but one works at a workshop far to the east."

Amina held an infant and another child by the hand. "I can scarcely get these two downstairs. Who helps him?"

Marco turned to the craftsmen. "Choose someone else who lives here. Practise the whole staircase before nightfall."

An older craftsman stepped forward, supporting his aching back. "My back hurts, but my legs still work." Zahra moved aside to let him pass.

Marco waited for them to choose the third helper, then ordered all three names written on the inside of the door. In the cloth cellar, he moved a bale away from a vent.

"This cellar will shelter ten. The others must use the workshop cellar opposite."

"That workshop belongs to another household," Zahra said, gripping her keys.

"Then take me to its owner." Marco examined the cellar door. "When the bells sound, everyone must know which doors open and who needs help downstairs first."

He handed his register to the district head, marking homes with elderly residents and young children.

Zahra poured tea and laughed. "Very well. But the workshop owner is harder to please than Mahmud."

Marco watched the three helpers practise with Mahmud. At the seventh step they caught against the banister and changed their grip; Zahra pulled a wicker chair out of their way.

"Do you intend to dismantle my whole house?" Mahmud grumbled. Reaching the courtyard, he pointed his stick at a board by the door. "And where will the cellar sign hang?"

"Beside the frame, where passers-by can see it," Zahra answered. She showed Marco a list of households written so small he had to approach the lamp to read it.

Outside, market loaves had shrunk and barley was measured sparingly. Rumours of Taza and Nador's fall passed from stall to stall. Marco climbed a step beside a bakery and unsealed a dispatch.

"Taza and Nador are still holding. The clerks will post fresh reports in the squares each morning and afternoon."

An old woman tugged his coat. "Colonel, how am I supposed to read those boards?"

Marco turned to the clerk. "Have the news read aloud in Castilian, Arabic and Berber, and in English in the English quarter."

"Will that silence the rumours?" Hassan asked beside the bakery.

"Let the truth be heard every day where people buy their bread." Marco folded the dispatch.

That afternoon Marco visited the southern glasshouses. Tifawt lifted canvas from beds of barley and turnips.

"If the railway is cut, this city must live on whatever still grows. Give us two more cartloads of coal each week to keep the soil warm, Colonel."

A lieutenant had called the furnace tenders away to dig trenches. Marco turned on him.

"Send them back. Waterworks attendants, bakers and glasshouse tenders are exempt from labour drafts."

He marked the transport register. "Three cartloads of coal go here. The third is held in reserve against a late train."

At the end of a glasshouse, a workman removed a worn brass valve and laid its rings on clean cloth. Marco crouched beside him. "What will keep the furnace hot tonight?"

"Three new sealing rings." The man showed him a cracked one. "I've waited since last week."

Tifawt looked at the vegetables near the door. "They take men to haul timber while these beds depend on this furnace."

Marco noted the rings and the train that might carry them. The smell of damp earth clung to his gloves as he left.

***

Darkness had fallen when Marco returned to Fes el-Bali. He thought the inspections finished, but Hassan said people were waiting at a large house near the Karouine quarter.

"How many?" Marco asked.

"Enough to make you sleep even less than Victoria allows."

Marco stared at him.

Hassan smiled. "The neighbourhood elders. You said you wanted their opinions."

Marco turned up his collar. "I did say that, didn't I?"

"And they remember."

"Unfortunate."

Behind an unremarkable wooden door lay a square courtyard beneath a canvas canopy. A large charcoal brazier burned at its centre, and teapots were continually refilled.

Chairs stood in a circle around the fire, not in rows before a speaker. Embroidered robes mingled with dye-stained wrists; some elders brought household registers, others keys to water stores. These people had kept Fes functioning through the winter without waiting for military orders.

Hassan sat at the outer edge and placed a teapot near Miriam. Chairs were found for latecomers until there was scarcely room around the map.

More than thirty people had gathered. Sheikh Ibrahim, representing Moorish families, sat beside the fire, white beard over his brown robe. Beside him was Miriam ben Ezra, a Jewish physician in her forties overseeing two civilian aid stations.

Opposite sat Aksel n'Tafukt, leader of Berber families who had come down from the mountains, alongside merchants, dyers, tanners, clerics, two teachers and Zahra. Thomas Hale was there too, without his red coat, seated at the rear as representative of the English quarter.

Marco removed his hat. "Thank you for coming."

Ibrahim smiled. "You summon us to our own house and thank us for coming. A very Castilian beginning."

A few laughed. Marco sat instead of delivering a speech.

"Then I'll begin again. I need your help because the army's plans still contain a great deal of foolishness."

The laughter grew, easing the tension enough for argument.

Marco spread three evacuation routes on the table. "Route Three took thirty-two minutes today, not eleven. I've cleared a few alleys, but I need you to show me what we've missed."

Zahra said she had warned them two years earlier that a stretcher could not pass through one alley. The clerk lowered his eyes, but Marco did not scold him. "Then we were at fault for asking the wrong people."

A merchant feared the army would drive whole streets from their homes. Marco pointed to nearby shelters: during bombardment people should take cover close by, and only districts on fire or with collapsed walls would withdraw in stages.

Aksel demanded to know who had given soldiers the right to decide which homes deserved defending.

Marco held his gaze. "If you know a better way, show me. But I won't call it courage to let children die in a house with no way out."

Miriam objected to gathering every patient in one place. Marco divided the map into smaller shelter groups and proposed distributing medicine as they did food.

"No," she interrupted. "Pain medicines, bandages and surgical instruments need three principal stores and six smaller depots, not a handful of bags scattered until every station lacks what it needs."

Marco handed her the pen, and she shifted two depots nearer the water stations. Ibrahim chuckled. "The Colonel really did come to ask."

"If I wanted people to nod, I'd have met my staff." They argued through supper, the maps filling with local notes.

Over bean soup, a market-gate keeper drew the map closer. "Close the gate at the alarm, and fewer outsiders will crowd this alley."

The district head opposite indicated the eastern turning. "Then everyone must detour through the dyers' quarter. That's where the stretcher stuck this morning."

Marco set down cold tea. "Tomorrow the engineers will test both routes. Record who leads the people before deciding which gates to close."

The clerk struck through the order he had just written and opened another page for the names of those responsible.

A church-bell keeper laid his keys on the table. "Three long peals reach the whole street. We can sound the danger that way."

A cleric from the east pushed his soup aside. "Our people have followed drums since childhood. At night they may mistake church bells for a call to worship."

Zahra tapped the district boundary. "The bells warn the whole city. Each quarter then uses its familiar drums or bells to guide people."

Miriam put a slip beside a shelter mark. "And flags on roofs by day. Deaf people must see where to go."

Marco wrote along the map's edge.

"Three common peals for the alarm. Local drums and bells for directions. Flags by day. We test it tomorrow."

A tannery owner touched two adjoining rooftops. "Build a wooden bridge here. The able-bodied can cross above, leaving the streets below to children and stretchers."

Marco laid down his ruler.

"How many must it bear? The engineers test it before laying the boards. No bridge goes on the evacuation map until it's proven sound."

Aksel put his palm on the table. "When Romans reach our alleys, how will families defend their doors?"

Marco surveyed the gathering. "Those who own a gun, raise your hand."

Many hands rose. "Who has fired in a narrow alley with a neighbour's house behind the target?"

Most hands fell. Only Hale and a few veterans kept theirs raised.

Miriam moved her medical notes. "Children need guides to the cellars; the wounded need stretcher bearers. Assign those people first."

Marco divided the register.

"Enter civilian volunteers in the register for their own districts. Those who want to fight train with veterans. Hale takes the English quarter and works with Moorish, Berber and Castilian groups along its borders."

Zahra turned a *Lifeblood* card in her hand. "Will you teach the whole street four languages before the enemy comes?"

Marco drew five marks. "Arrows for civilian routes, white circles for shelters, red crosses for aid stations, black bars for military passages and crossed marks for closed ways."

Miriam circled the cross with her pen. "Some people cannot tell those colours apart. Each mark needs a different shape."

Marco amended the drawings and handed them back. "Read them from the other side of the table."

Zahra caught his pen at a corner. "Put an arrow by this door and you'll send the entire crowd into that family's house."

Miriam raised a card to stretcher height. "The aid-station sign must hang above our heads. Those behind us need to see it."

Hale smoothed the map. "The English quarter will use the same marks, with English beside the local writing."

Marco set down another sheet. "Tomorrow, take the signs into the alleys and test them in furnace smoke. Show me whatever people misunderstand."

Near midnight, new ink had all but swallowed the original map. Unlike the first war council's map, where three officers had made North Africa into a machine of war, this one showed smaller things: a house where a man could no longer walk, a well whose approach must remain clear, a courtyard for two hundred, a bakery whose workers must stay, a rooftop that might become a passage if strengthened.

Marco studied it. This, too, was strategy, but every piece on this board had a name.

As the meeting dispersed, Ibrahim detained him. "Colonel Stones. You asked us today how people should retreat, but there's something armies dislike hearing."

"Please say it."

"Many will never leave Fes."

Marco sighed. "I know."

"You know in your head. I want you to understand in your belly." Ibrahim gestured towards the night-market sounds beyond the roof. "These alleys feed their families. Their parents lie buried here. Shops, wells, altars and memories are here. Some would rather die at home than take a train to an unknown place."

Marco listened.

"Treat them as fools the army must save from themselves," Ibrahim continued, "and they'll hide guns, people, even children. Your plans will die before the war arrives."

"Then what should I do?"

"Give them a part to play."

Marco watched him.

Ibrahim tapped the map.

"Those who stay must know why. Where to fight fires, which passages to guide others through, whom to bring water, and where to stand if they must fight. A man given responsibility will send his children away sooner than one told he's merely a civilian in the army's way."

Marco examined their symbols. "You're right."

Ibrahim smiled. "I know."

"You and Victoria would get along."

"That terrifying fair-haired woman?"

"You've met her?"

"She inspected our warehouses once. Three merchants couldn't sleep for a week afterwards."

Marco roared with laughter.

title_vi: Chapter Thirty-Nine: The Wards of Fes
title_en: Chapter Thirty-Nine: The Wards of Fes
text_en:
The following morning, Fes began to be divided into proper wards of the civilian watch. Each had a civilian leader, a shelter keeper, someone responsible for water and firefighting, a messenger to the medical stations and a list of households needing help. Those volunteering to fight were enrolled separately for training under veterans or regular soldiers instead of forming unruly armed bands.

Not every householder would put a name on the boards. Some feared service in the army; others did not want neighbours knowing a relative was ill. District heads went door to door explaining that names inside a doorway told rescuers where to knock first, while the watch had no right to make anyone bear arms.

Often the helper lived next door. Wooden tokens of responsibility passed between neighbours as simply as a borrowed ladder or a bucket carried across the alley.

Marco forbade grand names for the arrangement. Romeo was absent and could not object.

The first wooden signs went up at crossroads that day, painted large enough for smoky streets but revealing no military details. Children learned them faster than adults, making a race of finding the shelters. Marco discovered this outside a schoolroom.

A teacher held up a wooden card bearing a white circle. More than twenty pupils raised their hands when she asked its meaning.

"The shelter!"

"Don't push!"

"Help the little ones!"

A boy at the back shouted, "Don't go back for your toys!"

The class laughed, and Marco laughed at the doorway. The teacher moved to make everyone stand in greeting, but he shook his head and asked if they knew the three long bell peals.

A girl answered first. "Get ready, but don't run yet. Wait for the district signal."

"And if there's smoke in the house next door?"

"Tell an adult. Don't go in yourself."

Marco nodded. "Good."

As he left, he heard the boy whisper that Colonel Stones was shorter than rumour claimed. He stopped; the room went silent.

Marco looked back. "Rumours get many things wrong. Remember that."

The teacher turned away to conceal her laughter.

Three days later, the practice bells sounded amid the market. Teachers led children to shelter, Zahra's people helped Mahmud downstairs, and a stretcher cart passed the bend where a stretcher had stuck. Hassan's watch showed eleven minutes and fifty seconds, but a vegetable cart overturned in the main alley, while a district head raised the wrong flag and sent nearly two hundred people to the wrong shelter.

Marco put both failures on the notice board. Hassan feared the people would lose confidence, but Marco pointed to those caught in the crowd.

"They saw it happen. Hide it, and they won't heed the alarm next time."

Four days later, the second exercise saw no overturned cart. District heads diverted people from full shelters, and firefighters made a workshop owner put out his dye furnace before closing the doors. Door-to-door checks still found blocked back exits, cellars without flues and lamp oil stored beside stoves.

A widow withheld three barrels of oil until given a receipt. Marco moved them to a stone warehouse and wrote her name and compensation on the document. A silversmith's daughter asked to carry water rather than serve on the walls, and he assigned her that duty.

A Moorish veteran who had lost a leg at Algiers refused to be classed as helpless. Marco had him guide a child towards the shelter while a neighbour helped him downstairs.

Thus *Lifeblood* became part of the city's daily life. Signs had to be legible even to those who could not read, frightened and cold; lengthy rules belonged in the district registers, while the streets needed only clear marks.

The signs lacked the engineers' elegance. A white circle was crooked, an arrow leaned sideways, and children painted a moustache on a guide figure. Hassan complained, but Marco left them until repainting: at least the children recognised the signs and argued over which way to turn.

Near a water store, a woman asked for a sign to be corrected because a stretcher cart still could not pass the rear door. Marco sent workmen to measure it instead of demanding another long petition.

He had no time.

Refugees arrived by train from Taza in growing numbers, sometimes nearly a thousand in a day. One family carried a door carved with three generations of names; other children held chickens, blankets and key bundles that might never open another lock.

Warehouses filled quickly. Rather than build one vast camp outside the walls, Marco housed newcomers in stores, schools, merchants' courtyards and homes offering spare rooms. Rising coal prices and rents led him and Hassan to establish compensation by person and day of lodging, and to restrain extortionate landlords.

Victoria wrote warning him not to turn refuge into profiteering. Marco scribbled in the margin that she knew how to spoil everyone's pleasure; two days later, a parcel of *Lifeblood* cards arrived with her reply: "I take that as a compliment."

Fes still held markets and weddings, and hammers rang in the workshops. A tailor sold evacuation bags with sections for papers, dry bread and water flasks. Marco bought two with his own money for his wife and son in Madrid.

Millennia thanked him by letter, but said a bag could not replace a husband who must come home himself. Marco kept the folded letter in his breast pocket, where he felt it whenever he thought of missing supper.

Days later, a heating pipe cracked in an eastern dye workshop, igniting oil. Smoke spread beneath the canvas roofs; someone rang the wrong bell pattern, and a rumour that Romans had entered Fes raced through the alleys.

Marco rushed down the Governor's stairs, then stopped at the gate before the duty officer. "Fire in the east. What are the standing orders?"

"The district firefighters attend first, with a water cart from the nearest station. The garrison enters only if the district head requests it or flames spread beyond three rows of houses."

"Then follow it." Marco stayed beside the duty desk, his hand already resting on his riding gloves.

On the duty board, the newly agreed symbols marked the lines by which each district reported trouble. The young officer glanced repeatedly at Marco's cloak and gloves. Before, each alarm had sent soldiers charging after him; now they waited for the district head to request aid.

Marco checked where the reserve water cart stood, then laid down the gloves lest he pick them up. Outside, the bells changed to the proper rhythm. Each peal made standing still harder, but he let the appointed people work.

Ten minutes crawled past. The first report said firefighters had isolated two houses; the aid station had received seven people with minor burns and one with a broken leg. The second said the district head had diverted people from the smoke-filled main route; the third announced that the fire was controlled.

Hassan watched Marco lean over the table. "Disappointed that Fes doesn't need you, sir?"

"Half of me is." Marco listened until the fire carts faded, then smiled. "The other half is relieved to an irritating degree."

Afterwards, inspectors found the cracked pipe and the cause of the mistaken bell signal. The apprentice who had rung them was not punished; instead, the alarm was enclosed in a glazed case, with a hammer beside it to break the glass, and every heated workshop was examined again.

Marco slept seven hours that night. He did not tell Victoria, but Hassan did; the next day a note arrived from Marrakesh: "At last you've learned to live." Marco crumpled it, smoothed it out again and kept it beside Millennia's letter.

Beyond the walls, war advanced. Scouts at Taza saw more heavy guns, while Romeo reported destroying a supply bridge at the cost of two men. Marco lingered over their names longer than the victory report and reminded his mobile detachments to keep within their withdrawal limits.

Taza reported fewer evacuees. Those remaining either could not leave or refused to abandon their homes. Marco sent more carts for the sick and unaccompanied children, keeping his defensive orders: delay the Romans, force them to reveal their guns, waste ammunition, draw formations into prepared corridors and withdraw.

One evening Marco and Sheikh Ibrahim stood on a warehouse roof above Fes el-Bali. The lamps below followed no straight lines on a military map: they curved through alleys, gathered at wells and bathhouses, then vanished behind low domes. A woman climbed onto a chair to secure washing whipped by the wind, while a child crossed a distant courtyard between glowing cooking fires.

Ibrahim waited until Marco stopped judging the distances between passages, then offered him tea. He looked down as fondly as someone watching family sleep late.

The city was a sea of close-packed earthen roofs, with chimney smoke, washing lines, water cisterns and patches of unmelted snow. Lanterns made wandering trails of yellow light, unlike any straight line on a military chart.

"What do you see?" Ibrahim asked, passing him hot tea.

"Too many things that might burn."

The old man chuckled. "A soldier's answer."

"You asked."

"I see homes."

Marco looked again. Someone sang in a courtyard, hammers sounded farther away, and a family ate beside a brazier. Two children ran across a flat roof until an adult called them back from the slippery stones.

"Homes burn too," Marco said.

Ibrahim sipped his tea. "That's why they're worth defending."

They stood together in silence.

"Do you think Fes will win?" Ibrahim asked.

Marco hesitated. In his first weeks here, he might have boasted that the walls would hold, the artillery outranged the enemy, the garrison was strong enough and his plans covered everything. Now he knew more.

"I don't know."

Ibrahim turned to him.

"We're better prepared than last month," Marco continued. "My men will fight, and the people know their duties. But I've never faced this army. They may do something I haven't thought of."

"Do you say that to your troops?"

"Yes."

"Aren't you afraid they'll lose faith?"

Marco studied his tea. "I need them to trust one another and the arrangements we have practised, not believe I can see the future."

Ibrahim nodded. "Perhaps the Balancer suits you better than that laboratory story after all."

The wind shifted. A short bell announced the night train carrying flour, coal, medicines, artillery spares and the last refugees coming along the Taza line. Below, *Lifeblood* teams and the civilian watch waited to receive the goods and guide arrivals to their districts; Marco watched without descending to command.

The next morning he walked through Fes el-Bali. Fresh bread was on sale, and children's evacuation bags hung beneath school desks. Mahmud had moved downstairs, Hale's veterans showed the watch how to turn a stretcher through a tight corner, and Tifawt inspected new coal in the glasshouse.

Marco slowed beside the school. Children argued over bell signals until their teacher raised a hand and restored silence. Inside Zahra's door the helpers' names remained written; stretchers had new straps and the water station issued full vessels with proper labels.

He noted an unrepaired lock and a reserve lamp short of oil, assigning each to the proper keeper. Then he climbed to the watchtower and the awaiting military reports.

On the eastern wall, Hassan handed him a sealed letter from Taza. Scouts confirmed that the Western Romans had left their assembly grounds along several roads and heavy artillery was moving, though the direction of the main attack remained unknown.

"Is it time?" Hassan asked.

"Time to do what we've practised." Marco raised the alert and asked Taza and Nador to report more often, but did not close markets or send people to shelters before the signal.

That afternoon the notice board said three things: the Romans were advancing; Fes was not yet fighting; Taza still held. The tea seller returned to his stove and the silversmith took his children home a little early. Everyone checked water, bags and shelter paths.

At night, Marco stood on a wall strengthened with deep repairs; the gun that had left a blind angle had been moved. Fes remained lit below. The duty officer brought the final report: no fighting had begun.

"Wake me if anything changes," Marco said.

"And if nothing does, Colonel?"

"Then let me sleep."

Marco descended the stairs. The east was still dark. Behind him, people were still awake throughout the city, keeping its lights alive.

title_vi: Chapter Forty: A Bloody Charade
title_en: Chapter Forty: A Bloody Charade
text_en:
After Taza fell and the North African defensive line withdrew towards Fes, another bitter winter wind swept through Madrid.

Within a private chamber of the royal palace, the white queen was lifted from the chessboard. Testarossa turned the piece between two fingers, amusement glinting in her red eyes.

"Your Majesty moved too hastily. That silver hairpin has quite distracted you."

Across from her, Isabella stroked the head of her solitary king. Before the Queen could speak, the heavy wooden door burst open and a royal guardsman rushed in, his face stricken with alarm. He dropped to his knees upon the cold stone, struggling for breath.

The guardsman tried to steady himself, but his words came brokenly.

"Urgent news, Your Majesty. Rioting has broken out in the southern square, and the crowds are still gathering. The patrols fear they cannot hold the line without resorting to force."

Isabella rose and took up her cloak.

"Saddle the horses and hold the barricades. Until I give the order, no one is to fire upon the people."

She pulled her hood over her hair.

"I shall be there before another speaks in my name."

Soon two dark figures vanished into the capital's bitter winter night. At the corner of the square, Vestigium lamps shone upon a seething crowd, held back by dense ranks of royal soldiers with muskets and fixed bayonets. Their stifled murmuring hung in the air like ashes before a great storm.

Passing through the soldiers, Isabella and Testarossa entered the street. The Queen stopped before the grey sandstone wall of a chancery, where red paint ran towards the paving stones.

There, the dark crimson letters gleamed like fresh blood, still dripping slowly onto the stone:

"La Reina Ramera"

The square fell silent before the painted words. A hoarse cry sounded from the watchtower, and a two-headed eagle wheeled down to grip the stone ledge with its talons. All four red eyes fixed upon Testarossa, ignoring Isabella beside her.

Isabella looked up at the monstrous creature. The calm upon her face only made her concealed hand tighten beneath her cloak.

"Is it them?"

The two-headed eagle scraped its claws across the stone, its four eyes never leaving Testarossa. That wordless confirmation deepened the chill between the women.

Testarossa met its gaze from the tower with an arrogant smile.

"It is."

She tilted her head, as though she had awaited this moment for far too long.

"Those Habsburg rats have finally crawled out of their holes."

Isabella did not look at her smile. Her gaze returned to the red words upon the wall, where someone was trying to turn her anger into a trap.

Testarossa glanced towards the crowd beyond the bayonets.

"They have chosen the right place to emerge. A throne may withstand cannon fire, but whispers can make the one seated upon it doubt every face."

Isabella betrayed neither fear nor anger, concealing her clenched fist beneath the folds of her cloak.

"The time has come."

***

Snow began falling thickly across the Old Continent, whitening the roads of marching armies and extinguishing the last lingering warmth of autumn. The chessboard of the world shifted violently, each piece moving towards its appointed position.

A bitter north wind shrieked across the Plaza Mayor in the heart of Madrid.

Beneath the dreary winter sky, eleven thousand British soldiers stood in immaculate square formations. Their deep red woollen coats spread like a sea of blood upon the snow, while row after row of bare bayonets pointed straight into the air.

Edward walked along the ranks, his British officer's cloak snapping in the wind. Before the central formation, he drew the curved sabre from his hip and raised it against the darkened sky.

He surveyed thousands of weathered faces, men who had endured exile beside him, shed blood and risen from the ashes of their lost homeland.

"Back in our homeland, we were left with nothing," he began. "But here, behind you, stand your families, your homes and the future we have rebuilt with our own hands. Whoever wishes to turn Madrid into a graveyard must first pass through eleven thousand redcoats who know exactly whom they defend."

The front ranks remained motionless, yet Edward saw hands tighten around musket stocks. These men needed no further promises of glory; they needed to know their commander remembered that every red coat had a home behind it.

Edward paused, turning towards the English flag whipping in the wind.

"And I promise you this: when the firestorm has passed, England shall rise again from the ashes. Before long, our flag with its red cross shall fly once more. Those standing here today shall see the road home."

As one, the entire corps struck their musket butts against the stone and roared:

"For Sir Edward! For the Empire!"

***

Far to the north, the towering Pyrenees rose like a formidable natural barrier between two frontiers.

Seven Tercio legions crossed the mountain passes through deep snow. Cassandra reined in her horse upon a rocky outcrop, surveyed the descent into the French valley and raised her sword.

"Hold formation. Once we pass through the mountains, we must carve our own road."

Then seventy thousand muskets lowered together, and the great army surged across the border markers.

***

To the south, the Western Roman army advanced along the roads towards Fes, with heavy artillery following behind. Marco stood upon the city walls, watching the scouts return; every retreat route and storehouse within the city had already been marked.

From Tangier and Ceuta, Romeo sent supply wagons towards their appointed rendezvous. In Marrakesh, Victoria and Sultan Abd al-Rahman compared the positions of their cavalry, choosing routes by which they could relieve Fes if needed.

***

Inside the Berenguela Tower, a solitary candle illuminated the stone table before Rouge von Habsburg. Three admirals of the Western Coast had come to present themselves. Two bowed according to custom, but Don Trafalgar remained upright, his gloves gripped in one hand, his eyes upon the sea chart before Rouge.

Rouge tapped a finger against the table.

"For years you have allowed the throne to fall into Isabella's hands. I want to know how many ships and harbours you still possess, and how many men will obey your commands."

Trafalgar waited until Rouge had finished, then asked bluntly:

"And Edward Spencer? He holds Madrid. Before I order my ships to sail, I must know how we intend to deal with him."

Rouge swirled his wine, gripping the glass until a crack crept along its side. He set it down.

"Let Edward hold Madrid. He cannot watch every road and granary."

Trafalgar laid his gloves upon the table and indicated the ports whose supply routes must remain open.

"Then show me the supply lines before I accept orders to sail. A fleet cannot sail on promises."

***

At the Louvre, a thin crust of snow clung to the stone balustrade. In a firelit chamber, Pierrot de Kenway wiped a trace of salt from the hilt of his sabre, then sheathed it. Word of La Concha had reached Paris, along with two names: Edward Spencer and Isabella Testarossa.

He stepped onto the balcony, letting the wind from the Seine slip inside his collar. Below, wagons carrying the wounded crossed the paved courtyard beneath the ringing of the city's bells.
